# The layout language

https://salamlang.github.io/Salam/learn/layout/

Salam has a small language of its own for building web pages: the page language. You describe the page as a tree of elements in Salam, the compiler checks every name and value, and you get HTML, CSS and JavaScript back. This lesson is the tour; the lessons after it teach every element, every style property and every event one by one.

## A page

A `page:` block is a tree of page elements. Each element opens with its name and a colon and closes with `end`, and attributes and styles are written as `name = value` inside it, with no commas between them. The settings at the top of the block, such as `title`, `lang` and `dir`, belong to the page itself. In Persian the keyword is `صفحه:`. A page in a Persian file is right to left and has `lang = "fa"` without you saying so, and a page in an English file is left to right:

layout-page.salam

```salam
page:
    title = "My app"
    lang = "english"
    dir = "left to right"
    header:
        background = "#2563eb"
        color = "white"
        padding = "24px"
        heading: size = 1 content = "Welcome to Salam" end
    end
    box:
        padding = "20px"
        paragraph: content = "This page was built from Salam code." end
    end
end
```

## Building the page

`salam page build page.salam` turns that file into `page.html` and `page.css`, plus a `page.js` when the page has scripts. `--inline` puts everything into one self-contained HTML file. Given several files, `salam page build home.salam about.salam` writes one HTML file per page and a single `style.css` they share. With no file name at all it builds `main.salam` if there is one, and otherwise every layout page in the folder.

The styles do not end up on the elements. Each element that has styles gets a short generated class, such as `.a` or `.b`, and the rules go into the stylesheet, so the HTML stays small.

## Elements and attributes

Most HTML elements have a readable name: `box` is a `div`, `paragraph` a `p`, `link` an `a`, `list` and `item` are `ul` and `li`, and `nav`, `form`, `label`, `input` and `button` keep their HTML names. The text of an element is its `content`. Links and images both take `url`, which becomes `href` or `src` as needed, and some values have words of their own, such as `target = "new"` for a link that opens in a new tab:

layout-form.salam

```salam
page:
    title = "Contact us"
    nav:
        link: url = "/" content = "Home" end
        link: url = "/blog" content = "Blog" end
        link: url = "https://github.com/SalamLang/Salam" target = "new" content = "Source" end
    end
    image: url = "/logo.png" alt = "Salam logo" end
    form:
        id = "contact"
        label: for = "email" content = "Your email" end
        input: id = "email" type = "email" name = "email" placeholder = "you@example.com" required = true end
        label: for = "message" content = "Message" end
        input: id = "message" type = "text" name = "message" end
        button: type = "submit" content = "Send" end
    end
    list:
        item: content = "We answer within a day" end
        item: content = "No account needed" end
    end
end
```

A `true` attribute, such as `required = true`, becomes a bare HTML attribute, and a `false` one is left out. Every element is explained with its attributes and an example in lessons 25 to 30, and the element table lists their English and Persian names in one place.

## Styles

CSS properties are written the same way, with spaces instead of dashes: `border radius`, `font family`, `box sizing`. A property with `hover` in front of it applies while the pointer is over the element. A `global` element holds rules for the whole page: on its own it styles every element, and with `selector` it styles whatever the selector matches. Values can be built from constants declared above the layout, so a colour or a spacing is written once:

layout-style.salam

```salam
const ACCENT := "#0f766e"
const GAP := 16

page:
    title = "Pricing"
    global: box sizing = "border-box" end
    global: selector = "body" margin = "0" font family = "sans-serif" end
    section:
        display = "flex"
        gap = GAP + "px"
        padding = GAP * 2 + "px"
        box:
            border = "1px solid #ddd"
            border radius = "12px"
            padding = GAP + "px"
            heading: size = 2 content = "Free" end
            paragraph: content = "For trying things out" end
        end
        box:
            border = "2px solid " + ACCENT
            border radius = "12px"
            padding = GAP + "px"
            heading: size = 2 content = "Pro" color = ACCENT end
            button:
                content = "Upgrade"
                background = ACCENT
                color = "white"
                hover background = "#115e59"
                cursor = "pointer"
            end
        end
    end
end
```

The `Pro` box ends up with the rule `border:2px solid #0f766e` and its button with a `:hover` rule, all worked out while compiling. One thing to avoid: two elements with the same `class` and different styles would fight over that one class name, so the compiler stops with error E136. Leave `class` out on styled elements, or style a shared class once with `global`. Nearly the whole of CSS is covered this way, including grid, animation, scroll-driven timelines, anchor positioning and the SVG-only properties; lessons 31 to 38 explain every property with an example, and the property table lists them with their English and Persian names.

## Making it interactive

An attribute named after a browser event, such as `click`, `submit`, `key down` or `change`, takes a function instead of a value. A plain function name is compiled through the JavaScript backend and dropped into the page's own script, so the behaviour stays ordinary Salam instead of hand-written JS; an inline function works the same way and gets a generated name of its own:

layout-events.salam

```salam
import dom
import conv

mut count := 0

func increment():
    count += 1
    dom.SetText(dom.ById("count"), conv.FormatInt(count))
end

page:
    title = "Counter"
    box:
        heading: id = "count" content = "0" end
        button: click = increment content = "+1" end
    end
end
```

Inside the handler, `dom.ById` and `dom.Query` are checked against the ids actually used in the same file's layout, so a misspelled id such as `dom.ById("counter")` is caught before the page ever runs. A plain string such as `click = "alert(42)"` still works too, for a one-line call into existing JavaScript. Every event has its own lesson, starting with mouse events.

## Tables

One name can produce a different element depending on where it sits. Inside `table`, `header`, `main` and `footer` are `thead`, `tbody` and `tfoot`, and `column` becomes `th` in a header row and `td` everywhere else:

layout-table.salam

```salam
page:
    table:
        header:
            row:
                column: content = "Name" end
                column: content = "Score" end
            end
        end
        main:
            row:
                column: content = "Sara" end
                column: content = "18" end
            end
        end
    end
end
```

## Components

A `component` is a piece of page you define once and use as often as you like, as if it were a new element. Its parameters are set like attributes. Inside it, `content: end` marks the slot: whatever you nest inside the component where you use it lands there.

layout-component.salam

```salam
component Plan(name, price):
    box:
        border = "1px solid #ddd"
        border radius = "12px"
        padding = "16px"
        heading: size = 2 content = name end
        paragraph: content = "$" + price + " a month" end
        content: end
    end
end

page:
    title = "Plans"
    Plan: name = "Basic" price = 4 end
    Plan: name = "Pro" price = 9
        list:
            item: content = "Private projects" end
            item: content = "Email support" end
        end
    end
end
```

Both plans share one generated class, because their styles are identical. To share components between pages, put them in a file of their own and write `include = "parts.salam"` at the top of the layout; the path is relative to the page that includes it.

## Layouts with parameters

A layout can take a name and parameters, as in `layout Welcome(name: str):`. It then becomes a function that returns the page as a string of HTML, and a normal Salam program can call it with values it only knows while running:

layout-runtime.salam

```salam
page Card(name: str, score: int):
    title = "Card " + name
    heading: size = 2 content = name end
    if score >= 50:
        paragraph: content = "pass" end
    else:
        paragraph: content = "fail" end
    end
end

func main:
    println Card("Ali", 70)
end
```

Output:

```text
<!doctype html><html lang="en" dir="ltr"><head><meta charset="utf-8"><meta name="viewport" content="width=device-width, initial-scale=1"><title>Card Ali</title></head><body><h2>Ali</h2><p>pass</p></body></html>
```

Inside such a layout you can use `if`, `else` and `each`, and a component with typed parameters can be called on its own to get just its piece of HTML. Text that comes from a parameter is escaped for you, so a `<b>` or a `<script>` in the data shows up as text and never becomes part of the page:

layout-inbox.salam

```salam
component Badge(text: str):
    span: content = text background = "#fde68a" end
end

page Inbox(user: str, subjects: Vector<str>, unread: int):
    title = "Inbox of " + user
    heading: size = 1 content = "Hello, " + user end
    if unread == 0:
        paragraph: content = "No new messages" end
    else:
        paragraph: content = "Unread: " + unread end
        list:
            each i, s in subjects:
                item: content = (i + 1) + ". " + s end
            end
        end
    end
end

func main:
    mut subjects := Vector {} as Vector<str>
    defer subjects.free()
    subjects.push("Meeting at 10")
    subjects.push("<b>FREE</b> prize & more")
    println Inbox("Sara", subjects, subjects.len())
    println Badge("new")
end
```

Output:

```text
<!doctype html><html lang="en" dir="ltr"><head><meta charset="utf-8"><meta name="viewport" content="width=device-width, initial-scale=1"><title>Inbox of Sara</title></head><body><h1>Hello, Sara</h1><p>Unread: 2</p><ul><li>1. Meeting at 10</li><li>2. &lt;b&gt;FREE&lt;/b&gt; prize &amp; more</li></ul></body></html>
<style>.badge-a{background:#fde68a}</style><span class="badge-a">new</span>
```

The structure of the page is still fixed while compiling; only the values change. Two rules keep it that way. A layout with parameters is a `pure` function, so it cannot do anything else while building the page: even `subjects.len()` is not allowed inside it, which is why the count arrives as a parameter of its own. And a plain `str` cannot go where a URL, a colour or a length belongs, because text from a user could break out of it. Parse it first with `web.ParseUrl`, `web.ParseColor` or `web.ParseLength` from the `web` package, which reject anything unsafe, and give the layout the resulting `web.Url`, `web.Color` or `web.Length`.

## A page from a Salam program

Because a layout with parameters is just a function, a web server written in Salam can answer each request with a fresh page. This program serves a greeting at `http://localhost:8080/?name=Sara`:

layout-server.salam

```salam
import net.http
import net.router

page Greeting(name: str):
    title = "Hello " + name
    heading: size = 1 content = "Hello, " + name end
    paragraph: content = "This page was rendered on the server." end
end

func home(ctx: i64):
    mut name := http.Query(ctx, "name")
    if name == "":
        name = "guest"
    end
    http.Html(ctx, Greeting(name))
end

func main:
    mut r := router.NewRouter()
    router.Get(r, "/", home)
    mut s := http.NewServer(8080)
    http.Use(s, r)
    http.Run(s)
end
```

The server keeps running until you stop it, so the example has no output here. The name comes straight from the address bar, and thanks to the escaping, a visitor who sends `?name=<b>` sees the text `<b>` and nothing else.

## Web fonts

The `font` element produces an `@font-face`. `name` and `url` are required; if you leave `type` out, Salam works it out from the extension in the URL and then from the bytes of a file sitting next to the program. Use the font afterwards with `font family`:

layout-font.salam

```salam
page:
    font:
        name = "Estedad"
        url = "https://editor.salamlang.ir/fonts/Estedad-Light.ttf"
        display = "swap"
    end
    box:
        content = "Hello"
        font family = "Estedad"
    end
end
```

## Checked while compiling

Salam checks every element and attribute before it builds the page. A misspelled name, an attribute that element does not have, a malformed value such as a URL in the wrong shape, a required attribute left out, or an element in the wrong place is an error, and the message suggests the nearest valid name. For example, `hint = "x"` on an `input` gives "unknown attribute 'hint' on 'input'; did you mean 'enterkeyhint'?", and an `item` outside a `list` gives "element 'item' cannot be placed inside 'page'". Inside a page with parameters, an unknown element name is only a warning and is built as a `div`, so read the warnings there too.

The layout language turns into plain HTML and CSS, so anything you know about the web still applies. For the server side, the `net.http` and `net.router` packages used above handle requests, query strings and responses.


---

# Pages and text

https://salamlang.github.io/Salam/learn/page-text/

Most of a web page is text, and HTML has an element for every kind of text: a heading, a paragraph, a quotation, a piece of code, a date. In Salam you write them with plain readable names and the compiler turns them into the HTML tags. This lesson shows each one with an example you can run.

## The shape of a page

A `page:` block holds everything on the page. Before the first element you can set things that belong to the page itself: `title` is the text on the browser tab, `lang` and `dir` say which language and which direction the text has, and `background`, `color` and the other style properties at that level paint the whole page. Everything else is an element. An element opens with its name and a colon and closes with `end`, and what goes between is attributes and child elements, written as `name = value` with no commas.

The text of an element is its `content` attribute. It is always plain text: a `<` or an `&` in it is shown as it is and never becomes markup, so text that comes from a user can never break the page. Put several words in one string, or build a string with `+` from constants and numbers.

web-text-article.salam

```salam
page:
    title = "A short article"
    global: selector = "body" font family = "system-ui, sans-serif" max width = "34rem" margin = "2rem auto" line height = 1.6 end
    heading group:
        h1: content = "Why we write pages in Salam" end
        paragraph:
            content = "Published "
            time: datetime = "2026-10-26" content = "26 October 2026" end
        end
    end
    paragraph: content = "A page is a tree of elements. Each element has a name, some attributes and sometimes children." end
    heading: size = 2 content = "One language" end
    paragraph: content = "The page and the program that serves it are written in the same language, so a name that is wrong is found while compiling." end
    line: end
    small: content = "Written for the Salam course." end
end
```

The preview above is the real page the compiler built. The `global` line is a style rule for the whole page, and you will meet it again in the CSS lessons; here it only gives the page a readable font and a comfortable width.

## Headings

Headings give a page its outline. `heading` takes a `size` from 1 to 6, and `h1` to `h6` are the same thing under their HTML names. Use a single level 1 for the title of the page and then go down one level at a time: a level 3 belongs under a level 2, not directly under a level 1. Browsers draw the levels in decreasing sizes, but choose the level for its meaning and change the size with CSS. When a heading has a subtitle, wrap both in a `heading group` as the example above does.

## Paragraphs, breaks and rules

`paragraph` is a block of text, and browsers leave space above and below it. Inside a paragraph, `break` starts a new line, which is right for an address or a poem and wrong as a way to add space, because empty space is a job for CSS. `line` draws a horizontal rule between two topics, and `word break` marks where a long word may be cut if it does not fit.

A paragraph can hold child elements next to its own `content`. The `content` text always comes first, and the children follow in the order you write them. So a sentence with a bold word in the middle is written as the first part in `content`, then the bold element, then a `span` with the rest. The `span` is a neutral container: it adds no meaning and no look of its own, which makes it the element for styling a few words.

## Emphasis and inline text

Inline elements live inside a line of text. Several of them look alike in the browser and differ in meaning, and the meaning is what screen readers and search engines use. `strong` is important text and `bold` is only bold type. `emphasis` is stress, the word you say louder, and `italic` is a different voice, such as a foreign word. `mark` highlights what is relevant right now, `strikethrough` shows what is no longer true, and `small` is for small print. `subscript` and `superscript` raise and lower text for formulas. `code`, `keyboard`, `sample` and `variable` are the four ways to write about computers.

web-text-inline.salam

```salam
page:
    title = "Inline text"
    global: selector = "body" font family = "system-ui, sans-serif" margin = "1.5rem" line height = 1.7 end
    paragraph:
        content = "Water is H"
        subscript: content = "2" end
        span: content = "O and energy is E = mc" end
        superscript: content = "2" end
        span: content = ". " end
        strong: content = "Do not" end
        span: content = " drink the " end
        emphasis: content = "second" end
        span: content = " glass. Press " end
        keyboard: content = "Ctrl + S" end
        span: content = " to save, or call " end
        code: content = "save()" end
        span: content = " from your code. " end
        mark: content = "This part is highlighted." end
    end
end
```

Pick the element for what the text is, not for how it looks. Looks change in CSS in one place, but the meaning stays with the text, and a reader that cannot see your page, such as a screen reader, depends on it.

## Quotations, code and preformatted text

`quote` is a short quotation inside a sentence and browsers add the quotation marks. `block quote` is a longer quotation set apart from the text. Both can take a `cite` attribute with the address of the source, and `cite` as an element names a work such as a book or a film. For a listing where every space and line break matters, use `preformatted`: it shows its text in a monospace font and keeps the layout exactly. Write a line break inside the string as `\n`.

web-text-quote.salam

```salam
page:
    title = "Quotes and code"
    global: selector = "body" font family = "system-ui, sans-serif" margin = "1.5rem" end
    block quote:
        cite = "https://example.com/essay"
        content = "Everything should be made as simple as possible, but no simpler."
    end
    paragraph:
        content = "From "
        cite: content = "an essay on design" end
        span: content = ", as she put it: " end
        quote: content = "start small" end
        span: content = "." end
    end
    preformatted:
        content = "func main:\n    println \"Hello\"\nend"
        background = "#f3f4f6"
        padding = "12px"
        border radius = "8px"
    end
end
```

## Edits, dates and abbreviations

`deleted` and `inserted` show what was taken out and what was put in, and both accept a `datetime` and a `cite`. `time` holds a date or a time in words for people and in a fixed format in its `datetime` for programs, and `data` does the same for any other value. An `abbreviation` keeps its full form in `title`, and `definition` marks the word that a sentence defines.

web-text-edits.salam

```salam
page:
    title = "Edits and abbreviations"
    global: selector = "body" font family = "system-ui, sans-serif" margin = "1.5rem" line height = 1.7 end
    paragraph:
        content = "The meeting moved from "
        deleted: datetime = "2026-10-26" content = "Monday" end
        span: content = " to " end
        inserted: datetime = "2026-10-26" content = "Tuesday" end
        span: content = "." end
    end
    paragraph:
        definition: content = "Salam" end
        span: content = " is written in " end
        abbreviation: title = "Cascading Style Sheets" content = "CSS" end
        span: content = " and " end
        abbreviation: title = "HyperText Markup Language" content = "HTML" end
        span: content = " for you." end
    end
    paragraph:
        content = "Price: "
        strikethrough: content = "$20" end
        span: content = " " end
        data: value = "15" content = "$15" end
    end
end
```

## Mixed directions and ruby

A page in English often contains a Persian name, and a Persian page often contains an English one. Browsers decide the order of such text by a standard algorithm that usually works, but a name at the edge of a sentence can still pull the punctuation to the wrong side. Wrap a piece of text of unknown direction in `isolate` and it is laid out on its own, without affecting its neighbours. `direction override` is the blunt tool: it forces one direction whatever the characters say. `ruby` places a small annotation, usually a pronunciation, above the base text.

web-text-direction.salam

```salam
page:
    title = "Mixed directions"
    global: selector = "body" font family = "system-ui, sans-serif" margin = "1.5rem" line height = 1.8 end
    paragraph:
        content = "Comment from "
        isolate: content = "محمد" end
        span: content = " and from " end
        isolate: content = "Sara" end
        span: content = "." end
    end
    paragraph:
        content = "Forced: "
        direction override: dir = "rtl" content = "abc 123" end
    end
    paragraph:
        ruby:
            content = "東京"
            ruby text: content = "Tōkyō" end
        end
    end
end
```

## Reference: every text element

Each element below is shown with a short example. Wherever an element has attributes of its own they are listed under it, and the attributes that every element has are in the lesson on the head and global attributes. The examples are checked by the compiler, so you can paste any of them inside a `page:` block. Persian names work in any file, and the Persian lessons use them.

### `heading` (Persian: `سرتیتر`; HTML: `<h1>`)

A heading. The `size` attribute chooses the level, from 1 (the largest and most important) to 6. Search engines and screen readers build the outline of your page from its headings, so use one level 1 per page and do not skip levels.

```salam
heading: size = 2 content = "Our story" end
```

| Attribute | What it does | Example |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `size`
اندازه | The heading level as a whole number from 1 to 6. Without it the heading is level 1, and a number outside the range is cut to the nearest level, so 7 gives a level 6. [int] | `heading: size = 3 content = "Opening hours" end` |

### `h1` (HTML: `<h1>`)

A level 1 heading written with its HTML name. `heading` with `size = 1` produces exactly the same tag.

```salam
h1: content = "Welcome" end
```

### `h2` (HTML: `<h2>`)

A level 2 heading, used for the main sections under the page title.

```salam
h2: content = "Features" end
```

### `h3` (HTML: `<h3>`)

A level 3 heading, used for subsections of a level 2 section.

```salam
h3: content = "Speed" end
```

### `h4` (HTML: `<h4>`)

A level 4 heading.

```salam
h4: content = "Benchmarks" end
```

### `h5` (HTML: `<h5>`)

A level 5 heading.

```salam
h5: content = "Method" end
```

### `h6` (HTML: `<h6>`)

A level 6 heading, the smallest of the six.

```salam
h6: content = "Footnote" end
```

### `heading group` (Persian: `گروه سرتیتر`; HTML: `<hgroup>`)

Groups a heading with its subtitle or tagline so they count as one heading in the outline.

```salam
heading group:
    h1: content = "Salam" end
    paragraph: content = "A language for the web and beyond" end
end
```

### `paragraph` (Persian: `پاراگراف`; HTML: `<p>`)

A paragraph of text. It is the element you will use most. Browsers put space above and below it.

```salam
paragraph: content = "Salam compiles to fast native code." end
```

### `span` (Persian: `تکه`; HTML: `<span>`)

A neutral inline container with no meaning of its own. Use it to style or script a few words inside a line of text.

```salam
paragraph:
    content = "The total is "
    span: content = "42" color = "crimson" end
end
```

### `break` (Persian: `شکست`; HTML: `<br>`)

A line break inside a paragraph. It is a void element, so it takes no content. Use it for poems and addresses, not to add vertical space.

```salam
paragraph:
    content = "First line"
    break: end
    span: content = "Second line" end
end
```

Void element, it cannot have children

### `line` (Persian: `خط`; HTML: `<hr>`)

A thematic break, drawn as a horizontal rule. It marks a change of topic between paragraphs.

```salam
line: end
```

Void element, it cannot have children

### `word break` (Persian: `شکست واژه`; HTML: `<wbr>`)

Marks a place where the browser may break a very long word if it needs to. It is invisible otherwise.

```salam
paragraph:
    content = "super"
    word break: end
    span: content = "cali" end
    word break: end
    span: content = "fragilistic" end
end
```

Void element, it cannot have children

### `bold` (Persian: `پررنگ`; HTML: `<b>`)

Draws attention to text with bold type without saying it is important, such as a product name in a review.

```salam
paragraph:
    content = "Try the "
    bold: content = "Pro" end
    span: content = " plan." end
end
```

### `strong` (Persian: `قوی`; HTML: `<strong>`)

Text of strong importance. Browsers show it in bold and screen readers may stress it.

```salam
paragraph:
    strong: content = "Warning:" end
    span: content = " this cannot be undone." end
end
```

### `italic` (Persian: `کج`; HTML: `<i>`)

Text set apart from its surroundings in tone or voice, such as a technical term or a thought. Browsers show it in italics.

```salam
paragraph:
    content = "The word "
    italic: content = "salam" end
    span: content = " means peace." end
end
```

### `emphasis` (Persian: `تاکید`; HTML: `<em>`)

Stress emphasis, the word you would say louder. Browsers show it in italics and screen readers stress it.

```salam
paragraph:
    content = "I said "
    emphasis: content = "never" end
    span: content = "." end
end
```

### `underline` (Persian: `زیرخط`; HTML: `<u>`)

Text with an unarticulated annotation, such as a misspelling mark. Do not use it for links, because readers expect underlined text to be clickable.

```salam
paragraph:
    content = "Check the "
    underline: content = "speling" end
    span: content = " here." end
end
```

### `strikethrough` (Persian: `خط خورده`; HTML: `<s>`)

Text that is no longer accurate or relevant, drawn with a line through it, such as an old price.

```salam
paragraph:
    strikethrough: content = "$20" end
    span: content = " $15 today" end
end
```

### `small` (Persian: `ریز`; HTML: `<small>`)

Side comments and small print, such as copyright lines and legal notes. Browsers show it one size smaller.

```salam
small: content = "Prices include VAT." end
```

### `mark` (Persian: `برجسته`; HTML: `<mark>`)

Highlights text because it is relevant right now, like a search match. Browsers paint it with a yellow background.

```salam
paragraph:
    content = "Results for "
    mark: content = "salam" end
    span: content = ": 12 pages" end
end
```

### `subscript` (Persian: `زیرنویس`; HTML: `<sub>`)

Text set lower than the line, as in chemical formulas.

```salam
paragraph:
    content = "H"
    subscript: content = "2" end
    span: content = "O" end
end
```

### `superscript` (Persian: `بالانویس`; HTML: `<sup>`)

Text set higher than the line, as in exponents and footnote marks.

```salam
paragraph:
    content = "E = mc"
    superscript: content = "2" end
end
```

### `code` (Persian: `کد`; HTML: `<code>`)

A short piece of computer code inside text. Browsers use a monospace font.

```salam
paragraph:
    content = "Call "
    code: content = "println" end
    span: content = " to print." end
end
```

### `keyboard` (Persian: `صفحه کلید`; HTML: `<kbd>`)

Text the user types, usually a key or a shortcut.

```salam
paragraph:
    content = "Press "
    keyboard: content = "Ctrl + S" end
    span: content = " to save." end
end
```

### `sample` (Persian: `نمونه خروجی`; HTML: `<samp>`)

Sample output from a program, shown in a monospace font.

```salam
paragraph:
    content = "The program printed "
    sample: content = "Hello, World" end
end
```

### `variable` (Persian: `متغیر`; HTML: `<var>`)

The name of a variable in a formula or in programming text. Browsers show it in italics.

```salam
paragraph:
    content = "The area is "
    variable: content = "w" end
    span: content = " times " end
    variable: content = "h" end
end
```

### `abbreviation` (Persian: `کوته‌نوشت`; HTML: `<abbr>`)

An abbreviation or acronym. Put the full form in `title` so it shows when the pointer rests on it.

```salam
abbreviation: title = "HyperText Markup Language" content = "HTML" end
```

### `definition` (Persian: `تعریف`; HTML: `<dfn>`)

The term being defined in a sentence that defines it.

```salam
paragraph:
    definition: content = "Salam" end
    span: content = " is a compiled language with a built in page language." end
end
```

### `cite` (Persian: `نام اثر`; HTML: `<cite>`)

The title of a creative work, such as a book, a film or a paper. It is not for the name of a person.

```salam
paragraph:
    content = "I loved "
    cite: content = "The Little Prince" end
    span: content = "." end
end
```

### `quote` (Persian: `نقل قول`; HTML: `<q>`)

A short quotation that stays inside a paragraph. Browsers put quotation marks around it.

```salam
paragraph:
    content = "She said "
    quote: content = "see you soon" end
    span: content = " and left." end
end
```

| Attribute | What it does | Example |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `cite`
منبع نقل | The address of the page the quotation comes from. It is not shown, but tools can read it. [url] | `quote: cite = "https://example.com/talk" content = "less is more" end` |

### `block quote` (Persian: `نقل قول بلند`; HTML: `<blockquote>`)

A longer quotation set apart from the text around it, usually indented.

```salam
block quote:
    content = "Simplicity is the ultimate sophistication."
end
```

| Attribute | What it does | Example |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `cite`
منبع نقل | The address of the source of the quotation. [url] | `block quote: cite = "https://example.com/essay" content = "Make it simple." end` |

### `preformatted` (Persian: `پیش‌قالب`; HTML: `<pre>`)

Text that keeps its spaces and line breaks exactly, shown in a monospace font. It is the right choice for code listings and ASCII art.

```salam
preformatted: content = "line one\n    line two" end
```

### `time` (Persian: `زمان`; HTML: `<time>`)

A date or a time. The readable text can be anything, and `datetime` gives the exact value for programs.

```salam
time: datetime = "2026-10-26" content = "26 October 2026" end
```

| Attribute | What it does | Example |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `datetime`
زمان دقیق | The machine readable date or time, such as `2026-10-26` or `2026-10-26T09:30`. [datetime] | `time: datetime = "2026-10-26T09:30" content = "9:30 in the morning" end` |

### `data` (Persian: `داده`; HTML: `<data>`)

Links readable text to a value a program can use, such as a product number. `value` is required.

```salam
data: value = "4021" content = "Green tea" end
```

Required: `value`

| Attribute | What it does | Example |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `value`
مقدار | The machine readable value. It is required. [string] | `data: value = "7" content = "seven" end` |

### `deleted` (Persian: `حذف شده`; HTML: `<del>`)

Text that was removed from a document. Browsers draw it with a line through it.

```salam
paragraph:
    content = "Meet at "
    deleted: content = "5 pm" end
    inserted: content = "6 pm" end
end
```

| Attribute | What it does | Example |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `cite`
منبع نقل | The address of a page that explains why the text was removed. [url] | `deleted: cite = "https://example.com/changes" content = "old text" end` |

| `datetime`
زمان دقیق | When the text was removed, as a date or a date and time. [datetime] | `deleted: datetime = "2026-10-26" content = "old text" end` |

### `inserted` (Persian: `افزوده`; HTML: `<ins>`)

Text that was added to a document. Browsers underline it.

```salam
inserted: content = "New in this version" end
```

| Attribute | What it does | Example |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `cite`
منبع نقل | The address of a page that explains why the text was added. [url] | `inserted: cite = "https://example.com/changes" content = "new text" end` |

| `datetime`
زمان دقیق | When the text was added, as a date or a date and time. [datetime] | `inserted: datetime = "2026-10-26T09:30" content = "new text" end` |

### `ruby` (Persian: `آوانما`; HTML: `<ruby>`)

Annotation for East Asian and other scripts, a small pronunciation guide shown above or beside the base text. It holds the base text plus `ruby text` elements.

```salam
ruby:
    content = "漢"
    ruby text: content = "han" end
end
```

### `ruby text` (Persian: `متن آوانما`; HTML: `<rt>`)

The small annotation text of a `ruby`.

```salam
ruby:
    content = "東京"
    ruby text: content = "Tōkyō" end
end
```

Only inside: `ruby`

### `ruby parenthesis` (Persian: `پرانتز آوانما`; HTML: `<rp>`)

Parentheses shown only by browsers that cannot draw ruby, so the annotation still reads as `漢(han)`.

```salam
ruby:
    content = "漢"
    ruby parenthesis: content = "(" end
    ruby text: content = "han" end
    ruby parenthesis: content = ")" end
end
```

Only inside: `ruby`

### `isolate` (Persian: `جداساز جهت`; HTML: `<bdi>`)

Isolates a piece of text from the direction of the text around it. It is the safe way to put a name of unknown direction, such as a user name, inside a sentence.

```salam
paragraph:
    content = "User "
    isolate: content = "محمد" end
    span: content = " left a comment." end
end
```

### `direction override` (Persian: `جهت اجباری`; HTML: `<bdo>`)

Forces the direction of its text, ignoring what the characters say. `dir` is required.

```salam
direction override: dir = "rtl" content = "abc 123" end
```

Required: `dir`

## Try it yourself

- Write a recipe page with a level 1 title, an ordered list of steps and a `time` for the cooking time.

- Take the article above and add a `block quote` with a `cite` and a `mark` on the sentence you want people to notice.

- Change a `strong` to a `bold` and a `bold` to a `strong`. Does the page look different? What would a screen reader do?

# Page structure and lists

https://salamlang.github.io/Salam/learn/page-structure/

A page that only uses boxes looks fine in a browser and is a maze for everyone who cannot see it. This lesson shows the elements that name the parts of a page, the elements for lists, and the ones for things that open and close, and it ends with a complete blog page built from them.

## Boxes and landmarks

`box` and `span` are the generic containers. A `box` is a block, it starts on a new line and takes the full width. A `span` sits inside a line of text. Neither one says anything about its content, so they are the right tools when the only reason for the container is styling.

When a part of the page has a job, there is an element that names it. `header` holds the introduction, `nav` a group of navigation links, `main` the content the page is about, `aside` something related but separate, and `footer` the closing part. `section` is a themed group of content that usually starts with a heading, `article` is a piece that makes sense alone, such as a post or a comment, and `search` wraps the controls for searching. Browsers draw all of them like a plain box. The difference is for the people who cannot see the page: a screen reader lists these parts as landmarks and lets its user jump to the main content or to the navigation in one key press. Search engines read the outline in the same way.

web-structure-landmarks.salam

```salam
page:
    title = "Landmarks"
    global: selector = "body" font family = "system-ui, sans-serif" margin = 0 line height = 1.5 end
    header: background = "#0f766e" color = "white" padding = "10px 20px"
        h1: content = "Garden Notes" margin = 0 font size = "1.3rem" end
    end
    nav: background = "#ccfbf1" padding = "8px 20px" display = flex gap = 16
        link: url = "#soil" content = "Soil" end
        link: url = "#water" content = "Water" end
    end
    box: display = flex gap = 20 padding = 20
        main: flex = 1
            section: id = "soil"
                heading: size = 2 content = "Soil" end
                paragraph: content = "Dig in compost before you plant." end
            end
            section: id = "water"
                heading: size = 2 content = "Water" end
                paragraph: content = "Water early, when the air is cool." end
            end
        end
        aside: width = 160 background = "#f1f5f9" padding = 12 border radius = 8
            strong: content = "Tip" end
            paragraph: content = "A thick layer of mulch keeps the soil damp." end
        end
    end
    footer: padding = "10px 20px" border top = "1px solid #cbd5e1" color = "#475569"
        small: content = "Garden Notes, written by hand." end
    end
end
```

The example puts a `header` and a `nav` above, then a `main` with two sections and an `aside` next to it, then a `footer`. The `id` on each section is what the links `#soil` and `#water` point to: a link that starts with `#` scrolls to the element with that id. The `display = flex` and `gap` lines are CSS and are explained in the CSS lessons.

A page can have only one `main`, and it cannot sit inside an `article`. The compiler reports an error for a second one (E120). It also refuses a `header` or a `footer` inside another `header` or `footer`, and an `address` inside an `address`. A `header` or `footer` inside an `article` or a `section` is fine: it then belongs to that part and not to the whole page. When a page has two `nav` elements, tell them apart with `aria label`, for example `aria label = "Main"`, so that a screen reader can announce which one it is on.

## Lists

`list` is a bullet list. `ordered list` is a numbered one, for steps and rankings where the order matters. Only `item` elements can sit directly inside a list, and an `item` holds the text of the entry in its `content`. To nest a list, put it inside an `item`, after the `content`, as the example does under Olives. Browsers use a different marker for each level.

web-structure-lists.salam

```salam
page:
    title = "Lists"
    global: selector = "body" font family = "system-ui, sans-serif" margin = "1.5rem" line height = 1.6 end
    heading: size = 2 content = "Shopping" end
    list:
        item: content = "Bread" end
        item:
            content = "Olives"
            list:
                item: content = "Green" end
                item: content = "Black" end
            end
        end
        item: content = "Tea" end
    end
    heading: size = 2 content = "Countdown" end
    ordered list: reversed = true
        item: content = "Mix the dough" end
        item: content = "Let it rise" end
        item: content = "Bake" end
    end
    heading: size = 2 content = "Chapters" end
    ordered list: start = 4 type = "I"
        item: content = "The road" end
        item: content = "The inn" end
        item: value = 9 content = "The return" end
    end
end
```

An ordered list has three attributes. `reversed` counts down, so a list of three items is numbered 3, 2, 1. `start` is the number of the first item, and it can be zero or negative. `type` chooses the kind of marker: `1`, `a`, `A`, `i` or `I`. On a single `item`, `value` sets that item's number and the items after it carry on from there, which is why the last chapter above is IX. A bullet list ignores all of these. The marker can also be changed with the CSS property `list style type`, for example `persian` for Persian digits.

`menu` is a list of commands, for example the buttons of a toolbar. It holds `item` elements like `list` does. Do not use it for the links of a site: that is a `nav` with a `list` inside.

## Description lists

A `description list` is for name and value pairs: a glossary, the details of a product, the facts in a profile. A `term` is the name, and the `description` after it is the value. One term can have several descriptions, as the Footer entry in the first list shows, and several terms can share one description. Wrap each group in a `box` when you want to style a group as a unit, or to keep the groups visibly apart, as in the second list.

web-structure-definitions.salam

```salam
page:
    title = "Definitions"
    global: selector = "body" font family = "system-ui, sans-serif" margin = "1.5rem" line height = 1.6 end
    description list:
        term: content = "Header" font weight = "bold" end
        description: content = "The top of a page or of a section." end
        term: content = "Footer" font weight = "bold" end
        description: content = "Closing notes, links and the author." end
        description: content = "It can also close a section." end
    end
    description list:
        box: margin top = 16
            term: content = "Name" font weight = "bold" end
            description: content = "Salam" end
        end
        box: margin top = 16
            term: content = "Kind" font weight = "bold" end
            description: content = "Programming language" end
        end
    end
end
```

You always write `term` and `description`. The compiler tells the two situations apart by the parent: directly inside the list they are the plain elements, and inside a `box` that sits directly inside a list they are the variants called `term in box` and `description in box`. They produce the same tags. Outside a description list neither is allowed, and the compiler says so.

## Details and summary

`details` is a block the reader can open and close, with no script at all. Its first child must be a `summary`, and the compiler refuses it anywhere else. The summary is the line that is always visible and acts as the button. Everything after the summary is hidden until the block is opened. With `open = true` a block starts open. Give several blocks the same `name` and they become an exclusive group: opening one closes the others, which is exactly an accordion. A block without a name stays independent.

web-structure-details.salam

```salam
page:
    title = "Questions"
    global: selector = "body" font family = "system-ui, sans-serif" margin = "1.5rem" max width = "30rem" end
    global: selector = "details" border = "1px solid #cbd5e1" border radius = 8 padding = "8px 12px" margin bottom = 8 end
    global: selector = "summary" cursor = pointer font weight = "bold" end
    details: name = "faq" open = true
        summary: content = "What is a page block?" end
        paragraph: content = "It holds everything on the page." end
    end
    details: name = "faq"
        summary: content = "Can two be open at once?" end
        paragraph: content = "Not here. They share the name faq, so opening one closes the other." end
    end
    details:
        summary: content = "And this one?" end
        paragraph: content = "It has no name, so it opens and closes on its own." end
    end
end
```

In the example the first two blocks share the name `faq`, and the third has no name. Click them to see the difference. The `global` lines at the top only style the boxes and the pointer. They use plain tag names as selectors.

## Dialog

`dialog` is a box that floats above the page, for a message or a question. It has two ways of appearing. With `open = true` it is shown at once, with no dimming of the page behind it. To show it as a modal, a dialog that dims the page, traps the keyboard focus and closes on the Esc key, you have to ask the browser from a script. In Salam that is one call from a click handler: `dom.Call0(dom.ById("saved"), "showModal")`, and `"close"` in the same way to close it. The attribute `closedby` says what else may close it: `closerequest` (the Esc key and the device's close gesture), `any` (Esc or a click outside) or `none` (only your own code).

web-structure-dialog.salam

```salam
import dom

page:
    title = "Dialog"
    global: selector = "body" font family = "system-ui, sans-serif" margin = "1.5rem" end
    button: content = "Save the draft" click = (): dom.Call0(dom.ById("saved"), "showModal") end end
    paragraph: id = "state" content = "Nothing saved yet." end
    dialog: id = "saved" closedby = "any" padding = 20 border radius = 10
        heading: size = 2 content = "Saved" margin top = 0 end
        paragraph: content = "Your draft is stored. Press Esc, click outside or use the button." end
        button:
            content = "Close"
            click = (): dom.SetText(dom.ById("state"), "Draft saved.") dom.Call0(dom.ById("saved"), "close") end
        end
    end
end
```

The page starts with `import dom`, which is needed for the calls. `dom.ById` finds the element by its id, and the compiler checks that an element with that id exists in the same page. `dom.SetText` changes the text of the paragraph. Events and the `dom` package get their own lessons later.

## Figures and addresses

`figure` wraps something that belongs with the text but can stand on its own: a picture, a chart, a listing. The `figure caption` inside it names the figure, and a screen reader connects the two. The image gets its own text description in the `alt` attribute, and the next lesson explains why that is a different thing from the caption. `address` is for contact details of the author of the nearest article or of the whole page, not for any postal address you happen to mention. Browsers set it in italic, and the example turns that off with `font style = normal`.

web-structure-figure.salam

```salam
page:
    title = "Figure"
    global: selector = "body" font family = "system-ui, sans-serif" margin = "1.5rem" max width = "30rem" end
    figure: margin = 0
        image: url = "data:image/svg+xml,%3Csvg%20xmlns=%27http://www.w3.org/2000/svg%27%20viewBox=%270%200%20260%20120%27%3E%3Crect%20width=%27260%27%20height=%27120%27%20fill=%27%23bae6fd%27/%3E%3Ccircle%20cx=%27200%27%20cy=%2740%27%20r=%2724%27%20fill=%27%23facc15%27/%3E%3Crect%20y=%2790%27%20width=%27260%27%20height=%2730%27%20fill=%27%2316a34a%27/%3E%3C/svg%3E" alt = "A yellow sun over a green field" width = 260 height = 120 end
        figure caption: content = "Figure 1. The field at noon." color = "#475569" font size = "0.9rem" end
    end
    address: margin top = 20 font style = normal
        content = "Garden Notes"
        break: end
        link: url = "mailto:hello@example.com" content = "hello@example.com" end
    end
end
```

## A whole page

Here is a blog post that uses most of the elements above. The page `header` holds the name of the site and a `search` with its form. A `nav` follows. The `main` holds one `article`, which has a `header` of its own with the title and the date in a `time` element, and two `section` parts that each start with a level 2 heading. An `aside` next to it lists related reading, and the page `footer` holds the `address`. Read the code from the outside in, and notice that every element has a reason to be there.

web-structure-blog.salam

```salam
page:
    title = "A blog post"
    global: selector = "body" font family = "system-ui, sans-serif" margin = 0 line height = 1.6 color = "#1e293b" end
    header: display = flex justify content = "space-between" align items = center padding = "10px 20px" background = "#0f766e" color = "white"
        strong: content = "Garden Notes" end
        search:
            form: input: type = "search" placeholder = "Search" aria label = "Search the blog" end end
        end
    end
    nav: display = flex gap = 16 padding = "8px 20px" background = "#ccfbf1" aria label = "Main"
        link: url = "#" content = "Home" end
        link: url = "#" content = "Archive" end
    end
    box: display = flex gap = 24 padding = 20
        main: flex = 1
            article:
                header:
                    heading: size = 1 content = "Why mulch matters" margin bottom = 4 end
                    paragraph: margin top = 0 color = "#64748b"
                        content = "By Sara, "
                        time: datetime = "2026-10-26" content = "26 October 2026" end
                    end
                end
                section:
                    heading: size = 2 content = "Less watering" end
                    paragraph: content = "A layer of straw keeps the sun off the soil." end
                end
                section:
                    heading: size = 2 content = "Fewer weeds" end
                    paragraph: content = "Seeds in the dark do not sprout." end
                end
            end
        end
        aside: width = 170 aria label = "Related"
            heading: size = 2 content = "Related" font size = "1.1rem" end
            list: padding inline start = 20
                item: link: url = "#" content = "Compost basics" end end
                item: link: url = "#" content = "Rain barrels" end end
            end
        end
    end
    footer: padding = "10px 20px" border top = "1px solid #cbd5e1"
        address: font style = normal content = "Garden Notes, 12 Orchard Lane" end
    end
end
```

## Reference: structure and list elements

Every element of this lesson is below, with its attributes and a short example. The examples are checked by the compiler, so you can paste any of them inside a `page:` block. The attributes that every element has, such as `id` and `title`, are in the lesson on the head and global attributes.

### Containers and landmarks

### `box` (Persian: `جعبه`; HTML: `<div>`)

A generic block container (HTML `div`). It starts on a new line and takes the full width. It has no meaning of its own, so use it only to group things for layout or style when no other element fits.

```salam
box: padding = 12 background = "#f1f5f9" border radius = 8
    paragraph: content = "Two paragraphs share one box." end
    paragraph: content = "The box gives them a background." end
end
```

### `section` (Persian: `بخش`; HTML: `<section>`)

A themed group of content, almost always with a heading at its start. A page can have many sections; give each a heading so the outline makes sense.

```salam
section:
    heading: size = 2 content = "Watering" end
    paragraph: content = "Water early in the morning." end
end
```

### `article` (Persian: `مقاله`; HTML: `<article>`)

A self-contained piece that would make sense if it were copied somewhere else: a blog post, a news story, a product card, a comment. Articles can be nested, for example comments inside a post.

```salam
article:
    heading: size = 2 content = "Mulch matters" end
    paragraph: content = "A layer of straw keeps the soil damp." end
end
```

### `aside` (Persian: `کناری`; HTML: `<aside>`)

Content that is related to the main content but could be removed without breaking it: a sidebar, a note, a pull quote. Screen readers announce it as a complementary landmark.

```salam
aside: padding = 12 background = "#fef9c3" border radius = 8
    strong: content = "Tip" end
    paragraph: content = "Water the roots, not the leaves." end
end
```

### `header` (Persian: `سرصفحه`; HTML: `<header>`)

The introduction of the page or of a section: a title, a logo, a menu. Directly in the page it is the banner landmark. Inside an `article` or `section` it introduces only that part. It cannot be placed inside another `header` or `footer`.

```salam
header: background = "#0f766e" color = "white" padding = 12
    h1: content = "Garden Notes" margin = 0 end
end
```

### `footer` (Persian: `پاورقی`; HTML: `<footer>`)

The closing part of the page or of a section: author, copyright, related links. Directly in the page it is the content information landmark. It cannot be placed inside a `header` or another `footer`.

```salam
footer: padding = 12 border top = "1px solid #cbd5e1" color = "#475569"
    small: content = "Written by hand in Salam." end
end
```

### `nav` (Persian: `ناوبری`; HTML: `<nav>`)

A group of links for moving around the site or the page. Not every group of links is navigation, only the main ones. When a page has several, tell them apart with `aria label`.

```salam
nav: aria label = "Main" display = flex gap = 16
    link: url = "#" content = "Home" end
    link: url = "#" content = "Archive" end
end
```

### `main` (Persian: `اصلی`; HTML: `<main>`)

The content the page exists for. A page can have only one, and it cannot be inside an `article`, `aside`, `header`, `footer` or `nav`. A screen reader can jump straight to it.

```salam
main: max width = 600
    heading: size = 1 content = "Why mulch matters" end
    paragraph: content = "The page content goes here." end
end
```

### `search` (Persian: `جستجو`; HTML: `<search>`)

Wraps the controls used to search the page or the site. It is a landmark of its own, so a screen reader can jump to the search box. Put a form inside it.

```salam
search:
    form: input: type = "search" placeholder = "Search" aria label = "Search the blog" end end
end
```

### `address` (Persian: `آدرس`; HTML: `<address>`)

Contact information for the author of the nearest `article` or of the whole page. It is not for every postal address in a text. Browsers show it in italic; `font style = normal` turns that off. It cannot contain another `address`.

```salam
address: font style = normal
    content = "Garden Notes"
    break: end
    link: url = "mailto:hello@example.com" content = "hello@example.com" end
end
```

### Lists

### `list` (Persian: `فهرست`; HTML: `<ul>`)

A bullet list (HTML `ul`). Use it when the order of the entries does not matter. Only `item` elements can be its direct children.

```salam
list:
    item: content = "Bread" end
    item: content = "Olives" end
    item: content = "Tea" end
end
```

### `ordered list` (Persian: `فهرست شماره‌دار`; HTML: `<ol>`)

A numbered list (HTML `ol`) for steps and rankings, where the order matters. Its attributes change the counting and the look of the numbers.

```salam
ordered list:
    item: content = "Mix the dough" end
    item: content = "Let it rise" end
    item: content = "Bake" end
end
```

| Attribute | What it does | Example |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `reversed`
معکوس | A boolean. With `true` the list counts down, so three items are numbered 3, 2, 1. The items stay in the order you wrote them. [bool] | `ordered list: reversed = true
item: content = "Third place" end
item: content = "Second place" end
item: content = "Winner" end
end` |

| `start`
شروع | A whole number, the number of the first item. It may be zero or negative. The default is 1 (or the last number when the list is reversed). [int] | `ordered list: start = 5
item: content = "Fifth" end
item: content = "Sixth" end
end` |

| `type`
نوع | The kind of marker: `1` for numbers (the default), `a` or `A` for letters, `i` or `I` for Roman numerals in lower or upper case. [enum: ol_type] | `ordered list: type = "A"
item: content = "Apples" end
item: content = "Pears" end
end` |

### `item` (Persian: `مورد`; HTML: `<li>`)

One entry of a `list`, an `ordered list` or a `menu` (HTML `li`). Its text goes in `content`; a nested list goes after it.

```salam
list:
    item:
        content = "Olives"
        list:
            item: content = "Green" end
            item: content = "Black" end
        end
    end
end
```

Only inside: `list`, `ordered list`, `menu`

| Attribute | What it does | Example |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `value`
مقدار | A whole number. In an ordered list it sets the number of this item, and the items after it continue from there. In a bullet list it has no effect. [int] | `ordered list:
item: content = "One" end
item: value = 10 content = "Ten" end
item: content = "Eleven" end
end` |

### `menu` (Persian: `منو`; HTML: `<menu>`)

A list of commands, such as the buttons of a toolbar (HTML `menu`). It holds `item` elements like a `list`. Site navigation is a `nav` with a `list`, not a `menu`.

```salam
menu:
    item: button: content = "Cut" end end
    item: button: content = "Copy" end end
    item: button: content = "Paste" end end
end
```

### Description lists

### `description list` (Persian: `فهرست تعریف`; HTML: `<dl>`)

A list of name and value groups (HTML `dl`): a glossary, the facts about a product. Its children are `term` and `description` elements, or `box` elements that each wrap one group.

```salam
description list:
    term: content = "Salam" end
    description: content = "A programming language." end
    term: content = "Page" end
    description: content = "What the browser shows." end
end
```

### `term` (Persian: `واژه`; HTML: `<dt>`)

The name part of a group (HTML `dt`). It may be followed by one or more `description` elements. It is allowed directly inside a `description list`, and inside a `box` there.

```salam
description list:
    term: content = "Colour" end
    description: content = "Teal" end
end
```

Only inside: `description list`

### `description` (Persian: `شرح`; HTML: `<dd>`)

The value part of a group (HTML `dd`). A term can have several descriptions. It is allowed directly inside a `description list`, and inside a `box` there.

```salam
description list:
    term: content = "Sizes" end
    description: content = "Small" end
    description: content = "Large" end
end
```

Only inside: `description list`

### `term in box` (Persian: `واژه`; HTML: `<dt>`)

The same tag as `term`, used when the name sits inside a `box` that wraps one group of a `description list`. You write `term`; the compiler picks this variant from the parent. It is refused anywhere else.

```salam
description list:
    box:
        term: content = "Kind" end
        description: content = "Language" end
    end
end
```

### `description in box` (Persian: `شرح`; HTML: `<dd>`)

The same tag as `description`, used inside a `box` that wraps one group of a `description list`. You write `description`; the compiler picks this variant from the parent.

```salam
description list:
    box:
        term: content = "Born" end
        description: content = "2018" end
        description: content = "Tehran" end
    end
end
```

### Details, dialog and figures

### `details` (Persian: `جزئیات`; HTML: `<details>`)

A block the reader can open and close without any script. Its first child must be a `summary`, and the rest is hidden until the block is open.

```salam
details:
    summary: content = "More about mulch" end
    paragraph: content = "Straw, bark or leaves all work." end
end
```

| Attribute | What it does | Example |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `name`
نام | A string that makes `details` blocks with the same name an exclusive group: opening one closes the others. Blocks without a name do not affect each other. [string] | `details: name = "tips"
summary: content = "Spring" end
paragraph: content = "Sow seeds." end
end
details: name = "tips"
summary: content = "Autumn" end
paragraph: content = "Plant bulbs." end
end` |

| `open`
باز | A boolean. With `true` the block is open when the page loads. The reader can still close it. [bool] | `details: open = true
summary: content = "Read this first" end
paragraph: content = "It starts open." end
end` |

### `summary` (Persian: `خلاصه`; HTML: `<summary>`)

The always visible line of a `details` block; it works as the button that opens and closes it. It must be the first child of `details`.

```salam
details:
    summary: content = "Shipping" font weight = "bold" end
    paragraph: content = "Orders leave on Monday." end
end
```

Only inside: `details`

### `dialog` (Persian: `پنجره گفتگو`; HTML: `<dialog>`)

A box that floats above the page, for a message or a question. With `open = true` it is shown at once. To show it as a modal call `showModal` on it from a click handler, and `close` to hide it.

```salam
dialog: open = true padding = 16 border radius = 8
    paragraph: content = "Shown without a script." end
end
```

| Attribute | What it does | Example |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `open`
باز | A boolean. With `true` the dialog is visible when the page loads, as a normal, non-modal box with no dimmed backdrop. [bool] | `dialog: open = true
paragraph: content = "I am open." end
end` |

| `closedby`
بستن با | What may close a modal dialog besides your own code: `closerequest` (the Esc key and the device's close gesture), `any` (a close request or a click outside the dialog) or `none` (only code). [enum: closed_by] | `dialog: closedby = "any"
paragraph: content = "Click outside to close." end
end` |

### `figure` (Persian: `شکل`; HTML: `<figure>`)

Content that goes with the text but can stand on its own: an image, a chart, a code listing. It may hold one `figure caption`.

```salam
figure:
    preformatted: content = "1 + 1 = 2" end
    figure caption: content = "Listing 1. A sum." end
end
```

### `figure caption` (Persian: `زیرنویس شکل`; HTML: `<figcaption>`)

The caption of a `figure` (HTML `figcaption`). A figure can have only one.

```salam
figure:
    paragraph: content = "A chart would be here." end
    figure caption: content = "Figure 2. Rain per month." font size = "0.9rem" end
end
```

Only inside: `figure`

## Try it yourself

- Write the landmarks of your own home page: a `header` with a title, a `nav` with three links, a `main` with two sections and a `footer`. Then add a second `main` and read the error.

- Make a recipe: an `ordered list` of steps and, in a `description list`, the ingredients with their amounts. Make the steps start from 0.

- Build a page with a question and answer for each of three topics using `details`. Give them one `name`, then remove the name from one of them and see what changes.

- Add a button to the blog page that opens a `dialog` asking the reader to subscribe, and let a click outside close it.
