# Mouse events

https://salamlang.github.io/Salam/learn/events-mouse/

A page that only shows things is a document. A page that answers a click is a program. This lesson shows how to attach a Salam function to a mouse event, how to read where the pointer is, and how the twelve mouse events differ. Every example runs in the preview under it.

## Giving an element a handler

A handler is a function the browser calls when something happens to an element. In Salam you attach it with an attribute named after the event: `click = ...` on a `button` says what to do when the button is clicked. Events with two words have a space, as everywhere in the page language: `double click`, `mouse move`, `context menu`. The value of the attribute can be written in four ways.

web-mouse-forms.salam

```salam
import dom

mut named_clicks := 0

func named():
    named_clicks += 1
    dom.SetText(dom.ById("out"), "named function, click " + named_clicks)
end

func with_event(e: i64):
    dom.SetText(dom.ById("out"), "named function with the event, pointer at x " + dom.EventX(e))
end

page:
    title = "Four ways to handle a click"
    global: selector = "body" font family = "system-ui, sans-serif" margin = "1.5rem" end
    global: selector = "button" padding = "8px 14px" margin = "0 8px 8px 0" font size = "1rem" end
    paragraph: id = "out" content = "Press a button." end
    button: click = named content = "Named function" end
    button: click = with_event content = "With the event" end
    button: click = (): dom.SetText(dom.ById("out"), "lambda") end content = "Lambda" end
    button: click = "this.textContent = 'JS string was here'" content = "JS string" end
end
```

Here is what each form is for.

- A named function declared above the `page:` block. Use it when the code is longer than a line or when two elements share it. The function may have no parameters, as `named` has, or one parameter of type `i64`, as `with_event` has. That parameter receives the event, and you hand it to the helpers that read it: `dom.EventX(e)` and `dom.EventY(e)` for the pointer position, `dom.EventTarget(e)` for the element that was hit, `dom.PreventDefault(e)` and `dom.StopPropagation(e)` to change what the browser does next.

- A lambda written inline as `(): ... end`. It is the shortest form for one or two statements. In a page attribute a lambda takes no parameters, so it cannot see the event. When you need the event, use a named function.

- A JavaScript string such as `"this.textContent = 'hi'"`. It is copied into the HTML as it is, so inside it `this` is the element and `event` is the event. Use it only for tiny things the Salam helpers do not cover.

The functions you write in Salam are compiled to JavaScript and placed in one script at the end of the page. A browser finds the function named in `onclick="named()"` by looking it up on `window`, so the compiler also stores every handler there. You never write this yourself, but it explains why a handler must be a plain function of the page and not, say, a method.

State, for example a counter, lives in a top level `mut` variable above the page. The handler changes it and then writes the new value into the page with `dom.SetText`. The compiler checks your work: `dom.ById("x")` must name an id that exists in the same page (error E138), and an event must name a function that exists (error E137).

Do not name a handler like a built-in. The browser looks a name in an attribute up on the element, then on its form, then on the document, and only then on the window. A function called `clear`, `open`, `close`, `write`, `reset`, `submit`, `focus`, `click` or `name` loses to the built-in of that name, and nothing seems to happen. Some names are worse than useless: the window has read-only properties such as `closed`, `status`, `top` and `length`, and a handler with one of those names makes the whole page script stop with an error, so none of your handlers work. Choose names such as `clear_board` or `open_menu`.

A page script only knows the `dom` helpers and your own code. Helpers that do more than pass one call on, such as `dom.RandomInt`, and other packages such as `math` are not part of it. `dom.Random()` gives a number from 0 up to 1, so `(dom.Random() * 85.0) as i64` is a whole number from 0 to 84.

## Click: counting and switching

`click` fires when the user presses and releases the primary mouse button on the element, and also when a keyboard user presses Enter or Space on a focused button, so it is the right event for anything that acts like a button. Use it on a real `button` element and not on a `box`: a button can be reached with the Tab key, a box cannot.

The counter below keeps its number in `count`. Each handler is a lambda that changes the variable and calls `show`, a small function that copies the number into the heading. The two parts, the state and the code that draws it, stay separate, and that is the habit worth learning first.

web-mouse-counter.salam

```salam
import dom

mut count := 0

func show:
    dom.SetText(dom.ById("n"), "" + count)
end

page:
    title = "Click counter"
    global: selector = "body" font family = "system-ui, sans-serif" margin = "1.5rem" text align = center end
    heading: id = "n" size = 1 content = "0" font size = "4rem" margin = "0 0 12px 0" end
    button: id = "plus" click = (): count += 1 show() end content = "+1" padding = "8px 18px" font size = "1.1rem" end
    button: id = "reset" click = (): count = 0 show() end content = "Reset" padding = "8px 18px" font size = "1.1rem" margin = "0 0 0 8px" end
end
```

The second example needs no variable, because the page itself remembers the state: `dom.ToggleClass` adds a class when the element does not have it and removes it when it does. The look of each state is written in CSS, in a `style` element, and the script only flips the class. The `transition` property makes the change fade instead of jump.

web-mouse-toggle.salam

```salam
import dom

page:
    title = "Lamp"
    style: content = "#room.on { background: #fde68a; color: #422006 } #room.on .bulb { background: #f59e0b }" end
    global: selector = "body" font family = "system-ui, sans-serif" margin = "1.5rem" end
    box:
        id = "room"
        background = "#1e293b"
        color = "#e2e8f0"
        padding = 24
        border radius = 12
        text align = center
        transition = "background 0.3s"
        box: class = "bulb" width = 60 height = 60 margin = "0 auto 12px" background = "#475569" border radius = "50%" end
        button: id = "switch" click = (): dom.ToggleClass(dom.ById("room"), "on") end content = "Switch" padding = "6px 16px" end
    end
end
```

## Double click, other buttons and the context menu

`double click` fires after two quick clicks on the same element. The browser still sends the two ordinary `click` events first, so a handler on `click` runs twice before the double click arrives. Do not put two different actions on `click` and `double click` of the same element. `aux click` is the click of every button except the main one. The event's `button` number tells which: 0 is the main button, 1 the middle one, 2 the right one, and 3 and 4 are the back and forward buttons of some mice. `context menu` fires when the user asks for the context menu, which is a right click, the menu key or Shift and F10. Calling `dom.PreventDefault(e)` stops the browser's own menu.

web-mouse-buttons.salam

```salam
import dom

mut history := ""
mut lines := 0

func note(text: str):
    lines += 1
    if lines > 7:
        history = ""
        lines = 1
    end
    history = history + text + "\n"
    dom.SetText(dom.ById("log"), history)
end

func aux(e: i64):
    note("aux click, button " + (dom.GetNum(e, "button") as i64))
end

func menu(e: i64):
    dom.PreventDefault(e)
    note("context menu (the browser menu is blocked)")
end

page:
    title = "Kinds of clicks"
    global: selector = "body" font family = "system-ui, sans-serif" margin = "1.5rem" end
    box:
        id = "pad"
        click = (): note("click") end
        double click = (): note("double click") end
        aux click = aux
        context menu = menu
        content = "Click, double click, middle click or right click here"
        padding = 28
        background = "#e0f2fe"
        border radius = 10
        user select = none
    end
    paragraph: id = "log" content = "Nothing yet." white space = "pre-line" min height = "10em" end
end
```

The example reads the button number with `dom.GetNum(e, "button")`, which reads any number property of the event object. The log holds the last seven events, and `white space = "pre-line"` turns each `\n` in the text into a new line. `user select = none` stops a double click from selecting the words of the box.

That is enough to build your own menu. On `context menu` the handler prevents the default, moves a hidden box to the pointer and shows it. Any click on the area closes it again, and each item closes it as well.

web-mouse-menu.salam

```salam
import dom

func open_menu(e: i64):
    dom.PreventDefault(e)
    menu := dom.ById("menu")
    dom.SetStyle(menu, "left", "" + dom.EventX(e) + "px")
    dom.SetStyle(menu, "top", "" + dom.EventY(e) + "px")
    dom.SetStyle(menu, "display", "block")
end

func close_menu():
    dom.SetStyle(dom.ById("menu"), "display", "none")
end

func pick(what: str):
    dom.SetText(dom.ById("chosen"), "You chose: " + what)
    close_menu()
end

page:
    title = "Custom menu"
    global: selector = "body" font family = "system-ui, sans-serif" margin = 0 end
    box:
        id = "area"
        context menu = open_menu
        click = close_menu
        padding = 32
        min height = "260px"
        background = "#f1f5f9"
        paragraph: content = "Right click anywhere on this area." end
        paragraph: id = "chosen" content = "Nothing chosen." end
    end
    box:
        id = "menu"
        display = none
        position = fixed
        background = white
        border = "1px solid #cbd5e1"
        border radius = 8
        box shadow = "0 6px 18px rgba(0,0,0,0.18)"
        padding = 4
        button: id = "copy" click = (): pick("Copy") end content = "Copy" display = block width = "100%" end
        button: id = "rename" click = (): pick("Rename") end content = "Rename" display = block width = "100%" end
        button: id = "delete" click = (): pick("Delete") end content = "Delete" display = block width = "100%" end
    end
end
```

The menu box has `position = fixed`, which places it relative to the window, so `left` and `top` can be set straight from the pointer position `dom.EventX(e)` and `dom.EventY(e)`. Those two are measured from the top left corner of the window, which is the same corner a fixed box uses.

Use a custom context menu only where it adds something, as in an editor or a file list. A right click that does nothing useful, or hides the ordinary menu with its spell check and copy, annoys people. Keep every action of the menu reachable in another way too, because touch screens and keyboards do not right click.

## Pressing, releasing and moving

`mouse down` fires the moment a button goes down, `mouse up` when it comes up, and `click` is what the browser makes of a down and an up on the same element. `mouse move` fires again and again while the pointer moves, many times a second, so keep its handler short.

The position in the event is measured from the window. Most of the time you want it measured from some box, such as a drawing area. Ask the box where it is with `getBoundingClientRect` and subtract its `left` and `top`. In Salam that is `dom.Call0(box, "getBoundingClientRect")` for the rectangle and `dom.GetNum(rect, "left")` for each number. The first example shows the position inside the green box and moves a dot with it. The dot has `pointer events = none`, so it never gets in the way of the pointer.

web-mouse-coords.salam

```salam
import dom

func moved(e: i64):
    pad := dom.ById("pad")
    r := dom.Call0(pad, "getBoundingClientRect")
    x := (dom.EventX(e) - dom.GetNum(r, "left")) as i64
    y := (dom.EventY(e) - dom.GetNum(r, "top")) as i64
    dom.SetText(dom.ById("pos"), "x " + x + ", y " + y)
    dot := dom.ById("dot")
    dom.SetStyle(dot, "left", "" + x + "px")
    dom.SetStyle(dot, "top", "" + y + "px")
end

page:
    title = "Pointer position"
    global: selector = "body" font family = "system-ui, sans-serif" margin = "1.5rem" end
    box:
        id = "pad"
        mouse move = moved
        position = relative
        height = 180
        background = "#ecfccb"
        border radius = 10
        cursor = crosshair
        overflow = hidden
        box: id = "dot" position = absolute width = 12 height = 12 margin = "-6px 0 0 -6px" border radius = "50%" background = "#15803d" pointer events = none end
    end
    paragraph: id = "pos" content = "Move the mouse over the green area." end
end
```

The next example draws. A top level `mut` variable says whether the button is down. `mouse down` sets it and paints the first dot, `mouse move` paints while it is set, and `mouse up` clears it. `mouse leave` clears it too, because a button released outside the box would never reach the box. Each dot is a new element made with `dom.Create` and added with `dom.Append`, and the look of the dots comes from one CSS rule written in a `style` element.

web-mouse-draw.salam

```salam
import dom

mut drawing := false

func begin_stroke(e: i64):
    drawing = true
    paint(e)
end

func end_stroke:
    drawing = false
end

func paint(e: i64):
    if drawing:
        r := dom.Call0(dom.ById("board"), "getBoundingClientRect")
        dot := dom.Create("div")
        dom.SetAttr(dot, "class", "dot")
        dom.SetStyle(dot, "left", "" + (dom.EventX(e) - dom.GetNum(r, "left")) + "px")
        dom.SetStyle(dot, "top", "" + (dom.EventY(e) - dom.GetNum(r, "top")) + "px")
        dom.Append(dom.ById("board"), dot)
    end
end

func clear_board:
    dom.SetHtml(dom.ById("board"), "")
end

page:
    title = "Drawing"
    style: content = ".dot { position: absolute; width: 10px; height: 10px; margin: -5px 0 0 -5px; border-radius: 50%; background: #7c3aed; pointer-events: none }" end
    global: selector = "body" font family = "system-ui, sans-serif" margin = "1.5rem" end
    box:
        id = "board"
        mouse down = begin_stroke
        mouse move = paint
        mouse up = end_stroke
        mouse leave = end_stroke
        position = relative
        height = 200
        background = "#faf5ff"
        border = "2px dashed #c4b5fd"
        border radius = 10
        cursor = crosshair
        overflow = hidden
        user select = none
    end
    button: id = "clear" click = clear_board content = "Clear" margin = "10px 0 0 0" padding = "6px 14px" end
end
```

This draws dots, so a fast stroke leaves gaps. For a smooth line use a canvas, and see web/canvas. The pattern of down, move and up is the same for dragging an element by hand, and the next lessons build on it.

## Enter and leave, over and out

Four events tell you that the pointer has come or gone, and two pairs behave differently. `mouse enter` and `mouse leave` fire only for the element they are set on: when the pointer first comes into the element, and when it goes out of it altogether. Moving between the element and its children does not count. `mouse over` and `mouse out` also fire for the children, because they bubble up from them: moving from the outer box onto the inner one sends an `out` for the outer box and an `over` that rises from the inner one. Try both below and watch the counters. The left box says `enter 1, leave 0` while you are over it or its inner square, and the right box counts every step.

web-mouse-enter.salam

```salam
import dom

mut enters := 0
mut leaves := 0
mut overs := 0
mut outs := 0

func show_a:
    dom.SetText(dom.ById("count-a"), "enter " + enters + ", leave " + leaves)
end

func show_b:
    dom.SetText(dom.ById("count-b"), "over " + overs + ", out " + outs)
end

page:
    title = "Enter and leave"
    global: selector = "body" font family = "system-ui, sans-serif" margin = "1.5rem" end
    global: selector = ".zone" position = relative height = 90 width = 220 background = "#dbeafe" border radius = 10 padding = 10 box sizing = "border-box" end
    global: selector = ".inner" position = absolute right = 10 top = 10 width = 70 height = 70 background = "#2563eb" color = white border radius = 8 text align = center end
    box:
        display = flex
        gap = 24
        flex wrap = wrap
        box:
            heading: size = 3 content = "enter and leave" margin = "0 0 8px 0" end
            box:
                id = "a" class = "zone" content = "outer"
                mouse enter = (): enters += 1 show_a() end
                mouse leave = (): leaves += 1 show_a() end
                box: id = "a-inner" class = "inner" content = "inner" end
            end
            paragraph: id = "count-a" content = "enter 0, leave 0" end
        end
        box:
            heading: size = 3 content = "over and out" margin = "0 0 8px 0" end
            box:
                id = "b" class = "zone" content = "outer"
                mouse over = (): overs += 1 show_b() end
                mouse out = (): outs += 1 show_b() end
                box: id = "b-inner" class = "inner" content = "inner" end
            end
            paragraph: id = "count-b" content = "over 0, out 0" end
        end
    end
end
```

Most of the time you want enter and leave: a menu that opens while the pointer is over it, a tooltip, a highlight. Use over and out when you really want to know about each child, for example to light up the exact cell of a table the pointer touches.

Here is a tooltip that follows the pointer. `mouse enter` shows it with the right text, `mouse move` moves it, and `mouse leave` hides it. It sits 14 and 18 pixels away from the pointer, because a tooltip under the pointer would take the pointer's events and flicker. Its `pointer events = none` prevents the same problem.

web-mouse-tooltip.salam

```salam
import dom

func show_tip(text: str):
    tip := dom.ById("tip")
    dom.SetText(tip, text)
    dom.SetStyle(tip, "display", "block")
end

func hide_tip:
    dom.SetStyle(dom.ById("tip"), "display", "none")
end

func follow(e: i64):
    tip := dom.ById("tip")
    dom.SetStyle(tip, "left", "" + (dom.EventX(e) + 14.0) + "px")
    dom.SetStyle(tip, "top", "" + (dom.EventY(e) + 18.0) + "px")
end

page:
    title = "Tooltip"
    global: selector = "body" font family = "system-ui, sans-serif" margin = "1.5rem" end
    global: selector = "button" padding = "8px 14px" margin = "0 8px 0 0" font size = "1rem" end
    button: id = "save" content = "Save" mouse enter = (): show_tip("Save the file") end mouse move = follow mouse leave = hide_tip end
    button: id = "open" content = "Open" mouse enter = (): show_tip("Open a file from disk") end mouse move = follow mouse leave = hide_tip end
    button: id = "share" content = "Share" mouse enter = (): show_tip("Send a link to a friend") end mouse move = follow mouse leave = hide_tip end
    box: id = "tip" display = none position = fixed background = "#0f172a" color = white padding = "4px 10px" border radius = 6 font size = "0.85rem" pointer events = none end
end
```

## The target and bubbling

When you click the word inside a button inside a box, the event first goes to the word, and then it bubbles: it is offered to the button, then to the box, then upwards to the page. Every element on the way that has a `click` handler runs it. Inside a handler, `dom.EventTarget(e)` is the element that was really hit, even when the handler is set on an ancestor. This lets one handler on a list serve a hundred items. Call `dom.StopPropagation(e)` and the event goes no further.

web-mouse-bubble.salam

```salam
import dom

func outer(e: i64):
    who := dom.GetAttr(dom.EventTarget(e), "id")
    dom.SetText(dom.ById("log"), "The outer box heard a click from: " + who)
end

func inner_stop(e: i64):
    dom.StopPropagation(e)
    dom.SetText(dom.ById("log"), "The stopping button kept the click to itself.")
end

page:
    title = "Bubbling"
    global: selector = "body" font family = "system-ui, sans-serif" margin = "1.5rem" end
    global: selector = "button" padding = "8px 14px" margin = "0 8px 0 0" font size = "1rem" end
    box:
        id = "outer-box"
        click = outer
        padding = 20
        background = "#ede9fe"
        border radius = 10
        paragraph: content = "Outer box" margin = "0 0 10px 0" end
        button: id = "plain" content = "Plain button" end
        button: id = "stopper" click = inner_stop content = "Stopping button" end
        span: id = "label" content = "or the text here" end
    end
    paragraph: id = "log" content = "Click something." end
end
```

The outer box has one handler. It reads the target's id with `dom.GetAttr` and prints it. The plain button has no handler of its own and still reports to the box, and so does the text. The stopping button has a handler that stops the event, so the box never hears from it. Do not stop propagation without a reason: other code that listens higher up, such as a menu that wants to close on any click, stops working for that element.

Most events bubble. A few do not, and `mouse enter` and `mouse leave` are the ones from this lesson. This is why they count differently from `over` and `out` above.

## The wheel

`wheel` fires when the wheel turns, or two fingers slide on a touchpad. The event's `deltaY` is negative when the user scrolls up, away from themselves, and positive when they scroll down. By default the wheel scrolls the page. A handler that calls `dom.PreventDefault(e)` cancels that, which is what you want in a map or an image viewer and what you should not do on a normal page. Most browsers treat wheel handlers on the window, document and body as passive and ignore the cancel there, so put the handler on an element, as the example does.

web-mouse-wheel.salam

```salam
import dom

mut zoom := 1.0

func scroll_zoom(e: i64):
    dom.PreventDefault(e)
    if dom.GetNum(e, "deltaY") < 0.0:
        zoom = zoom * 1.1
    else:
        zoom = zoom / 1.1
    end
    if zoom > 3.0:
        zoom = 3.0
    end
    if zoom < 0.5:
        zoom = 0.5
    end
    percent := (zoom * 100.0) as i64
    dom.SetStyle(dom.ById("card"), "transform", "scale(" + zoom + ")")
    dom.SetText(dom.ById("level"), "Zoom " + percent + "%")
end

page:
    title = "Wheel zoom"
    global: selector = "body" font family = "system-ui, sans-serif" margin = "1.5rem" end
    box:
        id = "stage"
        wheel = scroll_zoom
        height = 200
        overflow = hidden
        background = "#f1f5f9"
        border radius = 10
        display = flex
        align items = center
        justify content = center
        box: id = "card" content = "Scroll the wheel over me" padding = 24 background = "#0f766e" color = white border radius = 10 end
    end
    paragraph: id = "level" content = "Zoom 100%" end
end
```

The handler multiplies or divides the zoom by 1.1 on each step and keeps it between 0.5 and 3, with two plain `if` statements, because the page script has no `math`. The result is written into `transform` as `scale(...)`. The box that is scaled is inside a stage with `overflow = hidden`, so what grows beyond the stage is cut off and the page does not move.

## Putting it together: a click game

This game uses what you have seen. The red square has a handler for `click` that counts a hit and moves the square to a random place. The yellow field around it also has a `click` handler that counts a miss. A click on the square would bubble to the field and count as a miss as well, so the square's handler first calls `dom.StopPropagation(e)`. Positions are set in percent, so the game works at any width.

web-mouse-game.salam

```salam
import dom

mut hits := 0
mut misses := 0

func show:
    dom.SetText(dom.ById("score"), "Hits " + hits + ", misses " + misses)
end

func move_target:
    t := dom.ById("target")
    dom.SetStyle(t, "left", "" + ((dom.Random() * 85.0) as i64) + "%")
    dom.SetStyle(t, "top", "" + ((dom.Random() * 75.0) as i64) + "%")
end

func hit(e: i64):
    dom.StopPropagation(e)
    hits += 1
    show()
    move_target()
end

func miss:
    misses += 1
    show()
end

page:
    title = "Catch the square"
    global: selector = "body" font family = "system-ui, sans-serif" margin = "1.5rem" end
    box:
        id = "field"
        click = miss
        position = relative
        height = 220
        background = "#fef9c3"
        border radius = 10
        overflow = hidden
        cursor = crosshair
        box: id = "target" click = hit position = absolute left = "40%" top = "30%" width = 44 height = 44 background = "#dc2626" border radius = 8 cursor = pointer end
    end
    paragraph: id = "score" content = "Hits 0, misses 0" end
end
```

## When CSS is the better tool

Before you write `mouse over` and `mouse out` to change how something looks, remember that CSS can do it alone. A style with the prefix `hover` applies while the pointer is over the element, and the browser takes it away again, with no code that can forget a case. The two buttons below look the same. The first uses `hover background` and states each colour once. The second needs two handlers, repeats the colours in the script, and does nothing when the script fails to load. CSS also takes the hover style away by itself in every case, while a script has to remember each way the pointer can leave.

web-mouse-hover.salam

```salam
import dom

page:
    title = "Hover"
    global: selector = "body" font family = "system-ui, sans-serif" margin = "1.5rem" end
    global: selector = "button" padding = "10px 18px" margin = "0 12px 0 0" font size = "1rem" border = "none" border radius = 8 color = white end
    button:
        id = "css"
        content = "Hover in CSS"
        background = "#0f766e"
        transition = "background 0.2s"
        hover background = "#115e59"
    end
    button:
        id = "js"
        content = "Hover in JS"
        background = "#0f766e"
        mouse over = (): dom.SetStyle(dom.ById("js"), "background", "#115e59") end
        mouse out = (): dom.SetStyle(dom.ById("js"), "background", "#0f766e") end
    end
    paragraph: content = "Both look the same. Only the first one needs no script." end
end
```

Use a mouse event when something must happen, such as a number that changes, a box that appears, a request that is sent. Use CSS when the page only has to look different. The CSS lessons come back to `hover`, `focus` and `active` in detail.

Touch screens have no pointer to hover with. A tooltip or a menu that appears only on hover is out of reach for a phone, so also offer a click or a tap.

## Reference: every mouse event

Each row gives the attribute, the name of the HTML attribute it becomes and when the event fires. The snippets are checked by the compiler. Where a handler needs the event itself, the snippet uses a JavaScript string, because a pasted snippet has no named function to call; in your own code use a named function with an `i64` parameter, as in the examples above.

| Attribute | When it fires | Example |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `click`
کلیک
onclick | Runs when the primary button is pressed and released on the element, or when a keyboard user activates a focused button with Enter or Space. It is the event for anything that acts like a button. | `button: click = (): dom.SetText(dom.ById("out"), "Clicked") end content = "Click me" end
paragraph: id = "out" content = "-" end` |

| `double click`
دو کلیک
ondblclick | Runs after two quick clicks on the same element. The two ordinary `click` events come first, so a `click` handler on the same element runs twice before this one. | `box: double click = (): dom.SetText(dom.ById("out"), "Double clicked") end content = "Double click here" padding = 20 background = "#e0f2fe" user select = none end
paragraph: id = "out" content = "-" end` |

| `aux click`
کلیک کمکی
onauxclick | Runs when a button other than the main one is clicked. The event property `button` says which: 1 is the middle button and 2 the right one, and 3 and 4 are the back and forward buttons of some mice. | `box: aux click = (): dom.SetText(dom.ById("out"), "Another button") end content = "Middle click here" padding = 20 background = "#fef3c7" end
paragraph: id = "out" content = "-" end` |

| `context menu`
منوی زمینه
oncontextmenu | Runs when the user asks for the context menu: a right click, the menu key or Shift and F10. `dom.PreventDefault(e)` stops the browser's own menu so the page can show its own. | `box: context menu = "event.preventDefault(); this.textContent = &#x27;Your own menu goes here&#x27;" content = "Right click here" padding = 20 background = "#fce7f3" end` |

| `mouse down`
فشردن ماوس
onmousedown | Runs the moment a mouse button goes down on the element, before the button is released. It is where dragging and drawing start. | `box: mouse down = (): dom.SetText(dom.ById("out"), "Button is down") end mouse up = (): dom.SetText(dom.ById("out"), "Button is up") end content = "Press and hold" padding = 20 background = "#e0e7ff" user select = none end
paragraph: id = "out" content = "-" end` |

| `mouse up`
رها کردن ماوس
onmouseup | Runs when a mouse button comes up over the element. A button released outside the element where it went down is reported to the element under the pointer, not to the first one. | `box: mouse up = (): dom.SetText(dom.ById("out"), "Released here") end content = "Release the button over me" padding = 20 background = "#dcfce7" user select = none end
paragraph: id = "out" content = "-" end` |

| `mouse move`
حرکت ماوس
onmousemove | Runs again and again while the pointer moves over the element, many times a second. Keep the handler short. The position is `dom.EventX(e)` and `dom.EventY(e)`, measured from the window. | `box: mouse move = "this.textContent = event.clientX + &#x27;, &#x27; + event.clientY" content = "Move over me" padding = 24 background = "#dcfce7" end` |

| `mouse enter`
ورود ماوس
onmouseenter | Runs once when the pointer comes into the element. It does not bubble and does not repeat when the pointer moves between the element and its children, which makes it the right choice for hover effects done in script. | `box: mouse enter = (): dom.SetText(dom.ById("out"), "Entered") end content = "Point at me" padding = 20 background = "#e0f2fe" end
paragraph: id = "out" content = "-" end` |

| `mouse leave`
خروج ماوس
onmouseleave | Runs once when the pointer leaves the element and all its children. It does not bubble. | `box: mouse leave = (): dom.SetText(dom.ById("out"), "Left") end content = "Point at me, then move away" padding = 20 background = "#e0f2fe" end
paragraph: id = "out" content = "-" end` |

| `mouse over`
عبور ماوس
onmouseover | Runs when the pointer comes onto the element or onto one of its children. It bubbles, so a handler on a parent hears about every child; use `dom.EventTarget(e)` to see which one. | `box: mouse over = (): dom.SetText(dom.ById("out"), "Over") end content = "Point at me" padding = 20 background = "#fef3c7" end
paragraph: id = "out" content = "-" end` |

| `mouse out`
بیرون رفتن ماوس
onmouseout | Runs when the pointer goes off the element or off one of its children. It bubbles, and it also fires when the pointer moves from the element onto its own child. | `box: mouse out = (): dom.SetText(dom.ById("out"), "Out") end content = "Point at me, then move away" padding = 20 background = "#fef3c7" end
paragraph: id = "out" content = "-" end` |

| `wheel`
چرخ ماوس
onwheel | Runs when the mouse wheel turns or two fingers slide on a touchpad. The event property `deltaY` is negative when scrolling up and positive when scrolling down. `dom.PreventDefault(e)` stops the page from scrolling. | `box: wheel = "event.preventDefault(); this.textContent = event.deltaY < 0 ? &#x27;Up&#x27; : &#x27;Down&#x27;" content = "Turn the wheel here" padding = 24 background = "#ede9fe" end` |

## Try it yourself

- Change the counter so that a double click adds ten and a click adds one. Watch the counter on a double click: what does it show? Why?

- Make the drawing board paint in a colour that depends on the button: left button purple, middle button green. Use `mouse down` and the `button` number.

- Add a "score" for the click game that counts how many hits in a row you made without a miss, and show it in the paragraph.

- Give the lamp example a second button and make both buttons control the same lamp with one named function.

# Keyboard and forms

https://salamlang.github.io/Salam/learn/events-keys-forms/

Mouse events start things. Keyboard and form events finish them: a search that filters as you type, a shortcut that saves, a message that says what is wrong with a field. This lesson goes through the events of keys, focus, text fields, forms, the clipboard and the elements that open and close, with an example you can try under each.

## Keys: down, up and press

Pressing a key sends `key down`. If you keep it pressed the browser sends `key down` again and again, with a property `repeat` set to true on the repeats. Letting go sends `key up`. An older third event, `key press`, fires only for keys that produce a character and is deprecated, so write new code with `key down` and `key up` and leave `key press` to old pages.

Key events go to the element that has focus: a text field the user clicked, a button reached with Tab, or an element with `tab index = 0`. They then bubble up to its ancestors, as clicks do, so a handler on a wrapper box hears the keys typed into everything inside it. You cannot put a handler on the page itself, so a shortcut works only while the focus is somewhere inside the element that carries the handler.

A handler that wants the event is a named function with one `i64` parameter, exactly as in the lesson on mouse events. `dom.EventKey(e)` returns the key as text. Other properties are read from the event with `dom.GetStr` and `dom.GetBool`. The example shows the two most useful: `code` and `repeat`. Click the field and press different keys, hold one down, and watch the lines change.

web-keys-echo.salam

```salam
import dom

func pressed(e: i64):
    dom.SetText(dom.ById("down"), "key down: " + dom.EventKey(e) + ", code " + dom.GetStr(e, "code"))
    if dom.GetBool(e, "repeat"):
        dom.SetText(dom.ById("note"), "The key is held, so the browser repeats it.")
    else:
        dom.SetText(dom.ById("note"), "")
    end
end

func released(e: i64):
    dom.SetText(dom.ById("up"), "key up: " + dom.EventKey(e))
    dom.SetText(dom.ById("note"), "")
end

page:
    title = "Which key?"
    global: selector = "body" font family = "system-ui, sans-serif" margin = "1.5rem" end
    input: id = "field" key down = pressed key up = released placeholder = "Click here, then press keys" width = "100%" padding = 10 font size = "1rem" box sizing = "border-box" end
    paragraph: id = "down" content = "key down: nothing yet" font family = monospace end
    paragraph: id = "up" content = "key up: nothing yet" font family = monospace end
    paragraph: id = "note" content = "" color = "#b45309" end
end
```

`key` is what the key means right now: `a`, `A` with Shift held, `Enter`, `Escape`, `Tab`, `Backspace`, a space is the one-character string `" "`, and the arrows are `ArrowUp`, `ArrowDown`, `ArrowLeft` and `ArrowRight`. `code` is which physical key it is, such as `KeyA`, whatever the keyboard layout. Use `key` when the character matters and `code` when the position matters, as in games. Modifiers are the booleans `shiftKey`, `ctrlKey`, `altKey` and `metaKey` (Command on a Mac), read with `dom.GetBool(e, "ctrlKey")`.

With a Persian or any other non-Latin layout, `key` for the key labelled S is a Persian letter, not `s`, so `Ctrl+S` written as `key == "s"` never matches. For shortcuts compare `code` (`KeyS`), which does not change with the layout.

## Enter, Escape, arrows and shortcuts

Most uses of key events are a small table: this key does that. The first one is a task list. Enter adds the text of the field as a new item, made with `dom.Create`, and empties the field. Escape only empties it. The handler checks that the field is not empty before it adds an item, with `dom.GetValue(field).len() > 0`.

web-keys-enter.salam

```salam
import dom

func typing(e: i64):
    field := dom.ById("task")
    key := dom.EventKey(e)
    if key == "Enter" and dom.GetValue(field).len() > 0:
        item := dom.Create("li")
        dom.SetText(item, dom.GetValue(field))
        dom.Append(dom.ById("list"), item)
        dom.SetValue(field, "")
    else key == "Escape":
        dom.SetValue(field, "")
    end
end

page:
    title = "Task list"
    global: selector = "body" font family = "system-ui, sans-serif" margin = "1.5rem" max width = "28rem" end
    input: id = "task" key down = typing placeholder = "New task, then Enter" width = "100%" padding = 10 font size = "1rem" box sizing = "border-box" end
    paragraph: content = "Enter adds the task. Escape clears the box." color = "#64748b" font size = "0.9rem" end
    list: id = "list" end
end
```

The second moves a ball with the arrow keys. The box has `tab index = 0`, which makes it reachable with Tab and lets it have focus, so it receives the key events. Without that attribute a box never gets them. The handler ignores every other key by returning early, and for arrows it calls `dom.PreventDefault(e)`, because the browser would otherwise scroll the page. The position lives in two `mut` variables and is written into `left` and `top` through `dom.SetStyle`.

web-keys-arrows.salam

```salam
import dom

mut x := 120
mut y := 60

func steer(e: i64):
    key := dom.EventKey(e)
    if key == "ArrowLeft":
        x -= 12
    else key == "ArrowRight":
        x += 12
    else key == "ArrowUp":
        y -= 12
    else key == "ArrowDown":
        y += 12
    else:
        ret
    end
    dom.PreventDefault(e)
    x = x < 0 ? 0 : (x > 270 ? 270 : x)
    y = y < 0 ? 0 : (y > 120 ? 120 : y)
    dom.SetStyle(dom.ById("ball"), "left", x + "px")
    dom.SetStyle(dom.ById("ball"), "top", y + "px")
end

page:
    title = "Arrow keys"
    global: selector = "body" font family = "system-ui, sans-serif" margin = "1.5rem" end
    box:
        id = "arena"
        tab index = 0
        key down = steer
        position = relative
        width = 300
        height = 150
        background = "#ecfeff"
        border = "2px solid #67e8f9"
        border radius = 10
        box: id = "ball" position = absolute left = 120 top = 60 width = 30 height = 30 border radius = "50%" background = "#0891b2" end
    end
    paragraph: content = "Click the box, then use the arrow keys." end
end
```

The third reads modifier keys. A wrapper box around a text area listens to `key down` for everything typed inside. When Ctrl (or Command) is held and the key is S, the handler prevents the default, which would open the browser's own save dialog, and runs its own action. Always prevent the default of a shortcut you take over, and never take over one the user depends on, such as Ctrl+C or Ctrl+W.

web-keys-shortcut.salam

```salam
import dom

func shortcut(e: i64):
    held := dom.GetBool(e, "ctrlKey") or dom.GetBool(e, "metaKey")
    key := dom.EventKey(e).lower()
    if held and key == "s":
        dom.PreventDefault(e)
        dom.SetText(dom.ById("status"), "Saved with Ctrl+S")
    else held and key == "enter":
        dom.PreventDefault(e)
        dom.SetText(dom.ById("status"), "Sent with Ctrl+Enter")
    end
end

page:
    title = "Shortcuts"
    global: selector = "body" font family = "system-ui, sans-serif" margin = "1.5rem" end
    box:
        id = "editor"
        key down = shortcut
        text area: id = "notes" rows = 5 placeholder = "Write here. Try Ctrl+S and Ctrl+Enter." width = "100%" padding = 10 font size = "1rem" box sizing = "border-box" end
    end
    paragraph: id = "status" content = "Nothing yet." color = "#047857" end
end
```

## Focus and blur

An element has focus when it is the one that receives the keys. `focus` runs when an element gains focus, by a click, by Tab or from a script, and `blur` when it loses it. Together they are the natural place for a hint that appears next to the field being filled, and for checking a field when the user leaves it. The first example does both: the hint changes with the field, and leaving the name field empty paints it red.

web-keys-focus.salam

```salam
import dom

func hint(text: str):
    dom.SetText(dom.ById("hint"), text)
end

func check_name:
    if dom.GetValue(dom.ById("name")).len() == 0:
        hint("The name is required.")
        dom.SetStyle(dom.ById("name"), "border-color", "#dc2626")
    else:
        hint("Thanks.")
        dom.SetStyle(dom.ById("name"), "border-color", "")
    end
end

page:
    title = "Focus and blur"
    global: selector = "body" font family = "system-ui, sans-serif" margin = "1.5rem" end
    global: selector = "input" display = block width = "100%" padding = 10 margin = "0 0 10px 0" font size = "1rem" border = "2px solid #cbd5e1" border radius = 6 box sizing = "border-box" end
    input: id = "name" placeholder = "Full name" focus = (): hint("Your name as it is on your card.") end blur = check_name end
    input: id = "email" placeholder = "Email" focus = (): hint("We never share it.") end blur = (): hint("") end end
    paragraph: id = "hint" content = "Click a field." color = "#475569" end
end
```

`focus` and `blur` do not bubble, so a handler on a wrapper never hears them from the fields inside. Their two siblings `focus in` and `focus out` do bubble, so one handler on a form section or a card can follow the focus of everything in it. They are also the way to style a whole group by what is inside it. CSS can do that too, with the `:focus-within` selector, and where it can you should use it.

web-keys-focusin.salam

```salam
import dom

page:
    title = "A group that follows focus"
    style: content = "#group.active { border-color: #2563eb; background: #eff6ff }" end
    global: selector = "body" font family = "system-ui, sans-serif" margin = "1.5rem" end
    global: selector = "input" display = block width = "100%" padding = 8 margin = "6px 0" font size = "1rem" box sizing = "border-box" end
    box:
        id = "group"
        focus in = (): dom.AddClass(dom.ById("group"), "active") end
        focus out = (): dom.RemoveClass(dom.ById("group"), "active") end
        padding = 14
        border = "2px solid #cbd5e1"
        border radius = 10
        transition = "background 0.2s"
        paragraph: content = "Delivery address" font weight = bold margin = 0 end
        input: id = "street" placeholder = "Street" end
        input: id = "city" placeholder = "City" end
    end
end
```

The group has one handler for each event. `focus in` adds the class that draws the blue border and `focus out` removes it. When you press Tab from one field to the next, `focus out` and `focus in` arrive one right after the other, before the browser draws anything, so the border does not flash. Inside a `focus out` handler, `event.relatedTarget` is the element that will receive the focus next, if you ever need to tell leaving the group from moving inside it.

## Typing in a field: input, change and before input

A text field has several events for the same act, and the difference is the moment. `input` fires after every change to the value: a typed letter, a deletion, a paste, a drop, an undo. `change` fires when the user is finished: when Enter is pressed in a one line field, or when the field loses focus after its value was changed. `before input` fires first, before the value changes, and its handler may call `preventDefault` to refuse the edit. Type into the field below and press Enter, then type some more and click away, and compare the two counters.

web-keys-input.salam

```salam
import dom

mut inputs := 0
mut changes := 0

func show:
    dom.SetText(dom.ById("counts"), "input fired " + inputs + " times, change fired " + changes + " times")
end

page:
    title = "Input and change"
    global: selector = "body" font family = "system-ui, sans-serif" margin = "1.5rem" end
    input: id = "field" input = (): inputs += 1 show() end change = (): changes += 1 show() end placeholder = "Type, then press Enter or click away" width = "100%" padding = 10 font size = "1rem" box sizing = "border-box" end
    paragraph: id = "counts" content = "input fired 0 times, change fired 0 times" end
    paragraph: content = "input follows every keystroke. change waits until you are done." color = "#64748b" end
end
```

A handler for `input` is what live features are made of. A character counter shows how much is left. Setting `maxlength` on the text area makes the browser stop typing at the limit, and the counter only has to show the length. It turns red near the end.

web-keys-counter.salam

```salam
import dom

func count:
    n := dom.GetValue(dom.ById("msg")).len()
    left := dom.ById("left")
    dom.SetText(left, n + " / 80")
    if n >= 70:
        dom.SetStyle(left, "color", "#b91c1c")
    else:
        dom.SetStyle(left, "color", "#475569")
    end
end

page:
    title = "Character counter"
    global: selector = "body" font family = "system-ui, sans-serif" margin = "1.5rem" end
    text area: id = "msg" input = count maxlength = 80 rows = 3 placeholder = "A short message" width = "100%" padding = 10 font size = "1rem" box sizing = "border-box" end
    paragraph: id = "left" content = "0 / 80" text align = right margin = "4px 0" end
end
```

A search box filters a list on every keystroke. The handler reads the field, makes it lower case and goes through the items found by `dom.QueryAll`: a matching item gets `display` set to an empty string, which puts back its normal look, and the others get `none`. Empty text matches everything, so clearing the box brings all items back with no extra code.

web-keys-filter.salam

```salam
import dom

func filter:
    needle := dom.GetValue(dom.ById("q")).lower()
    items := dom.QueryAll("#fruits li")
    repeat dom.CountOf(items) in i:
        item := dom.ItemAt(items, i)
        if dom.GetText(item).lower().includes(needle):
            dom.SetStyle(item, "display", "")
        else:
            dom.SetStyle(item, "display", "none")
        end
    end
end

page:
    title = "Live search"
    global: selector = "body" font family = "system-ui, sans-serif" margin = "1.5rem" end
    input: id = "q" input = filter placeholder = "Search fruit" width = "100%" padding = 10 font size = "1rem" box sizing = "border-box" end
    list: id = "fruits"
        item: content = "Apple" end
        item: content = "Banana" end
        item: content = "Cherry" end
        item: content = "Mango" end
        item: content = "Orange" end
        item: content = "Pear" end
    end
end
```

The loop uses `dom.CountOf` for the number of items and `dom.ItemAt` for each one. `QueryAll` returns the elements that exist at that moment, so call it inside the handler, as here, and not once at the start, if items may be added later.

## Selecting text

Three events report selection. `select` fires on a text field when the user selects some of its text, and not for a plain caret move. `selection change` fires whenever the selection or the caret in the field changes, which is also when the caret moves. `select start` fires when a new selection begins in any element, even one that is not editable, and a handler can call `preventDefault` to forbid the selection. The positions are the properties `selectionStart` and `selectionEnd` of the field, read with `dom.GetNum`.

web-keys-select.salam

```salam
import dom

func chosen:
    field := dom.ById("text")
    a := dom.GetNum(field, "selectionStart") as i64
    b := dom.GetNum(field, "selectionEnd") as i64
    dom.SetText(dom.ById("sel"), "select: " + (b - a) + " characters, from " + a + " to " + b)
end

func caret:
    at := dom.GetNum(dom.ById("text"), "selectionStart") as i64
    dom.SetText(dom.ById("caret"), "selection change: caret at " + at)
end

func started:
    dom.SetText(dom.ById("start"), "select start: a new selection began in the paragraph.")
end

page:
    title = "Selecting text"
    global: selector = "body" font family = "system-ui, sans-serif" margin = "1.5rem" end
    text area: id = "text" select = chosen selection change = caret rows = 3 content = "Select some of these words with the mouse or with Shift and the arrow keys." width = "100%" padding = 10 font size = "1rem" box sizing = "border-box" end
    paragraph: id = "sel" content = "select: nothing selected" end
    paragraph: id = "caret" content = "selection change: no caret yet" end
    paragraph: id = "para" select start = started content = "You can also select this paragraph." background = "#fef9c3" padding = 8 end
    paragraph: id = "start" content = "select start: nothing yet" end
end
```

Select with the mouse, or hold Shift and use the arrow keys. The lines under the text area show a count of characters and the caret position, and the yellow paragraph reports that a selection began in it. Support for `selection change` on a text field is newer than for the other two. A browser may send it only to the document, so test it in the browsers you care about.

## Submitting, resetting and form data

A form sends `submit` when the user presses a submit button, or presses Enter in a field, and the browser's own checks have passed. Left alone, the browser then sends the fields to the server and loads the answer. A page that handles the form itself calls `dom.PreventDefault(e)` first and then reads the fields with `dom.GetValue`. Put the handler on the form, not on the button, because Enter in a field submits without clicking the button. The `reset` event fires when a reset button is pressed or the form is reset by script, just before the fields go back to their starting values.

web-keys-submit.salam

```salam
import dom

func send(e: i64):
    dom.PreventDefault(e)
    who := dom.GetValue(dom.ById("who"))
    mail := dom.GetValue(dom.ById("mail"))
    dom.SetText(dom.ById("result"), "Thank you, " + who + ". We will write to " + mail + ".")
end

func cleared:
    dom.SetText(dom.ById("result"), "The form was cleared.")
end

page:
    title = "Sign up"
    global: selector = "body" font family = "system-ui, sans-serif" margin = "1.5rem" end
    global: selector = "input" display = block width = "100%" padding = 10 margin = "0 0 10px 0" font size = "1rem" box sizing = "border-box" end
    global: selector = "button" padding = "8px 16px" margin = "0 8px 0 0" font size = "1rem" end
    form:
        id = "signup"
        submit = send
        reset = cleared
        input: id = "who" placeholder = "Your name" end
        input: id = "mail" type = email placeholder = "Your email" end
        button: id = "go" type = submit content = "Sign up" end
        button: id = "clear" type = reset content = "Clear" end
    end
    paragraph: id = "result" content = "" color = "#047857" end
end
```

Give your fields and buttons ids that differ from the names of your functions. Inside a form, the browser looks up a name among the form's fields and buttons first, so a button with `id = "send"` hides a function called `send` and the handler reports "is not a function".

The third form event is `form data`. It fires every time the browser builds the list of fields of a form, which a submit does, and so does a script that writes `new FormData(form)`. A handler gets `event.formData` and may add or change entries before they are used. The example adds a hidden field when the button builds the data.

web-keys-formdata.salam

```salam
import dom

func extra(e: i64):
    data := dom.GetProp(e, "formData")
    _r := dom.CallS2(data, "append", "source", "newsletter")
    dom.SetText(dom.ById("out"), "form data: the form added a hidden field named source.")
end

page:
    title = "Form data"
    global: selector = "body" font family = "system-ui, sans-serif" margin = "1.5rem" end
    form:
        id = "news"
        form data = extra
        input: name = "email" value = "sara@example.com" padding = 10 font size = "1rem" end
        button: id = "build" type = button click = "new FormData(document.getElementById('news'))" content = "Build the form data" padding = "8px 16px" margin = "0 0 0 8px" end
    end
    paragraph: id = "out" content = "Nothing built yet." end
end
```

The button uses a short JavaScript string, because the `dom` helpers have no way to write `new`. The handler is a normal Salam function: `dom.GetProp(e, "formData")` gives the FormData object and `dom.CallS2` calls its `append` method with a name and a value.

## Checking fields: invalid

HTML can check fields without a line of script: `required`, `type = email`, `min`, `max`, `pattern` and `maxlength` all take part. When the browser checks a field and it fails, the field gets an `invalid` event. A check runs when the form is submitted, and also when a script calls `checkValidity()` or `reportValidity()` on the form or on a field. The second one also shows the browser's bubble with the message. `invalid` does not bubble, so the handler goes on the field itself.

The handler below replaces the browser's message with its own by calling `setCustomValidity` on the field. It looks at the field's `validity` object to tell an empty field from a wrong one. The message stays on the field until you remove it, so another handler, on `input`, sets it back to an empty string every time the user types. If you forget that, the field stays invalid forever, even after the user fixes it.

web-keys-validate.salam

```salam
import dom

func explain(e: i64):
    field := dom.EventTarget(e)
    if dom.GetBool(dom.GetProp(field, "validity"), "valueMissing"):
        _a := dom.CallS1(field, "setCustomValidity", "Please enter your email.")
    else:
        _b := dom.CallS1(field, "setCustomValidity", "That does not look like an email address.")
    end
    dom.SetText(dom.ById("why"), "invalid: " + dom.GetStr(field, "validationMessage"))
end

func retry:
    _c := dom.CallS1(dom.ById("mail"), "setCustomValidity", "")
end

func check_mail:
    _d := dom.Call0(dom.ById("form"), "reportValidity")
    if dom.GetBool(dom.GetProp(dom.ById("mail"), "validity"), "valid"):
        dom.SetText(dom.ById("why"), "The address is valid.")
    end
end

page:
    title = "Custom messages"
    global: selector = "body" font family = "system-ui, sans-serif" margin = "1.5rem" end
    form:
        id = "form"
        input: id = "mail" type = email required = true invalid = explain input = retry placeholder = "Your email" width = "100%" padding = 10 font size = "1rem" box sizing = "border-box" end
        button: id = "recheck" type = button click = check_mail content = "Check" margin = "10px 0 0 0" padding = "8px 16px" end
    end
    paragraph: id = "why" content = "Press Check." end
end
```

Checks in the browser are help for the user, not protection. Anybody can send a request with any values, so the server must check everything again.

## Copy, cut and paste

The three clipboard events fire when the user copies, cuts or pastes by keyboard or menu. They fire on the element that has the selection or the focus, and they bubble. `copy` and `cut` run before the browser does its part, so a handler can call `preventDefault` and put its own text on the clipboard with `clipboardData.setData`. `paste` gives the pasted content in `event.clipboardData`, and `getData("text")` is the plain text. A handler may prevent the default and insert a cleaned up version instead. A page cannot read the clipboard at any other time without the user's permission, and that is intended.

web-keys-clipboard.salam

```salam
import dom

mut copies := 0
mut cuts := 0

func counts:
    dom.SetText(dom.ById("stats"), "copied " + copies + " times, cut " + cuts + " times")
end

func copied:
    copies += 1
    counts()
end

func snipped:
    cuts += 1
    counts()
end

func pasted(e: i64):
    text := dom.CallS1(dom.GetProp(e, "clipboardData"), "getData", "text")
    dom.SetProp(dom.ById("last"), "textContent", text)
end

page:
    title = "Clipboard"
    global: selector = "body" font family = "system-ui, sans-serif" margin = "1.5rem" end
    input: id = "field" copy = copied cut = snipped paste = pasted value = "Copy, cut or paste in this box" width = "100%" padding = 10 font size = "1rem" box sizing = "border-box" end
    paragraph: id = "stats" content = "copied 0 times, cut 0 times" end
    paragraph:
        content = "Last pasted text: "
        span: id = "last" content = "none" font weight = bold end
    end
end
```

The paste handler passes the string to the page without touching it: `dom.CallS1` returns it as a JavaScript value, and `dom.SetProp` sets the `textContent` of the span with it. Select all in the box with Ctrl+A, then copy, cut and paste, and watch the counters and the last line.

## Details, popovers, dialogs and find in page

Some elements open and close by themselves, and they have events for it. `toggle` fires on a `details` element after it opens or closes, and on an element with the `popover` attribute after it is shown or hidden. A popover event carries `newState`, which is the text `open` or `closed`. The event fires a moment after the change, not at the same time. `before toggle` fires first, can be cancelled, and exists for popovers (and, in newer browsers, for dialogs). The example below shows the state that is about to start, `newState`, before the popover changes, and the state it reached after.

web-keys-toggle.salam

```salam
import dom

func opened:
    if dom.GetBool(dom.ById("more"), "open"):
        dom.SetText(dom.ById("dstate"), "The details are open.")
    else:
        dom.SetText(dom.ById("dstate"), "The details are closed.")
    end
end

func popped(e: i64):
    dom.SetText(dom.ById("pstate"), "The popover is now " + dom.GetStr(e, "newState") + ".")
end

func about_to(e: i64):
    dom.SetText(dom.ById("before"), "before toggle: about to be " + dom.GetStr(e, "newState") + ".")
end

page:
    title = "Toggle"
    global: selector = "body" font family = "system-ui, sans-serif" margin = "1.5rem" end
    details:
        id = "more"
        toggle = opened
        summary: content = "More about Salam" end
        paragraph: content = "Salam is a language for the web and for programs." end
    end
    paragraph: id = "dstate" content = "The details are closed." end
    button: popover target = "tip" content = "Show a tip" padding = "8px 16px" end
    box: id = "tip" popover = auto before toggle = about_to toggle = popped content = "Tips close when you press Escape." padding = 14 border radius = 8 end
    paragraph: id = "before" content = "No popover yet." end
    paragraph: id = "pstate" content = "" end
end
```

A `dialog` opened with `showModal()` is shown over the page and blocks everything behind it until it closes. `dom.Call0(dialog, "showModal")` opens it. When the user presses Escape the dialog sends `cancel`, which can be prevented to keep it open, and then it closes and sends `close`. A dialog closed by code, with `dom.CallS1(dialog, "close", "deleted")`, sends only `close`, and the text you passed is its `returnValue`.

web-keys-dialog.salam

```salam
import dom

func open_dialog:
    dom.SetText(dom.ById("log"), "Dialog is open.")
    _r := dom.Call0(dom.ById("dlg"), "showModal")
end

func canceled:
    dom.SetText(dom.ById("log"), "cancel fired (Escape was pressed).")
end

func finished:
    dom.SetText(dom.ById("end"), "close fired, return value: " + dom.GetStr(dom.ById("dlg"), "returnValue"))
end

func confirm_it:
    _r := dom.CallS1(dom.ById("dlg"), "close", "deleted")
end

page:
    title = "Dialog"
    global: selector = "body" font family = "system-ui, sans-serif" margin = "1.5rem" end
    button: id = "open" click = open_dialog content = "Delete the file" padding = "8px 16px" end
    dialog:
        id = "dlg"
        cancel = canceled
        close = finished
        paragraph: content = "Delete this file for good?" end
        button: id = "yes" click = confirm_it content = "Delete" padding = "6px 14px" end
    end
    paragraph: id = "log" content = "Nothing yet." end
    paragraph: id = "end" content = "" end
end
```

The last event is `before match`. An element with `hidden = "until-found"` is not drawn, but its text stays searchable. When the user finds it with the browser's find in page, or opens a link to its id, the browser shows it and sends `before match` just before. A handler can open the section around it, such as a closed accordion, so the match is visible. In the example, try Ctrl+F and look for pomegranate, or open the page with `#secret` at the end of its address. Not all browsers support it yet; in those the text simply stays hidden until a script shows it. Chrome does not run an inline `onbeforematch` attribute even though it fires the event, so this one event is registered from a `script` element with `addEventListener`, as the example does. The attribute `before match` is the spelling the standard defines, and where a browser honours it you can use it instead.

web-keys-match.salam

```salam
page:
    title = "Find in page"
    global: selector = "body" font family = "system-ui, sans-serif" margin = "1.5rem" end
    paragraph: id = "state" content = "The text below stays hidden until the browser finds it." end
    box: id = "secret" hidden = "until-found" content = "The secret word is pomegranate." padding = 14 background = "#fef3c7" border radius = 8 end
    script: content = "document.getElementById('secret').addEventListener('beforematch', function () { document.getElementById('state').textContent = 'before match fired: the browser is revealing the text'; });" end
end
```

## Reference: every keyboard and form event

Each row gives the attribute, the HTML attribute it becomes and when it fires. The snippets are checked by the compiler. Events that need the event object itself use a JavaScript string in these small snippets. The snippet for `before match` uses a `script` element for the reason given in the last section.

| Attribute | When it fires | Example |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `key down`
فشردن کلید
onkeydown | Runs when a key goes down on the focused element, and again for each repeat while the key is held (`repeat` is then true). `dom.EventKey(e)` is the key, such as `a`, `Enter` or `ArrowUp`. | `input: key down = (): dom.SetText(dom.ById("out"), "A key went down") end placeholder = "Press a key here" end
paragraph: id = "out" content = "-" end` |

| `key up`
رها کردن کلید
onkeyup | Runs when the key comes back up. There is exactly one `key up` for each press, however long the key was held. | `input: key up = (): dom.SetText(dom.ById("out"), "A key came up") end placeholder = "Press and release a key" end
paragraph: id = "out" content = "-" end` |

| `key press`
فشار کلید
onkeypress | Deprecated. Fires after `key down` for keys that produce a character, and not for Escape or the arrows. Use `key down` in new code. | `input: key press = (): dom.SetText(dom.ById("out"), "A character key was pressed") end placeholder = "Type a letter" end
paragraph: id = "out" content = "-" end` |

| `focus`
فوکوس
onfocus | Runs when the element gains focus, by a click, the Tab key or a script. It does not bubble; `focus in` is the bubbling version. | `input: focus = (): dom.SetText(dom.ById("out"), "The field has focus") end placeholder = "Click or Tab into me" end
paragraph: id = "out" content = "-" end` |

| `blur`
از دست رفتن فوکوس
onblur | Runs when the element loses focus. A good moment to check what the user typed. It does not bubble. | `input: blur = (): dom.SetText(dom.ById("out"), "The field lost focus") end placeholder = "Click in, then click away" end
paragraph: id = "out" content = "-" end` |

| `focus in`
ورود فوکوس
onfocusin | Like `focus`, but it bubbles, so one handler on a group hears the focus of every field inside. | `box: focus in = (): dom.SetText(dom.ById("out"), "Focus is inside the group") end input: placeholder = "First" end input: placeholder = "Second" end end
paragraph: id = "out" content = "-" end` |

| `focus out`
خروج فوکوس
onfocusout | Like `blur`, but it bubbles. `event.relatedTarget` is the element receiving the focus next, which lets you tell leaving the group from moving inside it. | `box: focus out = (): dom.SetText(dom.ById("out"), "Focus left a field of the group") end input: placeholder = "First" end input: placeholder = "Second" end end
paragraph: id = "out" content = "-" end` |

| `input`
ورودی
oninput | Runs after every change to the value of a field: typing, deleting, pasting, dropping, undoing. The right event for live features such as counters and filters. | `input: input = (): dom.SetText(dom.ById("out"), "You typed " + dom.GetValue(dom.ById("box")).len() + " characters") end id = "box" placeholder = "Type here" end
paragraph: id = "out" content = "-" end` |

| `before input`
پیش از ورودی
onbeforeinput | Runs before the value changes and can be cancelled, which refuses the edit. `event.data` holds the text about to be inserted. | `input: before input = "if (event.data === &#x27; &#x27;) { event.preventDefault(); }" placeholder = "No spaces allowed" end` |

| `change`
تغییر
onchange | Runs when the user has finished a change: Enter in a one line field, or the field losing focus after its value changed. For checkboxes, radio buttons and lists it runs at once. | `input: change = (): dom.SetText(dom.ById("out"), "The value was committed") end placeholder = "Type, then click away" end
paragraph: id = "out" content = "-" end` |

| `select`
انتخاب
onselect | Runs on a text field when the user selects some of its text. The range is in the properties `selectionStart` and `selectionEnd`. | `input: select = (): dom.SetText(dom.ById("out"), "Some text was selected") end value = "Select part of this text" end
paragraph: id = "out" content = "-" end` |

| `selection change`
تغییر انتخاب
onselectionchange | Runs when the selection or the caret changes in a text field. Support on the field itself is newer; some browsers send it only to the document. | `text area: selection change = (): dom.SetText(dom.ById("out"), "The caret moved") end content = "Click inside this text" end
paragraph: id = "out" content = "-" end` |

| `select start`
شروع انتخاب
onselectstart | Runs when the user starts a new selection, in any element, editable or not. It can be cancelled to forbid selecting. | `paragraph: select start = (): dom.SetText(dom.ById("out"), "A selection began") end content = "Select some of this text." end
paragraph: id = "out" content = "-" end` |

| `submit`
ارسال
onsubmit | Runs when a form is submitted by its submit button or by Enter in a field, after the browser's checks passed. Call `dom.PreventDefault(e)` to stop the browser from sending the form and loading a new page. | `form: submit = "event.preventDefault(); document.getElementById(&#x27;out&#x27;).textContent = &#x27;Sent: &#x27; + this.elements.name.value" input: name = "name" value = "Sara" end button: content = "Send" end end
paragraph: id = "out" content = "-" end` |

| `reset`
بازنشانی
onreset | Runs when the form is reset, by a reset button or by `form.reset()`, just before the fields go back to their starting values. It can be cancelled. | `form: reset = (): dom.SetText(dom.ById("out"), "The form was reset") end input: value = "Change me" end button: type = reset content = "Reset" end end
paragraph: id = "out" content = "-" end` |

| `invalid`
نامعتبر
oninvalid | Runs on a field that fails the browser's checks (`required`, `type = email`, `pattern`, ...) when the form is submitted or when `checkValidity()` or `reportValidity()` is called. It does not bubble, so it goes on the field. | `form: input: required = true invalid = (): dom.SetText(dom.ById("out"), "This field is required") end placeholder = "Required" end button: type = button click = "this.form.reportValidity()" content = "Check" end end
paragraph: id = "out" content = "-" end` |

| `form data`
داده فرم
onformdata | Runs on a form each time the browser builds its field list: on a submit, and on `new FormData(form)`. `event.formData` may be changed before it is used. | `form: id = "f" form data = (): dom.SetText(dom.ById("out"), "The form data was built") end input: name = "q" value = "x" end button: type = button click = "new FormData(document.getElementById(&#x27;f&#x27;))" content = "Build" end end
paragraph: id = "out" content = "-" end` |

| `copy`
رونوشت
oncopy | Runs when the user copies. A handler may call `preventDefault` and set its own text on the clipboard with `clipboardData.setData`. | `input: copy = (): dom.SetText(dom.ById("out"), "Copied") end value = "Select me and press Ctrl+C" end
paragraph: id = "out" content = "-" end` |

| `cut`
برش
oncut | Runs when the user cuts the selection, before the text is removed. | `input: cut = (): dom.SetText(dom.ById("out"), "Cut") end value = "Select me and press Ctrl+X" end
paragraph: id = "out" content = "-" end` |

| `paste`
چسباندن
onpaste | Runs when the user pastes, before the text is inserted. `event.clipboardData.getData('text')` is the pasted text. | `input: paste = (): dom.SetText(dom.ById("out"), "Pasted") end placeholder = "Press Ctrl+V here" end
paragraph: id = "out" content = "-" end` |

| `toggle`
تغییر حالت
ontoggle | Runs after a `details` element opens or closes, and after a popover is shown or hidden (`newState` is `open` or `closed`). It fires a moment after the change. | `details: toggle = (): dom.SetText(dom.ById("out"), "The details changed") end summary: content = "More" end paragraph: content = "Hidden text" end end
paragraph: id = "out" content = "-" end` |

| `before toggle`
پیش از تغییر حالت
onbeforetoggle | Runs just before a popover (and, in newer browsers, a dialog) opens or closes, and can be cancelled. `event.newState` is the state about to start. | `button: popover target = "tip" content = "Show" end
box: id = "tip" popover = auto before toggle = (): dom.SetText(dom.ById("out"), "About to change") end content = "A popover" end
paragraph: id = "out" content = "-" end` |

| `cancel`
انصراف
oncancel | Runs on a `dialog` when the user asks to close it with Escape. It can be cancelled to keep the dialog open. A dialog closed by code does not send it. | `button: click = "document.getElementById(&#x27;d&#x27;).showModal()" content = "Open" end
dialog: id = "d" cancel = (): dom.SetText(dom.ById("out"), "Escape was pressed") end paragraph: content = "Press Escape" end end
paragraph: id = "out" content = "-" end` |

| `close`
بسته شدن
onclose | Runs on a `dialog` after it has closed, by Escape, by `close()` or by a form with `method = dialog`. Its `returnValue` is the text passed to `close()`. | `button: click = "document.getElementById(&#x27;d&#x27;).showModal()" content = "Open" end
dialog: id = "d" close = (): dom.SetText(dom.ById("out"), "The dialog closed") end button: click = "this.parentNode.close(&#x27;ok&#x27;)" content = "Close" end end
paragraph: id = "out" content = "-" end` |

| `before match`
پیش از تطبیق
onbeforematch | Runs on an element with `hidden = "until-found"` just before the browser reveals it because find in page or a link to its id matched. A handler can open the section around it. Chrome fires the event but ignores the inline attribute, so register it from a `script` element with `addEventListener('beforematch', ...)`. | `paragraph: id = "out" content = "Find the word below with Ctrl+F." end
box: id = "s" hidden = "until-found" content = "Hidden word: pomegranate" end
script: content = "document.getElementById(&#x27;s&#x27;).addEventListener(&#x27;beforematch&#x27;, function () { document.getElementById(&#x27;out&#x27;).textContent = &#x27;Found it&#x27;; });" end` |

## Try it yourself

- Make the task list refuse an empty task and show a red message under the field instead. Clear the message the next time the user types.

- Let the ball in the arrow example move with the keys W, A, S and D as well, using `code` so that it works on every layout.

- Add to the search box a line that says how many items match. Update it from the same handler.

- Write a sign up form that needs two passwords. On `input` in either field, compare them and use `setCustomValidity` so that the form cannot be sent while they differ.
