# os/shell

https://salamlang.github.io/Salam/std/os-shell/

Running a command and getting its exit code, its output and its errors together.

The `os.shell` package runs a command, waits for it and gives back the whole result at once in a `CmdResult`: the exit code, the standard output and the error output. It is a thin layer over os.process (`StartCaptured`, `Wait`, read, `Cleanup`) for the common case where you want all three and do not need to run anything in parallel. Compared with `os.RunCapture` in os, it also captures the error output and, through `Run`, passes arguments without a shell.

The three functions differ in who reads the command:

| Function | Shell | Arguments | Result |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `Run(program, args)` | none | a vector, passed exactly | `CmdResult`; code -1 when the program cannot start |
| `Exec(command)` | none | the string split on single spaces | `CmdResult` |
| `System(command)` | `/bin/sh -c`, or `cmd` on Windows | the shell parses them | exit code only; output goes to the screen |

`Exec` splits the command on spaces alone and no shell is involved: pipes (`|`), redirection (`>`), quoting and tabs do not work. For those, call `sh -c` through `Run`, as the first example does.

Every call waits for the command to finish, with no timeout, and keeps the whole output in memory. The command gets an empty standard input, so a tool that asks a question reads end of file.

## Pipes and redirection through sh

For a pipeline, hand the whole script to `sh -c`. Wrapping that in a small function keeps the call sites short, and the result still has all three parts: the code of the last command, the output and the error output.

os-shell-guide-pipe.salam

```salam
import os.shell

func sh(script: str): shell.CmdResult:
    mut args := Vector {} as Vector<str>
    defer args.free()
    args.push("-c")
    args.push(script)
    ret shell.Run("sh", args)
end

func main:
    r := sh("printf 'red\\nblue\\nred\\ngreen\\nred\\n' | sort | uniq -c | sort -rn | head -n 1")
    if r.code != 0:
        println "the pipeline failed:", r.err
        ret 0
    end
    println "most common:", r.out.trim()
    r2 := sh("echo saved > notes.txt && cat notes.txt && rm notes.txt")
    println r2.code, r2.out.trim()
end
```

Output:

```text
most common: 3 red
0 saved
```

Only put text you wrote yourself into such a script. Values from users belong in separate arguments of `Run`, where no shell can read them.

## Work with the output line by line

Most tools print one item per line. Trim the output, split it on newlines and handle each line. The program below lists the current directory with `ls` and picks out the CSV files.

os-shell-guide-lines.salam

```salam
import os
import os.shell

func main:
    os.WriteFile("a.csv", "1,2\n")
    os.WriteFile("b.csv", "3,4\n")
    os.WriteFile("notes.txt", "hi\n")
    r := shell.Exec("ls")
    mut csv := 0
    each name in r.out.trim().split("\n"):
        if name.ends_with(".csv"):
            println "found", name
            csv += 1
        end
    end
    println csv, "csv files"
    os.Remove("a.csv")
    os.Remove("b.csv")
    os.Remove("notes.txt")
end
```

Output:

```text
found a.csv
found b.csv
2 csv files
```

To list files in a real program, prefer fs.dir or os: they need no external program and they work the same on Windows. Running a tool is the right choice when the tool does the real work, such as `git` or `ffmpeg`.

## Check whether a command worked

A command that fails returns a non-zero code and usually says why in the error output. Check `code` first; `err` is for the message you show or log. A program that cannot be found at all comes back with code -1 instead of stopping your program, and the reason is in os.error.

os-shell-guide-check.salam

```salam
import os.shell

func try(command: str):
    r := shell.Exec(command)
    if r.code == 0:
        println "ok:", command
        ret
    end
    println "failed:", command, "with code", r.code
    println "  has an error message:", r.err.len() > 0
end

func main:
    try("ls .")
    try("ls no-such-folder")
    println "exit code of false:", shell.System("false")
end
```

Output:

```text
ok: ls .
failed: ls no-such-folder with code 2
  has an error message: true
exit code of false: 1
```

The exact codes and messages belong to each tool and differ between systems: `ls` returns 2 for a missing folder on Linux and 1 on macOS. Test for zero or non-zero unless the tool documents its codes.

## Exec does not understand quotes

`Exec` only splits on spaces, so quotes stay in the text and a quoted phrase still becomes two arguments. When an argument contains a space, use `Run` with the arguments in a vector, or let `sh -c` read the quotes.

os-shell-guide-quote.salam

```salam
import os.shell

func main:
    r := shell.Exec("echo 'two words'")
    println "Exec:", r.out.trim()
    mut args := Vector {} as Vector<str>
    defer args.free()
    args.push("two words")
    r2 := shell.Run("echo", args)
    println "Run: ", r2.out.trim()
    mut script := Vector {} as Vector<str>
    defer script.free()
    script.push("-c")
    script.push("echo 'two words'")
    r3 := shell.Run("sh", script)
    println "sh -c:", r3.out.trim()
end
```

Output:

```text
Exec: 'two words'
Run:  two words
sh -c: two words
```

| Need | Use |
| --- | --- |
| A simple command with no quotes or special characters | `Exec` |
| Arguments with spaces or text from users | `Run` with a vector |
| Pipes, redirection, `&&` | `Run("sh", ...)` with `-c` |
| Only the exit code, output straight to the screen | `System` |
| Start without waiting, or stop a program | os.process |

## Types

### `CmdResult`

```salam
struct CmdResult
```

The result of a command.

| Name | Type | Description |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `code` | `int = 0` | The exit code; zero means success, 128 plus the signal number when a signal ended it, and -1 when the program could not start. |
| `out` | `str = ""` | The standard output, newlines included; it stops at the first zero byte. |
| `err` | `str = ""` | The error output. |

os-shell-Run.salam

```salam
import os.shell

func main:
    mut args := Vector {} as Vector<str>
    defer args.free()
    args.push("-n")
    args.push("hello")
    r := shell.Run("echo", args)
    println r.code, "[" + r.out + "]"
    r2 := shell.Exec("echo one two three")
    println r2.code, "[" + r2.out + "]"
    mut args2 := Vector {} as Vector<str>
    defer args2.free()
    args2.push("-c")
    args2.push("echo oops >&2; exit 3")
    r3 := shell.Run("sh", args2)
    println r3.code, "[" + r3.err + "]"
    println shell.System("true"), shell.System("false") != 0
end
```

Output:

```text
0 [hello]
0 [one two three
]
3 [oops
]
0 true
```

## Functions

### `Run`

```salam
func Run(command: str, args: Vector<str>): CmdResult
```

Runs a program with its arguments given separately (no shell, the name searched on `PATH`), waits for it to finish and returns the code, the output and the error output. Code -1 when it cannot start.

The example for this item is shown with the ones above: os-shell-Run.salam

### `Exec`

```salam
func Exec(command: str): CmdResult
```

Splits a command string on single spaces into a program and its arguments and runs it with `Run`, with no shell. Quotes are kept as ordinary characters.

The example for this item is shown with the ones above: os-shell-Run.salam

### `System`

```salam
func System(command: str): int
```

Runs a command in the real shell (`/bin/sh -c`, or `cmd` on Windows) and returns only the exit code; the output is printed directly. 127 when the shell cannot start.

The example for this item is shown with the ones above: os-shell-Run.salam

# os/temp

https://salamlang.github.io/Salam/std/os-temp/

Making a temporary file or directory under a unique name.

For data that is only needed while the program runs, make a temporary file or directory: an unpacked archive, a file being built before it is published, the output of a tool. `File` and `Directory` create an empty one in the system temporary folder under a random name (`salam-` and 16 hex digits from crypto), so several copies of the program running at once do not collide, and return its path. Removing it is up to you: nothing is cleaned up when the program exits.

Read and write the files with fs.file, and build paths inside a temporary directory with fs.path. For replacing a real file safely, `fs.file.AtomicWrite` is often the better tool.

What people get wrong:

- Not checking `Directory`. It returns empty text when it fails, and a later `path.Join("", name)` then writes into the current folder.

- Trusting `File` blindly. It always returns a path, even when the file could not be created, and it creates the file first and narrows its permissions right after, so for a moment it has the default permissions. For secrets, make a `Directory` (only you can enter it) and create the files inside it.

- Moving a finished file out with a rename. The temporary folder is often on another disk, where a rename fails; copy it instead.

## A scratch directory for one job

The usual pattern is three lines: make a directory with `Directory`, put `defer temp.RemoveDir(work)` right under it, and build every path inside it with path.Join. The deferred call runs on every way out of the function, an early `ret` included, so the directory is gone however the job ends. `Directory` returns an empty string when it cannot make the directory, so check for that before you use it.

os-temp-scratch.salam

```salam
import fs.dir
import fs.file
import fs.path
import os.temp

func main:
    work := temp.Directory()
    if work == "":
        println "could not make a work directory"
        ret 1
    end
    defer temp.RemoveDir(work)
    file.WriteText(path.Join(work, "part-1.txt"), "Salam ")
    file.WriteText(path.Join(work, "part-2.txt"), "world\n")
    mut joined := ""
    each name in ["part-1.txt", "part-2.txt"]:
        joined = joined + file.ReadText(path.Join(work, name))
    end
    print joined
    println dir.ListFiles(work).len(), "parts,", dir.Size(work), "bytes"
    ret 0
end
```

Output:

```text
Salam world
2 parts, 12 bytes
```

## Build a file in steps, then publish it

When a file is written in several steps, write it to a temporary file first and copy it to its real name only when it is complete. Whoever reads `people.csv` then never sees half of it. Use `file.Copy` here, not `file.Move`: the temporary directory is often on another disk (a `tmpfs` in memory on many Linux systems), and a rename cannot cross disks.

os-temp-staging.salam

```salam
import fs.file
import os.temp

func main:
    staging := temp.File()
    file.Append(staging, "id,name\n")
    file.Append(staging, "1,Sara\n")
    file.Append(staging, "2,Reza\n")
    rows := file.ReadLines(staging)
    println "staged", rows.len(), "lines"
    if file.Copy(staging, "people.csv") == 0:
        println "published people.csv,", file.Size("people.csv"), "bytes"
    end
    temp.Remove(staging)
    println "staging left behind:", file.Exists(staging)
    print file.ReadText("people.csv")
    file.Delete("people.csv")
end
```

Output:

```text
staged 3 lines
published people.csv, 22 bytes
staging left behind: false
id,name
1,Sara
2,Reza
```

When the whole content is ready in one string, fs.file.AtomicWrite is simpler: it writes the temporary copy next to the target, on the same disk, and renames it in one step.

## Who can read a temporary file

The system temporary directory is shared by every account on the machine. That is why `File` makes its file readable and writable by you alone (`600`) and `Directory` makes its directory open to you alone (`700`). A token or a downloaded document you put there stays out of reach of other users. Leave it like that, and widen the permissions with fs.Chmod only when another account really has to read the file.

os-temp-permissions.salam

```salam
import fs
import os.temp

func main:
    secret := temp.File()
    work := temp.Directory()
    println "file:", fs.Permissions(secret)
    println "directory:", fs.Permissions(work)
    temp.Remove(secret)
    temp.RemoveDir(work)
end
```

Output:

```text
file: 600
directory: 700
```

## Errors, and where the files go

`Remove` and `RemoveDir` return `0` on success and `-1` on failure, and they record an `IOError` in os.error. The usual failure is removing the same file twice. `RemoveDir` on a directory that is already gone counts as success.

os-temp-errors.salam

```salam
import os.error
import os.temp

func main:
    p := temp.File()
    println "first remove:", temp.Remove(p)
    error.Clear()
    println "second remove:", temp.Remove(p)
    if error.HasError():
        println "message:", error.LastMessage()
        println "is an I/O error:", error.LastCode() == error.IOError
    end
end
```

Output:

```text
first remove: 0
second remove: -1
message: failed to remove temp file
is an I/O error: true
```

The files go into the directory that os.TempDir names: the `TEMP`, `TMP` or `TMPDIR` environment variable, checked in that order, and `/tmp` when none is set. Nothing removes them when the program exits, and a program that crashes leaves them behind, so a long running service should give each job its own directory and remove it when the job is done. The names are random (`salam-` and hex digits), so never compare them or show them in output that someone reads later.

## Functions

### `File`

```salam
func File(): str
```

Makes an empty file named `salam-` plus 16 random hex digits and `.tmp` in the system temporary directory, sets its permissions to `600` and returns its path. It returns the path even when creation failed.

os-temp-File.salam

```salam
import os
import os.temp

func main:
    p := temp.File()
    println os.Exists(p)
    temp.Remove(p)
    println os.Exists(p)
    d := temp.Directory()
    println os.IsDir(d)
    temp.RemoveDir(d)
    println os.Exists(d)
end
```

Output:

```text
true
false
true
false
```

### `Directory`

```salam
func Directory(): str
```

Makes an empty directory under a unique name with permissions `700` and returns its path, or empty text (with an `os.error` record) when it cannot.

The example for this item is shown with the ones above: os-temp-File.salam

### `Remove`

```salam
func Remove(p: str): int
```

Removes a temporary file; 0 on success, -1 with an `os.error` record on failure.

The example for this item is shown with the ones above: os-temp-File.salam

### `RemoveDir`

```salam
func RemoveDir(p: str): int
```

Removes a temporary directory with everything in it, using `os.RemoveAll`; 0 on success or when it is already gone, -1 on failure. Like `os.RemoveAll`, it follows symbolic links to folders.

The example for this item is shown with the ones above: os-temp-File.salam

# os/user

https://salamlang.github.io/Salam/std/os-user/

Who is running the program, and the standard directories that belong to them.

The `os.user` package answers two questions: who is running the program (`Username`, `Uid`, `Gid`), and where that user's files belong (`HomeDir`, `ConfigDir`, `CacheDir`). Programs usually keep their settings in the user config directory and throwaway data in the user cache directory; this package gives the conventional path on each system, for instance `~/.config` on Linux and `%APPDATA%` on Windows. Note that macOS also gets `~/.config` and `~/.cache`, the convention of command line tools, rather than `~/Library`.

For the machine rather than the user, see os.platform; for reading other environment variables, env; for joining paths onto these folders, fs.path.

## How the directories are found

These functions do not ask the operating system for a list of folders. They read environment variables, the same way most command line tools do, which also means that whoever starts the program can point them somewhere else:

| Function | Linux, macOS and BSD | Windows |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `HomeDir` | `$HOME` | `%USERPROFILE%` |
| `ConfigDir` | `$XDG_CONFIG_HOME`, else `~/.config` | `%APPDATA%` |
| `CacheDir` | `$XDG_CACHE_HOME`, else `~/.cache` | `%LOCALAPPDATA%` |
| `Username` | `$USER`, else `$LOGNAME`, else the user database | `%USERNAME%` |

The example sets the variables itself with env.Set, so it prints the same on every Unix machine:

os-user-resolve.salam

```salam
import env
import os.user

func main:
    env.Set("HOME", "/home/sara")
    env.Unset("XDG_CONFIG_HOME")
    env.Unset("XDG_CACHE_HOME")
    println "home:  ", user.HomeDir()
    println "config:", user.ConfigDir()
    println "cache: ", user.CacheDir()
    env.Set("XDG_CONFIG_HOME", "/data/sara/config")
    env.Set("XDG_CACHE_HOME", "/fast-disk/cache")
    println "config:", user.ConfigDir()
    println "cache: ", user.CacheDir()
end
```

Output:

```text
home:   /home/sara
config: /home/sara/.config
cache:  /home/sara/.cache
config: /data/sara/config
cache:  /fast-disk/cache
```

## Settings and cache for your own program

Give your program its own folder inside each of these directories, named after the program, and create it with dir.MkdirAll before the first write: on a fresh account even `~/.config` may not exist yet. Settings belong in the config folder. Anything you can rebuild, such as downloads or a search index, belongs in the cache folder, which the user or a cleanup tool may empty at any time.

The first line of this example points `HOME` at a folder in the current directory so that running it does not touch your real settings. A real program leaves that line out.

os-user-app-dirs.salam

```salam
import env
import fs.dir
import fs.file
import fs.path
import os
import os.user

func main:
    env.Set("HOME", path.Join(os.Cwd(), "demo-home"))
    env.Unset("XDG_CONFIG_HOME")
    env.Unset("XDG_CACHE_HOME")
    config := path.Join(user.ConfigDir(), "notes")
    cache := path.Join(user.CacheDir(), "notes")
    dir.MkdirAll(config)
    dir.MkdirAll(cache)
    settings := path.Join(config, "settings.ini")
    repeat 2 in run:
        if file.Exists(settings):
            println "run", run + 1, "found", file.ReadText(settings).trim()
        else:
            file.WriteText(settings, "theme=dark\n")
            println "run", run + 1, "wrote the default settings"
        end
    end
    file.WriteText(path.Join(cache, "index.bin"), "0123456789")
    println "settings at ~/" + path.Rel(user.HomeDir(), settings)
    println "cache holds", dir.Size(cache), "bytes"
    dir.RemoveAll(user.HomeDir())
end
```

Output:

```text
run 1 wrote the default settings
run 2 found theme=dark
settings at ~/.config/notes/settings.ini
cache holds 10 bytes
```

## Expanding ~ in paths from users

The shell turns `~/notes` into a full path before your program sees it, but a path read from a settings file or typed at a prompt still starts with `~`. Neither fs.file nor fs.path expands it, so replace it yourself with `HomeDir`:

os-user-expand-home.salam

```salam
import env
import fs.path
import os.user
import str

func expand(p: str): str:
    if p == "~": ret user.HomeDir() end
    if str.StartsWith(p, "~/"):
        ret path.Join(user.HomeDir(), p.substr(2, p.len() - 2))
    end
    ret p
end

func main:
    env.Set("HOME", "/home/sara")
    each p in ["~", "~/notes/today.md", "/etc/hosts", "reports/may.csv"]:
        println p, "->", expand(p)
    end
end
```

Output:

```text
~ -> /home/sara
~/notes/today.md -> /home/sara/notes/today.md
/etc/hosts -> /etc/hosts
reports/may.csv -> reports/may.csv
```

## Things to watch for

- `Username` is fine for a greeting or a log line, but it comes from environment variables that anyone starting the program can change. Never use it to decide what someone is allowed to do.

- `Uid` and `Gid` are `-1` on Windows. On Unix a `Uid` of `0` means the program runs as root, which is worth a warning in a tool that should not.

- When its variable is not set, for example in a service started with an empty environment, `HomeDir` returns an empty string, and `ConfigDir` and `CacheDir` on Unix then return the relative paths `.config` and `.cache`. Check `HomeDir` first; otherwise your files silently land in the current directory.

## Functions

### `Username`

```salam
func Username(): str
```

The name of the current user: `$USER`, else `$LOGNAME`, else the system user database; `%USERNAME%` on Windows. It can be changed by whoever starts the program.

os-user-Username.salam

```salam
import os.user

func main:
    println user.Username().len() > 0
    println user.Uid() >= 0, user.Gid() >= 0
    println user.HomeDir().len() > 0
    println user.ConfigDir().len() > 0, user.CacheDir().len() > 0
end
```

Output:

```text
true
true true
true
true true
```

### `Uid`

```salam
func Uid(): int
```

The numeric user id from the system, 0 for root; minus one on Windows.

The example for this item is shown with the ones above: os-user-Username.salam

### `Gid`

```salam
func Gid(): int
```

The numeric group id of the user; minus one on Windows.

The example for this item is shown with the ones above: os-user-Username.salam

### `HomeDir`

```salam
func HomeDir(): str
```

The home directory of the user, from `$HOME` (`%USERPROFILE%` on Windows); empty when the variable is not set.

The example for this item is shown with the ones above: os-user-Username.salam

### `ConfigDir`

```salam
func ConfigDir(): str
```

The standard directory for program settings: `$XDG_CONFIG_HOME` or `~/.config`, `%APPDATA%` on Windows. It may not exist yet.

The example for this item is shown with the ones above: os-user-Username.salam

### `CacheDir`

```salam
func CacheDir(): str
```

The standard directory for program caches: `$XDG_CACHE_HOME` or `~/.cache`, `%LOCALAPPDATA%` on Windows. It may not exist yet.

The example for this item is shown with the ones above: os-user-Username.salam

# fs

https://salamlang.github.io/Salam/std/fs/

File times and permissions; the base of the file, dir and path packages.

The `fs` package holds a few functions about a file's metadata (its times and its permissions) and three sub-packages you will use far more often: fs.file for reading and writing files, fs.dir for folders and fs.path for building paths. The simpler os package covers whole-file reads, folder listings and existence checks; come here for when a file changed and who may read it.

Times are whole seconds since the start of 1970 (Unix time), as an `i64`. Every function returns `-1` when the path does not exist or the system cannot answer.

Write permissions in octal, such as `0o644`, meaning the owner reads and writes and everyone else reads. `Permissions` returns the same digits as an ordinary number, such as `644`, so that it reads easily. The two are not the same number (`0o644` is 420), so never pass the result of `Permissions` back to `Chmod` unchanged.

## Keep a secret file private

A new file gets the system default permissions, usually `644`, which lets every account on the machine read it. For tokens, keys and passwords, write the file and then narrow it to `0o600`. Keep the two notations apart: `Chmod` takes octal (`0o600`), while `Permissions` gives the same digits back as an ordinary number (`600`). That is why `p % 100 == 0` below means that the group and everyone else have no rights at all.

fs-guide-private.salam

```salam
import fs
import fs.file

func main:
    file.WriteText("token.txt", "s3cr3t")
    fs.Chmod("token.txt", 0o644)
    println "before:", fs.Permissions("token.txt")
    fs.Chmod("token.txt", 0o600)
    p := fs.Permissions("token.txt")
    println "after: ", p
    if p % 100 == 0:
        println "only the owner can read it"
    end
    file.Delete("token.txt")
end
```

Output:

```text
before: 644
after:  600
only the owner can read it
```

## Reading the permission digits

The three digits are for the owner, the group and everyone else, in that order. Inside one digit, 4 means read, 2 means write and 1 means execute, and the digit is their sum:

| Digit | Letters | Meaning |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `7` | `rwx` | read, write and run |
| `6` | `rw-` | read and write |
| `5` | `r-x` | read and run |
| `4` | `r--` | read only |
| `0` | `---` | nothing |

This example turns the number into the letters that `ls -l` prints. A script needs the execute bit for its owner (`0o755` or `0o700`) before the shell runs it, and a directory needs it before anyone can open it.

fs-guide-rwx.salam

```salam
import fs
import fs.file

func letters(digit: int): str:
    mut out := ""
    if digit >= 4: out = out + "r" else: out = out + "-" end
    if digit % 4 >= 2: out = out + "w" else: out = out + "-" end
    if digit % 2 == 1: out = out + "x" else: out = out + "-" end
    ret out
end

func show(p: int): str:
    ret letters(p / 100) + letters(p / 10 % 10) + letters(p % 10)
end

func main:
    file.WriteText("deploy.sh", "echo deploying\n")
    each mode in [0o755, 0o750, 0o644, 0o600]:
        fs.Chmod("deploy.sh", mode)
        p := fs.Permissions("deploy.sh")
        println p, show(p)
    end
    file.Delete("deploy.sh")
end
```

Output:

```text
755 rwxr-xr-x
750 rwxr-x---
644 rw-r--r--
600 rw-------
```

## Rebuild only what changed

`ModTime` is how build tools such as `make` decide what to do: an output is out of date when its source changed after the output was written. For a path that does not exist `ModTime` returns `-1`, which the example reads as "build it". Times are in whole seconds, so a source and an output written in the same second count as up to date. That is the right answer here, because the output was written after the source.

fs-guide-rebuild.salam

```salam
import fs
import fs.file

func needs_build(src: str, out: str): bool:
    built := fs.ModTime(out)
    if built < 0: ret true end
    ret fs.ModTime(src) > built
end

func main:
    file.WriteText("page.md", "# Hello\n")
    println "first run, build:", needs_build("page.md", "page.html")
    file.WriteText("page.html", "<h1>Hello</h1>\n")
    println "after building, build:", needs_build("page.md", "page.html")
    file.Delete("page.html")
    println "output deleted, build:", needs_build("page.md", "page.html")
    file.Delete("page.md")
end
```

Output:

```text
first run, build: true
after building, build: false
output deleted, build: true
```

## Platform notes

- `CreatedTime` is `0` where the file system does not record a creation time, which is common on Linux. Use `ModTime` when you need a value that is always there.

- On Linux, macOS and BSD the time functions and `Permissions` run the system `stat` command through the shell, with the path quoted. That is quick for a handful of files, but over thousands of files in a loop the process starts add up. `Chmod` calls the system directly.

- Windows has no Unix permission bits, only a read only flag, so `Chmod` can only switch that flag, and `Permissions` returns 292 (`0o444`) for a read only file and 438 (`0o666`) otherwise: the octal value, not the digits it gives on Unix. Write permission logic for Unix and test it there.

## Functions

### `ModTime`

```salam
func ModTime(path: str): i64
```

When the file's content was last changed, in Unix seconds; -1 when the path does not exist.

fs-ModTime.salam

```salam
import fs
import fs.file

func main:
    file.WriteText("report.txt", "hello")
    t := fs.ModTime("report.txt")
    println t > 0, fs.AccessedTime("report.txt") > 0, fs.CreatedTime("report.txt") >= 0
    fs.Chmod("report.txt", 0o644)
    println fs.Permissions("report.txt")
end
```

Output:

```text
true true true
644
```

### `AccessedTime`

```salam
func AccessedTime(path: str): i64
```

When the file was last read, in Unix seconds. Many systems update it lazily or not at all (`noatime`), so do not rely on it.

The example for this item is shown with the ones above: fs-ModTime.salam

### `CreatedTime`

```salam
func CreatedTime(path: str): i64
```

When the file was created, in Unix seconds, or zero where the file system does not keep it.

The example for this item is shown with the ones above: fs-ModTime.salam

### `Chmod`

```salam
func Chmod(path: str, mode: int): int
```

Changes a file's permissions; give them in octal, such as `0o644`. Returns 0 on success and -1 on failure. On Windows only the read only flag can change.

The example for this item is shown with the ones above: fs-ModTime.salam

### `Permissions`

```salam
func Permissions(path: str): int
```

A file's permissions as their octal digits read as a decimal number, such as `644`; -1 when the path does not exist. On Windows it returns 292 or 438 instead.

The example for this item is shown with the ones above: fs-ModTime.salam

# fs/dir

https://salamlang.github.io/Salam/std/fs-dir/

Creating, listing, copying, moving and removing directories.

The `fs.dir` package covers everything you do with directories: create them, list them, walk a tree, measure it, copy, move and delete it. It is built on the folder functions of os and adds two things: when a function fails it records the detail (an `IOError` with the operation and the path) in os.error, and `Move` works across disks. For files use fs.file, and to build the paths fs.path.

Listing functions return bare names; `Walk` returns full paths. Functions that change the disk return 0 or -1.

What people get wrong:

- Using `Exists` for files. Here it is true only for a directory; for files use `fs.file.Exists`.

- Expecting `Copy` and `Move` to refuse an existing target. Both merge into it: files with the same name are replaced and other files stay.

- Pointing `RemoveAll`, `Walk`, `Size` or `Copy` at a tree with symbolic links. They follow a link to a folder as if it were part of the tree, so `RemoveAll` deletes the contents of the link's target and a link loop never ends.

## Create a project layout

`MkdirAll` creates every missing parent and succeeds when the folder is already there, so it is the safe choice for setting up a layout that may partly exist. `List`, `ListDirs` and `ListFiles` return bare names, not full paths, in whatever order the file system keeps them, and that order differs between systems. Sort them with sort.Sort before you show or compare them.

fs-dir-guide-skeleton.salam

```salam
import fs.dir
import fs.file
import sort

func main:
    each d in ["shop/src/models", "shop/src/views", "shop/tests", "shop/docs"]:
        dir.MkdirAll(d)
    end
    file.WriteText("shop/main.salam", "func main:\nend\n")
    file.WriteText("shop/README.md", "# Shop\n")
    file.WriteText("shop/src/models/order.salam", "")
    top := dir.ListDirs("shop")
    sort.Sort(top)
    println "folders:", top
    files := dir.ListFiles("shop")
    sort.Sort(files)
    println "files:  ", files
    println "src has", dir.ListDirs("shop/src").len(), "folders"
    dir.RemoveAll("shop")
end
```

Output:

```text
folders: ["docs", "src", "tests"]
files:   ["README.md", "main.salam"]
src has 2 folders
```

## Walk a whole tree

`Walk` returns the path of every file below a directory, already joined to the directory you passed in, so each one can go straight to an fs.file function. Directories themselves are not in the list, and like the listing functions it has no fixed order. This example counts files by extension and adds up their sizes, which is what `Size` does in one call.

fs-dir-guide-walk.salam

```salam
import fs.dir
import fs.file
import fs.path

func main:
    dir.MkdirAll("site/pages/blog")
    dir.MkdirAll("site/assets/img")
    file.WriteText("site/pages/index.html", "<h1>Home</h1>")
    file.WriteText("site/pages/blog/first.html", "<p>First post</p>")
    file.WriteText("site/assets/style.css", "body { margin: 0 }")
    file.WriteText("site/assets/img/logo.svg", "<svg/>")
    counts := HashMap {} as HashMap<str, int>
    mut bytes := 0 as i64
    each p in dir.Walk("site"):
        ext := path.Ext(p)
        if counts.has(ext): counts.put(ext, counts.get(ext) + 1) else: counts.put(ext, 1) end
        bytes += file.Size(p)
    end
    each ext in [".html", ".css", ".svg"]:
        println ext, counts.get(ext)
    end
    println "total:", bytes, "bytes, same as dir.Size:", bytes == dir.Size("site")
    dir.RemoveAll("site")
end
```

Output:

```text
.html 2
.css 1
.svg 1
total: 54 bytes, same as dir.Size: true
```

## Keep rotating backups

`Copy` copies a tree with everything in it (file contents only; permissions are not kept), and `Move` renames one, falling back to copy and delete when the rename fails, for example because the target is on another disk. Together they make a simple rotation: drop the oldest backup, shift the others up by one, and copy the live folder to `.bak1`. The oldest is removed first so that its name is free before anything moves onto it.

fs-dir-guide-backup.salam

```salam
import fs.dir
import fs.file
import str

func backup(src: str, keep: int):
    dir.RemoveAll(src.concat(".bak").concat(str.FromInt(keep)))
    mut n := keep - 1
    until n >= 1:
        from := src.concat(".bak").concat(str.FromInt(n))
        if dir.Exists(from): dir.Move(from, src.concat(".bak").concat(str.FromInt(n + 1))) end
        n -= 1
    end
    dir.Copy(src, src.concat(".bak1"))
end

func main:
    dir.MkdirAll("notes")
    repeat 1 to 4 in day:
        file.WriteText("notes/today.txt", "day ".concat(str.FromInt(day)))
        backup("notes", 3)
    end
    repeat 1 to 3 in n:
        name := "notes.bak".concat(str.FromInt(n))
        println name, file.ReadText(name.concat("/today.txt"))
    end
    println "notes.bak4 exists:", dir.Exists("notes.bak4")
    each d in ["notes", "notes.bak1", "notes.bak2", "notes.bak3"]: dir.RemoveAll(d) end
end
```

Output:

```text
notes.bak1 day 4
notes.bak2 day 3
notes.bak3 day 2
notes.bak4 exists: false
```

## Errors and pitfalls

Every function that changes the disk returns `0` or `-1`, and on failure it leaves a short message in os.error. The message names the operation that failed, not the reason, so when the reason matters, check the likely causes yourself: the folder already exists, its parent is missing, or it is not empty.

fs-dir-guide-errors.salam

```salam
import fs.dir
import fs.file
import os.error

func report(what: str, rc: int):
    if rc == 0:
        println what, "ok"
    else:
        println what, "failed:", error.LastMessage()
    end
end

func main:
    report("mkdir data", dir.Mkdir("data"))
    report("mkdir data again", dir.Mkdir("data"))
    report("mkdir a/b/c", dir.Mkdir("a/b/c"))
    file.WriteText("data/x.txt", "x")
    report("remove data", dir.Remove("data"))
    println "data/x.txt is a dir:", dir.Exists("data/x.txt"), "is a file:", file.Exists("data/x.txt")
    report("remove all data", dir.RemoveAll("data"))
    println "listing a missing dir:", dir.List("data").len()
end
```

Output:

```text
mkdir data ok
mkdir data again failed: mkdir failed
mkdir a/b/c failed: mkdir failed
remove data failed: rmdir failed
data/x.txt is a dir: false is a file: true
remove all data ok
listing a missing dir: 0
```

- `Mkdir` fails when the folder exists or its parent is missing; `MkdirAll` handles both.

- `Remove` only removes an empty folder. `RemoveAll` deletes everything inside without asking, so build its argument carefully and never pass it a path straight from user input; path.IsSafe checks that a path stays inside a base folder.

- `Exists` is false for a file, and `List` on a missing folder gives an empty vector rather than an error.

## Which function for which job

| Job | Function |
| --- | --- |
| Create one folder in an existing parent | `Mkdir` |
| Create a whole path of folders | `MkdirAll` |
| Names inside one folder | `List`, or `ListDirs` and `ListFiles` for one kind only |
| Every file below a folder, with paths | `Walk` |
| Total size of a tree | `Size` |
| Duplicate a tree | `Copy` |
| Rename or move a tree | `Move` |
| Delete an empty folder | `Remove` |
| Delete a folder and its contents | `RemoveAll` |

## Functions

### `Mkdir`

```salam

```

Creates one directory; fails (-1, with an `os.error` record) when it exists or its parent is missing.

fs-dir-List.salam

```salam
import fs.dir
import fs.file

func main:
    dir.Mkdir("library")
    dir.MkdirAll("library/poetry/hafez")
    file.WriteText("library/index.txt", "3 books")
    file.WriteText("library/poetry/hafez/ghazal.txt", "a line of verse")
    println dir.Exists("library"), dir.IsDir("library/index.txt")
    println dir.List("library").len(), dir.ListDirs("library"), dir.ListFiles("library")
    println dir.Walk("library").len(), dir.Size("library") > 0
    println dir.Permissions("library") > 0, dir.ModTime("library") > 0
    dir.Copy("library", "backup")
    dir.Move("backup", "archive")
    println dir.Exists("backup"), dir.Exists("archive/poetry/hafez"), file.Exists("archive/poetry/hafez/ghazal.txt")
    dir.Mkdir("empty")
    dir.Remove("empty")
    dir.RemoveAll("library")
    dir.RemoveAll("archive")
    println dir.Exists("library"), dir.Exists("empty")
end
```

Output:

```text
true false
2 ["poetry"] ["index.txt"]
2 true
true true
false true true
false false
```

# fs/file

https://salamlang.github.io/Salam/std/fs-file/

Reading and writing files, file information, copying and moving, and MD5 and SHA digests.

The `fs.file` package is the fullest set of tools for working with one file: read it whole or as lines, write, append, replace it safely, copy, move and delete it, look up its size, times and permissions, hash it and guess its MIME type. Its copy, move, delete and atomic write functions record failures in os.error; reads and plain writes do not, so check what they return. For folders use fs.dir, for paths fs.path, and for streaming a large file the handle functions of io.

Writes return the number of bytes written, or -1. Reads return empty text when the file cannot be opened, the same as for an empty file; ask `Exists` when the difference matters.

What people get wrong:

- Treating it as binary-safe. Every read and write goes through a `str`, which ends at the first zero byte, so `ReadAll`, `ReadBytes`, `WriteBytes` and the digest functions cut a binary file short. For images, archives and other binary data use `ReadBinaryFile` and `WriteBinaryFile` from archive, which carry a pointer and a length, and the pointer forms in crypto such as `Sha256Bytes`.

- Expecting `Move` to cross disks. It is a rename and fails between file systems; `fs.dir.Move` falls back to copying, or copy and delete yourself.

- Assuming `AtomicWrite` keeps the old file's permissions. It writes a new file, which gets the default permissions; a file you had narrowed to `0o600` becomes readable again unless you `Chmod` it after each save.

- Using `Exists` to mean "is a file". It is true for directories too; combine it with `fs.dir.IsDir`.

## Read a settings file line by line

`ReadLines` splits a file at its line breaks and drops a trailing `\r`, so a file saved on Windows reads the same as one saved on Linux. That makes simple `key = value` files easy: trim each line, skip blank lines and comments, and split at the first `=`.

fs-file-guide-config.salam

```salam
import fs.file
import str

func main:
    file.WriteText("app.conf", "# shop settings\nname = Corner Shop\n\nport = 8080\ncurrency = IRR\n")
    settings := HashMap {} as HashMap<str, str>
    each line in file.ReadLines("app.conf"):
        t := line.trim()
        if t.len() == 0 or str.StartsWith(t, "#"): continue end
        eq_at := str.IndexOf(t, "=")
        if eq_at < 0: continue end
        settings.put(t.substr(0, eq_at).trim(), t.substr(eq_at + 1, t.len() - eq_at - 1).trim())
    end
    println settings.size(), "settings"
    println "name:", settings.get("name")
    println "port:", settings.get("port")
    file.Delete("app.conf")
end
```

Output:

```text
3 settings
name: Corner Shop
port: 8080
```

For a format with sections, quoting or nesting, use a real parser such as encoding.toml, encoding.json or encoding.envfile.

## Append to a log

`Append` opens the file, adds the text at the end and closes it again, and creates the file on the first call. Each call is a separate open and close, which is fine for a line now and then. For a busy log, open the file once with `Open(p, "ab")`, write through io.Write and `Close` it at the end.

fs-file-guide-log.salam

```salam
import fs.file

func log(line: str):
    file.Append("app.log", line.concat("\n"))
end

func main:
    log("started")
    log("loaded 3 orders")
    log("sent invoice 1042")
    log("stopped")
    lines := file.ReadLines("app.log")
    println "log has", lines.len(), "lines,", file.Size("app.log"), "bytes"
    println "last two:"
    mut i := lines.len() - 2
    until i < lines.len():
        println " ", lines.get(i)
        i += 1
    end
    file.Delete("app.log")
end
```

Output:

```text
log has 4 lines, 50 bytes
last two:
  sent invoice 1042
  stopped
```

## Check that a file arrived intact

Download pages often publish a SHA-256 digest next to each file. Compute the digest of your copy with `Sha256Hex` and compare the two: a change of even one byte gives a completely different digest. `Md5Hex` and `Sha1Hex` are fine for noticing accidental changes, such as a cache key, but anyone can build two different files with the same MD5 or SHA-1 on purpose, so do not trust them against an attacker.

fs-file-guide-checksum.salam

```salam
import fs.file

func verify(p: str): bool:
    want := file.ReadText(p.concat(".sha256")).trim()
    ret file.Sha256Hex(p) == want
end

func main:
    file.WriteBytes("release.tar", "pretend this is a release archive")
    file.WriteText("release.tar.sha256", file.Sha256Hex("release.tar").concat("\n"))
    println "intact:", verify("release.tar")
    file.Append("release.tar", "!")
    println "after a change:", verify("release.tar")
    file.Delete("release.tar")
    file.Delete("release.tar.sha256")
end
```

Output:

```text
intact: true
after a change: false
```

The digest functions read the file into a string first, and a Salam string ends at the first zero byte. For text files that does not matter. A binary file that contains a zero byte, which most archives and images do, is hashed only up to that byte, so check such files with the system `sha256sum` or with the buffer functions in crypto, such as `Sha256Bytes`. The same limit applies to `ReadAll`, `ReadText`, `ReadBytes` and `WriteBytes`.

## Save without losing the old version

`AtomicWrite` writes the new content to `name.tmp` next to the target and then renames it over the target in one step. A program that crashes in the middle leaves either the old file or the new one, never half of each. It does not flush the data to the disk first, so after a power cut a file saved a moment earlier can still be lost on some file systems, and two programs saving the same file at once share the same `.tmp` name. Copying the old file to `.bak` first also keeps one previous version. When the folder does not exist, `AtomicWrite` returns `-1` and leaves its message in os.error.

fs-file-guide-save.salam

```salam
import fs.file
import os.error

func save(p: str, data: str): bool:
    if file.Exists(p): file.Copy(p, p.concat(".bak")) end
    if file.AtomicWrite(p, data) != 0:
        println "save failed:", error.LastMessage()
        ret false
    end
    ret true
end

func main:
    save("profile.json", "{\"name\": \"Sara\"}")
    save("profile.json", "{\"name\": \"Sara\", \"city\": \"Tabriz\"}")
    println "current:", file.ReadText("profile.json")
    println "backup: ", file.ReadText("profile.json.bak")
    println "temp file left:", file.Exists("profile.json.tmp")
    save("no-such-dir/profile.json", "{}")
    file.Delete("profile.json")
    file.Delete("profile.json.bak")
end
```

Output:

```text
current: {"name": "Sara", "city": "Tabriz"}
backup:  {"name": "Sara"}
temp file left: false
save failed: atomic write failed
```

## Serve files with the right type

A web server has to send a `Content-Type` with each file. `MimeType` picks it from the extension alone, without upper and lower case mattering, and knows the common web, image, audio, video and archive types; anything else is `application/octet-stream`, which browsers download instead of showing. `Extension` keeps the dot and the original case, and is empty when the name has no extension.

fs-file-guide-mime.salam

```salam
import fs.file

func main:
    each name in ["index.html", "app.js", "logo.SVG", "photo.jpeg", "data.json", "notes", "backup.7z"]:
        ext := file.Extension(name)
        if ext == "": println name, "(no extension)", file.MimeType(name)
        else: println name, ext, file.MimeType(name)
        end
    end
end
```

Output:

```text
index.html .html text/html
app.js .js text/javascript
logo.SVG .SVG image/svg+xml
photo.jpeg .jpeg image/jpeg
data.json .json application/json
notes (no extension) application/octet-stream
backup.7z .7z application/octet-stream
```

An HTTP server usually wants net.mime instead: its `MimeType` adds `; charset=utf-8` to text types and knows web fonts, and the package also parses `Content-Type` headers and multipart bodies.

## Which function for which job

| Job | Function |
| --- | --- |
| Read a small text file whole | `ReadText`, or `ReadLines` for a vector of lines |
| Read only the start of a file | `ReadBytes` |
| Replace a file's content | `WriteText`, or `AtomicWrite` when the file matters |
| Add to the end of a file | `Append` |
| Work through a big file piece by piece | `Open`, then the io functions, then `Close` |
| Size, times and permissions in one call | `Stat` |
| Duplicate, move or delete | `Copy`, `Move` (or `Rename`), `Delete` |
| Check a download | `Sha256Hex` |
| Content type for a web response | `MimeType` |

## Types

### `FileInfo`

```salam
struct FileInfo
```

Everything about a file.

| Name | Type | Description |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `size` | `i64 = 0` | The size in bytes. |
| `mod_time` | `i64 = 0` | When it was last changed. |
| `accessed_time` | `i64 = 0` | When it was last read. |
| `created_time` | `i64 = 0` | When it was created. |
| `permissions` | `int = 0` | The permissions, as octal digits such as `644`. |
| `exists` | `bool = false` | True when the path exists (a directory counts); the other fields are 0 when it does not. |

fs-file-Stat.salam

```salam
import fs.file

func main:
    file.WriteText("picture.png", "PNG")
    info := file.Stat("picture.png")
    println info.exists, info.size, info.mod_time > 0, info.permissions > 0
    println file.Size("picture.png"), file.Exists("picture.png")
    println file.ModTime("picture.png") > 0, file.AccessedTime("picture.png") > 0, file.CreatedTime("picture.png") >= 0
    file.Chmod("picture.png", 0o600)
    println file.Permissions("picture.png")
    println file.Extension("picture.png"), file.MimeType("picture.png"), file.MimeType("letter.pdf")
    println file.Stat("missing.txt").exists
end
```

Output:

```text
true 3 true true
3 true
true true true
600
.png image/png application/pdf
false
```

```salam
import fs.file

func main:
    file.WriteText("poem.txt", "The children of Adam are limbs of one body\n")
    file.Append("poem.txt", "having been created of one essence\n")
    print file.ReadText("poem.txt")
    println file.ReadAll("poem.txt") == file.ReadText("poem.txt")
    lines := file.ReadLines("poem.txt")
    println lines.len(), lines.get(1)
    file.WriteBytes("data.bin", "ABCDEF")
    println file.ReadBytes("data.bin", 3)
    file.AtomicWrite("settings.txt", "language=english")
    println file.ReadText("settings.txt")

    println f.readline()
    file.Close(f)
end
```

```text
true
2 having been created of one essence
ABC

The children of Adam are limbs of one body
```

### `Copy`

```salam
import fs.file

func main:
    file.WriteText("original.txt", "hello")
    file.Copy("original.txt", "copy.txt")
    file.Move("copy.txt", "moved.txt")
    file.Rename("moved.txt", "final.txt")
    println file.Exists("copy.txt"), file.Exists("final.txt"), file.ReadText("final.txt")
    file.Delete("final.txt")
    println file.Exists("final.txt")
end
```

Output:

```text
false true hello
false
```

# fs/path

https://salamlang.github.io/Salam/std/fs-path/

Working with file paths: joining them, separating the name and the extension, absolute and relative paths, and a safety check.

The `fs.path` package takes paths apart and puts them together: join, split, clean, make absolute or relative, and check that a path from a user stays inside a folder. Every function is a thin name over the same function in filepath (with `Filename` for `Base`, `Dirname` and `Parent` for `Dir`), so pick one of the two packages and use it throughout a program. One name differs in meaning: `filepath.Base` keeps the extension, while `path.Basename` drops it; `fs.path` reads naturally next to fs.file and fs.dir.

Do not build paths by concatenating strings; `Join` puts the separator in for you. The separator is always `/`, on Windows too: every function first turns `\` into `/`, and Windows accepts `/` in paths. When a path comes from a user, check it with `IsSafe` before opening it, so that nobody climbs out of the permitted directory with `../..`.

Every function here works on the text of the path alone. None of them looks at the disk, except `Abs`, `Rel` and `IsSafe` with a relative path, which read the current directory. To create, read or list files, combine this package with fs.dir, fs.file or io, as the guide below does.

What people get wrong:

- Expecting `Join` to clean up. It only adds or merges the separator, so `Join("a/b", "../c")` is `a/b/../c`; pass the result through `Clean`. An absolute second part does not replace the first either, unlike Python's `os.path.join`.

- Reading `Ext` as the whole extension. It is only the last one: `.gz` for `backup.tar.gz`, and empty for a dot file such as `.bashrc`.

- Comparing paths as text without `Clean`. `docs/./cv.pdf` and `docs/cv.pdf` are the same file. Comparisons are also case sensitive, which is wrong on Windows and on default macOS disks.

## Serving a file a user asked for

A download handler gets a name such as `2026/report.pdf` from the request and has to turn it into a file inside one folder. `IsSafe` simplifies the joined path first and then checks that it still starts with the folder, so `a/../b.txt` is fine while `../secret.txt` and `a/../../etc/passwd` are refused. An empty name is refused too.

fs-path-guide-safe.salam

```salam
import fs.path

func resolve(root: str, requested: str): str:
    if not path.IsSafe(root, requested): ret "" end
    ret path.Clean(path.Join(root, requested))
end

func main:
    root := "/srv/uploads"
    each name in ["avatar.png", "2026/report.pdf", "a/../b.txt", "../secret.txt", "a/../../etc/passwd", "/etc/passwd", ""]:
        full := resolve(root, name)
        if full.len() == 0:
            println "refused", "[" + name + "]"
        else:
            println "serve  ", full
        end
    end
end
```

Output:

```text
serve   /srv/uploads/avatar.png
serve   /srv/uploads/2026/report.pdf
serve   /srv/uploads/b.txt
refused [../secret.txt]
refused [a/../../etc/passwd]
serve   /srv/uploads/etc/passwd
refused []
```

Look at the `/etc/passwd` line: `Join` does not let an absolute second part replace the first, so the result lands inside the folder and is safe. The check works on text only; it does not follow symbolic links, so do not put links that point outside the folder in a directory you serve.

## Mapping one folder tree onto another

A static site generator reads `content/blog/hello.md` and writes `public/blog/hello.html`. `Rel` gives the part below the source folder, `Dirname` and `Stem` take it apart, and `Join` and `Clean` build the new path. `Stem` removes only the last extension, so `salam.v2.md` keeps its `.v2`.

fs-path-guide-output.salam

```salam
import fs.path

func output_for(src_root: str, out_root: str, file: str): str:
    rel := path.Rel(src_root, file)
    folder := path.Join(out_root, path.Dirname(rel))
    page := path.Stem(rel).concat(".html")
    ret path.Clean(path.Join(folder, page))
end

func main:
    src := "/site/content"
    out := "/site/public"
    each file in ["/site/content/index.md", "/site/content/blog/hello.md", "/site/content/blog/2026/salam.v2.md"]:
        println path.Rel(src, file), "->", output_for(src, out, file)
    end
end
```

Output:

```text
index.md -> /site/public/index.html
blog/hello.md -> /site/public/blog/hello.html
blog/2026/salam.v2.md -> /site/public/blog/2026/salam.v2.html
```

For a file directly in the source folder `Dirname` returns `.`; the final `Clean` removes the `/.` that `Join` leaves behind. The example uses absolute paths because `Rel` makes relative ones absolute against the current directory first.

## Making a new name next to a file

To put a backup, a thumbnail or a converted copy next to the original, keep the folder and change only the name. Here `Stem` and `Ext` turn `plan.md` into `plan.bak.md`, and fs.dir and io do the actual work on disk.

fs-path-guide-backup.salam

```salam
import fs.path
import fs.dir
import io

func backup_name(p: str): str:
    name := path.Stem(p).concat(".bak").concat(path.Ext(p))
    ret path.Join(path.Dirname(p), name)
end

func main:
    dir.MkdirAll("notes/2026")
    each p in ["notes/todo.txt", "notes/2026/plan.md"]:
        io.WriteFile(p, "draft of ".concat(path.Filename(p)))
        copy := backup_name(p)
        io.WriteFile(copy, io.ReadFile(p))
        println p, "saved as", copy
    end
    println io.ReadFile("notes/2026/plan.bak.md")
end
```

Output:

```text
notes/todo.txt saved as notes/todo.bak.txt
notes/2026/plan.md saved as notes/2026/plan.bak.md
draft of plan.md
```

## Which function for which job

Several functions here have close names. `Filename` keeps the extension; `Basename` and `Stem` both drop it. `Normalize` only changes `\` to `/`; `Clean` is the one that resolves `.` and `..`.

| You want | Call | For `/home/sara/docs/cv.pdf` |
| --- | --- | --- |
| The folder | `Dirname` or `Parent` | `/home/sara/docs` |
| The name with its extension | `Filename` | `cv.pdf` |
| The name without its extension | `Stem` or `Basename` | `cv` |
| The extension | `Ext` | `.pdf` |
| Folder and name at once | `Split` | `dir` and `base` fields |
| Remove `.`, `..` and double slashes | `Clean` | unchanged |
| The path from one folder to another | `Rel` | `docs/cv.pdf` from `/home/sara` |
| Check a path from a user | `IsSafe` | `true` inside the base folder |

`Validate` only rejects an empty string. It is not a security check; use `IsSafe` for that.

## Types

### `PathParts`

```salam
struct PathParts
```

The two parts of a path.

| Name | Type | Description |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `dir` | `str = ""` | The directory part. |
| `base` | `str = ""` | The file name. |

fs-path-Join.salam

```salam
import fs.path

func main:
    p := path.Join("/home/sara", "docs/cv.pdf")
    println p
    parts := path.Split(p)
    println parts.dir, parts.base
    println path.Dirname(p), path.Parent(p), path.Filename(p), path.Basename(p)
    println path.Ext(p), path.Stem(p)
    println path.Normalize("/a/./b/../c//d"), path.Clean("a/b/../../c")
    println path.IsAbs(p), path.IsAbs("docs"), path.IsAbs(path.Abs("docs"))
    println path.Rel("/home/sara", "/home/sara/docs/cv.pdf")
    println path.IsSafe("/srv/files", "a/b.txt"), path.IsSafe("/srv/files", "../../etc/passwd")
    println path.Validate("docs/cv.pdf"), path.Validate("")
end
```

Output:

```text
/home/sara/docs/cv.pdf
/home/sara/docs cv.pdf
/home/sara/docs /home/sara/docs cv.pdf cv
.pdf cv
/a/./b/../c//d c
true false true
docs/cv.pdf
true false
true false
```

The path of `target` relative to `base`, with `..` steps when it lies outside; `.` when they are the same. Both are made absolute first.

The directory part of a path: `.` when there is none, `/` for a file at the root. A trailing `/` is ignored.

# filepath

https://salamlang.github.io/Salam/std/filepath/

Path functions that never touch the file system; the same work as the fs/path package.

The `filepath` package takes path strings apart and builds them: `Join`, `Dir`, `Base`, `Ext`, `Stem`, `Clean`, `Abs`, `Rel` and the `IsSafe` check for paths that come from users. It works on strings alone and never touches the file system, apart from `Abs`, `Rel` and `IsSafe`, which read the current directory for a relative path. Use it in build tools, static site generators, upload handlers and anywhere a path is computed rather than typed. To act on the files themselves, pair it with fs.file, fs.dir or os.

The fs.path package is a set of other names for the same functions; use whichever reads better to you, but one per program. The names differ a little: `Base` here is `Filename` there, and `Dir` is `Dirname`. Watch out for `path.Basename`, which is `Stem` and drops the extension, unlike `Base`. Paths always come out with `/` as the separator, on Windows too, and Windows accepts that.

What people get wrong:

- Expecting `Join` to clean the result. It only places one `/` between the parts: `Join("a/b", "../c")` is `a/b/../c`, and an absolute second part is appended, not substituted. Call `Clean` afterwards.

- Comparing paths as plain text. Clean both first, and remember that the comparison is case sensitive.

- Trusting a user's path without `IsSafe`. Even after `Join`, `../../etc/passwd` climbs out of your folder.

## Windows paths

A path pasted by a Windows user, or read from a Windows config file, uses `\`. Every function here calls `Normalize` first, so `Dir`, `Base` and `Join` accept both kinds. `IsAbs` also treats a drive letter such as `C:/` as absolute.

filepath-guide-windows.salam

```salam
import filepath

func main:
    raw := "C:\\Users\\Sara\\Documents\\cv.pdf"
    p := filepath.Normalize(raw)
    println p
    println filepath.IsAbs(p), filepath.IsAbs("Documents\\cv.pdf")
    println filepath.Dir(p)
    println filepath.Base(p), filepath.Stem(p), filepath.Ext(p)
    println filepath.Join("C:\\Users\\Sara", "Pictures\\cat.jpg")
    println filepath.Clean("D:/games/../music/./song.mp3")
end
```

Output:

```text
C:/Users/Sara/Documents/cv.pdf
true false
C:/Users/Sara/Documents
cv.pdf cv .pdf
C:/Users/Sara/Pictures/cat.jpg
D:/music/song.mp3
```

In a Salam string a single backslash is written `\\`. `Clean` treats the drive as an ordinary first part, so `C:/../x` becomes `x`; do not climb above the drive with `..`.

## Edge cases worth knowing

The table below runs `Dir`, `Base`, `Ext` and `Clean` over inputs that often cause bugs: the root, an empty string, a trailing slash, a dot file and a double extension.

filepath-guide-edges.salam

```salam
import filepath
import fmt

func show(p: str):
    print fmt.PadRight("[" + p + "]", 20)
    print fmt.PadRight(filepath.Dir(p), 10)
    print fmt.PadRight(filepath.Base(p), 16)
    print fmt.PadRight("[" + filepath.Ext(p) + "]", 8)
    println filepath.Clean(p)
end

func main:
    println "path                dir       base            ext     clean"
    each p in ["/", "", "docs/", "/var/log/app.log", ".bashrc", "backup.tar.gz", "../up/x.txt", "a/./b/../c.txt"]:
        show(p)
    end
end
```

Output:

```text
path                dir       base            ext     clean
[/]                 /         /               []      /
[]                  .         .               []      .
[docs/]             .         docs            []      docs
[/var/log/app.log]  /var/log  app.log         [.log]  /var/log/app.log
[.bashrc]           .         .bashrc         []      .bashrc
[backup.tar.gz]     .         backup.tar.gz   [.gz]   backup.tar.gz
[../up/x.txt]       ../up     x.txt           [.txt]  ../up/x.txt
[a/./b/../c.txt]    a/./b/..  c.txt           [.txt]  a/c.txt
```

The rules it shows: a trailing slash is ignored; an empty path counts as `.`; a name that starts with a dot, like `.bashrc`, has no extension; `Ext` returns only the last extension, so test for `.tar.gz` with `str.EndsWith` when you need it. `Dir` does not simplify, so call `Clean` first when the path may contain `.` or `..`.

## Grouping files by extension

`Ext` with a `HashMap` counts files by type, for a report or to pick a handler for each file. A second vector remembers the order in which the extensions first appeared, so the output does not depend on the map's internal order.

filepath-guide-group.salam

```salam
import filepath

func main:
    files := ["src/main.salam", "src/util.salam", "README.md", "docs/guide.md", "logo.svg", "Makefile", "docs/intro.md"]
    order := Vector {} as Vector<str>
    defer order.free()
    counts := HashMap {} as HashMap<str, int>
    each f in files:
        mut ext := filepath.Ext(f)
        if ext.len() == 0: ext = "(none)" end
        if counts.has(ext):
            counts.put(ext, counts.get(ext) + 1)
        else:
            counts.put(ext, 1)
            order.push(ext)
        end
    end
    each ext in order:
        println ext, counts.get(ext)
    end
end
```

Output:

```text
.salam 2
.md 3
.svg 1
(none) 1
```

`Ext` keeps the case of the name, so `photo.JPG` gives `.JPG`. Pass it through `str.Lower` before comparing when the files come from a camera or from Windows.

## Constants and variables

### `Separator`

```salam

import filepath

func main:

    println p, filepath.Separator
    println filepath.Dir(p), filepath.Base(p), filepath.Ext(p), filepath.Stem(p)
    println filepath.Normalize("a//b/./c/"), filepath.Clean("a/b/../c")
    println filepath.IsAbs("/usr/bin"), filepath.IsAbs(p), filepath.IsAbs(filepath.Abs(p))
    println filepath.Rel("/a/b", "/a/b/c/d")
    println filepath.IsSafe("/srv", "x/y"), filepath.IsSafe("/srv", "../etc")
    println filepath.Validate("a/b")
end
```

Output:

```text
projects/salam/main.salam /
projects/salam main.salam .salam main
a//b/./c/ a/c
true false true
c/d
true false
true
```

# env

https://salamlang.github.io/Salam/std/env/

Environment variables: reading them with the right type, .env files, the run profile, and masking sensitive values.

Settings such as a server port, a database address and API keys belong in environment variables rather than in the code, the "twelve-factor" way of configuring a service. The `env` package reads them with the right type and a default, masks secrets for logs, loads `.env` files, picks files per environment and fills `${NAME}` templates. For the bare value of one variable, os.Env is enough; to parse or write `.env` files as data without touching the environment, use encoding/envfile; for command line options, flag.

The "profile" says whether the program is running in development, test or production. It is read from `SALAM_ENV`; when that is unset or empty, `APP_ENV` and then `ENV` are tried, and the default is `development`. `Profile` returns the value lower-cased but otherwise as written. `IsProduction`, `IsDevelopment` and `IsTest` also accept `prod`, `dev` and `testing`, but `LoadProfile` uses the name as written, so `SALAM_ENV=prod` loads `.env.prod`, not `.env.production`.

What people get wrong:

- Trusting the typed getters to validate. `GetInt` turns `abc` into 0 and `12px` into 12, and `GetBool` knows only lower case `true`, `1`, `yes` and `on`, so `DEBUG=True` is false.

- Expecting a `.env` file to win. `Load` and `LoadProfile` never replace a variable that is already set, which is right in production; `Overload` and `LoadDotEnv` do replace.

- Logging secrets. Pass them through `Mask`, and keep `.env.local` files out of version control.

## Reading the whole configuration at start-up

Read every setting once, in one function, into a struct. The rest of the program then takes the struct and never calls `env` itself, which keeps the list of variables in one place and makes the code easy to test. Print the configuration at start-up, but pass secrets through `Mask` first.

env-guide-config.salam

```salam
import env
import str

struct Config:
    pub host: str = ""
    pub port: i64 = 0
    pub workers: i64 = 0
    pub debug: bool = false
    pub db_url: str = ""
    pub api_key: str = ""
end

func load_config(): Config:
    ret Config {
        host = env.GetOr("APP_HOST", "127.0.0.1"),
        port = env.GetInt("APP_PORT", 8080),
        workers = env.GetInt("APP_WORKERS", 4),
        debug = env.GetBool("APP_DEBUG", false),
        db_url = env.GetOr("APP_DB_URL", "sqlite://app.db"),
        api_key = env.Get("APP_API_KEY")
    }
end

func main:
    env.Set("APP_PORT", "9000")
    env.Set("APP_DEBUG", "yes")
    env.Set("APP_API_KEY", "sk-test-1234567890")
    env.Unset("APP_HOST")
    env.Unset("APP_WORKERS")
    env.Unset("APP_DB_URL")
    c := load_config()
    println "listening on", c.host + ":" + str.FromInt(c.port as int)
    println "workers:", c.workers, "debug:", c.debug
    println "database:", c.db_url
    println "api key:", env.Mask(c.api_key)
    if c.api_key.len() == 0: println "warning: APP_API_KEY is not set" end
end
```

Output:

```text
listening on 127.0.0.1:9000
workers: 4 debug: true
database: sqlite://app.db
api key: sk****90
```

## What a .env file can contain

A `.env` file has one `NAME=value` per line. Lines starting with `#` are comments, a leading `export` is allowed so the same file works with a shell, and values may be in double or single quotes. Inside double quotes and unquoted values, `${NAME}` is replaced; single quotes keep the text exactly as written.

env-guide-dotenv.salam

```salam
import env
import io

func main:
    io.WriteFile(".env", "# local settings\nexport APP_NAME=\"Salam Shop\"\nAPP_PORT=8080\nAPP_URL=http://localhost:${APP_PORT}\nAPP_GREETING='hello ${APP_NAME}'\nEMPTY=\n")
    env.Set("APP_PORT", "3000")
    println "read:", env.Load(".env")
    println env.Get("APP_NAME")
    println env.Get("APP_PORT")
    println env.Get("APP_URL")
    println env.Get("APP_GREETING")
    println env.Has("EMPTY"), "[" + env.Get("EMPTY") + "]", env.GetOr("EMPTY", "fallback")
end
```

Output:

```text
read: 4
Salam Shop
3000
http://localhost:8080
hello ${APP_NAME}
true [] fallback
```

Three things to notice. `Load` never replaces a variable that is already set, so `APP_PORT` stays `3000`, and the number it returns counts only the variables it actually set. A `${APP_PORT}` inside the file uses the file's own value. And an empty value is set but empty: `Has` says true while `GetOr` gives the default.

## One set of files per environment

`LoadProfile` reads up to four files from a folder, later ones winning over earlier ones: `.env`, `.env.local`, `.env.<profile>` and `.env.<profile>.local`. Commit the first and third, and keep the `.local` files, which hold each developer's own values and secrets, out of version control. A variable that is already set in the real environment still wins over every file.

env-guide-profiles.salam

```salam
import env
import io

func main:
    io.WriteFile(".env", "DB_HOST=localhost\nLOG_LEVEL=debug\nCACHE=off\n")
    io.WriteFile(".env.local", "DB_HOST=127.0.0.1\n")
    io.WriteFile(".env.production", "DB_HOST=db.internal\nLOG_LEVEL=warn\n")
    io.WriteFile(".env.production.local", "LOG_LEVEL=error\n")
    env.Set("SALAM_ENV", "production")
    env.Set("CACHE", "on")
    println "profile:", env.Profile(), env.IsProduction()
    println "loaded:", env.LoadProfile(".")
    println "DB_HOST =", env.Get("DB_HOST")
    println "LOG_LEVEL =", env.Get("LOG_LEVEL")
    println "CACHE =", env.Get("CACHE")
end
```

Output:

```text
profile: production true
loaded: 2
DB_HOST = db.internal
LOG_LEVEL = error
CACHE = on
```

Here `DB_HOST` comes from `.env.production`, `LOG_LEVEL` from `.env.production.local`, and `CACHE` stays `on` because it was set before loading. Missing files are skipped without an error.

## Filling a template with variables

`Expand` replaces `${NAME}` in any text, and `${NAME:-default}` uses the default when the variable is unset or empty. It suits connection strings and paths that are partly configured. An unknown name without a default becomes an empty string, so check the important variables with `Has` first.

env-guide-expand.salam

```salam
import env

func main:
    env.Set("DB_USER", "shop")
    env.Set("DB_NAME", "orders")
    env.Unset("DB_HOST")
    env.Unset("DB_PORT")
    template := "postgres://${DB_USER}@${DB_HOST:-localhost}:${DB_PORT:-5432}/${DB_NAME}"
    println env.Expand(template)
    env.Set("DB_HOST", "db.example.com")
    println env.Expand(template)
    println env.Expand("missing: [${NOT_SET_ANYWHERE}]")
end
```

Output:

```text
postgres://shop@localhost:5432/orders
postgres://shop@db.example.com:5432/orders
missing: []
```

## Pitfalls

- `GetInt` and `GetFloat` return the default only when the variable is unset or empty. A value that is not a number is not rejected: `abc` gives `0` and `12px` gives `12`. Check the value yourself when a wrong setting must stop the program.

- `GetBool` treats anything it does not recognise as `false`, whatever the default. It compares case-sensitively and accepts only `true`, `1`, `yes` and `on`; `TRUE` and `Yes` are false.

- `Load` keeps existing values, `Overload` replaces them, and `LoadDotEnv` replaces them too. Use `Load` when the real environment should win, which is what you want in production.

- `Set` changes the environment of this program and of the processes it starts afterwards, never the shell that started it.

## Functions

### `Get`

```salam
func Get(name: str): str
```

The value of a variable, or an empty string when it is not set; an empty and an unset variable look the same here.

env-Get.salam

```salam
import env

func main:
    env.Set("PORT", "8080")
    env.Set("DEBUG", "true")
    env.Set("RATIO", "0.75")
    println env.Get("PORT"), env.Has("PORT"), env.Has("NOPE")
    println env.GetInt("PORT", 80), env.GetInt("NOPE", 80)
    println env.GetBool("DEBUG", false), env.GetFloat("RATIO", 1.0)
    println env.GetOr("HOST", "localhost")
    env.Unset("PORT")
    println env.Has("PORT")
    env.Set("API_KEY", "example-not-a-real-key")
    println env.Mask("example-not-a-real-key"), env.GetMasked("API_KEY")
    env.Set("NAME", "Salam")
    println env.Expand("${NAME} on port ${PORT:-3000}")
end
```

Output:

```text
8080 true false
8080 80
true 0.75
localhost
false
ex****ey ex****ey
Salam on port 3000
```

### `Load`

```salam
func Load(path: str): int
```

Loads a `KEY=VALUE` file without changing variables that are already set, expanding `${NAME}` references. It returns how many variables it set; a missing file sets none.

env-Load.salam

```salam
import env
import io

func main:
    io.WriteFile(".env", "DB_HOST=localhost\nDB_PORT=5432\n# a comment\n")
    println env.Load(".env"), env.Get("DB_HOST")
    env.Set("DB_PORT", "1")
    env.Load(".env")
    println env.Get("DB_PORT")
    env.Overload(".env")
    println env.Get("DB_PORT")
    println env.LoadText("A=1\nB=2"), env.Get("B")
    println env.LoadDotEnv(".env")
    io.WriteFile(".env.test", "MODE=testing\n")
    env.Set("SALAM_ENV", "test")
    println env.LoadProfile("."), env.Get("MODE")
end
```

Output:

```text
2 localhost
1
5432
2 2
2
1 testing
```

The example for this item is shown with the ones above: env-Load.salam

