---

# flag

https://salamlang.github.io/Salam/std/flag/

Reading command line options such as `--port 8080` and `-v` with the right type, and generating the help text.

The `flag` package reads command line options. Each flag has a long name (`--port`), an optional short name (`-p`), a kind (bool, string, int or float), a default value and a line of help. The value can be given either way: `--port=8080` or `--port 8080`. Any argument that is not a flag is "positional", and after `--` everything counts as positional. For a program with subcommands such as `tool build` and `tool test`, see cli; for settings from the environment, env.

The steps are always the same: `New`, one `Add...` per flag, `Parse` with the arguments (without the program's own name), then check `Parse`'s result and `HelpWanted` before reading values with `GetStr`, `GetInt`, `GetFloat` and `GetBool`. `--help` and `-h` are always recognised and reserved, and the `Usage` text is generated for you.

What people get wrong:

- Forgetting that a value flag takes the next argument whatever it is. `--name --verbose` sets the name to `--verbose`.

- Passing negative numbers as positional arguments. `-5` looks like a flag and gives "unknown flag"; put `--` before it, or use `--offset=-5` for a flag value.

- Expecting a bad boolean to be an error. `--verbose=maybe` is accepted and reads as false; only `true`, `1`, `yes` and `on` are true.

## Reading the real command line

os.Args returns every argument, with the program's own name first. `cli.RemainingArgs` drops that first item, which gives exactly what `Parse` wants. A program then checks three things in order: did parsing fail, was help asked for, and only then does it read the values. Exit with code 2 on a usage error, as most command line tools do.

flag-guide-args.salam

```salam
import cli
import flag
import os

func main:
    mut argv := cli.RemainingArgs(os.Args())
    defer argv.free()
    if argv.len() == 0:
        each a in ["--name", "Sara", "-n", "2", "--excited"]: argv.push(a) end
    end
    mut f := flag.New("greet", "prints a greeting")
    defer flag.Free(f)
    flag.AddStr(f, "name", "", "world", "who to greet")
    flag.AddInt(f, "times", "n", 1, "how many times")
    flag.AddBool(f, "excited", "e", false, "end with three exclamation marks")
    if not flag.Parse(f, argv):
        println "greet:", flag.Error(f)
        ret 2
    end
    if flag.HelpWanted(f):
        print flag.Usage(f)
        ret 0
    end
    line := "Hello, " + flag.GetStr(f, "name") + (flag.GetBool(f, "excited") ? "!!!" : ".")
    repeat flag.GetInt(f, "times") as int:
        println line
    end
    ret 0
end
```

Output:

```text
Hello, Sara!!!
Hello, Sara!!!
```

Run it as `salam run greet.salam --name Ali -n 3` to pass your own arguments. When it gets none, as here, it uses a built-in sample so that the output above stays the same.

## Reporting bad input

`Parse` stops at the first problem and returns false, and `Error` says what went wrong in one line, ready to print. There are four kinds: a value that is not a whole number, a value that is not a decimal, a flag that was never declared, and a flag at the end of the line with no value after it.

flag-guide-errors.salam

```salam
import flag
import str

func try_line(line: str): int:
    argv := str.Split(line, " ")
    defer argv.free()
    mut f := flag.New("resize", "resizes images")
    defer flag.Free(f)
    flag.AddInt(f, "width", "w", 800, "the new width in pixels")
    flag.AddFloat(f, "quality", "q", 0.9, "the JPEG quality")
    flag.AddStr(f, "out", "o", "out", "the output directory")
    if not flag.Parse(f, argv):
        println "error:", flag.Error(f)
        ret 2
    end
    println "ok: width", flag.GetInt(f, "width"), "quality", flag.GetFloat(f, "quality"), "files", flag.Positional(f)
    ret 0
end

func main:
    each line in ["-w 640 a.jpg", "--width=wide a.jpg", "--quality=0,5 a.jpg", "--height 100", "a.jpg -o"]:
        println "$ resize", line
        println "exit code", try_line(line)
    end
end
```

Output:

```text
$ resize -w 640 a.jpg
ok: width 640 quality 0.9 files ["a.jpg"]
exit code 0
$ resize --width=wide a.jpg
error: invalid int value for --width: wide
exit code 2
$ resize --quality=0,5 a.jpg
error: invalid float value for --quality: 0,5
exit code 2
$ resize --height 100
error: unknown flag: --height
exit code 2
$ resize a.jpg -o
error: missing value for flag: -o
exit code 2
```

The messages are in English. Unknown flags and missing values stop the parse where they occur; numbers are checked after the whole line has been read, in the order the flags were declared. Decimal values need a dot (or the Persian `٫`), so `0,5` is rejected. Number flags accept Persian digits as well. When a flag is given twice, the last value wins.

## Flag, then environment, then default

Many programs read a setting from a flag, fall back to an environment variable, and use a built-in default last. `WasSet` makes that possible: it tells "the user typed `--port 8080`" apart from "8080 is just the default", which `GetInt` alone cannot.

flag-guide-precedence.salam

```salam
import env
import flag
import str

func port_from(line: str): i64:
    argv := str.Split(line, " ")
    defer argv.free()
    mut f := flag.New("server", "")
    defer flag.Free(f)
    flag.AddInt(f, "port", "p", 8080, "the port to listen on")
    flag.Parse(f, argv)
    if flag.WasSet(f, "port"): ret flag.GetInt(f, "port") end
    ret env.GetInt("PORT", flag.GetInt(f, "port"))
end

func main:
    env.Unset("PORT")
    println "nothing set:", port_from("app.log")
    env.Set("PORT", "3000")
    println "PORT=3000:", port_from("app.log")
    println "PORT=3000 and -p 9000:", port_from("-p 9000")
    println "PORT=3000 and --port=8080:", port_from("--port=8080")
end
```

Output:

```text
nothing set: 8080
PORT=3000: 3000
PORT=3000 and -p 9000: 9000
PORT=3000 and --port=8080: 8080
```

The last line matters: `--port=8080` is the same number as the default, but the user asked for it explicitly, so it wins over `PORT`. See env for the environment side.

## Short names, booleans and positional arguments

Flags and positional arguments can come in any order. A boolean flag never takes the next argument as its value; to turn off one that defaults to true, write `--name=false`. After `--`, even arguments that look like flags are positional, which is how a program accepts a file called `-r`.

flag-guide-positional.salam

```salam
import flag
import str

func main:
    argv := str.Split("-r --dry-run=false --depth ۳ src docs -- --not-a-flag -r", " ")
    defer argv.free()
    mut f := flag.New("sync", "copies folders")
    defer flag.Free(f)
    flag.AddBool(f, "recursive", "r", false, "go into subfolders")
    flag.AddBool(f, "dry-run", "n", true, "only print what would happen")
    flag.AddInt(f, "depth", "d", 1, "how deep to go")
    println flag.Parse(f, argv), "[" + flag.Error(f) + "]"
    println "recursive:", flag.GetBool(f, "recursive")
    println "dry run:", flag.GetBool(f, "dry-run")
    println "depth:", flag.GetInt(f, "depth")
    pos := flag.Positional(f)
    defer pos.free()
    each i, p in pos:
        println "arg", i, p
    end
end
```

Output:

```text
true []
recursive: true
dry run: false
depth: 3
arg 0 src
arg 1 docs
arg 2 --not-a-flag
arg 3 -r
```

Short names cannot be combined: `-rv` is read as one flag called `rv` and gives an "unknown flag" error. Write `-r -v` instead.

## Types

### `FlagSet`

```salam
struct FlagSet
```

A program's set of flags and the result of parsing.

| Name | Type | Description |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `prog` | `str = ""` | The program's name, for the help text. |
| `desc` | `str = ""` | The program's description, for the help text. |
| `names` | `Vector` | The long names of the flags. |
| `shorts` | `Vector` | The short names of the flags. |
| `kinds` | `Vector` | The kind of each flag. |
| `vals` | `Vector` | The current value of each flag, as text. |
| `defs` | `Vector` | The default value of each flag. |
| `helps` | `Vector` | The help line of each flag. |
| `was_set` | `Vector` | Whether each flag appeared on the command line. |
| `pos` | `Vector` | The positional arguments. |
| `err` | `str = ""` | The message of the last parse error. |
| `help_wanted` | `bool = false` | True when `--help` was given. |

flag-Parse.salam

```salam
import flag

func main:
    mut f := flag.New("copy", "copies files")
    defer flag.Free(f)
    flag.AddBool(f, "verbose", "v", false, "report everything")
    flag.AddStr(f, "out", "o", "output", "the destination directory")
    flag.AddInt(f, "jobs", "j", 1, "how many jobs at once")
    flag.AddFloat(f, "ratio", "r", 1.0, "the compression ratio")
    mut args := Vector {} as Vector<str>
    defer args.free()
    each a in ["-v", "--out=backup", "-j", "4", "a.txt", "b.txt"]:
        args.push(a)
    end
    println flag.Parse(f, args), "[" + flag.Error(f) + "]"
    println flag.GetBool(f, "verbose"), flag.GetStr(f, "out"), flag.GetInt(f, "jobs"), flag.GetFloat(f, "ratio")
    println flag.WasSet(f, "jobs"), flag.WasSet(f, "ratio")
    println flag.Positional(f), flag.HelpWanted(f)
    println flag.FlagKindBool, flag.FlagKindStr, flag.FlagKindInt, flag.FlagKindFloat
end
```

Output:

```text
true []
true backup 4 1
true false
["a.txt", "b.txt"] false
0 1 2 3
```

## Functions

### `Parse`

```salam
func Parse(fs &: FlagSet, arglist: Vector<str>): bool
```

Parses the arguments, not including the program name. On an unknown flag, a missing value or a bad number it returns false and `Error` says why. `--help` does not make it fail; check `HelpWanted`.

The example for this item is shown with the ones above: flag-Parse.salam

### `GetStr`

```salam

```

The value of a string flag, or its default; empty for a name that was never declared.

The example for this item is shown with the ones above: flag-Parse.salam

### `GetInt`

```salam

```

```salam
import flag

func main:
    mut f := flag.New("tool", "an example tool")
    defer flag.Free(f)
    flag.AddBool(f, "quiet", "q", false, "say nothing")
    flag.AddInt(f, "port", "p", 8080, "the port")
    mut args := Vector {} as Vector<str>
    defer args.free()
    args.push("--help")
    flag.Parse(f, args)
    if flag.HelpWanted(f):
        print flag.Usage(f)

    mut f2 := flag.New("tool", "")
    defer flag.Free(f2)

end
```

# cli

https://salamlang.github.io/Salam/std/cli/

Command line programs with several commands, like `git commit`, and asking the user questions.

Many tools have several commands: `git commit`, `salam build`, `salam run`. The `cli` package holds the list of commands, works out from the first argument which one was asked for, and builds the overall help text. It also asks the user questions in the terminal with `Prompt`, `PromptOr` and `Confirm`.

It is deliberately small and does not parse options. Pick the package by the shape of your program:

- One command with options, such as `resize --width 800 photo.png`: flag alone is enough.

- Several commands, each with its own options: `cli` picks the command and a flag set per command reads its options.

- Full-screen or coloured terminal output: term.

The things people get wrong:

- `Dispatch` wants the arguments without the program's name. os.Args includes it, so pass `RemainingArgs(os.Args())`.

- `help`, `-h`, `--help`, `version`, `-v` and `--version` are taken by `Dispatch`, and inside each command flag treats `-h` and `--help` as a help request. Never register `h` as a short flag of your own.

- Command names match exactly: no prefixes, aliases or case folding, and `Register` does not reject a duplicate (the first one wins).

- `RemainingArgs` returns a new vector; free it with `defer rest.free()`.

## A tool with several commands

The usual shape: `Dispatch` picks the command from the first argument, `RemainingArgs` hands everything after it to that command, and each command declares its own flag set, so `todo add` and `todo list` can have different options. Each command returns an exit code.

cli-guide-subcommands.salam

```salam
import cli
import flag
import str

func cmd_add(argv: Vector<str>): int:
    mut f := flag.New("todo add", "adds a task")
    defer flag.Free(f)
    flag.AddInt(f, "priority", "p", 3, "1 is the most urgent")
    if not flag.Parse(f, argv):
        println "todo add:", flag.Error(f)
        ret 2
    end
    if flag.HelpWanted(f):
        print flag.Usage(f)
        ret 0
    end
    words := flag.Positional(f)
    defer words.free()
    println "added [" + str.Join(words, " ") + "] with priority", flag.GetInt(f, "priority")
    ret 0
end

func cmd_list(argv: Vector<str>): int:
    mut f := flag.New("todo list", "lists the tasks")
    defer flag.Free(f)
    flag.AddBool(f, "all", "a", false, "include finished tasks")
    if not flag.Parse(f, argv):
        println "todo list:", flag.Error(f)
        ret 2
    end
    println "listing", flag.GetBool(f, "all") ? "all tasks" : "open tasks"
    ret 0
end

func run(app &: cli.App, line: str): int:
    argv := str.Split(line, " ")
    defer argv.free()
    command := cli.Dispatch(app, argv)
    rest := cli.RemainingArgs(argv)
    defer rest.free()
    if command == "add": ret cmd_add(rest) end
    if command == "list": ret cmd_list(rest) end
    if command == cli.CmdVersion:
        println app.name, app.version
        ret 0
    end
    if command == cli.CmdUnknown: println "todo: unknown command:", argv.get(0) end
    print cli.Usage(app)
    ret command == cli.CmdHelp ? 0 : 2
end

func main:
    mut app := cli.New("todo", "a small task list", "0.3.0")
    cli.Register(app, "add", "add a task")
    cli.Register(app, "list", "show the tasks")
    each line in ["add -p 1 buy milk", "list --all", "add --priority=high call mom", "add --help", "--version", "remove 3"]:
        println "$ todo", line
        println "exit", run(app, line)
    end
end
```

Output:

```text
$ todo add -p 1 buy milk
added [buy milk] with priority 1
exit 0
$ todo list --all
listing all tasks
exit 0
$ todo add --priority=high call mom
todo add: invalid int value for --priority: high
exit 2
$ todo add --help
Usage: todo add [options] [args]
  adds a task
Options:
  -p, --priority <int>  1 is the most urgent (default: 3)
  -h, --help  show this help
exit 0
$ todo --version
todo 0.3.0
exit 0
$ todo remove 3
todo: unknown command: remove
todo 0.3.0
a small task list

Usage: todo <command> [options]

Commands:
  add           add a task
  list          show the tasks

Run 'todo <command> --help' for help on a specific command.
exit 2
```

`cli.Usage` ends with a hint to run `todo <command> --help`, but answering it is each command's job: check `flag.HelpWanted` after parsing and print `flag.Usage`, as `add` does here. Both help texts are generated in English; only your descriptions appear as you wrote them.

## Wiring it to the real arguments

In a real program the arguments come from os.Args. Drop the program's own name with `RemainingArgs` and pass the rest to `Dispatch`. With no arguments at all `Dispatch` returns `CmdHelp`, so running the tool bare prints its help, which is what users expect.

cli-guide-main.salam

```salam
import cli
import os

func main:
    mut app := cli.New("notes", "keeps short notes", "1.2.0")
    cli.Register(app, "new", "write a new note")
    cli.Register(app, "show", "print every note")
    argv := cli.RemainingArgs(os.Args())
    defer argv.free()
    command := cli.Dispatch(app, argv)
    if command == cli.CmdHelp:
        print cli.Usage(app)
        ret 0
    else command == cli.CmdVersion:
        println app.version
        ret 0
    else command == cli.CmdUnknown:
        println "notes: no such command:", argv.get(0)
        ret 2
    end
    println "running", command, "with", cli.RemainingArgs(argv)
    ret 0
end
```

Output:

```text
notes 1.2.0
keeps short notes

Usage: notes <command> [options]

Commands:
  new           write a new note
  show          print every note

Run 'notes <command> --help' for help on a specific command.
```

The output above is what it prints with no arguments. Try `salam run notes.salam show --all` or `salam run notes.salam --version`.

## Required flags

A flag with no sensible default, such as the server to deploy to, should be required. `RequireFlags` takes the names that must appear and returns the ones that did not, so you can report all of them at once instead of one per run.

cli-guide-required.salam

```salam
import cli
import flag
import str

func deploy(line: str): int:
    argv := str.Split(line, " ")
    defer argv.free()
    mut f := flag.New("deploy", "uploads a release")
    defer flag.Free(f)
    flag.AddStr(f, "host", "H", "", "the server to deploy to")
    flag.AddStr(f, "user", "u", "", "the login name")
    flag.AddInt(f, "port", "p", 22, "the SSH port")
    if not flag.Parse(f, argv):
        println "deploy:", flag.Error(f)
        ret 2
    end
    mut required := Vector {} as Vector<str>
    defer required.free()
    required.push("host")
    required.push("user")
    missing := cli.RequireFlags(f, required)
    defer missing.free()
    if missing.len() > 0:
        println "deploy: missing --" + str.Join(missing, ", --")
        ret 2
    end
    println "deploying to", flag.GetStr(f, "user") + "@" + flag.GetStr(f, "host"), "port", flag.GetInt(f, "port")
    ret 0
end

func main:
    each line in ["-H example.com -u sara", "--host=example.com -p 2222", "-p 2222"]:
        println "$ deploy", line
        println "exit", deploy(line)
    end
end
```

Output:

```text
$ deploy -H example.com -u sara
deploying to sara@example.com port 22
exit 0
$ deploy --host=example.com -p 2222
deploy: missing --user
exit 2
$ deploy -p 2222
deploy: missing --host, --user
exit 2
```

It uses `flag.WasSet`, so it checks that the flag was typed, not that it has a value: `--host=` counts as given. Check for an empty string too when that matters.

## Questions that also work in scripts

`PromptOr` and `Confirm` read one line from standard input. When nothing is typed, or the program runs in a script with no terminal, `PromptOr` returns its default and `Confirm` returns false, so a forgotten question never does something dangerous. Give every question a flag too, here `--name` and `--yes`, so the program can run without anyone at the keyboard.

cli-guide-noninteractive.salam

```salam
import cli
import flag
import str

func main:
    argv := str.Split("--name demo", " ")
    defer argv.free()
    mut f := flag.New("init", "creates a project")
    defer flag.Free(f)
    flag.AddStr(f, "name", "", "", "the project name")
    flag.AddBool(f, "yes", "y", false, "do not ask for confirmation")
    flag.Parse(f, argv)
    mut name := flag.GetStr(f, "name")
    if name.len() == 0: name = cli.PromptOr("project name", "my-app") end
    language := cli.PromptOr("language", "english")
    println ""
    mut go_on := flag.GetBool(f, "yes")
    if not go_on: go_on = cli.Confirm("create " + name + " in " + language + "?") end
    println ""
    if go_on:
        println "created", name
    else:
        println "nothing created; pass --yes to skip the question"
    end
end
```

Output:

```text
language (english):
create demo in english? [y/N]:
nothing created; pass --yes to skip the question
```

This output is what happens with standard input empty, as in a CI job: the language question takes its default and the confirmation is refused. The questions end without a line break because nobody pressed Enter.

## Types

### `App`

```salam
struct App
```

A command line program and its commands.

| Name | Type | Description |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `name` | `str = ""` | The program's name. |
| `desc` | `str = ""` | The program's description. |
| `version` | `str = ""` | The program's version. |
| `cmd_names` | `Vector` | The names of the commands. |
| `cmd_descs` | `Vector` | The descriptions of the commands. |

cli-Dispatch.salam

```salam
import cli
import str

func run(app &: cli.App, line: str):
    args := str.Split(line, " ")
    command := cli.Dispatch(app, args)
    if command == cli.CmdHelp:
        println "help was asked for"
    else command == cli.CmdVersion:
        println "version:", app.version
    else command == cli.CmdUnknown:
        println "unknown command"
    else:
        println "running:", command, cli.RemainingArgs(args)
    end
    args.free()
end

func main:
    mut app := cli.New("salamctl", "project management", "1.0.0")
    cli.Register(app, "build", "build the project")
    cli.Register(app, "test", "run the tests")
    println cli.HasCommand(app, "build"), cli.CommandDesc(app, "test")
    each line in ["build --fast", "--help", "--version", "deploy"]:
        run(app, line)
    end
    print cli.Usage(app)
end
```

Output:

```text
true run the tests
running: build ["--fast"]
help was asked for
version: 1.0.0
unknown command
salamctl 1.0.0
project management

Usage: salamctl <command> [options]

Commands:
  build         build the project
  test          run the tests

Run 'salamctl <command> --help' for help on a specific command.
```

### `RequireFlags`


Of the names you give, returns the flags that were not typed on the command line, in the same order. A flag given with an empty value, such as `--host=`, counts as typed.

cli-RequireFlags.salam

```salam
import cli
import flag

func main:
    mut f := flag.New("deploy", "")
    defer flag.Free(f)
    flag.AddStr(f, "host", "H", "", "the server")
    flag.AddStr(f, "user", "u", "", "the user")
    mut args := Vector {} as Vector<str>
    defer args.free()
    args.push("--host=example.com")
    flag.Parse(f, args)
    mut required := Vector {} as Vector<str>
```


### `Confirm`


Prints the question with `[y/N]: ` and reads one line. `y` or `yes`, in any case and with spaces around it, is true; anything else, an empty line or the end of input is false.

```salam
import cli

func main:

    end
end
```


Prints the question followed by `: `, reads one line and returns it with surrounding spaces trimmed. Do not end the question with a colon yourself. At the end of input it returns an empty string.

# config

https://salamlang.github.io/Salam/std/config/

Reading and writing INI, env and YAML settings files with dotted keys.

The `config` package reads a program's settings from INI, YAML or env files and keeps them as one ordered list of keys and text values. Keys in sections are dotted: the key `host` in the `[db]` section of an INI file, or under `db:` in YAML, becomes `db.host`. Whatever the file format, the rest of the program reads settings the same way.

Use it for flat settings files that people edit by hand. For neighbouring jobs:

- A single environment variable of the running process: env or os.

- A `.env` file with full control over quoting, `export` lines and errors: encoding/envfile, which this package uses underneath.

- YAML with lists or nested data you want to walk: encoding/yaml. JSON or TOML: encoding/json, encoding/toml.

- Command line options: flag.

The usual pattern is to read the default settings, `Merge` the current environment's settings on top, and then read the values with the right type. Every value is stored as text; `GetInt`, `GetFloat` and `GetBool` convert it when you read it, and their last argument is the value to use when the key is not there at all.

The things people get wrong:

- Nothing here reports an error. A missing or unreadable file gives an empty config, a line without `=` is skipped, and a value that is not a number reads as 0. Check the file and the important keys yourself, as the guides below show.

- `GetBool` is true only for `true`, `1`, `yes` and `on`, written in lower case. `TRUE` and `Yes` are false.

- In INI and env files a `#` after a space starts a comment (in INI a `;` does too). Put quotes around values that contain them, such as passwords.

- A `Config` owns its memory: free each one you make, including the new ones that `Merge` and `Section` return, and free the vector `Keys` returns.

## Layered settings: defaults, then overrides

Most programs read settings from more than one place: defaults shipped with the program, a file for the server it runs on, and a few values given on the command line. `Merge` takes two configs and returns a third in which the second one wins. Chain it to stack as many layers as you need. Keys keep the order of the base, and keys that only the override has are added at the end.

config-layers.salam

```salam
import config

func main:
    defaults := "name = shop\nworkers = 4\ndebug = false\n\n[db]\nhost = localhost\nport = 5432\n"
    production := "workers = 16\n\n[db]\nhost = db.internal\npool = 20\n"
    mut base := config.ParseINI(defaults)
    defer config.Free(base)
    mut prod := config.ParseINI(production)
    defer config.Free(prod)
    mut flags := config.New()
    defer config.Free(flags)
    config.Set(flags, "debug", "yes")
    mut step := config.Merge(base, prod)
    defer config.Free(step)
    mut final := config.Merge(step, flags)
    defer config.Free(final)
    print config.FormatINI(final)
    println "workers:", config.GetInt(final, "workers", 1)
    println "debug:", config.GetBool(final, "debug", false)
    println "db:", config.Get(final, "db.host"), config.GetInt(final, "db.port", 5432), config.GetInt(final, "db.pool", 5)
end
```

Output:

```text
name = shop
workers = 16
debug = yes
[db]
host = db.internal
port = 5432
pool = 20
workers: 16
debug: true
db: db.internal 5432 20
```

The production file only names what differs (`workers`, `db.host` and a new `db.pool`), so the defaults stay the single place that lists every setting. `db.port` was never overridden and keeps its default.

## Sections and your own settings struct

Passing one big config around means every part of the program sees every key. `Section` cuts out the keys under one name and drops the prefix, so a function that sets up the database only gets `host`, `port` and `pool`. Reading those into a struct once, at startup, keeps the rest of the code free of key names and string conversions.

config-sections.salam

```salam
import config

struct Database:
    pub host: str = ""
    pub port: i64 = 0
    pub pool: i64 = 0
end

func read_database(c &: config.Config): Database:
    ret Database {
        host = config.GetOr(c, "host", "localhost"),
        port = config.GetInt(c, "port", 5432),
        pool = config.GetInt(c, "pool", 10)
    }
end

func main:
    text := "server:\n  port: 8080\n  host: 0.0.0.0\ndatabase:\n  host: db.local\n  port: 6432\nlog: warn\n"
    mut c := config.ParseYAML(text)
    defer config.Free(c)
    mut server := config.Section(c, "server")
    defer config.Free(server)
    keys := config.Keys(server)
    defer keys.free()
    each k in keys:
        println "server", k, "=", config.Get(server, k)
    end
    mut dbc := config.Section(c, "database")
    defer config.Free(dbc)
    d := read_database(dbc)
    println d.host, d.port, d.pool
    println config.Len(c), config.Has(c, "log"), config.Has(c, "server")
end
```

Output:

```text
server port = 8080
server host = 0.0.0.0
db.local 6432 10
5 true false
```

A YAML map such as `server:` is flattened into dotted keys, so the config holds only the leaf values: `Has(c, "server")` is false, while `Has(c, "server.port")` is true. `Keys` lists the keys in file order.

## Reading files: comments, quotes and missing files

`LoadINI`, `LoadYAML` and `LoadEnv` read the whole file and parse it. If the file is not there they return an empty config without a word, so a typo in the path quietly leaves every setting at its default. Check the path first with fs/file and decide what a missing file means for your program.

config-files.salam

```salam
import config
import fs.file
import io

func load_settings(path: str): config.Config:
    if not file.Exists(path):
        println "no", path, "found, using built-in defaults"
        mut c := config.New()
        config.Set(c, "server.port", "8080")
        ret c
    end
    ret config.LoadINI(path)
end

func main:
    io.WriteFile("shop.ini", "[server]\nport = 9000   # the public port\n\n[db]\npassword = \"s3cret#2024\"\nmode = TRUE\ntags: fast\n")
    mut c := load_settings("shop.ini")
    defer config.Free(c)
    keys := config.Keys(c)
    defer keys.free()
    each k in keys:
        println k, "=", "[" + config.Get(c, k) + "]"
    end
    println "db.mode as bool:", config.GetBool(c, "db.mode", false)
    mut missing := load_settings("missing.ini")
    defer config.Free(missing)
    println "port:", config.GetInt(missing, "server.port", 0)
end
```

Output:

```text
server.port = [9000]
db.password = [s3cret#2024]
db.mode = [TRUE]
db.mode as bool: false
no missing.ini found, using built-in defaults
port: 8080
```

Three details show up in the output. The comment after `9000` was cut off, and the spaces before it with it. The quoted password kept its `#`. The line `tags: fast` has no `=`, so it was dropped without a warning, and `mode = TRUE` was read but is not true for `GetBool`.

## Check the settings at startup

The typed getters never fail. The default is used only when the key is missing; a key that is present but holds bad text is still converted. `GetInt` turns `eighty` into 0, not into your default, and `GetBool` is true only for `true`, `1`, `yes` and `on`, so `enabled` reads as false. It is worth checking the important keys once, when the program starts, and refusing to run with a clear list of problems.

config-validate.salam

```salam
import config
import str

func check(c &: config.Config): Vector<str>:
    mut problems := Vector {} as Vector<str>
    required := ["APP_PORT", "DATABASE_URL"]
    each key in required:
        if config.Has(c, key) == false:
            problems.push("missing " + key)
        end
    end
    if config.Has(c, "APP_PORT"):
        raw := config.Get(c, "APP_PORT")
        if str.FromInt(config.GetInt(c, "APP_PORT", 0)) != raw:
            problems.push("APP_PORT is not a whole number: " + raw)
        end
    end
    ret problems
end

func report(name: str, text: str):
    mut c := config.ParseEnv(text)
    defer config.Free(c)
    problems := check(c)
    defer problems.free()
    if problems.len() == 0:
        println name, "is fine, port", config.GetInt(c, "APP_PORT", 8080)
        ret
    end
    println name, "has", problems.len(), "problems:"
    each p in problems:
        println " ", p
    end
end

func main:
    mut c := config.ParseEnv("APP_PORT=eighty\nAPP_DEBUG=enabled\n")
    defer config.Free(c)
    println config.GetInt(c, "APP_PORT", 8080), config.GetInt(c, "APP_WORKERS", 4)
    println config.GetBool(c, "APP_DEBUG", true), config.GetBool(c, "APP_CACHE", true)
    report("broken.env", "APP_PORT=eighty\n")
    report("good.env", "APP_PORT=9000\nDATABASE_URL=postgres://db/shop\n")
end
```

Output:

```text
0 4
false true
broken.env has 2 problems:
  missing DATABASE_URL
  APP_PORT is not a whole number: eighty
good.env is fine, port 9000
```

The check for a number compares the text with the number written back out with `str.FromInt`. If they differ, the text was not a plain whole number.

## Change a file and write it back

`Set` adds or replaces a key and `Remove` deletes one, returning false when the key was not there. `FormatINI` writes the keys without a section first, then one `[section]` block for each prefix, and puts quotes around values that need them. Write the text with io and the next `LoadINI` reads back the same settings.

config-save.salam

```salam
import config
import io

func main:
    io.WriteFile("app.ini", "theme = light\n\n[editor]\nfont = mono\nsize = 12\n")
    mut c := config.LoadINI("app.ini")
    defer config.Free(c)
    config.Set(c, "theme", "dark")
    config.Set(c, "editor.size", "14")
    config.Set(c, "editor.title", "My notes")
    config.Set(c, "window.width", "1200")
    println config.Remove(c, "editor.font"), config.Remove(c, "editor.font")
    io.WriteFile("app.ini", config.FormatINI(c))
    print io.ReadFile("app.ini")
    mut again := config.LoadINI("app.ini")
    defer config.Free(again)
    println config.Get(again, "editor.title"), config.Len(again) == config.Len(c)
end
```

Output:

```text
true false
theme = dark
[editor]
size = 14
title = "My notes"
[window]
width = 1200
My notes true
```

Comments and blank lines from the original file are not kept: `ParseINI` skips them, so a file the program rewrites loses them. Keep hand written notes in a separate defaults file that the program only reads.

## Which function for which job

| You want | Use |
| --- | --- |
| Read a file from disk | `LoadINI`, `LoadYAML`, `LoadEnv` |
| Read text you already have | `ParseINI`, `ParseYAML`, `ParseEnv` |
| A value as text, with a fallback | `GetOr` |
| A number or a flag | `GetInt`, `GetFloat`, `GetBool` |
| Overrides on top of defaults | `Merge` |
| Only the keys of one section | `Section` |
| Write settings out again | `FormatINI`, `FormatEnv`, `FormatEnvExport` |

`ParseYAML` keeps only maps as dotted keys. A list becomes one value holding its text, so `tags: [a, b]` or a block list reads as `["a", "b"]`; parse that with encoding/yaml when you need the items.

## Types

### `Config`

```salam
struct Config
```

A set of settings: dotted keys with text values, in the order they were first set.

| Name | Type | Description |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `m` | `collections.OrderedMap` | The ordered map that keeps the keys and values in order. |

config-Get.salam

```salam
import config

func main:
    mut c := config.New()
    defer config.Free(c)
    config.Set(c, "name", "salam")
    config.Set(c, "port", "8080")
    config.Set(c, "debug", "yes")
    config.Set(c, "ratio", "0.5")
    println config.Len(c), config.Has(c, "port"), config.Get(c, "name")
    println config.GetInt(c, "port", 80), config.GetFloat(c, "ratio", 1.0), config.GetBool(c, "debug", false)
    println config.GetOr(c, "host", "localhost")
    println config.Remove(c, "ratio"), config.Keys(c)
end
```

Output:

```text
4 true salam
8080 0.5 true
localhost
true ["name", "port", "debug"]
```

config-ParseINI.salam

```salam
import config
import io

func main:
    text := "name = salam\n\n[db]\nhost = localhost\nport = 5432\n"
    mut c := config.ParseINI(text)
    defer config.Free(c)
    println config.Keys(c)
    mut db := config.Section(c, "db")
    defer config.Free(db)
    println config.Get(db, "port")
    print config.FormatINI(db)
    io.WriteFile("app.ini", text)
    mut loaded := config.LoadINI("app.ini")
    defer config.Free(loaded)
    println config.Get(loaded, "db.host")
end
```

```text
5432
host = localhost
port = 5432
localhost
```

### `Merge`

```salam
func Merge(base &: Config, override &: Config): Config
```

New settings with every key of `base` and then of `override`; where both have a key, `override` wins and the key keeps its place from `base`. Free the result.

config-ParseEnv.salam

```salam
import config
import io

func main:
    mut base := config.ParseEnv("MODE=dev\nPORT=3000\n")
    mut over := config.ParseEnv("PORT=80\nLOG=info\n")
    defer config.Free(base)
    defer config.Free(over)
    mut merged := config.Merge(base, over)
    defer config.Free(merged)
    print config.FormatEnv(merged)
    print config.FormatEnvExport(over)
    io.WriteFile(".env", "TOKEN=abc\n")
    mut loaded := config.LoadEnv(".env")
    defer config.Free(loaded)
    println config.Get(loaded, "TOKEN")
end
```

Output:

```text
MODE=dev
PORT=80
LOG=info
export PORT=80
export LOG=info
abc
```

# log

https://salamlang.github.io/Salam/std/log/

Recording what a program does, with levels, a prefix, structured fields, JSON output and writing to a file.

For a program running on a server, `println` is not enough: you need to know how important each message is and when it was written, and to be able to silence the unimportant ones. The `log` package has four levels, debug, info, warn and error, and records only the messages at or above the level you set; the default level is info. Each line goes out in plain text or as one JSON object, to standard error, standard output or a file that can rotate.

A text line looks like `2026-10-17 13:09:22 [INFO] shop order 1042 accepted`: the local time, the level, the prefix and the message. The examples below turn the time off with `ShowTime(false)` so their output is stable.

All settings are global to the program: call `SetLevel`, `SetFormat`, `SetPrefix` and one of `ToStderr`, `ToStdout` or `ToFile` once near the start of `main`, and every package that imports `log` writes the same way. For a quick look at a value while you work on the code, debug is the better tool; for timing and memory figures, runtime.

The things people get wrong:

- A file log is buffered. Lines reach the disk when the buffer fills or at `CloseFile`, so `tail -f` lags behind and a crash loses the last lines. Call `CloseFile` on every way out of the program.

- The text format writes the message as it is. A value from a user that holds a line break starts a fake log line; use JSON, which escapes it (see below).

- The settings are plain globals with no lock. Change them at startup only, not while other threads are logging.

- The time is local time with no zone offset, also in JSON. Run servers with `TZ=UTC` when logs from several machines are compared.

## Choose the level from the settings

The level should not be fixed in the code. During development you want debug messages; on a busy server you want warnings and errors only. Read the level as text from a settings file or the environment and turn it into a number with `ParseLevel`. It accepts `debug`, `info`, `warn`, `warning` and `error` in any case, and falls back to info for anything else, so a typo never silences the log completely.

log-level-config.salam

```salam
import log
import config

func setup(text: str):
    mut c := config.ParseEnv(text)
    defer config.Free(c)
    level := log.ParseLevel(config.GetOr(c, "LOG_LEVEL", "info"))
    log.SetLevel(level)
    log.SetPrefix(config.GetOr(c, "APP_NAME", "app"))
    println "-- level", log.LevelName(log.GetLevel())
end

func work():
    log.Debug("cache lookup for key user:7")
    log.Info("order 1042 accepted")
    log.Warn("payment provider answered slowly")
    log.Error("could not send the receipt email")
end

func main:
    log.ToStdout()
    log.ShowTime(false)
    setup("LOG_LEVEL=debug\nAPP_NAME=shop\n")
    work()
    setup("LOG_LEVEL=warning\nAPP_NAME=shop\n")
    work()
    setup("LOG_LEVEL=loud\n")
    work()
end
```

Output:

```text
-- level DEBUG
[DEBUG] shop cache lookup for key user:7
[INFO] shop order 1042 accepted
[WARN] shop payment provider answered slowly
[ERROR] shop could not send the receipt email
-- level WARN
[WARN] shop payment provider answered slowly
[ERROR] shop could not send the receipt email
-- level INFO
[INFO] app order 1042 accepted
[WARN] app payment provider answered slowly
[ERROR] app could not send the receipt email
```

The `config` package used here is described on its own page, config. The prefix is a good place for the program's name, so that lines from several programs in one log stay apart.

## JSON logs for a log collector

Text lines are easy to read; JSON lines are easy for tools such as Loki, Elasticsearch or a cloud log service to search. `SetFormat(FormatJSON)` turns every line into one JSON object with `level`, the optional `prefix`, `msg`, and one member for each key given to the `...KV` functions. With the time switched on, a `time` member in ISO 8601 comes first.

log-json-requests.salam

```salam
import log
import str

struct Request:
    pub method: str = ""
    pub path: str = ""
    pub status: int = 0
    pub ms: int = 0
end

func record(r: Request):
    mut keys := Vector {} as Vector<str>
    mut vals := Vector {} as Vector<str>
    defer keys.free()
    defer vals.free()
    keys.push("method")
    vals.push(r.method)
    keys.push("path")
    vals.push(r.path)
    keys.push("status")
    vals.push(str.FromInt(r.status as i64))
    keys.push("ms")
    vals.push(str.FromInt(r.ms as i64))
    if r.status >= 500:
        log.ErrorKV("request failed", keys, vals)
    else r.status >= 400:
        log.WarnKV("request rejected", keys, vals)
    else:
        log.InfoKV("request served", keys, vals)
    end
end

func main:
    log.ToStdout()
    log.ShowTime(false)
    log.SetFormat(log.FormatJSON)
    log.SetPrefix("api")
    record(Request { method = "GET", path = "/products", status = 200, ms = 12 })
    record(Request { method = "POST", path = "/login", status = 401, ms = 3 })
    record(Request { method = "GET", path = "/report \"q3\"", status = 503, ms = 950 })
end
```

Output:

```text
{"level": "INFO", "prefix": "api", "msg": "request served", "method": "GET", "path": "/products", "status": "200", "ms": "12"}
{"level": "WARN", "prefix": "api", "msg": "request rejected", "method": "POST", "path": "/login", "status": "401", "ms": "3"}
{"level": "ERROR", "prefix": "api", "msg": "request failed", "method": "GET", "path": "/report \"q3\"", "status": "503", "ms": "950"}
```

Picking the level from the result, error for a 5xx answer and warn for a 4xx one, lets you alert on errors without reading every request. Quotes inside a value are escaped, so each line stays valid JSON. All values are written as JSON strings, numbers included.

## Log to a file that does not grow forever

`ToFile` appends to a file and returns 0, or minus one when the file cannot be opened. `SetRotation(max_bytes, max_backups)` keeps it in check: when the file has reached `max_bytes`, the next line first renames it to `.1`, shifts the older copies up by one and starts a new, empty file. Copies past `max_backups` are deleted.

log-rotation.salam

```salam
import log
import os
import io
import str

func first_line(path: str): str:
    lines := io.ReadFile(path).split("\n")
    defer lines.free()
    ret lines.get(0)
end

func main:
    files := ["worker.log", "worker.log.1", "worker.log.2", "worker.log.3"]
    each f in files:
        os.Remove(f)
    end
    log.ShowTime(false)
    if log.ToFile("worker.log") != 0:
        println "cannot open worker.log"
        ret 1
    end
    log.SetRotation(120, 2)
    repeat 24 in i:
        log.Info("processed job " + str.FromInt(i as i64))
    end
    log.CloseFile()
    each f in files:
        if os.Exists(f):
            println f, "starts with", first_line(f)
        else:
            println f, "does not exist"
        end
    end
end
```

Output:

```text
worker.log starts with [INFO] processed job 22
worker.log.1 starts with [INFO] processed job 17
worker.log.2 starts with [INFO] processed job 12
worker.log.3 does not exist
```

The limit here is tiny so that the example rotates a few times. A real service uses something like `10 * 1024 * 1024` bytes and five backups. The size is checked before each line is written, so a file can end up one line longer than the limit. Call `CloseFile` before the program ends, or the last lines stay in the buffer; `Fatal` closes the file for you before it exits with status 1.

## Key and value fields in text logs

For text logs, `Field`, `FieldInt` and `FieldBool` build `key=value` pieces and `KV` joins them after a message. `Field` puts quotes around a value that contains a space or a quote, and escapes the quotes inside, so a line can still be split into fields by a program.

log-fields.salam

```salam
import log

func login_line(user: str, attempts: i64, ok: bool, agent: str): str:
    mut fields := Vector {} as Vector<str>
    defer fields.free()
    fields.push(log.Field("user", user))
    fields.push(log.FieldInt("attempts", attempts))
    fields.push(log.FieldBool("ok", ok))
    fields.push(log.Field("agent", agent))
    ret log.KV("login", fields)
end

func main:
    log.ToStdout()
    log.ShowTime(false)
    log.Info(login_line("sara", 1, true, "curl/8.5"))
    log.Warn(login_line("guest user", 3, false, "my \"test\" bot"))
    println log.Field("empty", "")
    println log.Field("path", "/a b")
end
```

Output:

```text
[INFO] login user=sara attempts=1 ok=true agent=curl/8.5
[WARN] login user="guest user" attempts=3 ok=false agent="my \"test\" bot"
empty=
path="/a b"
```

An empty value is written as `key=` with nothing after it. Only spaces and quotes trigger the quoting: a tab, a backslash or a line break goes through unchanged. These helpers only build text; the level filter still applies when you pass the result to `Info` or `Warn`.

## Formatted messages and values from users

`Infof` and the other `...f` functions fill each `{}` with the next string from a vector, which reads better than a chain of `+`. They do not clean the values. Here a user name with a line break forges an `[ERROR]` line in the text log, while the JSON line keeps it inside one string as `\n`.

log-untrusted.salam

```salam
import log

func pair(a: str, b: str): Vector<str>:
    mut v := Vector {} as Vector<str>
    v.push(a)
    v.push(b)
    ret v
end

func main:
    log.ToStdout()
    log.ShowTime(false)
    name := "mina\n[ERROR] disk full"
    args := pair(name, "10.0.0.7")
    defer args.free()
    log.Infof("user {} signed in from {}", args)
    keys := pair("user", "ip")
    defer keys.free()
    log.SetFormat(log.FormatJSON)
    log.InfoKV("user signed in", keys, args)
    log.SetFormat(log.FormatText)
    log.SetLevel(log.LevelError + 1)
    log.Error("nobody sees this")
    log.SetLevel(log.LevelInfo)
    log.Info("logging is back on")
end
```

Output:

```text
[INFO] user mina
[ERROR] disk full signed in from 10.0.0.7
{"level": "INFO", "msg": "user signed in", "user": "mina\n[ERROR] disk full", "ip": "10.0.0.7"}
[INFO] logging is back on
```

The end of the example shows a trick for tests and quiet tools: a level above `LevelError` silences everything, and setting it back turns logging on again.

## Which function for which job

| You want | Use |
| --- | --- |
| A plain message | `Debug`, `Info`, `Warn`, `Error` |
| A message with values filled in | `Infof` and the other `...f` functions, with `{}` placeholders |
| Fields that tools can search | `InfoKV` and the other `...KV` functions, best with `FormatJSON` |
| The level as a variable | `Log(level, msg)` |
| Stop the program after an unrecoverable error | `Fatal` |
| Output for a container or systemd | the default, `ToStderr` |

## Constants and variables

```salam
import log

func main:
    log.ToStdout()
```

```text
0 ERROR 2 1
```

### `FormatText`

The readable text format.

log-InfoKV.salam

```salam
import log

func main:
    log.ToStdout()
    log.ShowTime(false)
    mut keys := Vector {} as Vector<str>
    mut values := Vector {} as Vector<str>
    defer keys.free()
    defer values.free()
    keys.push("user")
    values.push("sara")
    keys.push("ms")
    values.push("42")
    log.InfoKV("request served", keys, values)
    log.WarnKV("it was slow", keys, values)
    log.ErrorKV("it failed", keys, values)
    log.SetLevel(log.LevelDebug)
    log.DebugKV("the details", keys, values)
    log.SetFormat(log.FormatJSON)
    log.Info("as JSON")
    println log.GetFormat() == log.FormatJSON, log.FormatText
    mut fields := Vector {} as Vector<str>
    defer fields.free()
    fields.push(log.Field("path", "/login"))
    fields.push(log.FieldInt("status", 200))
    fields.push(log.FieldBool("cached", false))
    println log.KV("response", fields)
end
```

Output:

```text
[INFO] request served user=sara ms=42
[WARN] it was slow user=sara ms=42
[ERROR] it failed user=sara ms=42
[DEBUG] the details user=sara ms=42
{"level": "INFO", "msg": "as JSON"}
true 0
response path=/login status=200 cached=false
```

### `FormatJSON`

```salam

```

The JSON format, one object per line, for log collectors.

The example for this item is shown with the ones above: log-InfoKV.salam

# debug

https://salamlang.github.io/Salam/std/debug/

Tools for finding a bug: assertions, a hand-kept call stack, tracing and timing.

The `debug` package holds a few small tools for when the program is not doing the right thing. `Assert` checks a condition that should always hold. `Enter` and `Exit` keep a call stack by hand, so an error message can say where in the program it happened. `Trace` prints what the program is doing, the timers show which part is slow, and `MemStats` counts allocations to find a leak.

It is meant for development. For messages a running service keeps, use log; for exact timing and allocation counters in your own code, runtime and mem; for benchmarks inside tests, testing.

The things people get wrong:

- `Assert` is an ordinary function: it runs in release builds too, and its message is built even when the condition holds. Keep expensive work out of the message.

- The stack, the trace switch and the timers are globals with no lock, shared by every thread. In a program with threads the stack mixes frames from all of them.

- The stack is only as good as its `Enter` and `Exit` calls. Always pair them with `defer debug.Exit()`.

- `MemStats` only has numbers in a build with memory counting on; a normal run gets a line saying so.

Trace lines and failed assertions go to standard error, so they do not mix with the program's normal output.

## Say where an error happened

An error message like empty price is hard to act on in a big program: which item, and who asked for it? Call `Enter` at the start of the functions you care about and `defer debug.Exit()` right after it, so the frame is removed on every return path. `Stack` then gives the path from the outermost frame to the current one, joined with `>`. The frame is just text, so it can carry the item being worked on.

debug-stack-errors.salam

```salam
import debug

func fail(msg: str): bool:
    println "error in", debug.Stack() + ":", msg
    ret false
end

func parse_price(text: str): bool:
    debug.Enter("parse_price")
    defer debug.Exit()
    if text.len() == 0:
        ret fail("empty price")
    end
    ret true
end

func load_item(name: str, price: str): bool:
    debug.Enter("load_item " + name)
    defer debug.Exit()
    ret parse_price(price)
end

func load_catalogue(): int:
    debug.Enter("load_catalogue")
    defer debug.Exit()
    mut loaded := 0
    if load_item("tea", "4.50"): loaded += 1 end
    if load_item("cake", ""): loaded += 1 end
    if load_item("milk", "1.20"): loaded += 1 end
    ret loaded
end

func main:
    println load_catalogue(), "items loaded, depth now", debug.Depth()
end
```

Output:

```text
error in load_catalogue > load_item cake > parse_price: empty price
2 items loaded, depth now 0
```

After the outer function returns, `Depth` is back at 0. If it is not, some function called `Enter` without a matching `Exit`, which is exactly the bug that `defer` prevents.

## Trace the calls of a recursive function

`EnableTrace(true)` switches tracing on: from then on `Enter` and `Exit` print an `enter` and an `exit` line, and `Trace` prints its message after the current stack. With tracing off, `Trace` prints nothing, so trace calls can stay in the code and be switched on with a flag, for instance from a setting or a command line option.

debug-trace-calls.salam

```salam
import debug
import str

func fib(n: int): int:
    debug.Enter("fib " + str.FromInt(n as i64))
    defer debug.Exit()
    if n < 2:
        debug.Trace("base case")
        ret n
    end
    ret fib(n - 1) + fib(n - 2)
end

func main:
    debug.Trace("not printed, tracing is off")
    debug.EnableTrace(true)
    result := fib(3)
    debug.EnableTrace(false)
    debug.Trace("not printed either")
    printerrln "fib(3) =", result
end
```

Output:

```text
[TRACE] fib 3: enter
[TRACE] fib 3 > fib 2: enter
[TRACE] fib 3 > fib 2 > fib 1: enter
[TRACE] fib 3 > fib 2 > fib 1: base case
[TRACE] fib 3 > fib 2 > fib 1: exit
[TRACE] fib 3 > fib 2 > fib 0: enter
[TRACE] fib 3 > fib 2 > fib 0: base case
[TRACE] fib 3 > fib 2 > fib 0: exit
[TRACE] fib 3 > fib 2: exit
[TRACE] fib 3 > fib 1: enter
[TRACE] fib 3 > fib 1: base case
[TRACE] fib 3 > fib 1: exit
[TRACE] fib 3: exit
fib(3) = 2
```

Reading the lines from top to bottom shows the order of the calls; the indentation you would draw by hand is the length of each stack. All of it goes to standard error, like the last line, which this example prints with `printerrln`.

## Time parts of a program

`StartTimer` starts a named timer and `StopTimer` returns the milliseconds since it started, measured with the monotonic clock, so a change of the system time does not disturb it. Starting a timer that already exists restarts it. `StopTimer` does not remove the timer: calling it again later gives a larger number, which is handy for lap times. A name that was never started gives 0.

debug-timers.salam

```salam
import debug

func busy(n: int): int:
    mut total := 0
    repeat n in i:
        total = (total + i * i) % 1000003
    end
    ret total
end

func main:
    debug.StartTimer("all")
    debug.StartTimer("step")
    a := busy(200000)
    first := debug.StopTimer("step")
    debug.StartTimer("step")
    b := busy(200000)
    second := debug.StopTimer("step")
    total := debug.StopTimer("all")
    later := debug.StopTimer("all")
    println a == b
    println "both steps fit in the total:", first + second <= total
    println "a timer keeps running after StopTimer:", later >= total
    println "unknown timer:", debug.StopTimer("never started")
end
```

Output:

```text
true
both steps fit in the total: true
a timer keeps running after StopTimer: true
unknown timer: 0
```

Times differ from run to run and from machine to machine, so the example only prints comparisons. In your own program print the numbers themselves, for instance with log at the debug level. Measure a part several times, or over many iterations, before deciding it is slow; the first run often includes one time costs.

## Assertions guard your own promises

`Assert` is for conditions that must hold if the code is correct, such as a balance that never goes below zero after a checked withdrawal. It is not for bad input from users or files: those are expected, and the program should answer them with an error value, as `withdraw` does with `false` when the balance is too small.

debug-assert.salam

```salam
import debug

struct Account:
    pub owner: str = ""
    pub balance: int = 0
end

func withdraw(a &: Account, amount: int): bool:
    debug.Assert(amount > 0, "withdraw needs a positive amount")
    if amount > a.balance:
        ret false
    end
    a.balance -= amount
    debug.Assert(a.balance >= 0, "a balance never goes below zero")
    ret true
end

func main:
    mut acc := Account { owner = "Sara", balance = 100 }
    println withdraw(acc, 30), acc.balance
    println withdraw(acc, 500), acc.balance
    println withdraw(acc, 70), acc.balance
end
```

Output:

```text
true 70
false 70
true 0
```

When an assertion fails, the program prints the message to standard error and stops at once with `abort`, so the exit status is 134 on Linux and no deferred code runs. With the first assertion broken, the run ends like this:

```salam
assertion failed: withdraw needs a positive amount
Aborted (core dumped)
```

Under a debugger (`salam debug file.salam`) the abort stops in the failing function, so you can look at its variables. `Break` stops there on purpose, without a failed condition. Do not leave it in code that runs without a debugger: with nothing attached, the program is stopped by the signal.

## Find a leak with MemStats

`MemStats` returns one line with the number of allocations and frees, the bytes still in use (`live`) and the most that was ever in use (`peak`). The counting is compiled in only when you ask for it, so build or run with `-DSALAM_MEM_DEBUG` (or `--asan`). Print the line before and after a piece of work that should leave nothing behind: if `live` keeps growing every time it runs, that work leaks.

debug-memstats.salam

```salam
import debug

func average_score(n: int, free_it: bool): int:
    mut scores := Vector {} as Vector<int>
    repeat n in i:
        scores.push(60 + i % 40)
    end
    mut total := 0
    each s in scores: total += s end
    if free_it: scores.free() end
    ret total / n
end

func main:
    println "start: ", debug.MemStats()
    repeat 100 in _:
        average_score(500, true)
    end
    println "freed: ", debug.MemStats()
    repeat 100 in _:
        average_score(500, false)
    end
    println "leaked:", debug.MemStats()
end
```

The example is not run on this page because it needs the flag. With `salam run -DSALAM_MEM_DEBUG leak.salam` it prints:

```salam
start:  allocs=1 frees=0 live=64 peak=64
freed:  allocs=103 frees=101 live=97 peak=2081
leaked: allocs=205 frees=102 live=204936 peak=204936
```

After the first loop `live` is back near where it started; after the second it has grown by about 2 KB per call, the 500 numbers each forgotten vector held. `salam memcheck file.salam` goes further and runs the program under AddressSanitizer, which reports where each leaked block was allocated.

## Functions

### `Assert`

```salam
func Assert(cond: bool, msg: str)
```

If the condition is false, prints `assertion failed: ` and the message to standard error and stops the program with `abort`. It also runs in release builds.

debug-Enter.salam

```salam
import debug

func child():
    debug.Enter("child")
    println debug.Depth()
    println debug.Stack()
    debug.Exit()
end

func main:
    debug.Enter("root")
    child()
    debug.Exit()
    println debug.Depth()
    debug.Assert(1 + 1 == 2, "the arithmetic holds")
    debug.AssertNotNil(debug.MemStats() as void*, "the memory statistics")
    debug.EnableTrace(true)
    println debug.TraceEnabled()
    debug.Trace("a trace message")
    debug.StartTimer("loop")
    mut total := 0
    repeat 1000 in i:
        total += i
    end
    println total, debug.StopTimer("loop") >= 0.0
    if total < 0:
        debug.Break()
    end
end
```

Output:

```text
2
root > child
0
true
[TRACE] a trace message
499500 true
```

# runtime

https://salamlang.github.io/Salam/std/runtime/

Facts about the running program: the system, the memory, the uptime and the build options.

The `runtime` package answers questions about the running program and the machine under it: which system and processor, how many cores, how much memory, how long the program has been up and how it was compiled. It is what a `/health` route, a startup log line or a benchmark guard needs.

It gathers facts from os/platform and adds the uptime and the build flags. For details such as the host name or the kernel version, use os/platform directly; for the program's own allocation counts, mem; for timing a piece of code, time or the timers in debug.

Where the numbers come from:

| System | CpuCount | TotalMemory | AvailableMemory, UsedMemory |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Linux | a system call | reads `/proc/meminfo` | reads `/proc/meminfo` |
| Windows | the `NUMBER_OF_PROCESSORS` variable | runs PowerShell | runs PowerShell |
| macOS, BSD | runs `sysctl` | runs `sysctl` | minus one |

The things people get wrong:

- The memory functions are not free everywhere. On Linux they read a small file, but on Windows each call starts PowerShell and takes a good part of a second. Cache the numbers, or refresh them on a timer, instead of reading them on every request.

- Every number can be minus one when the system does not report it. Check before you do arithmetic.

- The memory figures are for the whole machine, not this program. In a container you see the host's memory, not the container's limit.

- The uptime counts from `MarkStart`. Without it the clock starts at the first `UptimeMs` call, so the first health check reports 0. It uses the wall clock, so changing the system time moves it.

## A /health route

A load balancer, Docker's `HEALTHCHECK` or a monitoring service calls a health route every few seconds to see whether the program is alive. Call `MarkStart` first thing in `main`, so the uptime counts from the start of the program and not from the first request, and answer with a small JSON object built from the runtime facts.

runtime-health.salam

```salam
import runtime
import net.http
import net.router
import conv
import str

func health(ctx: i64):
    mut body := `{"status": "ok", "os": "` + runtime.OS() + `", "arch": "` + runtime.Arch() + `"`
    body = body + `, "cpus": ` + conv.FormatInt(runtime.CpuCount() as i64)
    body = body + `, "uptime_ms": ` + conv.FormatInt(runtime.UptimeMs())
    body = body + `, "used_memory": ` + conv.FormatInt(runtime.UsedMemory())
    body = body + `, "build": "` + runtime.BuildFlags() + `"}`
    http.Json(ctx, body)
end

func main:
    runtime.MarkStart()
    mut r := router.NewRouter()
    router.Get(r, "/health", health)
    mut s := http.NewServer(19734)
    http.Use(s, r)
    println http.RunBackground(s)
    res := http.Get("http://127.0.0.1:19734/health")
    body := http.Body(res)
    println http.Status(res), http.GetHeader(res, "content-type")
    println str.StartsWith(body, `{"status": "ok"`), str.Contains(body, `"uptime_ms": `)
end
```

Output:

```text
true
200 application/json
true true
```

The example starts the server in the background with net/http and calls its own route, so it runs without anything else. The numbers in the body change on every run, so it prints only the status, the content type and two checks. A real body looks like `{"status": "ok", "os": "linux", "arch": "x64", "cpus": 8, "uptime_ms": 5412, "used_memory": 6442450944, "build": "release"}`.

## Report memory in a readable way

`TotalMemory` and `AvailableMemory` return bytes, and minus one where the system does not report them. `UsedMemory` is the difference, or minus one when either is missing. Turn the bytes into MiB for people, and handle the minus one before doing any arithmetic, or a percentage of a negative number ends up on a dashboard.

runtime-memory.salam

```salam
import runtime
import conv

func mib(bytes: i64): str:
    if bytes < 0: ret "unknown" end
    ret conv.FormatInt(bytes / (1024 * 1024)) + " MiB"
end

func memory_line(total: i64, available: i64): str:
    if total < 0 or available < 0:
        ret "memory: not reported on this system"
    end
    percent := (total - available) * 100 / total
    ret "memory: " + mib(total - available) + " of " + mib(total) + " in use (" + conv.FormatInt(percent) + "%)"
end

func main:
    println memory_line(8589934592, 2147483648)
    println memory_line(17179869184, 15032385536)
    println memory_line(0 - 1, 0 - 1)
    line := memory_line(runtime.TotalMemory(), runtime.AvailableMemory())
    println line.len() > 0
    used := runtime.UsedMemory()
    println used <= runtime.TotalMemory()
end
```

Output:

```text
memory: 6144 MiB of 8192 MiB in use (75%)
memory: 2048 MiB of 16384 MiB in use (12%)
memory: not reported on this system
true
true
```

The first three lines use fixed numbers so the output is the same everywhere; the last two call the real functions.

## Size a worker pool from the core count

A server or a batch job often starts one worker per core. `CpuCount` gives the cores that are online, but a sensible rule also lets the operator override it, puts a ceiling on very large machines and falls back to a small number when the count is unknown. `Summary` puts the main facts in one line, which is handy to log once at startup.

runtime-workers.salam

```salam
import runtime
import str

func pick_workers(cpus: int, configured: int): int:
    if configured > 0: ret configured end
    if cpus < 1: ret 2 end
    if cpus > 16: ret 16 end
    ret cpus
end

func main:
    println "8 cores, nothing configured:", pick_workers(8, 0)
    println "64 cores, nothing configured:", pick_workers(64, 0)
    println "core count unknown:", pick_workers(0 - 1, 0)
    println "configured by hand:", pick_workers(8, 3)
    workers := pick_workers(runtime.CpuCount(), 0)
    println "here:", workers >= 1 and workers <= 16
    line := runtime.Summary()
    println str.Contains(line, " cpus="), str.Contains(line, " build=")
end
```

Output:

```text
8 cores, nothing configured: 8
64 cores, nothing configured: 16
core count unknown: 2
configured by hand: 3
here: true
true true
```

A real `Summary` line looks like `linux/x64 cpus=8 uptime_ms=3 build=release`.

## Know how the program was built

`BuildFlags` returns `release` for a `--release` build, or the checks that are compiled in, joined with commas: `safe` for the default development build with bounds checks, `mem_debug` and `asan` for the memory checking builds. `IsSafeBuild`, `IsMemDebugBuild` and `IsAsanBuild` test each one. These are fixed when the program is compiled, so checking them costs nothing.

runtime-build-check.salam

```salam
import runtime

func check_benchmark_build(): bool:
    flags := runtime.BuildFlags()
    if flags == "release":
        ret true
    end
    println "warning: this is a", flags, "build, so the timings would be too slow"
    if runtime.IsSafeBuild():
        println "  bounds checks are on; build with --release"
    end
    if runtime.IsAsanBuild() or runtime.IsMemDebugBuild():
        println "  memory checking is on; build without --asan or -DSALAM_MEM_DEBUG"
    end
    ret false
end

func main:
    if check_benchmark_build() == false:
        println "skipping the benchmark"
        ret
    end
    println "running the benchmark"
end
```

Output:

```text
warning: this is a safe build, so the timings would be too slow
  bounds checks are on; build with --release
skipping the benchmark
```

`salam run` makes a development build, which is why this example warns. Build it with `salam build file.salam --release` and the same program runs the benchmark. The same check is useful at startup of a server, to log a warning when a debug build reaches production by mistake.

```salam
    free := runtime.AvailableMemory()

    println runtime.UptimeMs() >= 0, runtime.UptimeSeconds() >= 0.0
```

# testing

https://salamlang.github.io/Salam/std/testing/

Writing tests for your code: equality assertions, a pass and fail count, and a summary at the end.

A test is a small program that checks your code does what it should. The `testing` package has assertions that print a clear message when they fail but do not stop the program, so every check runs and `Summary` says at the end how many passed and how many failed. Put tests in a file whose name ends in `_test.salam`, write each one as a function whose name starts with `test_`, and run them all with `salam test`, locally or in CI (see below). A test file can also be an ordinary program with its own `main`, started with `salam run`.

`Summary` returns the number of failures, and returning it from `main` makes the program end with a non-zero code when something failed, which is what turns a CI job red. For checks inside the program itself, conditions that must never be false in production code, use `Assert` from debug instead, which stops the program. To time code, see debug and time.

The things people get wrong:

- A failure line says what differed, not where. In a loop over cases, use `AssertMsg` and put the case name in the message (see below).

- Strings are printed without quotes, so a stray space is invisible in `got hello  want hello`. Put brackets around values in your own messages.

- An exit code only has 8 bits, so 256 failures read as exit code 0. A suite that can have that many should return `failures > 0 ? 1 : 0`.

- The counters are plain globals with no lock: call the assertions from the main thread only.

## Running tests with salam test

`salam test` finds every `*_test.salam` file under the current directory (or the files and directories you name), and in each one calls every function whose name starts with `test_` (`آزمون` in a Persian file) and that takes no arguments. You do not write `main`: the runner writes its own, in memory, and reports each test by name:

```salam
salam test                      # every test file under this directory
salam test calc_test.salam      # one file
salam test --run=parse          # only tests whose name contains "parse"
salam test '--run=^test_add$'   # exactly test_add (^ and $ anchor the name)
salam test --interp             # on the interpreter, no C compiler needed
```

Each file runs in its own process, so a crash fails that file and the others still run. The command ends with exit code 1 when any test failed, when a test file does not compile, and when `--run` matches no test at all. `--format=teamcity` prints TeamCity service messages instead of plain lines, which is what the JetBrains plugin reads to show the test tree; a file that has its own `main` and no `test_` functions is run as one test that passes when it exits with 0.

## Table driven tests

When one function has to give the right answer for many inputs, put the inputs and the expected answers in an array of small structs and loop over it. Adding a case is then one line, and every case runs even when an earlier one fails.

testing-guide-table.salam

```salam
import testing
import str

struct Case:
    pub n: int = 0
    pub want: str = ""
end

func fizzbuzz(n: int): str:
    if n % 15 == 0:
        ret "FizzBuzz"
    else n % 3 == 0:
        ret "Fizz"
    else n % 5 == 0:
        ret "Buzz"
    end
    ret str.FromInt(n)
end

func main:
    cases := [
        Case { n = 1, want = "1" },
        Case { n = 3, want = "Fizz" },
        Case { n = 5, want = "Buzz" },
        Case { n = 9, want = "Fizz" },
        Case { n = 10, want = "Buzz" },
        Case { n = 15, want = "FizzBuzz" },
        Case { n = 98, want = "98" }
    ]
    each c in cases:
        testing.AssertEqStr(fizzbuzz(c.n), c.want)
    end
    ret testing.Summary()
end
```

Output:

```text
--
tests: 7 passed, 0 failed
```

The program returns what `Summary` returns, so it ends with exit code 0 when everything passed. Run it like any other program:

```salam
salam run fizzbuzz_test.salam
echo $?
```

## Failure messages that point at the case

`AssertEqStr` inside a loop prints `strings differ: got ... want ...`, which leaves you to work out which row of the table it was. Give each case a name and build the message yourself with `AssertMsg`. Brackets around the values show spaces at the edges, which is exactly the bug in this example.

testing-guide-labels.salam

```salam
import testing
import str

struct Case:
    pub name: str = ""
    pub input: str = ""
    pub want: str = ""
end

func slug(title: str): str:
    ret str.Replace(str.Lower(title), " ", "-")
end

func check(c: Case):
    got := slug(c.input)
    testing.AssertMsg(got == c.want, c.name + ": got [" + got + "] want [" + c.want + "]")
end

func main:
    cases := [
        Case { name = "plain words", input = "Hello World", want = "hello-world" },
        Case { name = "trailing space", input = "Release notes ", want = "release-notes" },
        Case { name = "one word", input = "Salam", want = "salam" }
    ]
    each c in cases:
        check(c)
    end
    failures := testing.Summary()
    println "exit code:", failures > 0 ? 1 : 0
end
```

Output:

```text
FAIL: trailing space: got [release-notes-] want [release-notes]
--
tests: 2 passed, 1 failed
exit code: 1
```

## Group the tests of each function

A long test file is easier to read when each function under test gets its own test function. `Failed` counts every failure so far; remember it at the start of a group and compare at the end to report the group as a whole.

testing-guide-groups.salam

```salam
import testing

func clamp(v: int, low: int, high: int): int:
    if v < low:
        ret low
    end
    if v > high:
        ret high
    end
    ret v
end

func average(values: Vector<int>): f64:
    if values.len() == 0:
        ret 0.0
    end
    mut total := 0
    each v in values:
        total += v
    end
    ret total as f64 / values.len() as f64
end

func report(name: str, failed before: int):
    if testing.Failed() == failed before:
        println "ok  ", name
    else:
        println "FAIL", name
    end
end

func test clamp():
    before := testing.Failed()
    testing.AssertEqInt(clamp(5, 0, 10), 5)
    testing.AssertEqInt(clamp(-3, 0, 10), 0)
    testing.AssertEqInt(clamp(42, 0, 10), 10)
    report("clamp", before)
end

func test average():
    before := testing.Failed()
    mut v := Vector {} as Vector<int>
    defer v.free()
    testing.AssertEqFloat(average(v), 0.0, 0.000001)
    v.push(1)
    v.push(2)
    v.push(4)
    testing.AssertEqFloat(average(v), 2.333333, 0.00001)
    report("average", before)
end

func main:
    test clamp()
    test average()
    ret testing.Summary()
end
```

Output:

```text
ok   clamp
ok   average
--
tests: 5 passed, 0 failed
```

Floats are compared with `AssertEqFloat` and a tolerance, never with `==`: 7 / 3 has no exact binary form, so the last digits differ from any decimal you write down.

## Test the error paths too

The code that runs when something goes wrong is the code that is run least, so test it on purpose. For a function that reports problems through an `err &:` out parameter, call it with bad input and check both the result and the message. `AssertContains` checks for a key word, so the test keeps passing when the wording around it is improved.

testing-guide-errors.salam

```salam
import testing

func parse port(text: str, err &: str): int:
    err = ""
    if text.len() == 0:
        err = "the port is empty"
        ret 0
    end
    n := text.to_int()
    if n < 1 or n > 65535:
        err = "the port must be between 1 and 65535"
        ret 0
    end
    ret n
end

func main:
    mut err := ""
    testing.AssertEqInt(parse port("8080", err), 8080)
    testing.AssertEqStr(err, "")

    testing.AssertEqInt(parse port("", err), 0)
    testing.AssertContains(err, "empty")

    testing.AssertEqInt(parse port("70000", err), 0)
    testing.AssertNeStr(err, "")
    testing.AssertContains(err, "65535")
    ret testing.Summary()
end
```

Output:

```text
--
tests: 7 passed, 0 failed
```

## What a failure looks like

A failed assertion prints a `FAIL:` line with what it got and what it wanted, and the program carries on with the next check. The failure lines go to standard error and the summary to standard output, so a CI log shows both but a pipe can separate them.

testing-guide-failure.salam

```salam
import testing

func initials(name: str): str:
    parts := name.split(" ")
    mut out := ""
    each p in parts:
        out = out + p.substr(0, 1)
    end
    ret out
end

func main:
    testing.AssertEqStr(initials("Ada Lovelace"), "AL")
    testing.AssertEqStr(initials("grace hopper"), "GH")
    testing.AssertEqInt(testing.Failed(), 1)
    failures := testing.Summary()
    println "exit code a CI job would see:", failures
end
```

Output:

```text
FAIL: strings differ: got gh want GH
--
tests: 2 passed, 1 failed
exit code a CI job would see: 1
```

This example prints the failure count instead of returning it, so the page can show its output. A real test file ends with `ret testing.Summary()`, and the non-zero exit code is what makes the CI job fail.

## Which assertion to use

| You are checking | Use | Why |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Two whole numbers | `AssertEqInt`, `AssertEqInt64` | The message shows both values |
| Two strings | `AssertEqStr` | The message shows both strings |
| Floats | `AssertEqFloat` with a small tolerance | Rounding makes `==` unreliable |
| Part of a longer text | `AssertContains` | Survives changes to the rest of the text |
| That something changed | `AssertNeInt`, `AssertNeStr` | For ids, tokens and hashes |
| A pointer was or was not set | `AssertNil`, `AssertNotNil` | For C libraries and allocations |
| Any other condition | `AssertMsg` | Say in words what went wrong |

Prefer the specific assertions to `Assert`. "ints differ: got 4 want 5" tells you far more than "assertion failed". `Reset` sets both counters back to zero, for a program that runs several separate suites in a row.

## Functions

### `Assert`

```salam
import testing

func add(a: int, b: int): int:
    ret a + b
end

func main:
    testing.Reset()
    testing.Assert(add(2, 2) == 4)
    testing.AssertMsg(add(1, 1) == 2, "one and one")
    testing.AssertTrue(true)
    testing.AssertFalse(add(0, 0) == 1)
    testing.AssertEqInt(add(3, 4), 7)
    testing.AssertEqInt64(10000000000 as i64, 10000000000 as i64)
    testing.AssertEqFloat(0.1 + 0.2, 0.3, 0.0001)
    testing.AssertContains("the Salam language", "Salam")
    testing.AssertEqStr("hello", "hello")
    testing.AssertEqBool(1 < 2, true)
    testing.AssertNeInt(1, 2)
    testing.AssertNeStr("a", "b")
    testing.AssertNil(null)
    testing.AssertEqInt(add(2, 2), 5)
    println testing.Passed(), testing.Failed()
    println testing.Summary()
end
```

Output:

```text
FAIL: ints differ: got 4 want 5
13 1
--
tests: 13 passed, 1 failed
1
```
