### `ClockTime`

```salam
struct ClockTime
```

A time of day.

| Name | Type | Description |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `hour` | `int = 0` | The hour, 0 to 23. |
| `minute` | `int = 0` | The minute. |
| `second` | `int = 0` | The second. |

calendar-Epoch.salam

```salam
import calendar
import time

func main:
    t := 1710943509
    zone := calendar.TZLocal(t)
    g := calendar.EpochToGregorian(t)
    println calendar.CompareGregorian(g, calendar.WallClockGregorian(t, zone)) == 0
    println calendar.CompareJalali(calendar.EpochToJalali(t), calendar.WallClockJalali(t, zone)) == 0
    println calendar.CompareHijri(calendar.EpochToHijri(t), calendar.WallClockHijri(t, zone)) == 0
    println calendar.FormatClockTime(calendar.EpochToClockTime(t)) == calendar.FormatClockTime(calendar.WallClockTime(t, zone))
    j := calendar.JalaliDate { year = 1403, month = 1, day = 1 }
    println calendar.JalaliToUnixUTC(j, 14, 5, 9) == t
    println calendar.GregorianToUnixUTC(calendar.GregorianDate { year = 2024, month = 3, day = 20 }, 14, 5, 9)
    println calendar.HijriToUnixUTC(calendar.HijriDate { year = 1445, month = 9, day = 10 }, 0, 0, 0)
    println calendar.CompareGregorian(calendar.TodayGregorian(), calendar.EpochToGregorian(time.Now())) >= 0, calendar.TodayGregorian().year >= 2024, calendar.TodayJalali().year >= 1403, calendar.TodayHijri().year >= 1445
    c := calendar.NowClockTime()
    println c.hour < 24, c.minute < 60, c.second < 61
end
```

Output:

```text
true
true
true
true
true
1710943509
1710892800
true true true true
true true true
```

### `TimeZone`

```salam
struct TimeZone
```

A time zone with a fixed offset from UTC.

| Name | Type | Description |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `name` | `str = "UTC"` | The zone name, such as `Asia/Tehran`. |
| `offset_minutes` | `int = 0` | The offset from UTC in minutes; 210 for Tehran. |

calendar-TimeZone.salam

```salam
import calendar

func main:
    t := 1710943509
    tehran := calendar.TZTehran()
    println tehran.name, tehran.offset_minutes
    println calendar.FormatJalali(calendar.WallClockJalali(t, tehran)), calendar.FormatClockTime(calendar.WallClockTime(t, tehran))
    println calendar.FormatGregorian(calendar.WallClockGregorian(t, calendar.TZTokyo())), calendar.FormatClockTime(calendar.WallClockTime(t, calendar.TZTokyo()))
    println calendar.FormatHijri(calendar.WallClockHijri(t, calendar.TZMecca()))
    each zone in [calendar.TZUTC(), calendar.TZKabul(), calendar.TZRiyadh(), calendar.TZDubai(), calendar.TZIstanbul(), calendar.TZLondon(), calendar.TZNewYork()]:
        println zone.name, zone.offset_minutes, calendar.FormatClockTime(calendar.WallClockTime(t, zone))
    end
    g := calendar.GregorianDate { year = 2024, month = 3, day = 20 }
    c := calendar.ClockTime { hour = 23, minute = 0, second = 0 }
    println calendar.ZonedGregorianToEpoch(g, c, tehran)
    println calendar.FormatGregorian(calendar.ConvertZonedGregorian(g, c, tehran, calendar.TZTokyo())), calendar.FormatClockTime(calendar.ConvertZonedTime(g, c, tehran, calendar.TZTokyo()))
    fixed := calendar.FixedOffsetZone("UTC+05:30", 330)
    println fixed.name, calendar.FormatClockTime(calendar.WallClockTime(t, fixed))
    local := calendar.TZLocal(t)
    println local.name, local.offset_minutes == calendar.LocalOffsetMinutes(t)
end
```

Output:

```text
Asia/Tehran 210
1403-01-01 17:35:09
2024-03-20 23:05:09
1445-09-10
UTC 0 14:05:09
Asia/Kabul 270 18:35:09
Asia/Riyadh 180 17:05:09
Asia/Dubai 240 18:05:09
Europe/Istanbul 180 17:05:09
Europe/London 0 14:05:09
America/New_York -300 09:05:09
1710963000
2024-03-21 04:30:00
UTC+05:30 19:35:09
Local true
```

### `JalaliToJDN`

```salam

```

The example for this item is shown with the ones above: calendar-Convert.salam


The example for this item is shown with the ones above: calendar-Convert.salam

### `IsLeapJalali`

```salam
func IsLeapJalali(year: int): bool
```

True when the Jalali year is a leap year, meaning Esfand has 30 days.

calendar-Jalali.salam

```salam
import calendar

func main:
    println calendar.IsLeapJalali(1403), calendar.IsLeapJalali(1404), calendar.DaysInJalaliYear(1403)
    println calendar.DaysInJalaliMonth(1403, 1), calendar.DaysInJalaliMonth(1403, 7), calendar.DaysInJalaliMonth(1403, 12), calendar.DaysInJalaliMonth(1404, 12)
    println calendar.IsValidJalaliDate(1404, 12, 30), calendar.IsValidJalaliDate(1403, 12, 30)
    println calendar.JalaliMonthNameFa(1), calendar.JalaliMonthNameEn(1), calendar.JalaliMonthNameFa(12)
    j := calendar.JalaliDate { year = 1403, month = 6, day = 31 }
    d := calendar.JalaliToJDN(j)
    println calendar.JalaliWeekday(d), calendar.JalaliWeekdayNameFa(calendar.JalaliWeekday(d))
    println calendar.WeekdayJalali(j), calendar.WeekdayNameFa(calendar.WeekdayJalali(j))
    println calendar.FormatJalali(calendar.AddDaysJalali(j, 1)), calendar.FormatJalali(calendar.AddWeeksJalali(j, 2))
    println calendar.FormatJalali(calendar.AddMonthsJalali(j, 1)), calendar.FormatJalali(calendar.AddYearsJalali(j, -1))
    println calendar.FormatJalali(calendar.StartOfMonthJalali(j)), calendar.FormatJalali(calendar.EndOfMonthJalali(calendar.AddMonthsJalali(j, 6)))
    nowruz := calendar.JalaliDate { year = 1404, month = 1, day = 1 }
    println calendar.DaysBetweenJalali(j, nowruz), calendar.CompareJalali(j, nowruz), calendar.CompareJalali(nowruz, nowruz)
end
```

Output:

```text
true false 366
31 30 30 29
false true
فروردین Farvardin اسفند
0 شنبه
6 شنبه
1403-07-01 1403-07-14
1403-07-30 1402-06-31
1403-06-01 1403-12-30
181 -1 0
```

### `IsLeapGregorian`

```salam
func IsLeapGregorian(year: int): bool
```

True when the Gregorian year is a leap year.

calendar-Gregorian.salam

```salam
import calendar

func main:
    println calendar.IsLeapGregorian(2024), calendar.IsLeapGregorian(1900), calendar.DaysInGregorianYear(2024)
    println calendar.DaysInGregorianMonth(2024, 2), calendar.DaysInGregorianMonth(2023, 2), calendar.IsValidGregorianDate(2023, 2, 29)
    g := calendar.GregorianDate { year = 2024, month = 1, day = 31 }
    w := calendar.WeekdayGregorian(g)
    println w, calendar.WeekdayNameEn(w), calendar.WeekdayNameFa(w), calendar.WeekdayNameAr(w)
    println calendar.Weekday(calendar.GregorianToJDN(g)), calendar.GregorianMonthNameEn(1)
    println calendar.FormatGregorian(calendar.AddMonthsGregorian(g, 1)), calendar.FormatGregorian(calendar.AddYearsGregorian(calendar.GregorianDate { year = 2024, month = 2, day = 29 }, 1))
    println calendar.FormatGregorian(calendar.AddDaysGregorian(g, 30)), calendar.FormatGregorian(calendar.AddWeeksGregorian(g, -1))
    println calendar.FormatGregorian(calendar.StartOfMonthGregorian(g)), calendar.FormatGregorian(calendar.EndOfMonthGregorian(calendar.AddMonthsGregorian(g, 1)))
    println calendar.FormatGregorian(calendar.NextWeekdayOnOrAfter(g, 5))
    year_end := calendar.GregorianDate { year = 2024, month = 12, day = 31 }
    println calendar.DaysBetweenGregorian(g, year_end), calendar.CompareGregorian(year_end, g)
end
```

Output:

```text
true false 366
29 28 false
3 Wednesday چهارشنبه الأربعاء
3 January
2024-02-29 2025-02-28
2024-03-01 2024-01-24
2024-01-01 2024-02-29
2024-02-02
335 1
```

```salam
    println calendar.IsLeapHijri(1445), calendar.IsLeapHijri(1446)
    println calendar.DaysInHijriMonth(1445, 9), calendar.DaysInHijriMonth(1445, 12), calendar.DaysInHijriMonth(1446, 12)

    println calendar.HijriMonthNameFa(9), calendar.HijriMonthNameAr(9), calendar.HijriMonthNameEn(9)
    println calendar.FormatHijri(calendar.AddDaysHijri(h, 1)), calendar.FormatHijri(calendar.AddWeeksHijri(h, 1))
    println calendar.FormatHijri(calendar.AddMonthsHijri(h, 3)), calendar.FormatHijri(calendar.AddYearsHijri(h, 1))
    println calendar.FormatHijri(calendar.StartOfMonthHijri(h)), calendar.FormatHijri(calendar.EndOfMonthHijri(h))

    println calendar.WeekdayNameFa(calendar.WeekdayHijri(h))
end
```

```text
دوشنبه
```

# thread

https://salamlang.github.io/Salam/std/thread/

Holding and waiting for the threads that `spawn` creates.

In Salam you start a function that should run alongside the rest of the program with `spawn`. It takes a function with no parameters and no result and gives back a number, the thread's handle. `join`, or `thread.Join`, waits for that thread to finish.

The `thread` package wraps that handle in a `Thread` so you can keep several of them in a vector and wait for all of them at once, and `SpawnStack` starts a thread with a stack of the size you choose. Threads share the program's globals and heap; for shared data use sync or atomic, to pass values between threads chan, and to spread a loop over every core pool. A thread cannot be stopped from outside; to ask one to finish early, use ctx or an atomic flag it checks.

## Split one job across threads

The most common use of threads is to cut a big job into parts and give each part its own thread. Give each thread its own piece of memory to write its answer into, start them all, then wait for all of them with `JoinAll`. Because no two threads write to the same place, there is nothing to lock. `spawn` also takes a second argument, a pointer the function receives as its parameter; that is how each thread learns which part is its own.

thread-guide-split.salam

```salam
import thread
import mem

struct Part:
    pub first: i64 = 0
    pub last: i64 = 0
    pub sum: i64 = 0
end

func add range(p: Part*):
    mut total := 0 as i64
    mut i := p[0].first
    until i <= p[0].last:
        total += i
        i += 1
    end
    p[0].sum = total
end

func new part(first: i64, last: i64): Part*:
    p := mem.Allocate(sizeof(Part)) as Part*
    p[0] = Part { first = first, last = last }
    ret p
end

func main:
    size := 250 as i64
    mut parts := Vector {} as Vector<Part*>
    defer parts.free()
    mut group := Vector {} as Vector<thread.Thread>
    defer group.free()
    repeat 4 in w:
        p := new part((w as i64) * size + 1, (w as i64 + 1) * size)
        parts.push(p)
        group = thread.Collect(group, spawn(add range, p))
    end
    thread.JoinAll(group)
    mut total := 0 as i64
    each p in parts:
        println p[0].first, "to", p[0].last, "=", p[0].sum
        total += p[0].sum
        mem.Free(p as void*)
    end
    println "total:", total
end
```

Output:

```text
1 to 250 = 31375
251 to 500 = 93875
501 to 750 = 156375
751 to 1000 = 218875
total: 500500
```

The parts may finish in any order, but the program reads the answers only after `JoinAll` and in the order it stored them, so the output is always the same.

## Do something else while a thread works

A thread does not have to be part of a group. Start one slow task in the background, carry on with other work on the main thread, and call `Join` at the point where you need the result. Until `Join` returns, do not read what the thread is writing.

thread-guide-background.salam

```salam
import thread

mut words := 0
mut lines := 0

func count text():
    text := "the quick brown fox\njumps over\nthe lazy dog"
    mut reading := false
    lines = 1
    repeat text.len() in i:
        c := text[i]
        if c == '\n':
            lines += 1
        end
        if c == ' ' or c == '\n':
            reading = false
        else not reading:
            reading = true
            words += 1
        end
    end
end

func main:
    worker := thread.New(spawn(count text))
    println "main thread: loading settings"
    println "main thread: opening the report"
    thread.Join(worker)
    println "lines:", lines, "words:", words
end
```

Output:

```text
main thread: loading settings
main thread: opening the report
lines: 3 words: 9
```

Here only the main thread prints. If both threads printed, the lines could come out in a different order on every run.

## Deep recursion on a bigger stack

A thread from `spawn` gets the system's default stack, which deep recursion can overflow. `SpawnStack` starts the function on a stack of the size you ask for. The system may refuse a very large stack, so check the thread with `Valid` and have a plan for the case where it is not.

thread-guide-fallback.salam

```salam
import thread

mut depth := 0 as i64

func walk(n: i64): i64:
    if n == 0:
        ret 0
    end
    ret 1 + walk(n - 1)
end

func deep work(_arg: void*):
    depth = walk(300000)
end

func main:
    t := thread.SpawnStack(deep work, null, (128 * 1024 * 1024) as u64)
    if thread.Valid(t):
        thread.Join(t)
    else:
        println "no big stack, running on this thread"
        deep work(null)
    end
    println "depth reached:", depth
end
```

Output:

```text
depth reached: 300000
```

The function given to `SpawnStack` takes a `void*`, so the same function can also be called directly with `null` when no thread could be started.

## Pitfalls, and which tool to use

- Join every thread you start. A program that returns from `main` while threads are still running cuts them off midway.

- Globals are shared by every thread. Two threads that change the same variable without a lock give a different answer from run to run.

- Output from several threads interleaves in no fixed order. Collect results and print them from one thread.

- A handle of zero means the thread did not start. `Join` on it does nothing, so check `Valid` when it matters.

- Join each thread exactly once. On Linux and macOS `Join` also frees the handle, so a second `Join` of the same thread uses freed memory and can crash.

- `Collect` returns the vector it was given, grown by one; always assign the result back, as in `group = thread.Collect(group, spawn(work))`.

| You want to | Use |
| --- | --- |
| Wait for one or a few threads | `spawn` with `thread.Join` or `JoinAll` |
| Run the turns of a loop on all cores | pool.`ParallelFor` |
| Let threads change shared data | sync.`Mutex` or atomic.`I64` |
| Pass values from one thread to another | chan.`Chan` |
| Know when many tasks are done without keeping their handles | sync.`WaitGroup` |

## Types

### `Thread`

```salam
struct Thread
```

A thread, running or finished.

| Name | Type | Description |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `handle` | `i64 = 0` | The handle `spawn` returned; zero means invalid. |

thread-Join.salam

```salam
import thread
import sync

mut total := 0
mut lock := sync.Mutex {}

func worker():
    repeat 1000:
        sync.Lock(lock)
        total += 1
        sync.Unlock(lock)
    end
end

func main:
    lock = sync.NewMutex()
    first := thread.New(spawn(worker))
    println thread.Valid(first), thread.Handle(first) != 0
    mut group := Vector {} as Vector<thread.Thread>
    defer group.free()
    repeat 3:
        group = thread.Collect(group, spawn(worker))
    end
    thread.Join(first)
    thread.JoinAll(group)
    println group.len(), total
    empty := thread.New(0)
    println thread.Valid(empty), empty.handle
    thread.Join(empty)
    sync.Destroy(lock)
end
```

Output:

```text
true true
3 4000
false 0
```

## Functions

### `New`

### `SpawnStack`

```salam
func SpawnStack(fn: i64, arg: void*, stack: u64): Thread
```

Starts a function on a new thread with a stack of the size you give, in bytes, for work that needs more than the default, such as deep recursion. The function takes a `void*` and returns nothing. If the system cannot give that stack it returns an invalid handle, so check with `Valid`.

thread-SpawnStack.salam

```salam
import thread

mut total := 0 as i64

func count(n: i64): i64:
    if n <= 0:
        ret 0
    end
    ret 1 + count(n - 1)
end

func work(_arg: void*):
    total = count(200000)
end

func main:
    stack := (64 * 1024 * 1024) as u64
    t := thread.SpawnStack(work, null, stack)
    println thread.Valid(t)
    thread.Join(t)
    println total
end
```

Output:

```text
true
200000
```

# sync

https://salamlang.github.io/Salam/std/sync/

Mutexes, condition variables, wait groups, read-write locks, semaphores and once, for coordinating threads.

When several threads change the same variable they have to take turns, or the result depends on the order the threads happen to run in. The `sync` package has the classic tools for taking turns, built on the operating system's threads library:

- A mutex: each thread takes the lock before touching the data and releases it afterwards. An RWMutex lets many readers in at once.

- A condition variable: a thread sleeps until another one says that something has changed.

- A wait group: call `Add` before starting a piece of work, `Done` at its end, and `Wait` until the count is back to zero.

- A semaphore caps how many threads are inside a part at once, and a once runs setup a single time.

Threads themselves come from `spawn` and the thread package. For a single shared number, atomic is cheaper than a lock; to hand values from one thread to another, chan does the locking and waiting for you; to cancel work, ctx.

The things people get wrong:

- Using a value that was never created. Every tool here is made with a `New...` function; a zero `sync.Mutex {}` has no lock inside and crashes on `Lock`. Globals are declared with `{}` and created at the top of `main`.

- Locking twice. A mutex is not reentrant: a thread that calls `Lock` on a mutex it already holds waits forever. `Do` holds a lock while its function runs, so calling `Do` on the same `Once` from inside it hangs too.

- Waiting on a condition without a loop. `WaitCond` can return before the condition is true; always wait inside `until not condition:`.

- Forgetting `Destroy...`. Each tool holds operating system memory; destroy it after the last thread that uses it has been joined.

## Keep data consistent with a mutex

A lock is not only for counters. Anything that has to stay true across several variables, such as "the money in all accounts adds up to the same total", needs every change to happen while the lock is held. Take the lock at the top of the function and put `Unlock` in a `defer`, so it is released on every return path, including the early `ret`.

sync-guide-transfer.salam

```salam
import sync

mut accounts := Vector {} as Vector<int>
mut lock := sync.Mutex {}
mut group := sync.WaitGroup {}

func transfer(from: int, dest: int, amount: int): bool:
    sync.Lock(lock)
    defer sync.Unlock(lock)
    if accounts.get(from) < amount:
        ret false
    end
    accounts.set(from, accounts.get(from) - amount)
    accounts.set(dest, accounts.get(dest) + amount)
    ret true
end

func clerk():
    repeat 1000 in i:
        transfer(i % 3, (i + 1) % 3, 7)
    end
    sync.Done(group)
end

func main:
    lock = sync.NewMutex()
    group = sync.NewWaitGroup()
    accounts.push(500)
    accounts.push(300)
    accounts.push(200)
    sync.Add(group, 4)
    mut workers := Vector {} as Vector<i64>
    defer workers.free()
    repeat 4:
        workers.push(spawn(clerk))
    end
    sync.Wait(group)
    each t in workers:
        join(t)
    end
    total := accounts.get(0) + accounts.get(1) + accounts.get(2)
    println "money in the bank:", total
    println "a transfer that is too big:", transfer(0, 1, 100000)
    accounts.free()
    sync.DestroyWaitGroup(group)
    sync.Destroy(lock)
end
```

Output:

```text
money in the bank: 1000
a transfer that is too big: false
```

Four threads move money around 4000 times and the total is still 1000. Without the lock two threads could read the same balance at once and one of the changes would be lost.

## Many readers, few writers

When data is read far more often than it is changed, such as settings or a cache, a plain mutex makes readers wait for each other for no reason. An `RWMutex` lets any number of readers in together with `RLock`, and gives a writer the data to itself with `WLock`.

sync-guide-settings.salam

```salam
import sync

mut settings := HashMap {} as HashMap<str, int>
mut guard := sync.RWMutex {}
mut reads := 0
mut count lock := sync.Mutex {}

func reader():
    repeat 200:
        sync.RLock(guard)
        limit := settings.get("limit")
        sync.RUnlock(guard)
        if limit > 0:
            sync.Lock(count lock)
            reads += 1
            sync.Unlock(count lock)
        end
    end
end

func writer():
    repeat 1 to 5 in v:
        sync.WLock(guard)
        settings.put("limit", v * 10)
        sync.WUnlock(guard)
    end
end

func main:
    guard = sync.NewRWMutex()
    count lock = sync.NewMutex()
    settings.put("limit", 5)
    a := spawn(reader)
    b := spawn(reader)
    w := spawn(writer)
    join(a)
    join(b)
    join(w)
    println "reads:", reads
    println "final limit:", settings.get("limit")
    settings.free()
    sync.Destroy(count lock)
    sync.DestroyRWMutex(guard)
end
```

Output:

```text
reads: 400
final limit: 50
```

A reader must never write while holding only the read lock. If a reader may need to change the data, take the write lock instead.

## Limit how many run at once

A `Semaphore` holds a number of permits. `Acquire` takes one and waits when none are left, `Release` gives it back. With two permits, at most two threads are inside the guarded part at any moment, which is how you cap parallel downloads or database connections.

sync-guide-limit.salam

```salam
import sync

mut slots := sync.Semaphore {}
mut lock := sync.Mutex {}
mut running := 0
mut busiest := 0
mut finished := 0

func download():
    sync.Acquire(slots)
    sync.Lock(lock)
    running += 1
    if running > busiest:
        busiest = running
    end
    sync.Unlock(lock)
    sync.SleepMs(20)
    sync.Lock(lock)
    running -= 1
    finished += 1
    sync.Unlock(lock)
    sync.Release(slots)
end

func main:
    slots = sync.NewSemaphore(2)
    lock = sync.NewMutex()
    mut jobs := Vector {} as Vector<i64>
    defer jobs.free()
    repeat 6:
        jobs.push(spawn(download))
    end
    each t in jobs:
        join(t)
    end
    println "downloads finished:", finished
    println "never more than two at once:", busiest <= 2
    sync.Destroy(lock)
    sync.DestroySemaphore(slots)
end
```

Output:

```text
downloads finished: 6
never more than two at once: true
```

`TryAcquire` takes a permit only if one is free and returns `false` at once otherwise, for work that should be skipped rather than queued.

## Set something up exactly once

Some setup is expensive and should happen only when it is first needed, but several threads may need it at the same moment. `Do` runs its function the first time it is called on a `Once`; every other caller waits until that run has finished and then goes on without running it again.

sync-guide-once.salam

```salam
import sync

mut setup := sync.Once {}
mut table := Vector {} as Vector<int>
mut builds := 0

func build table():
    builds += 1
    repeat 10 in i:
        table.push(i * i)
    end
end

func square(n: int): int:
    sync.Do(setup, (): build table() end)
    ret table.get(n)
end

func worker():
    _ := square(3)
end

func main:
    setup = sync.NewOnce()
    a := spawn(worker)
    b := spawn(worker)
    c := spawn(worker)
    join(a)
    join(b)
    join(c)
    println "square of 7:", square(7)
    println "table built", builds, "time"
    table.free()
    sync.DestroyOnce(setup)
end
```

Output:

```text
square of 7: 49
table built 1 time
```

## A work queue: wait for work, wait for the end

A condition variable is how a thread sleeps until there is something to do instead of checking in a busy loop. The workers below wait on `has_work` while the queue is empty, and the main thread calls `Signal` after each push to wake one of them. A wait group counts the jobs: `Add` before each push, `Done` when it is processed, and `Wait` returns when all are done. To stop the workers, set a flag and `Broadcast`, which wakes all of them.

sync-guide-queue.salam

```salam
import sync

mut lock := sync.Mutex {}
mut has_work := sync.CondVar {}
mut jobs_done := sync.WaitGroup {}
mut queue := Vector {} as Vector<int>
mut taken := 0
mut closed := false
mut total := 0

func worker():
    sync.Lock(lock)
    until true:
        until taken == queue.len() and not closed:
            sync.WaitCond(has_work, lock)
        end
        if taken == queue.len(): break end
        size := queue.get(taken)
        taken += 1
        sync.Unlock(lock)
        cost := size * 2
        sync.Lock(lock)
        total += cost
        sync.Done(jobs_done)
    end
    sync.Unlock(lock)
end

func main:
    lock = sync.NewMutex()
    has_work = sync.NewCondVar()
    jobs_done = sync.NewWaitGroup()
    workers := [spawn(worker), spawn(worker), spawn(worker)]
    repeat 1 to 10 in size:
        sync.Add(jobs_done, 1)
        sync.Lock(lock)
        queue.push(size)
        sync.Signal(has_work)
        sync.Unlock(lock)
    end
    sync.Wait(jobs_done)
    println "all 10 jobs done, total cost", total
    sync.Lock(lock)
    println "nobody signals, waited 20 ms, woken:", sync.WaitCondTimeout(has_work, lock, 20)
    closed = true
    sync.Broadcast(has_work)
    sync.Unlock(lock)
    each t in workers: join(t) end
    println "workers stopped"
    queue.free()
    sync.DestroyWaitGroup(jobs_done)
    sync.DestroyCondVar(has_work)
    sync.Destroy(lock)
end
```

Output:

```text
all 10 jobs done, total cost 110
nobody signals, waited 20 ms, woken: false
workers stopped
```

`WaitCond` releases the lock while it sleeps and takes it again before it returns, which is why the worker can check the queue right after it. `WaitCondTimeout` does the same with a time limit, returning true when it was woken and false when the time ran out. The wait group does not replace `join`: every spawned thread still has to be joined once.

## Pitfalls, and which tool to use

- When two locks are needed, every thread must take them in the same order. Taking A then B in one thread and B then A in another can stop both.

- Keep the locked part short. Do slow work, such as file or network calls, before taking the lock or after releasing it.

- Every `New...` has a matching `Destroy...`. Call it after the last thread using the value has been joined.

| Situation | Use |
| --- | --- |
| Several threads change the same data | `Mutex` |
| Data is read much more often than written | `RWMutex` |
| Wait until N tasks are done | `WaitGroup` |
| At most N tasks at a time | `Semaphore` |
| Setup that must run once | `Once` |
| Wait until some condition becomes true | `CondVar` with a `Mutex` |
| A single shared number | atomic.`I64` |
| Hand values from one thread to another | chan.`Chan` |

## Types

### `Mutex`

```salam
struct Mutex
```

A mutex; only one thread holds it at a time.

| Name | Type | Description |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `handle` | `void*` | The operating system's lock. |

sync-Mutex.salam

```salam
import sync

mut balance := 0
mut lock := sync.Mutex {}
mut group := sync.WaitGroup {}

func deposit():
    repeat 500:
        sync.Lock(lock)
        balance += 1
        sync.Unlock(lock)
    end
    sync.Done(group)
end

func main:
    lock = sync.NewMutex()
    group = sync.NewWaitGroup()
    sync.Wait(group)
    sync.Add(group, 4)
    a := spawn(deposit)
    b := spawn(deposit)
    c := spawn(deposit)
    d := spawn(deposit)
    sync.Wait(group)
    join(a)
    join(b)
    join(c)
    join(d)
    println "balance:", balance
    sync.DestroyWaitGroup(group)
    sync.Destroy(lock)
end
```

Output:

```text
balance: 2000
```

### `CondVar`

```salam
struct CondVar
```

A condition variable: threads sleep on it until another thread wakes them.

| Name | Type | Description |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `handle` | `void*` | The operating system's condition variable. |

sync-CondVar.salam

```salam
import sync

mut ready := false
mut lock := sync.Mutex {}
mut cond := sync.CondVar {}

func producer():
    sync.SleepMs(20)
    sync.Lock(lock)
    ready = true
    sync.Broadcast(cond)
    sync.Unlock(lock)
end

func main:
    lock = sync.NewMutex()
    cond = sync.NewCondVar()
    start := sync.NowMs()
    sync.Lock(lock)
    println sync.WaitCondTimeout(cond, lock, 10)
    t := spawn(producer)
    until not ready:
        sync.WaitCond(cond, lock)
    end
    sync.Unlock(lock)
    join(t)
    println ready, sync.NowMs() - start >= 20
    sync.Signal(cond)
    sync.DestroyCondVar(cond)
    sync.Destroy(lock)
end
```

Output:

```text
false
true true
```

### `WaitGroup`

```salam
struct WaitGroup
```

A wait group: a count of unfinished work.

| Name | Type | Description |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `counter` | `i64*` | The number of unfinished pieces of work. |
| `mu` | `void*` | The internal lock. |
| `cv` | `void*` | The internal condition variable. |

The example for this item is shown with the ones above: sync-Mutex.salam

### `RWMutex`

```salam
struct RWMutex
```

A read-write lock: several readers together, or one writer alone.

| Name | Type | Description |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `state` | `i64*` | The internal state: the readers, the writer and the waiting writers. |
| `mu` | `void*` | The internal lock. |
| `cv` | `void*` | The internal condition variable. |

sync-RWMutex.salam

```salam
import sync

func main:
    rw := sync.NewRWMutex()
    sync.RLock(rw)
    sync.RLock(rw)
    println "two readers together"
    sync.RUnlock(rw)
    sync.RUnlock(rw)
    sync.WLock(rw)
    println "one writer alone"
    sync.WUnlock(rw)
    sync.DestroyRWMutex(rw)

    sem := sync.NewSemaphore(2)
    sync.Acquire(sem)
    println sync.TryAcquire(sem), sync.TryAcquire(sem)
    sync.Release(sem)
    println sync.TryAcquire(sem)
    sync.DestroySemaphore(sem)

    once := sync.NewOnce()
    repeat 3:
        sync.Do(once, (): println "only once" end)
    end
    sync.DestroyOnce(once)
end
```

Output:

```text
two readers together
one writer alone
true false
true
only once
```

# atomic

https://salamlang.github.io/Salam/std/atomic/

A counter and a flag that several threads can change safely without taking a lock by hand.

For a simple counter that several threads increment, you do not have to build a lock yourself: `I64` in this package does each operation in one indivisible step. `CompareAndSwap` is the base of most lock-free algorithms: it changes the value only if it is still the one you expected.

With gcc, clang and the LLVM backend each operation is one of the processor's atomic instructions. Under tcc, which lacks them, each cell is protected by a small lock instead; the results are the same, only slower.

There are two types: `I64`, a shared 64-bit whole number, and `Flag`, a shared true or false. Both are small handles to a cell on the heap, so passing one to a function or a thread by value shares the same cell. For anything bigger than one value, use sync; to pass values between threads, chan.

The things people get wrong:

- Using a cell that was never created. `atomic.I64 {}` has no cell and crashes on the first `Add`; make it with `NewI64` or `NewFlag`, for a global at the top of `main`.

- Combining two operations. `if Load(a) < 10: Add(a, 1) end` is two steps, and another thread can act in between; that is what `CompareAndSwap` in a loop is for.

- Destroying too early. `DestroyI64` frees the cell for every copy of the handle; call it once, after every thread that uses it has been joined.

There is no subtract: `Add(a, -1)` counts down.

## Hand out unique numbers

`Add` returns the value after the addition, and no two callers can get the same one. That makes it a ready made source of unique ids, ticket numbers or slot indexes, shared by any number of threads with no lock in sight.

atomic-guide-ids.salam

```salam
import atomic

mut next id := atomic.I64 {}
mut taken := Vector {} as Vector<i64>

func hand out():
    repeat 100:
        id := atomic.Add(next id, 1)
        taken.set(id as int - 1, taken.get(id as int - 1) + 1)
    end
end

func main:
    next id = atomic.NewI64(0)
    repeat 400:
        taken.push(0)
    end
    a := spawn(hand out)
    b := spawn(hand out)
    c := spawn(hand out)
    d := spawn(hand out)
    join(a)
    join(b)
    join(c)
    join(d)
    mut twice := 0
    each n in taken:
        if n != 1:
            twice += 1
        end
    end
    println "last id:", atomic.Load(next id)
    println "ids given out more than once:", twice
    taken.free()
    atomic.DestroyI64(next id)
end
```

Output:

```text
last id: 400
ids given out more than once: 0
```

Four threads took 100 ids each, and every id from 1 to 400 was given out exactly once. Each thread then writes only to the slot its own id names, which is why the vector needs no lock either.

## Update with CompareAndSwap

Some updates are not a plain addition: "keep the largest value seen so far" has to read the value, decide, and write. Doing that in two steps would let another thread slip in between. The answer is a loop: read the value, compute the new one, and ask `CompareAndSwap` to store it only if the value has not changed meanwhile. If it has, read again and retry.

atomic-guide-max.salam

```salam
import atomic

mut highest := atomic.I64 {}

func record(value: i64):
    mut seen := atomic.Load(highest)
    until value > seen:
        if atomic.CompareAndSwap(highest, seen, value):
            ret
        end
        seen = atomic.Load(highest)
    end
end

func low readings():
    repeat 500 in i:
        record((i * 7 % 900) as i64)
    end
end

func high readings():
    repeat 500 in i:
        record((i * 13 % 1000) as i64)
    end
end

func main:
    highest = atomic.NewI64(0)
    a := spawn(low readings)
    b := spawn(high readings)
    join(a)
    join(b)
    println "highest reading:", atomic.Load(highest)
    atomic.DestroyI64(highest)
end
```

Output:

```text
highest reading: 993
```

The loop also stops as soon as the stored value is already at least as large, so most calls do not write at all.

## A stop signal for a worker

A `Flag` is the simplest way to tell a long running thread to finish: the worker checks it each round, and the main thread sets it when it is time. A plain `bool` global is not enough, because nothing guarantees the worker ever sees the change.

atomic-guide-stop.salam

```salam
import atomic
import sync

mut stop := atomic.Flag {}
mut rounds := atomic.I64 {}

func worker():
    until not atomic.Get(stop):
        atomic.Add(rounds, 1)
        sync.SleepMs(1)
    end
end

func main:
    stop = atomic.NewFlag(false)
    rounds = atomic.NewI64(0)
    t := spawn(worker)
    until atomic.Load(rounds) < 20:
        sync.SleepMs(1)
    end
    atomic.Set(stop, true)
    join(t)
    println "worker ran at least 20 rounds:", atomic.Load(rounds) >= 20
    println "stop flag:", atomic.Get(stop)
    atomic.DestroyFlag(stop)
    atomic.DestroyI64(rounds)
end
```

Output:

```text
worker ran at least 20 rounds: true
stop flag: true
```

## Only the first one wins

`TestAndSet` turns the flag on and tells you whether you were the one who did it. When several threads race for one job, such as sending a single alert or doing a one time cleanup, exactly one of them gets `true`.

atomic-guide-first.salam

```salam
import atomic

mut claimed := atomic.Flag {}
mut winners := atomic.I64 {}
mut losers := atomic.I64 {}

func try claim():
    if atomic.TestAndSet(claimed):
        atomic.Add(winners, 1)
    else:
        atomic.Add(losers, 1)
    end
end

func main:
    claimed = atomic.NewFlag(false)
    winners = atomic.NewI64(0)
    losers = atomic.NewI64(0)
    mut threads := Vector {} as Vector<i64>
    defer threads.free()
    repeat 8:
        threads.push(spawn(try claim))
    end
    each t in threads:
        join(t)
    end
    println "winners:", atomic.Load(winners), "losers:", atomic.Load(losers)
    atomic.DestroyFlag(claimed)
    atomic.DestroyI64(winners)
    atomic.DestroyI64(losers)
end
```

Output:

```text
winners: 1 losers: 7
```

## Atomic or a lock?

An atomic value is right when the shared state is one number or one flag. As soon as two values must change together, such as a balance and a history, use a sync.`Mutex`: two atomic operations in a row are not atomic together. For setup that must run once, `sync.Once` is clearer than a hand made flag.

| Job | Function |
| --- | --- |
| Count events from many threads | `Add(a, 1)` |
| Take the next free number | `Add`, using its result |
| Read the latest value for a report | `Load` |
| Reset and get the old total | `Swap(a, 0)` |
| Any read, compute, write update | `CompareAndSwap` in a loop |
| Tell a thread to stop | `Flag` with `Set` and `Get` |
| Let exactly one thread do something | `TestAndSet` |

## Types

### `I64`

```salam
struct I64
```

A 64-bit whole number shared between threads.

| Name | Type | Description |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `cell` | `i64*` | The address of the value. |
| `mu` | `sync.Mutex` | The internal lock. |

atomic-I64.salam

```salam
import atomic

mut counter := atomic.I64 {}

func worker():
    repeat 1000:
        atomic.Add(counter, 1)
    end
end

func main:
    counter = atomic.NewI64(0)
    a := spawn(worker)
    b := spawn(worker)
    join(a)
    join(b)
    println atomic.Load(counter)
    atomic.Store(counter, 10)
    println atomic.Swap(counter, 20), atomic.Load(counter)
    println atomic.CompareAndSwap(counter, 20, 30), atomic.CompareAndSwap(counter, 20, 40), atomic.Load(counter)
    atomic.DestroyI64(counter)
    flag := atomic.NewFlag(false)
    println atomic.TestAndSet(flag), atomic.TestAndSet(flag), atomic.Get(flag)
    atomic.Set(flag, false)
    println atomic.Get(flag)
    atomic.DestroyFlag(flag)
end
```

Output:

```text
2000
10 20
true false 30
true false true
false
```

# chan

https://salamlang.github.io/Salam/std/chan/

A channel for passing values from one thread to another, with a buffer, timeouts and closing.

A channel is a queue that several threads send values into at one end and receive from at the other; it handles the locks and the waiting for you. You give the value type when you create it, as in `chan.Chan<i64>`, and call `init` with a capacity before using it.

When the buffer is full, `send` waits; when it is empty, `recv` does. A channel of capacity zero is "unbuffered": the sender waits until a receiver takes the value. After `close`, sending returns false but receivers still get the values that are left; once the channel is empty, `ok` turns false and a receiving loop can end.

Use a channel when one thread produces values and another consumes them. For shared data that several threads change in place, sync is the better fit; for a counter, atomic; for running the turns of a loop on every core, pool; and for telling workers to stop, ctx.

The things people get wrong:

- Forgetting `init`. A channel declared with `chan.Chan {}` has no buffer or lock yet and crashes on the first `send`.

- Using the value from a failed receive. When `ok` is false the result is a zero value that means nothing.

- Telling a timeout from the end. `recv_timeout` sets `ok` to false both when the time ran out and when the channel is closed and empty; ask `is_closed` to know which.

- Sending a `Vector` or a pointer and then changing it. The channel copies the value, which for those types is only the handle, so both threads see the same memory.

## The receive loop

Almost every consumer looks the same: receive in an endless `until true:` loop and `break` when `ok` turns false. That happens only after the channel is closed and empty, so no value is lost. The rule that goes with it: the side that sends is the side that closes, once it has nothing more to send.

chan-guide-loop.salam

```salam
import chan

mut orders := chan.Chan {} as chan.Chan<str>

func checkout():
    each id in ["A-1001", "A-1002", "A-1003"]:
        orders.send(id)
    end
    orders.close()
    println "after close, send works:", orders.send("A-1004")
end

func main:
    orders.init(8)
    t := spawn(checkout)
    join(t)
    println "waiting in the buffer:", orders.len()
    mut ok := true
    until true:
        id := orders.recv(ok)
        if not ok: break end
        println "packing", id
    end
    println "closed and empty:", orders.is_closed(), orders.len()
    orders.free()
end
```

Output:

```text
after close, send works: false
waiting in the buffer: 3
packing A-1001
packing A-1002
packing A-1003
closed and empty: true 0
```

The sender filled the buffer and closed the channel before the receiver even started, and still every order came out. A `send` after `close` returns false instead of waiting.

## A pipeline of stages

Channels connect stages that each do one thing. Here one thread generates numbers, a second squares them, and the main thread adds them up. Each stage closes its output channel when its input runs dry, so the end of the data flows down the pipeline by itself and every loop stops on its own.

chan-guide-pipeline.salam

```salam
import chan

mut numbers := chan.Chan {} as chan.Chan<i64>
mut squares := chan.Chan {} as chan.Chan<i64>

func generate():
    repeat 1 to 10 in n:
        numbers.send(n as i64)
    end
    numbers.close()
end

func square():
    mut ok := true
    until true:
        n := numbers.recv(ok)
        if not ok:
            break
        end
        squares.send(n * n)
    end
    squares.close()
end

func main:
    numbers.init(2)
    squares.init(2)
    a := spawn(generate)
    b := spawn(square)
    mut total := 0 as i64
    mut count := 0
    mut ok := true
    until true:
        v := squares.recv(ok)
        if not ok:
            break
        end
        total += v
        count += 1
    end
    join(a)
    join(b)
    println "values through the pipeline:", count
    println "sum of squares:", total
    numbers.free()
    squares.free()
end
```

Output:

```text
values through the pipeline: 10
sum of squares: 385
```

The channels hold only two values each. When the last stage is slow, the earlier ones wait in `send` instead of piling up memory, which is called back pressure.

## Ask and wait for an answer

Two channels make a request and reply pair: one carries questions to a worker, the other brings the answers back. With capacity zero, each `send` waits until the other side has taken the value, so the two threads move in step and the answers come back in the order the questions went out.

chan-guide-reply.salam

```salam
import chan

mut requests := chan.Chan {} as chan.Chan<str>
mut replies := chan.Chan {} as chan.Chan<str>

func server():
    mut ok := true
    until true:
        name := requests.recv(ok)
        if not ok:
            break
        end
        replies.send("hello, " + name)
    end
end

func main:
    requests.init(0)
    replies.init(0)
    t := spawn(server)
    mut ok := true
    each name in ["Sara", "Reza", "Mina"]:
        requests.send(name)
        println replies.recv(ok)
    end
    requests.close()
    join(t)
    requests.free()
    replies.free()
end
```

Output:

```text
hello, Sara
hello, Reza
hello, Mina
```

## Many senders, one receiver

When several threads send into one channel, none of them can close it, because each one only knows that it is done. Count the senders with a sync.`WaitGroup` and let one more small thread wait for the group and then close the channel.

chan-guide-fanin.salam

```salam
import chan
import sync

mut events := chan.Chan {} as chan.Chan<i64>
mut senders := sync.WaitGroup {}

func sensor(base: i64):
    repeat 5 in i:
        events.send(base + i as i64)
    end
    sync.Done(senders)
end

func sensor a(): sensor(100) end
func sensor b(): sensor(200) end
func sensor c(): sensor(300) end

func closer():
    sync.Wait(senders)
    events.close()
end

func main:
    events.init(4)
    senders = sync.NewWaitGroup()
    sync.Add(senders, 3)
    a := spawn(sensor a)
    b := spawn(sensor b)
    c := spawn(sensor c)
    d := spawn(closer)
    mut per sensor := [0, 0, 0]
    mut ok := true
    until true:
        v := events.recv(ok)
        if not ok:
            break
        end
        per sensor[v / 100 - 1] += 1
    end
    join(a)
    join(b)
    join(c)
    join(d)
    println "from sensor a:", per sensor[0]
    println "from sensor b:", per sensor[1]
    println "from sensor c:", per sensor[2]
    sync.DestroyWaitGroup(senders)
    events.free()
end
```

Output:

```text
from sensor a: 5
from sensor b: 5
from sensor c: 5
```

Values from different senders arrive interleaved in no fixed order, so the program counts them per sender instead of printing them as they come.

## When the channel is full

`send` waits for room, which is not always what you want. A server under load is often better off refusing extra work at once than making every caller wait. `try_send` returns `false` immediately when there is no room, and `try_recv` does the same for an empty channel.

chan-guide-shed.salam

```salam
import chan

func main:
    mut queue := chan.Chan {} as chan.Chan<int>
    queue.init(3)
    mut accepted := 0
    mut dropped := 0
    repeat 1 to 8 in request:
        if queue.try_send(request):
            accepted += 1
        else:
            dropped += 1
        end
    end
    println "accepted:", accepted, "dropped:", dropped, "waiting:", queue.len()
    mut ok := true
    until true:
        r := queue.try_recv(ok)
        if not ok:
            break
        end
        println "handling request", r
    end
    println "queue empty:", queue.len() == 0
    queue.free()
end
```

Output:

```text
accepted: 3 dropped: 5 waiting: 3
handling request 1
handling request 2
handling request 3
queue empty: true
```

Between the two extremes are `send_timeout` and `recv_timeout`, which wait at most the given number of milliseconds.

| If the channel is full or empty | Send | Receive |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Wait as long as it takes | `send` | `recv` |
| Wait up to some milliseconds | `send_timeout` | `recv_timeout` |
| Do not wait at all | `try_send` | `try_recv` |

Two mistakes to avoid: receiving from a channel nobody will ever close or send to waits forever, and calling `free` while another thread is still using the channel. Join the threads first, then free.

## Types

### `Chan`

```salam
struct Chan<T>
```

A channel of values of type `T`.

| Name | Type | Description |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `buf` | `T*` | The buffer of values. |
| `ctl` | `i64*` | The internal state: the head and tail of the queue, the count and whether it is closed. |
| `cap` | `i64 = 0` | The capacity. |
| `zidx` | `i64 = 0` | The buffer slot holding the type's zero value, for when nothing was received. |
| `mu` | `sync.Mutex` | The internal lock. |
| `not_empty` | `sync.CondVar` | Waking the receivers. |
| `not_full` | `sync.CondVar` | Waking the senders. |
| `taken` | `sync.CondVar` | The signal that a value was taken, on an unbuffered channel. |

chan-Chan.salam

```salam
import chan
import sync

mut jobs := chan.Chan {} as chan.Chan<i64>
mut results := chan.Chan {} as chan.Chan<i64>
mut group := sync.WaitGroup {}

func worker():
    mut open := true
    until true:
        n := jobs.recv(open)
        if not open:
            break
        end
        results.send(n * n)
    end
    sync.Done(group)
end

func main:
    jobs.init(4)
    results.init(16)
    group = sync.NewWaitGroup()
    sync.Add(group, 2)
    a := spawn(worker)
    b := spawn(worker)
    repeat 1 to 11 in n:
        jobs.send(n)
    end
    jobs.close()
    sync.Wait(group)
    join(a)
    join(b)
    results.close()
    mut total := 0 as i64
    mut open := true
    until true:
        v := results.recv(open)
        if not open:
            break
        end
        total += v
    end
    println "sum of the squares:", total
    println jobs.is_closed(), jobs.len(), jobs.capacity(), jobs.send(1)
    sync.DestroyWaitGroup(group)
    jobs.free()
    results.free()
end
```

Output:

```text
sum of the squares: 506
true 0 4 false
```

```salam
import chan

func main:
    mut c := chan.Chan {} as chan.Chan<str>
    c.init(1)
    println c.try_send("hello"), c.try_send("again")
    println c.send_timeout("late", 20)
    mut open := true
    println c.try_recv(open), open
    _ := c.recv_timeout(open, 20)
    println "after 20 milliseconds:", open
    println c.send_deadline("a", 0, false)
    println c.recv_deadline(open, 20, true), open

```

# pool

https://salamlang.github.io/Salam/std/pool/

Running one loop in parallel across several processor cores.

If each turn of a loop is independent of the others, such as processing each slot of an array on its own, `ParallelFor` spreads the turns across several worker threads and waits for all of them. The loop body is a function taking an `i64`, the turn's number.

Despite the name there is no pool that lives on: each call to `ParallelFor` starts its worker threads, hands out the turn numbers one at a time to whichever worker is free, and joins every worker before it returns. That makes it the shortest way to use every core for one loop. For work that arrives over time, use your own threads from thread fed by a chan; for shared state, sync and atomic.

The things people get wrong:

- Relying on the order of the turns, or changing shared data from them without a lock. Each turn writing to its own slot is safe; anything else needs atomic or a mutex.

- Making the turns too small. Taking the next turn number costs a lock, and every call starts and joins threads, so a turn should do a fair amount of work (see chunks).

- Calling `ParallelFor` in a hot loop. Each call pays for creating threads; parallelize the outer loop instead of the inner one.

## One turn per row

The natural fit for `ParallelFor` is data laid out in rows, such as the pixels of an image or the lines of a table. Make each turn handle one row: the turns touch different memory, so they need no lock, and the result is the same whatever order they ran in.

pool-guide-pixels.salam

```salam
import pool
import mem
import str

mut pixels := null as int*
width := 8
height := 6

func brighten row(y: i64):
    repeat width in x:
        i := (y as int) * width + x
        mut v := pixels[i] + 60
        if v > 255:
            v = 255
        end
        pixels[i] = v
    end
end

func main:
    pixels = mem.AllocateZeroed(sizeof(int) * ((width * height) as u64)) as int*
    repeat width * height in i:
        pixels[i] = (i * 37) % 256
    end
    pool.ParallelFor(height, 3, (y: i64): brighten row(y) end)
    repeat height in y:
        mut line := ""
        repeat width in x:
            line = line + str.FromInt(pixels[y * width + x]) + " "
        end
        println line.trim()
    end
    mem.Free(pixels as void*)
end
```

Output:

```text
60 97 134 171 208 245 255 63
100 137 174 211 248 255 66 103
140 177 214 251 255 69 106 143
180 217 254 255 72 109 146 183
220 255 255 75 112 149 186 223
255 255 78 115 152 189 226 255
```

The loop body here is a short lambda that calls a named function. Keeping the real work in a named function makes it easy to test on its own, without any threads.

## Chunks, not single items

Each turn has a small cost of its own, so a million turns that each add one number spend more time on bookkeeping than on adding. Cut the work into a few large chunks instead, let each turn handle one chunk and write its partial result to its own slot, and combine the slots on the main thread at the end.

pool-guide-chunks.salam

```salam
import pool
import mem

mut partial := null as i64*
total numbers := 1000000 as i64
chunks := 8

func add chunk(c: i64):
    size := total numbers / (chunks as i64)
    first := c * size + 1
    mut last := first + size - 1
    if c == chunks as i64 - 1:
        last = total numbers
    end
    mut s := 0 as i64
    mut n := first
    until n <= last:
        s += n
        n += 1
    end
    partial[c] = s
end

func main:
    partial = mem.AllocateZeroed(sizeof(i64) * (chunks as u64)) as i64*
    pool.ParallelForAuto(chunks, (c: i64): add chunk(c) end)
    mut sum := 0 as i64
    repeat chunks in c:
        sum += partial[c]
    end
    println "chunks:", chunks
    println "sum of 1 to", total numbers, "=", sum
    println "check:", sum == total numbers * (total numbers + 1) / 2
    mem.Free(partial as void*)
end
```

Output:

```text
chunks: 8
sum of 1 to 1000000 = 500000500000
check: true
```

`ParallelForAuto` picks the number of workers from the processor count. A few chunks per worker is a good size: enough for the work to even out when some chunks are slower, few enough that the overhead stays small.

## Combine results with an atomic counter

When the turns produce something that has to be added into one place, such as a count of matches, the simplest safe choice is an atomic.`I64`. Here every number below 100000 is one turn, and each turn that finds a prime adds one to the shared counter.

pool-guide-primes.salam

```salam
import pool
import atomic

mut found := atomic.I64 {}

func is prime(n: i64): bool:
    if n < 2:
        ret false
    end
    mut d := 2 as i64
    until d * d <= n:
        if n % d == 0:
            ret false
        end
        d += 1
    end
    ret true
end

func main:
    found = atomic.NewI64(0)
    pool.ParallelFor(100000, pool.CPUCount(), (n: i64):
        if is prime(n):
            atomic.Add(found, 1)
        end
    end)
    println "primes below 100000:", atomic.Load(found)
    atomic.DestroyI64(found)
end
```

Output:

```text
primes below 100000: 9592
```

An atomic add per match is fine when matches are rare compared with the work of each turn. If every turn would update the counter, use partial results per chunk as in the previous section instead.

## Rules for the loop body

- Never rely on the order of the turns. Turn 5 can finish before turn 0.

- A turn may write to its own slot freely. Anything shared needs a sync.`Mutex` or an atomic.

- Do not print from the loop body; the lines come out mixed up. Store the results and print after `ParallelFor` returns.

- `ParallelFor` waits for every turn, so as soon as it returns all results are ready and no join is needed.

- Small loops are faster without threads. Parallelize only when one run of the loop takes noticeable time.

## Functions

### `CPUCount`

```salam
func CPUCount(): i64
```

The number of processor cores that are online, at least one.

pool-ParallelFor.salam

```salam
import pool
import mem

mut squares := null as i64*

func main:
    println pool.CPUCount() >= 1
    squares = mem.AllocateZeroed(80 as u64) as i64*
    pool.ParallelFor(10, 4, (i: i64): squares[i] = i * i end)
    mut total := 0 as i64
    repeat 10 in i:
        total += squares[i]
    end
    println total
    pool.ParallelForAuto(10, (i: i64): squares[i] = -i end)
    println squares[9]
    mem.Free(squares as void*)
end
```

Output:

```text
true
285
-9
```

### `ParallelFor`

```salam
func ParallelFor(n: i64, workers: i64, body: func(i64))
```

Runs the body for the numbers zero to `n - 1` on `workers` new threads, at most `n` of them, and returns when every turn is done. Nothing happens when `n` is zero or less.

The example for this item is shown with the ones above: pool-ParallelFor.salam

### `ParallelForAuto`

```salam
func ParallelForAuto(n: i64, body: func(i64))
```

Like `ParallelFor`, with one thread per core from `CPUCount`.

The example for this item is shown with the ones above: pool-ParallelFor.salam

# ctx

https://salamlang.github.io/Salam/std/ctx/

A context for cancellation and deadlines, passed from the main piece of work down to the smaller ones.

A context tells long-running work when to stop: either someone called `Cancel`, or its deadline passed. Contexts form a tree: you start from `Background` and make a child each time with `WithCancel`, `WithTimeout` or `WithDeadline`.

Cancelling a context ends all its children, but not its parent. The work should check `IsDone` from time to time, or wait on it with `Wait`. Free each context with `Free` when you are done with it, children before parents.

Use a context when work that may take long has to stop early: a request whose client went away, a batch job with a time budget, a background thread at shutdown. It is built on sync and works across threads. For one stop flag and nothing else, an atomic.`Flag` is enough; to pass results back, use a chan.

The things people get wrong:

- Expecting a context to interrupt a call. No standard library function takes one: a network request, a file read or a `sync.SleepMs` runs to its end. Check `IsDone` between steps, sleep with `Wait`, and give network calls their own timeout options.

- Freeing in the wrong order. A child keeps a copy of its parent that points at the parent's memory, and freeing the root destroys the lock the whole tree shares. Free children first, the root last, each exactly once.

- Assuming the deadlines follow a steady clock. They are measured with `sync.NowMs`, which on Linux and macOS is the wall clock, so setting the system time moves them.

## Guide: one context per request

The usual shape is one context for a whole piece of work, such as an HTTP request or a batch job, and a child for every smaller task it starts. When the request is cancelled, every task under it sees `IsDone` turn true, while work hanging from another branch keeps going. The program below builds that tree and cancels the request in the middle.

ctx-guide-tree.salam

```salam
import ctx

func show(name: str, c: ctx.Context):
    if ctx.IsDone(c):
        println name, "stopped:", ctx.Err(c)
    else:
        println name, "running"
    end
end

func main:
    root := ctx.Background()
    request := ctx.WithCancel(root)
    db_query := ctx.WithCancel(request)
    cache := ctx.WithCancel(request)
    audit := ctx.WithCancel(root)

    ctx.Cancel(request)

    show("request", request)
    show("db query", db_query)
    show("cache", cache)
    show("audit", audit)
    show("root", root)

    ctx.Free(audit)
    ctx.Free(cache)
    ctx.Free(db_query)
    ctx.Free(request)
    ctx.Free(root)
end
```

Output:

```text
request stopped: cancelled
db query stopped: cancelled
cache stopped: cancelled
audit running
root running
```

Cancelling goes down the tree, never up: `root` and `audit` are untouched. That is why each task should get its own child instead of sharing the parent: you can stop one task alone by cancelling its child, or all of them by cancelling the parent.

## Guide: check between steps

A context does not stop anything by force. The work has to look at it, and the right place is between steps, before each item of a loop or before each slow call. Pass the context as the first argument of every function that may take long, and return early when it is done.

ctx-guide-steps.salam

```salam
import ctx

func copy_files(c: ctx.Context, files: Vector<str>): int:
    mut copied := 0
    each name in files:
        if ctx.IsDone(c):
            println "  stopped before", name, "(" + ctx.Err(c) + ")"
            ret copied
        end
        println "  copied", name
        copied += 1
    end
    ret copied
end

func main:
    mut files := Vector {} as Vector<str>
    files.push("a.txt")
    files.push("b.txt")
    files.push("c.txt")
    root := ctx.Background()

    println "normal run:"
    live := ctx.WithCancel(root)
    println "  total", copy_files(live, files)

    println "cancelled by the user:"
    stopped := ctx.WithCancel(root)
    ctx.Cancel(stopped)
    println "  total", copy_files(stopped, files)

    println "deadline already passed:"
    late := ctx.WithDeadline(root, 1)
    println "  total", copy_files(late, files)

    ctx.Free(late)
    ctx.Free(stopped)
    ctx.Free(live)
    ctx.Free(root)
    files.free()
end
```

Output:

```text
normal run:
  copied a.txt
  copied b.txt
  copied c.txt
  total 3
cancelled by the user:
  stopped before a.txt (cancelled)
  total 0
deadline already passed:
  stopped before a.txt (deadline exceeded)
  total 0
```

The same function serves all three cases, and the caller decides which one applies. `Err` tells the two reasons apart: `cancelled` when someone called `Cancel`, `deadline exceeded` when the time ran out. `WithDeadline(root, 1)` uses an instant long past, so its context is done from the start.

## Guide: time budgets

A child can never outlive its parent. A child with a longer timeout than its parent still ends at the parent's deadline, and `Deadline` reports the nearest deadline of the context and all its parents. A child with a shorter timeout ends earlier on its own, and its parent goes on.

ctx-guide-budget.salam

```salam
import ctx

func main:
    root := ctx.Background()
    request := ctx.WithTimeout(root, 2000)
    lookup := ctx.WithTimeout(request, 60000)
    quick := ctx.WithTimeout(request, 50)

    println "root has a deadline:", ctx.Deadline(root) != 0
    println "lookup keeps the request budget:", ctx.Deadline(lookup) == ctx.Deadline(request)
    println "quick is tighter:", ctx.Deadline(quick) < ctx.Deadline(request)

    println "quick finished within 1 s:", ctx.Wait(quick, 1000), ctx.Err(quick)
    println "request still running:", not ctx.IsDone(request)

    ctx.Free(quick)
    ctx.Free(lookup)
    ctx.Free(request)
    ctx.Free(root)
end
```

Output:

```text
root has a deadline: false
lookup keeps the request budget: true
quick is tighter: true
quick finished within 1 s: true deadline exceeded
request still running: true
```

So a request can get a total budget of two seconds at the top, and a step deep inside can ask for a minute without breaking it. `Wait` returns `true` as soon as the context finishes, here after about 50 milliseconds, and `false` if its own time limit ran out first.

## Guide: stopping a thread

A context is safe to share between threads, so it is the clean way to tell a background thread to stop. The thread loops until `IsDone` is true and sleeps with `Wait` between rounds, so a `Cancel` from the main thread wakes it at once instead of after its next sleep.

ctx-guide-worker.salam

```salam
import ctx
import sync

mut root := ctx.Background()
mut job := ctx.WithCancel(root)
mut wg := sync.NewWaitGroup()
mut finished := false

func worker():
    until ctx.IsDone(job):
        _ := ctx.Wait(job, 100)
    end
    finished = true
    sync.Done(wg)
end

func main:
    sync.Add(wg, 1)
    t := spawn(worker)
    sync.SleepMs(50)
    println "asking the worker to stop"
    ctx.Cancel(job)
    sync.Wait(wg)
    join(t)
    println "worker finished:", finished, "reason:", ctx.Err(job)

    sync.DestroyWaitGroup(wg)
    ctx.Free(job)
    ctx.Free(root)
end
```

Output:

```text
asking the worker to stop
worker finished: true reason: cancelled
```

A loop that calls `sync.SleepMs` instead of `Wait` would also stop, but only after the sleep ends. Free the context only after the thread is joined, since the thread still reads it until it returns.

## Which function for which job

| You want | Use |
| --- | --- |
| A root for a new tree | `Background`, which never finishes by itself |
| A task you stop by hand | `WithCancel`, then `Cancel` |
| A task with a time limit | `WithTimeout(parent, ms)` |
| A task that must end at a fixed time | `WithDeadline(parent, at_ms)` with an instant from `sync.NowMs` |
| To check without blocking | `IsDone`, and `Err` for the reason |
| To sleep but wake on cancel | `Wait(c, ms)` |

Two mistakes are common. Freeing a parent while its children are still in use leaves them pointing at freed memory, so free children first. And a context only helps when the work checks it: a long call that never looks at `IsDone` runs to the end however early you cancel.

## Types

### `Context`

```salam
struct Context
```

A context.

| Name | Type | Description |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `state` | `i64*` | The internal state: cancelled, the deadline and whether there is one. |
| `parent` | `Context*` | The parent context, or null for the root. |
| `mu` | `sync.Mutex` | The lock every context in one tree shares. |
| `cv` | `sync.CondVar` | The condition variable that cancellation wakes. |
| `is_root` | `bool = false` | Whether this context is the root. |

ctx-Context.salam

```salam
import ctx

func main:
    root := ctx.Background()
    cancellable := ctx.WithCancel(root)
    timed := ctx.WithTimeout(cancellable, 30)
    println ctx.IsDone(timed), "[" + ctx.Err(timed) + "]", ctx.Deadline(timed) > 0, ctx.Deadline(root)
    println ctx.Wait(timed, 10)
    println ctx.Wait(timed, 1000), ctx.Err(timed)
    ctx.Cancel(cancellable)
    println ctx.IsDone(cancellable), ctx.Err(cancellable), ctx.IsDone(root)
    past := ctx.WithDeadline(root, 1)
    println ctx.IsDone(past), ctx.Err(past)
    ctx.Free(past)
    ctx.Free(timed)
    ctx.Free(cancellable)
    ctx.Free(root)
end
```

Output:

```text
false [] true 0
false
true deadline exceeded
true cancelled false
true deadline exceeded
```

# encoding

https://salamlang.github.io/Salam/std/encoding/

Turning text and data into Base64, hexadecimal and URL encoding.

This package holds the common ways of writing bytes as plain text: Base64 for fitting binary data into JSON or email, hexadecimal for showing bytes, and URL encoding for putting text or special characters into a web address.

The larger formats, such as JSON, YAML and XML, have sub-packages of their own, listed in this same group.

Every function takes and returns `str`, except the two `...Bytes` forms, which work on a pointer and a length for binary data. Neighbouring packages: encoding/binary for numbers packed into bytes, crypto for hashes that you then show in hex, and jwt for tokens, which use the URL-safe Base64 alphabet that this package does not have.

The things people get wrong:

- Decoding binary into a `str`. A `str` ends at the first zero byte, so `Base64Decode` and `HexDecode` cut binary data short; use `Base64DecodeBytes` into a buffer.

- Expecting `HexDecode` to report bad input. It stops at the first pair that is not hex and returns what it decoded so far, and an odd last digit is dropped. Check the length and the characters first when the text comes from outside.

- Feeding it URL-safe Base64 (`-` and `_` instead of `+` and `/`, often without padding). The lenient decoder skips those characters and returns damaged bytes; the strict one refuses.

- `URLEncode` writes a space as `%20`, while `URLDecode` reads both `%20` and `+` as a space.

## Guide: an HTTP Basic login header

HTTP Basic authentication sends `user:password` in Base64 after the word `Basic`. Base64 is not encryption, anyone can decode it, so this only belongs on HTTPS. Building the header is one call; reading it on the server side means decoding with `Base64DecodeStrict` and splitting at the first colon, since the password itself may contain more colons.

encoding-guide-basic-auth.salam

```salam
import encoding

func basic_header(user: str, password: str): str:
    ret "Basic " + encoding.Base64Encode(user + ":" + password)
end

func read_header(header: str, user &: str, password &: str): bool:
    if header.find("Basic ") != 0:
        ret false
    end
    mut ok := false
    pair := encoding.Base64DecodeStrict(header.substr(6, header.len() - 6), ok)
    colon := pair.find(":")
    if not ok or colon < 0:
        ret false
    end
    user = pair.substr(0, colon)
    password = pair.substr(colon + 1, pair.len() - colon - 1)
    ret true
end

func main:
    h := basic_header("sara", "p@ss:2026")
    println "Authorization:", h

    mut user := ""
    mut password := ""
    if read_header(h, user, password):
        println "user:", user
        println "password:", password
    end
    println "bad header accepted:", read_header("Basic !!not-base64!!", user, password)
end
```

Output:

```text
Authorization: Basic c2FyYTpwQHNzOjIwMjY=
user: sara
password: p@ss:2026
bad header accepted: false
```

The strict decoder reports through its `ok` argument whether the text was valid Base64, so a garbled header is refused instead of being turned into a random user name.

## Guide: strict or lenient Base64

`Base64Decode` never fails: it skips characters it does not know and accepts missing padding. That is handy for text you produced yourself. For anything that comes from outside, use `Base64DecodeStrict`, which accepts only padded standard Base64 and tells you when the input is broken.

encoding-guide-strict.salam

```salam
import encoding

func check(label: str, s: str):
    mut ok := false
    text := encoding.Base64DecodeStrict(s, ok)
    if ok:
        println label, "ok:", text
    else:
        println label, "rejected"
    end
end

func main:
    check("padded   ", "U2FsYW0=")
    check("unpadded ", "U2FsYW0")
    check("typo     ", "U2Fs*W0=")
    check("wrapped  ", "U2Fs\nYW0=")
    check("persian  ", encoding.Base64Encode("سلام"))
    println "lenient on the typo: [" + encoding.Base64Decode("U2Fs*W0=") + "]"
    println "lenient unpadded: [" + encoding.Base64Decode("U2FsYW0") + "]"
end
```

Output:

```text
padded    ok: Salam
unpadded  rejected
typo      rejected
wrapped   ok: Salam
persian   ok: سلام
lenient on the typo: [Sal[]
lenient unpadded: [Salam]
```

Line breaks are allowed in both, because MIME and PEM files wrap Base64 at 76 or 64 characters. A typo is where the two differ: the strict form says no, the lenient form quietly returns damaged bytes. For binary data use `Base64EncodeBytes` and `Base64DecodeBytes`, which work on a pointer and a length, because a `str` stops at the first zero byte.

## Guide: seeing the bytes with hex

Hexadecimal writes each byte as two digits, which makes it the easiest way to see what a string really holds. Persian letters take two bytes each in UTF-8, so `len` of a Persian word counts bytes, not letters. Hex is also the usual form for hashes, keys and colours.

encoding-guide-hex.salam

```salam
import encoding

func main:
    words := ["A", "é", "س", "سلام"]
    each w in words:
        println w, "is", w.len(), "bytes:", encoding.HexEncode(w)
    end

    stored := "d8b3d984d8a7d985"
    println "decoded:", encoding.HexDecode(stored)
    println "upper case works too:", encoding.HexDecode("D8B3D984D8A7D985")
end
```

Output:

```text
A is 1 bytes: 41
é is 2 bytes: c3a9
س is 2 bytes: d8b3
سلام is 8 bytes: d8b3d984d8a7d985
decoded: سلام
upper case works too: سلام
```

`HexEncode` writes lower case; `HexDecode` reads both cases.

## Guide: putting text into a URL

A query value cannot contain spaces, `&`, `=` or non-ASCII letters as they are. `URLEncode` escapes everything except letters, digits and `- _ . ~`, so the result is safe anywhere in a URL. `URLDecode` undoes it and also reads `+` as a space, the way HTML forms send it.

encoding-guide-url.salam

```salam
import encoding

func link(base: str, q: str, city: str): str:
    ret base + "?q=" + encoding.URLEncode(q) + "&city=" + encoding.URLEncode(city)
end

func main:
    url := link("https://example.com/search", "coffee & cake", "تهران")
    println url

    part := "coffee%20%26%20cake"
    println "q is", encoding.URLDecode(part)
    println "plus means space:", encoding.URLDecode("tea+time")
    println "round trip:", encoding.URLDecode(encoding.URLEncode("a/b?c=d")) == "a/b?c=d"
end
```

Output:

```text
https://example.com/search?q=coffee%20%26%20cake&city=%D8%AA%D9%87%D8%B1%D8%A7%D9%86
q is coffee & cake
plus means space: tea time
round trip: true
```

Encode each value on its own and join them with `&`, as `link` does: encoding the whole URL at once would also escape the `?` and `&` that hold it together. For whole query strings with repeated keys, encoding/query does the bookkeeping, and encoding/url parses and rebuilds complete URLs.

## Which encoding for which job

| Job | Use |
| --- | --- |
| Binary data inside JSON, email or a header | `Base64Encode`, `Base64EncodeBytes` |
| Reading Base64 from a client or a file | `Base64DecodeStrict`, `Base64DecodeBytes` |
| Hashes, keys, debugging output | `HexEncode`, `HexDecode` |
| One value in a URL path or query | `URLEncode`, `URLDecode` |

## Functions

### `Base64Encode`

```salam
func Base64Encode(data: str): str
```

Turns text into standard Base64, padded with `=`.

encoding-Base64.salam

```salam
import encoding
import mem

func main:
    e := encoding.Base64Encode("hello world")
    println e
    println encoding.Base64Decode(e)
    mut ok := false
    println "[" + encoding.Base64DecodeStrict("***", ok) + "]", ok
    println encoding.Base64DecodeStrict("YWJj", ok), ok
    b := mem.Allocate(3 as u64)
    mem.Set(b, 255, 3 as u64)
    println encoding.Base64EncodeBytes(b, 3)
    out := mem.Allocate(8 as u64)
    println encoding.Base64DecodeBytes("AAEC", out, 8, ok), ok
    mem.Free(b)
    mem.Free(out)
end
```

Output:

```text
aGVsbG8gd29ybGQ=
hello world
[] false
abc true
////
3 true
```

Turns `n` bytes of memory into Base64.

The example for this item is shown with the ones above: encoding-Base64.salam

### `Base64Decode`

```salam

```

Turns Base64 back into text. It never fails: spaces, newlines and characters outside the Base64 alphabet are skipped, and missing padding is accepted.

The example for this item is shown with the ones above: encoding-Base64.salam

### `HexEncode`

```salam

```

Writes each byte of the text as two lower case hexadecimal digits.

encoding-Hex.salam

```salam
import encoding

func main:
    h := encoding.HexEncode("Hi!")
    println h, encoding.HexDecode(h)
    println encoding.HexVal("f"), encoding.HexVal("A"), encoding.HexVal("z")
    u := encoding.URLEncode("name=Ali & age=30")
    println u
    println encoding.URLDecode(u)
end
```

Output:

```text
486921 Hi!
15 10 -1
name%3DAli%20%26%20age%3D30
name=Ali & age=30
```

### `HexVal`

The example for this item is shown with the ones above: encoding-Hex.salam

### `HexDecode`

```salam
func HexDecode(s: str): str
```

Turns a hexadecimal string back into bytes, reading upper and lower case. It stops at the first invalid pair and drops an odd last digit, without an error.

The example for this item is shown with the ones above: encoding-Hex.salam

### `URLEncode`

```salam
func URLEncode(s: str): str
```

Percent-encodes text for a web address, byte by byte with upper case hex; letters, digits and `-_.~` are left as they are, and a space becomes `%20`.

The example for this item is shown with the ones above: encoding-Hex.salam

### `URLDecode`

```salam
func URLDecode(s: str): str
```

Undoes percent encoding and turns `+` into a space. A `%` not followed by two hex digits is kept as it is.

The example for this item is shown with the ones above: encoding-Hex.salam

### `Base64DecodeStrict`

```salam
func Base64DecodeStrict(s: str, ok &: bool): str
```

Like `Base64Decode`, but only padded standard Base64 is accepted; any other character, misplaced `=` or wrong length makes `ok` false and returns an empty string. Whitespace is still allowed.

The example for this item is shown with the ones above: encoding-Base64.salam

### `Base64DecodeBytes`

```salam
func Base64DecodeBytes(s: str, out: void*, cap: int, ok &: bool): int
```

Decodes strict Base64 into the buffer `out`, of capacity `cap`, and returns how many bytes it wrote. Bad input, or more bytes than `cap`, makes `ok` false and returns 0.

The example for this item is shown with the ones above: encoding-Base64.salam
