# encoding/json

https://salamlang.github.io/Salam/std/encoding-json/

Building and reading JSON: from a plain string through automatic struct conversion to streaming.

There are three ways to work with JSON here. For simple jobs, functions such as `Member`, `Object` and `Get` work directly on JSON text. For real programs, `Marshal` and `Unmarshal` convert a Salam struct to JSON and back. For data whose shape you do not know in advance, `Decode` returns a dynamic Value.

Set the key name of a field with `@json "name"` above it; `@json "-"` leaves the field out. Without it, the field's own name becomes the key.

Use this package for APIs, config files and anything another program will read. Its neighbours: encoding/yaml and encoding/toml for files people edit, encoding/msgpack when the data should be small and binary, and encoding/serde to read or write the same struct in several formats.

The things people get wrong:

- `GetInt` returns an `int`, 32 bits, and clamps anything larger: `3000000000` comes back as `2147483647`. For ids and timestamps, read the field with `Unmarshal` into an `i64`, or parse the text from `Get`.

- `Get`, `GetInt` and `Has` look only at the top level of an object. For nested values use `GetPath`, such as `GetPath(text, "user.address.city")`.

- Strict or lenient. `Unmarshal` fails on a missing field, an unknown key or a type that does not match; `UnmarshalLenient` keeps the struct's defaults for missing fields and skips unknown keys, but a wrong type still fails.

- Key order. `Marshal` writes fields in struct order, but a decoded `Value` object does not keep the order of its keys; pass `sort_keys` to `Encode` when output must be stable.

## Guide: load a config file into a struct

A config file is the most common JSON a program reads. Describe it as structs, give every field the default you want, and let `UnmarshalLenient` fill in what the file has. Nested objects map to nested structs and arrays map to `Vector` fields.

encoding-json-guide-config.salam

```salam
import encoding.json
import encoding.encerr

struct Database:
    pub host: str = "localhost"
    pub port: int = 5432
    pub pool: int = 4
end

struct Config:
    pub name: str = "app"
    pub debug: bool = false
    pub db: Database = Database {}
    pub admins: Vector<str> = Vector {}
end

func main:
    text := `{
  "name": "shop",
  "db": {"host": "db.internal", "port": 6432},
  "admins": ["sara", "reza"]
}`
    mut cfg := Config {}
    mut e := encerr.NoError()
    if not json.UnmarshalLenient(text, cfg, e):
        println "bad config:", e.message
        ret 1
    end
    println "name:", cfg.name
    println "debug:", cfg.debug
    println "database:", cfg.db.host, cfg.db.port, "pool", cfg.db.pool
    println "admins:", cfg.admins.len(), cfg.admins.get(0), cfg.admins.get(1)
end
```

Output:

```text
name: shop
debug: false
database: db.internal 6432 pool 4
admins: 2 sara reza
```

The file left out `debug` and `db.pool`, so they keep their defaults. That is the reason for the lenient form here: plain `Unmarshal` is strict and fails with `missing key 'pool'` when a field is absent, and with `unknown key` when the file has a key the struct does not. Strict is right for messages between programs, where a missing field is a bug; lenient is right for files people edit by hand. To read a file from disk, pass the text of `file.ReadAll` from fs/file.

## Guide: build an API response

Going the other way, `Marshal` turns a struct into compact JSON for the wire and `MarshalIndent` into readable JSON for logs and files. A `Vector` of structs becomes an array of objects, quotes inside strings are escaped, and the field order is the order of the struct.

encoding-json-guide-response.salam

```salam
import encoding.json

struct Item:
    pub sku: str = ""
    pub title: str = ""
    @json "price_cents"
    pub price: int = 0
    pub in_stock: bool = true
end

struct Page:
    pub page: int = 1
    pub total: int = 0
    pub items: Vector<Item> = Vector {}
    @json "-"
    pub cache_key: str = ""
end

func main:
    mut p := Page { page = 2, total = 14, cache_key = "products:2" }
    p.items.push(Item { sku = "BK-01", title = "Notebook", price = 1250 })
    p.items.push(Item { sku = "PN-07", title = "Pen \"fine\"", price = 300, in_stock = false })

    println json.Marshal(p)
    println json.MarshalIndent(p, "  ")
end
```

Output:

```text
{"page":2,"total":14,"items":[{"sku":"BK-01","title":"Notebook","price_cents":1250,"in_stock":true},{"sku":"PN-07","title":"Pen \"fine\"","price_cents":300,"in_stock":false}]}
{
  "page": 2,
  "total": 14,
  "items": [
    {
      "sku": "BK-01",
      "title": "Notebook",
      "price_cents": 1250,
      "in_stock": true
    },
    {
      "sku": "PN-07",
      "title": "Pen \"fine\"",
      "price_cents": 300,
      "in_stock": false
    }
  ]
}
```

`@json "price_cents"` renames a field in the JSON without renaming it in the code, and `@json "-"` keeps internal fields such as `cache_key` out of the output. Use it for passwords and tokens too, so they can never leak into a response by accident.

## Guide: explore JSON of unknown shape

When you do not know the shape ahead of time, for example a webhook from another service, `Decode` gives a tree of Value nodes. Ask each node what it is with `IsString`, `IsInt`, `IsObject` and the rest, then read it with the matching `As` function.

encoding-json-guide-dynamic.salam

```salam
import encoding.json
import encoding.value
import encoding.encerr
import str

func describe(v: value.Value): str:
    if value.IsString(v): ret "string " + value.AsString(v) end
    if value.IsInt(v): ret "int " + str.FromInt(value.AsInt(v)) end
    if value.IsFloat(v): ret "float " + str.FromFloat(value.AsFloat(v)) end
    if value.IsBool(v):
        if value.AsBool(v): ret "bool true" end
        ret "bool false"
    end
    if value.IsArray(v): ret "array of " + str.FromInt(value.ArrayLen(v)) end
    if value.IsObject(v): ret "object with " + str.FromInt(value.ObjectLen(v)) + " keys" end
    ret "null"
end

func main:
    mut e := encerr.NoError()
    doc := json.Decode(`{"id": 7, "name": "Lamp", "price": 19.5, "sale": true, "tags": ["home", "light"], "size": {"w": 20, "h": 45}, "note": null}`, e)
    if encerr.IsError(e):
        println "parse error:", e.message
        ret 1
    end
    println "keys:", value.ObjectLen(doc)
    keys := ["id", "name", "price", "sale", "tags", "size", "note", "color"]
    each k in keys:
        if not value.ObjectHas(doc, k):
            println k, "is missing"
            continue
        end
        println k, "=", describe(value.ObjectGet(doc, k))
    end
    size := value.ObjectGet(doc, "size")
    println "area:", value.AsInt(value.ObjectGet(size, "w")) * value.AsInt(value.ObjectGet(size, "h"))
end
```

Output:

```text
keys: 7
id = int 7
name = string Lamp
price = float 19.5
sale = bool true
tags = array of 2
size = object with 2 keys
note = null
color is missing
area: 900
```

Whole numbers come back as `int` and numbers with a fraction as `float`; `IsNumber` accepts both. An object does not keep the order of its keys, so when the order matters, walk a list of the keys you expect, as this program does, and use `ObjectHas` for the optional ones.

## Guide: report bad input

Every decoding function takes an `EncodingError` from encoding/encerr. When it fails, `message` says what was wrong and `position` is the byte offset where the reader stopped, which is what you show the user. The text helpers like `Get` never fail; they return an empty string for a missing key, so check with `Has` or `Valid` first when that matters.

encoding-json-guide-errors.salam

```salam
import encoding.json
import encoding.encerr

struct Signup:
    pub email: str = ""
    pub age: int = 0
end

func load(text: str):
    mut s := Signup {}
    mut e := encerr.NoError()
    if json.Unmarshal(text, s, e):
        println "ok:", s.email, s.age
    else:
        println "error at", e.position, "->", e.message
    end
end

func load_lenient(text: str):
    mut s := Signup {}
    mut e := encerr.NoError()
    if json.UnmarshalLenient(text, s, e):
        println "lenient ok:", s.email, s.age
    end
end

func main:
    load(`{"email": "a@example.com", "age": 31}`)
    load(`{"email": "a@example.com", "age": "31"}`)
    load(`{"email": "a@example.com", "age": 31`)
    load(`{"email": "a@example.com", "age": 31, "plan": "pro"}`)
    load_lenient(`{"email": "a@example.com", "age": 31, "plan": "pro"}`)

    println "valid:", json.Valid(`[1, 2, 3]`), json.Valid(`[1, 2,]`)
    println "missing key gives [" + json.Get(`{"a": 1}`, "b") + "]"
end
```

Output:

```text
ok: a@example.com 31
error at 34 -> value does not match the expected type
error at 36 -> expected ',' or '}'
error at 46 -> unknown key
lenient ok: a@example.com 31
valid: true false
missing key gives []
```

## Guide: stream newline-delimited JSON

Logs and exports often hold one JSON value per line (NDJSON). A decoder reads them one at a time: `More` says whether another value is left, and `Decode` returns the next one. `NewBufDecoder` reads from a string and `NewDecoder` from an open file. Encoders write the same format, one value per line.

encoding-json-guide-ndjson.salam

```salam
import encoding.json
import encoding.value

func main:
    logs := `{"level": "info", "msg": "started", "ms": 3}
{"level": "warn", "msg": "slow query", "ms": 820}
{"level": "info", "msg": "request", "ms": 41}
{"level": "error", "msg": "timeout", "ms": 5000}
{"level": "info", "msg": "request", "ms": 37}
`
    mut counts := HashMap {} as HashMap<str, int>
    mut slow := 0
    mut d := json.NewBufDecoder(logs)
    until d.More():
        line := d.Decode()
        level := value.AsString(value.ObjectGet(line, "level"))
        counts.put(level, counts.get_or(level, 0) + 1)
        if value.AsInt(value.ObjectGet(line, "ms")) > 500:
            slow += 1
        end
    end
    println "info:", counts.get_or("info", 0), "warn:", counts.get_or("warn", 0), "error:", counts.get_or("error", 0)
    println "slower than 500 ms:", slow

    mut out := json.NewBufEncoder()
    out.Encode(value.ValueString("summary"))
    out.Encode(value.ValueInt(slow))
    println out.String()
    out.Close()
end
```

Output:

```text
info: 3 warn: 1 error: 1
slower than 500 ms: 2
"summary"
2
```

`until d.More():` reads naturally as "while there is more", because `until` in Salam runs while its condition holds.

## Which function for which job

| Job | Use |
| --- | --- |
| Read one field from a small JSON text | `Get`, `GetInt`, `GetPath` |
| Build a small JSON text by hand | `Member`, `MemberInt`, `Object`, `Array` |
| Struct to JSON | `Marshal`, `MarshalIndent` |
| JSON to struct, exact | `Unmarshal` |
| JSON to struct, with defaults and extra keys | `UnmarshalLenient` |
| Unknown shape | `Decode`, `Encode` |
| One value per line | `NewDecoder`, `NewEncoder` |
| Pretty print or shrink existing text | `Indent`, `Minify` |
| A JSON Schema for a struct | `Schema` |

## Types

### `JSONOptions`

```salam
struct JSONOptions
```

The options for `Encode`.

| Name | Type | Description |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `indent` | `str = ""` | The indent unit; empty means one line. |
| `sort_keys` | `bool = false` | Write the keys in alphabetical order. Without it the key order is not fixed. |
| `ignore_null` | `bool = false` | Leave out the keys whose value is null. |

encoding-json-Value.salam

```salam
import encoding.json
import encoding.value
import encoding.encerr
import fs.file

func main:
    mut e := encerr.NoError()
    v := json.Decode(`{"city": "Tehran", "zones": [1, 2, 22]}`, e)
    println encerr.IsError(e), value.AsString(value.ObjectGet(v, "city"))
    println json.EncodeDefault(v)
    opts := json.JSONOptions { indent = "  ", sort_keys = true }
    println json.Encode(v, opts)
    _ := json.Decode("[1, 2", e)
    println encerr.IsError(e), e.position
    mut enc := json.NewBufEncoder()
    enc.Encode(value.ValueInt(1))
    enc.Encode(value.ValueString("two"))
    println enc.String()
    enc.Close()
    mut pretty := json.NewBufEncoderIndent("  ")
    pretty.Encode(v)
    println pretty.String()
    pretty.Close()
    out := file.Open("lines.ndjson", "wb")
    mut lines := json.NewEncoder(out)
    lines.Encode(value.ValueInt(10))
    lines.Encode(value.ValueInt(20))
    lines.Close()
    mut tabbed := json.NewEncoderIndent(file.Open("pretty.json", "wb"), "\t")
    tabbed.Encode(v)
    tabbed.Close()
    mut reader := json.NewDecoder(file.Open("lines.ndjson", "rb"))
    mut total := 0 as i64
    until reader.More():
        total += value.AsInt(reader.Decode())
    end
    println total
    mut two := json.NewBufDecoder("{\"a\": 1}\n{\"a\": 2}\n")
    until two.More():
        println json.EncodeDefault(two.Decode())
    end
end
```

Output:

```text
false Tehran
{"city": "Tehran", "zones": [1, 2, 22]}
{
  "city": "Tehran",
  "zones": [
    1,
    2,
    22
  ]
}
true 5
1
"two"
{
  "city": "Tehran",
  "zones": [
    1,
    2,
    22
  ]
}
30
{"a": 1}
{"a": 2}
```

### `Valid`

```salam

```

True when the text is valid JSON.

encoding-json-Build.salam

```salam
import encoding.json

func main:
    mut tags := Vector {} as Vector<str>
    tags.push(json.Str("hello"))
    tags.push(json.Str(`a "quoted" line`))
    mut members := Vector {} as Vector<str>
    members.push(json.Member("name", "Ali"))
    members.push(json.MemberInt("age", 30))
    members.push(json.MemberBool("admin", false))
    members.push(json.MemberFloat("score", 18.5))
    members.push(json.MemberRaw("tags", json.Array(tags)))
    text := json.Object(members)
    println text
    println json.Valid(text), json.Valid("{broken")
    println json.Get(text, "name"), json.GetInt(text, "age"), json.GetFloat(text, "score")
    println json.Has(text, "admin"), json.Has(text, "email"), json.Keys(text)
    println json.Escape("one\ttwo")
    pretty := json.Indent(text)
    println pretty
    println json.Minify(pretty) == json.Minify(text)
    println json.Indent4(`{"a":1}`)
    println json.IndentTabs(`{"a":1}`) == "{\n\t\"a\": 1\n}", json.IndentWith(`[1]`, "--")
    nested := `{"user":{"tags":["a","b"],"name":"Ali"}}`
    println json.GetPath(nested, "user.name"), json.GetPath(nested, "user.tags.1"), json.Items(json.GetPath(nested, "user.tags")).len()
    println json.Unquote(`"\u0633\u0644\u0627\u0645"`)
end
```

```text
one\ttwo

    "hello",
```

### `SchemaEnvelope`

```salam
func SchemaEnvelope<T>(v: T): str
```

Builds the JSON Schema of a value's type, along with the definitions of the nested types, inside an envelope to be combined later with `SchemaMerge`.

encoding-json-Marshal.salam

```salam
import encoding.json
import encoding.encerr

struct User:
    @json "name"
    pub name: str = ""
    @json "age"
    pub age: int = 0
    @json "tags"
    pub tags: Vector<str> = Vector {}
    @json "-"
    pub password: str = ""
end

func main:
    mut u := User { name = "Maryam", age = 28, password = "secret" }
    u.tags.push("admin")
    println json.Marshal(u)
    println json.MarshalIndent(u, "  ")
    mut loaded := User {}
    mut e := encerr.NoError()
    println json.Unmarshal(`{"name": "Reza", "age": 41, "tags": ["a", "b"]}`, loaded, e)
    println loaded.name, loaded.age, loaded.tags.len()
    println json.Unmarshal(`{"name": "Reza", "age": "forty"}`, loaded, e), e.message
    mut lenient := User {}
    println json.UnmarshalLenient(`{"name": "Sara", "extra": 1}`, lenient, e), lenient.name
    println json.Schema(u)
    envelope := json.SchemaEnvelope(u)
    println json.SchemaMerge(envelope) == json.Schema(u)
end
```

Output:

```text
{"name":"Maryam","age":28,"tags":["admin"]}
{
  "name": "Maryam",
  "age": 28,
  "tags": [
    "admin"
  ]
}
true
Reza 41 2
false value does not match the expected type
true Sara
{"$schema":"https://json-schema.org/draft/2020-12/schema","$defs":{"User":{"title":"User","type":"object","properties":{"name":{"type":"string"},"age":{"type":"integer","format":"int32"},"tags":{"type":"array","items":{"type":"string"}}},"required":["name","age","tags"],"additionalProperties":false}},"$ref":"#/$defs/User"}
true
```

# encoding/yaml

https://salamlang.github.io/Salam/std/encoding-yaml/

Reading YAML by path, building and writing it, and converting it to JSON.

YAML is the usual format for configuration files. This package converts YAML to JSON internally, which is what makes its reading functions simple and what lets it work alongside the json package.

The reading functions take a path: keys separated by dots, with a list index in square brackets, as in `app.hosts[1]`. A path that is not there gives an empty string or zero; to tell that apart from a real value, use `Has`.

It reads the YAML that configuration files use: nested maps, lists in dashed and `[flow]` form, quoted strings, `|` and `>` block text, comments and several documents. For flat `key = value` settings with sections and overrides, config is simpler, and it reads YAML too.

The things people get wrong:

- Anchors and aliases (`&base`, `*base`, `<<: *base`) are not supported. A value like `&a 1` is read as the string `&a 1`, and an anchor on a map, as in `base: &base` followed by indented keys, loses the rest of the document without an error. Write such files out in full, or expand them with another tool first.

- `yes`, `no`, `on` and `off` are strings, as in YAML 1.2, so `GetBool` is false for them. Only `true` and `false` are booleans.

- `GetInt` returns a 32-bit `int` and wraps around for larger numbers. Read sizes, ids and timestamps through `ToJSON` into an `i64` field (see below).

- Every path function parses the whole text again. For many reads from a large file, call `ToJSON` or `Decode` once and work on the result.

## Guide: read a config file with defaults

The path functions are the quickest way to read a config file. Check first that the sections you depend on exist with `HasKeys`, then read each setting with the typed getter. For optional settings, wrap `Get` in a small helper that falls back to a default when `Has` says the key is not there.

encoding-yaml-guide-config.salam

```salam
import encoding.yaml

func setting(text: str, path: str, def: str): str:
    if yaml.Has(text, path):
        ret yaml.Get(text, path)
    end
    ret def
end

func main:
    text := `# settings for the shop
server:
  host: 0.0.0.0
  port: 8080
  workers: 4
log:
  level: debug
features:
  search: true
  beta: false
`
    mut required := Vector {} as Vector<str>
    required.push("server")
    required.push("log")
    if not yaml.HasKeys(text, required):
        println "config is missing a section"
        ret 1
    end

    println "listen on", yaml.Get(text, "server.host") + ":" + yaml.Get(text, "server.port")
    println "workers:", yaml.GetInt(text, "server.workers")
    println "log level:", setting(text, "log.level", "info")
    println "log file:", setting(text, "log.file", "stdout")
    println "search on:", yaml.GetBool(text, "features.search"), "beta on:", yaml.GetBool(text, "features.beta")
    println "feature flags:", yaml.Keys(text, "features")
end
```

Output:

```text
listen on 0.0.0.0:8080
workers: 4
log level: debug
log file: stdout
search on: true beta on: false
feature flags: ["search", "beta"]
```

Comments starting with `#` are ignored. `GetInt` and `GetBool` return 0 and `false` for a missing key, which is also a real value, so a default other than zero needs the `Has` check.

## Guide: YAML into a struct

For a config with many fields, a struct is easier to pass around than a text and a list of paths. There is no YAML `Unmarshal` of its own, but there does not need to be: `ToJSON` turns the YAML into JSON, and encoding/json fills the struct, with the same `@json` names and defaults.

encoding-yaml-guide-struct.salam

```salam
import encoding.yaml
import encoding.json
import encoding.encerr

struct Service:
    pub name: str = ""
    pub image: str = ""
    pub replicas: int = 1
    pub ports: Vector<int> = Vector {}
end

func main:
    text := `name: api
image: shop/api:2.3
ports:
  - 80
  - 443
`
    mut s := Service {}
    mut e := encerr.NoError()
    if not json.UnmarshalLenient(yaml.ToJSON(text), s, e):
        println "bad service:", e.message
        ret 1
    end
    println s.name, "runs", s.image
    println "replicas:", s.replicas
    println "ports:", s.ports.len(), s.ports.get(0), s.ports.get(1)
end
```

Output:

```text
api runs shop/api:2.3
replicas: 1
ports: 2 80 443
```

`replicas` is not in the file, so it keeps its default of 1 because the lenient form was used. With `json.Unmarshal` the missing key would be an error.

## Guide: walk a list of records

A list of objects, such as the jobs of a CI file, is read with `Len` and an index in the path. Build the path for item `i` once and add the field names to it. `[lint]` is the short flow form of a list, and reads the same way as the dashed form.

encoding-yaml-guide-list.salam

```salam
import encoding.yaml
import str

func main:
    text := `jobs:
  - name: lint
    run: salam format --check
  - name: test
    run: sh tests/run.sh
    needs: [lint]
  - name: deploy
    run: sh deploy.sh
    needs: [test]
    branch: main
`
    n := yaml.Len(text, "jobs")
    println n, "jobs"
    repeat n in i:
        at := "jobs[" + str.FromInt(i) + "]"
        line := yaml.Get(text, at + ".name") + ": " + yaml.Get(text, at + ".run")
        if yaml.Has(text, at + ".needs"):
            println line, "(after", yaml.Get(text, at + ".needs[0]") + ")"
        else:
            println line
        end
        if yaml.Has(text, at + ".branch"):
            println "  only on", yaml.Get(text, at + ".branch")
        end
    end
end
```

Output:

```text
3 jobs
lint: salam format --check
test: sh tests/run.sh (after lint)
deploy: sh deploy.sh (after test)
  only on main
```

## Guide: several documents in one file

Kubernetes manifests and some log formats put several YAML documents in one file, separated by a line with `---`. `SplitDocuments` cuts them apart, and each piece is then an ordinary YAML text for the other functions.

encoding-yaml-guide-multi.salam

```salam
import encoding.yaml

func main:
    text := `kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: web
spec:
  replicas: 3
---
kind: Service
metadata:
  name: web
spec:
  port: 80
---
kind: ConfigMap
metadata:
  name: web-config
`
    docs := yaml.SplitDocuments(text)
    println docs.len(), "documents"
    each d in docs:
        println "-", yaml.Get(d, "kind"), yaml.Get(d, "metadata.name"), "valid:", yaml.Valid(d)
    end
    println "deployment as JSON:", yaml.ToJSON(docs.get(0))
end
```

Output:

```text
3 documents
- Deployment web valid: true
- Service web valid: true
- ConfigMap web-config valid: true
deployment as JSON: {"kind": "Deployment", "metadata": {"name": "web"}, "spec": {"replicas": 3}}
```

`ToJSON` is also how you hand YAML to anything that speaks JSON, such as an HTTP API. Going the other way, `Dump` writes JSON text as YAML.

## Guide: what type did the value get?

YAML decides the type of a value from how it looks, and the result is not always what the author meant. `TypeOf` shows what the reader saw. Here `yes` stayed a string, `007` kept its zeros as a string, and the five gigabyte limit is too big for `GetInt` but fine for an `i64` field.

encoding-yaml-guide-types.salam

```salam
import encoding.yaml
import encoding.json
import encoding.encerr

struct Limits:
    pub max_upload: i64 = 0
    pub public: bool = false
    pub code: str = ""
end

func load(text: str):
    mut l := Limits {}
    mut err := encerr.EncodingError {}
    if json.UnmarshalLenient(yaml.ToJSON(text), l, err):
        println "  loaded:", l.max_upload, l.public, l.code
    else:
        println "  refused:", err.message
    end
end

func main:
    text := "max_upload: 5368709120\npublic: yes\ncode: 007\n"
    println "public is a", yaml.TypeOf(text, "public"), "so GetBool says", yaml.GetBool(text, "public")
    println "code is a", yaml.TypeOf(text, "code"), "with the text", yaml.Get(text, "code")
    println "GetInt overflows:", yaml.GetInt(text, "max_upload")
    println "as JSON:", yaml.ToJSON(text)
    load(text)
    load("max_upload: 5368709120\npublic: true\ncode: \"007\"\n")
end
```

Output:

```text
public is a string so GetBool says false
code is a string with the text 007
GetInt overflows: 1073741824
as JSON: {"max_upload": 5368709120, "public": "yes", "code": "007"}
  refused: value does not match the expected type
  loaded: 5368709120 true 007
```

The struct route also checks the types for you: `public: yes` is refused instead of read as false. Writing `true` and quoting values that must stay text, such as `"007"`, makes the file mean the same to every reader.

## Which function for which job

| Job | Use |
| --- | --- |
| Read a few settings | `Get`, `GetInt`, `GetBool`, `GetFloat` |
| Tell a missing key from an empty one | `Has`, `HasKeys` |
| Look at the structure | `TypeOf`, `Len`, `Keys` |
| A whole file into a struct | `ToJSON` and `json.UnmarshalLenient` |
| Unknown shape | `Decode` to a Value, `Encode` back |
| Write YAML | `Object`, `Member`, or `Dump` from JSON |
| Files with `---` | `SplitDocuments` |

## Functions

### `Decode`

```salam
func Decode(text: str, err &: encerr.EncodingError): value.Value
```

Turns YAML into a dynamic `Value`.

encoding-yaml-Build.salam

```salam
import encoding.yaml
import encoding.value
import encoding.encerr
import str

func main:
    mut members := Vector {} as Vector<str>
    members.push(yaml.Member("name", "salam"))
    members.push(yaml.MemberInt("port", 8080))
    members.push(yaml.MemberBool("debug", false))
    members.push(yaml.MemberFloat("ratio", 0.25))
    mut hosts := Vector {} as Vector<str>
    hosts.push(yaml.Str("a: b"))
    members.push(yaml.MemberRaw("hosts", yaml.Array(hosts)))
    object := yaml.Object(members)
    println object
    println yaml.Dump(object)
    println str.Contains(yaml.DumpTabs(`{"a": {"b": 1}}`), "\tb: 1"), yaml.DumpWith(`{"a": [1]}`, "    ")
    println yaml.Escape("one: two")
    println yaml.Parse("x: 1")
    mut e := encerr.NoError()
    v := yaml.Decode("city: Tehran\npopulation: 9000000\n", e)
    println value.AsInt(value.ObjectGet(v, "population"))
    println yaml.Encode(v)
end
```

Output:

```text
{"name": "salam", "port": 8080, "debug": false, "ratio": 0.25, "hosts": ["a: b"]}
name: salam
port: 8080
debug: false
ratio: 0.25
hosts:
  - "a: b"
true a:
    - 1
one: two
{"x": 1}
9000000
city: Tehran
population: 9000000
```

```salam
import encoding.yaml

func main:
```

# encoding/csv

https://salamlang.github.io/Salam/std/encoding-csv/

Reading and writing CSV files, with correct quoting and conversion to a dynamic value.

CSV is the simplest table format: one row per line, fields separated by commas. A field containing a comma, a quote or a line break is wrapped in quotes, and a quote inside it is doubled. This package reads and writes that format, one line at a time with `ReadLine` and `WriteLine` or a whole text with `ReadAll` and `WriteAll`, and converts it to and from a Value for encoding/json.

Every field is a string; CSV has no numbers or booleans. For spreadsheets with several sheets, formulas or types, see excel; for CSV that feeds a machine learning model, data.

The things people get wrong:

- The separator is always a comma. A file from a European Excel with `;` between fields, or a tab-separated file, reads as one field per line; replace the separator or split those lines yourself.

- A quoted field must be followed directly by a comma or the end of the line. In `"Pen" ,blue` the space after the quote ends the row, and the rest of the line is dropped without an error.

- Line breaks inside a quoted field cannot be read back: `ReadAll` splits the text into lines first. `WriteLine` quotes such a field correctly for other tools, but this reader cuts it in two.

- `FromValue` takes the columns from the keys of the first object, and an object does not keep its key order, so the columns can come out in a different order from the file you read. When the order matters, write the rows yourself with `WriteLine`.

## Guide: totals from a CSV export

The typical job is a spreadsheet export: read every row, skip the header, convert the number columns and add them up. `ReadAll` gives a `CSVTable` whose `rows` each hold a `fields` vector, one string per column. A `HashMap` keeps the totals and a `Vector` keeps the cities in the order they first appeared.

encoding-csv-guide-report.salam

```salam
import encoding.csv

func main:
    text := `date,city,product,amount
2026-10-01,Tehran,tea,120
2026-10-01,Shiraz,coffee,90
2026-10-02,Tehran,coffee,75
2026-10-02,Tabriz,tea,40
2026-10-03,Shiraz,tea,60
`
    mut table := csv.ReadAll(text)
    mut cities := Vector {} as Vector<str>
    mut totals := HashMap {} as HashMap<str, int>
    mut grand := 0
    each i, row in table.rows:
        if i == 0 or row.fields.len() < 4:
            continue
        end
        city := row.fields.get(1)
        amount := row.fields.get(3).to_int()
        if not totals.has(city):
            cities.push(city)
        end
        totals.put(city, totals.get_or(city, 0) + amount)
        grand += amount
    end
    each c in cities:
        println c, totals.get(c)
    end
    println "total", grand
    csv.FreeTable(table)
end
```

Output:

```text
Tehran 195
Shiraz 150
Tabriz 40
total 385
```

Guard against short rows, as the `row.fields.len() < 4` check does: a blank line or a hand-edited file can have fewer columns than the header. Free the table with `FreeTable` when you are done.

## Guide: write a CSV file

`WriteLine` joins one row and adds quotes only where they are needed: around a field with a comma, a quote or a line break, with inner quotes doubled. That is what Excel, LibreOffice and most import tools expect, and writing the rows yourself keeps the columns in the order you choose.

encoding-csv-guide-export.salam

```salam
import encoding.csv

struct Contact:
    pub name: str = ""
    pub company: str = ""
    pub note: str = ""
end

func main:
    mut people := Vector {} as Vector<Contact>
    people.push(Contact { name = "Sara Ahmadi", company = "Nik, Ltd.", note = "prefers email" })
    people.push(Contact { name = "Reza", company = "Pars", note = `said "call me Monday"` })

    mut out := ""
    mut header := Vector {} as Vector<str>
    header.push("name")
    header.push("company")
    header.push("note")
    out = out + csv.WriteLine(header) + "\n"
    each p in people:
        mut f := Vector {} as Vector<str>
        f.push(p.name)
        f.push(p.company)
        f.push(p.note)
        out = out + csv.WriteLine(f) + "\n"
    end
    print out

    row := csv.ReadLine(`Reza,Pars,"said ""call me Monday"""`)
    println "read back:", row.get(2)
end
```

Output:

```text
name,company,note
Sara Ahmadi,"Nik, Ltd.",prefers email
Reza,Pars,"said ""call me Monday"""
read back: said "call me Monday"
```

Write the header row the same way as the data rows. `WriteLine` does not add the line break, so add `"\n"` yourself, or `"\r\n"` for tools that insist on it. To save the result, write `out` with fs/file.

## Guide: CSV to JSON

`ToValue` uses the header row as keys and turns every other row into an object, which encoding/json can then print. That is a small CSV to JSON converter in a few lines. `FromValue` goes back from an array of objects to CSV text.

encoding-csv-guide-json.salam

```salam
import encoding.csv
import encoding.json
import encoding.value

func main:
    text := "sku,title,stock\nBK-01,Notebook,12\nPN-07,\"Pen, blue\",0\n"
    rows := csv.ToValue(text)
    println value.ArrayLen(rows), "rows"
    opts := json.JSONOptions { indent = "  ", sort_keys = true }
    println json.Encode(rows, opts)

    first := value.ArrayGet(rows, 0)
    println "stock is a string:", value.IsString(value.ObjectGet(first, "stock"))
end
```

Output:

```text
2 rows
[
  {
    "sku": "BK-01",
    "stock": "12",
    "title": "Notebook"
  },
  {
    "sku": "PN-07",
    "stock": "0",
    "title": "Pen, blue"
  }
]
stock is a string: true
```

Every field stays a string, even `12`, because CSV has no types. Convert the columns you know are numbers with `to_int()` or `to_float()`. With `CSVOptions { header = false }`, `ToValueWith` reads a file without a header: every row, the first one included, becomes an object with the keys `col0`, `col1` and so on.

## Guide: edge cases

The reader keeps fields exactly as they are written. That matters in a few places:

encoding-csv-guide-pitfalls.salam

```salam
import encoding.csv

func show(line: str):
    f := csv.ReadLine(line)
    mut s := ""
    each x in f:
        s = s + "[" + x + "]"
    end
    println f.len(), "fields:", s
end

func main:
    show("a,b,c")
    show("a,,c")
    show(" a , b ")
    show(`"x,y",z`)
    show(`"she said ""hi""",ok`)
    show("trailing,")
    show(`"Pen" ,blue,3`)
    show("sku;title;stock")

    mut t := csv.ReadAll("id,name\r\n1,Ali\r\n2,Sara\r\n")
    println "rows with CRLF:", t.rows.len(), t.rows.get(2).fields.get(1)
    csv.FreeTable(t)
end
```

Output:

```text
3 fields: [a][b][c]
3 fields: [a][][c]
2 fields: [ a ][ b ]
2 fields: [x,y][z]
2 fields: [she said "hi"][ok]
2 fields: [trailing][]
1 fields: [Pen]
1 fields: [sku;title;stock]
rows with CRLF: 3 Sara
```

- An empty field, including one after a trailing comma, is an empty string, not a missing column.

- Spaces around a field are kept; trim them with `str.Trim` if your source pads columns.

- Windows line endings (`\r\n`) are handled by `ReadAll`.

- `ReadAll` skips blank lines, so a table never has empty rows.

- A space between a closing quote and the comma ends the row: `"Pen" ,blue,3` gives one field.

- A line with semicolons is one field, because only commas separate fields.

- `ReadAll` splits the text into lines before it reads the fields, so a quoted field that contains a line break comes back cut in two. If your data can hold line breaks, replace them before writing the file.

## Types

### `CSVRow`

```salam
struct CSVRow
```

One row.

| Name | Type | Description |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `fields` | `Vector` | The row's fields. |

encoding-csv-Table.salam

```salam
import encoding.csv
import encoding.value

func main:
    text := "name,city\nAli,Tehran\n\"Sara, engineer\",\"Shiraz\"\n"
    mut table := csv.ReadAll(text)
    println table.rows.len()
    each row in table.rows:
        println row.fields.len(), row.fields[0]
    end
    println csv.WriteAll(table)
    csv.FreeTable(table)
    println csv.ReadLine(`a,"b,c",d`)
    mut fields := Vector {} as Vector<str>
    fields.push("plain")
    fields.push(`with "quotes"`)
    println csv.WriteLine(fields)
    v := csv.ToValue("name,age\nAli,30\n")
    println value.ArrayLen(v), value.AsString(value.ObjectGet(value.ArrayGet(v, 0), "name"))
    println csv.FromValue(v)
    opts := csv.CSVOptions { header = false }
    rows := csv.ToValueWith("1,2\n3,4\n", opts)
    println value.ArrayLen(rows), csv.FromValueWith(rows, opts)
end
```

Output:

```text
3
2 name
2 Ali
2 Sara, engineer
name,city
Ali,Tehran
"Sara, engineer",Shiraz
["a", "b,c", "d"]
plain,"with ""quotes"""
1 Ali
age,name
30,Ali
2 1,2
3,4
```

### `CSVOptions`


| Name | Type | Description |

| `header` | `bool = true` | The first row is a header; true by default. When false, every row becomes an object with the keys `col0`, `col1` and so on, and `FromValueWith` writes no header row. |

The example for this item is shown with the ones above: encoding-csv-Table.salam

# encoding/toml

https://salamlang.github.io/Salam/std/encoding-toml/

Reading and writing TOML configuration files.

TOML is the configuration format of `[section]` tables and `key = value` lines used by `Cargo.toml`, `pyproject.toml` and many server configs. This package reads TOML text into a dynamic Value and writes a Value back as TOML. It has five functions: `DecodeStrict`, `Decode` and `Valid` for reading, `EncodeStrict` and `Encode` for writing.

Pick TOML for files people edit by hand. For data that programs exchange use encoding/json; for YAML files such as CI or Kubernetes configs use encoding/yaml; for `KEY=value` secrets files use encoding/envfile. If you only want settings loaded from a file with defaults and environment overrides, config may already do the job.

### How TOML maps to a Value

| TOML | Value |
| --- | --- |
| `[table]`, `[a.b]`, inline `{ k = v }`, dotted keys `a.b = 1` | object (nested) |
| `[[name]]` | array of objects |
| `"basic"` with escapes, `'literal'` | string |
| `42`, `-7`, `1_000`, `0x1F`, `0o17`, `0b101` | int (64-bit) |
| `3.5`, `1e6`, `inf`, `nan` | float |
| `true`, `false` | bool |
| dates and times such as `1979-05-27T07:32:00Z` | string, unchanged |

### What trips people up

- Use `DecodeStrict`, not `Decode`, on files people edit. `Decode` never reports an error: on broken input it returns whatever it read before the mistake, so a typo silently drops the rest of the file.

- The parser is lenient. It checks syntax, not every rule of the TOML specification. A key or `[table]` defined twice is accepted (the tables merge, the later key wins), and an unquoted word such as `mode = fast` is read as the string `"fast"` instead of being rejected.

- Some syntax is missing. Multi-line strings in triple quotes (`"""` or `'''`) make the document invalid, and the 8-digit `\U` escape is not decoded. Dates stay strings; parse them with time if you need them.

- Writing is not formatting. `Encode` writes keys in no fixed order, drops keys whose value is null, and writes an array of objects as an inline array `[{...}, {...}]` rather than `[[table]]` blocks. The result is valid TOML that reads back to the same data, but comments and layout of an original file are lost.

## Guide: read a project manifest

Project files such as `Cargo.toml` or `pyproject.toml` mix plain tables, inline tables and arrays of tables. `DecodeStrict` reads the whole file into a Value and tells you through `ok` whether it was valid; from there the `value` functions walk it.

encoding-toml-guide-manifest.salam

```salam
import encoding.toml
import encoding.value
import sort

func main:
    text := `[package]
name = "shop"
version = "1.4.0"
authors = ["Sara", "Reza"]

[dependencies]
http = "2.1"
json = { version = "1.0", optional = true }
log = "0.9"

[[bin]]
name = "shop"
path = "src/main.salam"

[[bin]]
name = "shop-admin"
path = "src/admin.salam"
`
    mut ok := false
    doc := toml.DecodeStrict(text, ok)
    if not ok:
        println "not valid TOML"
        ret 1
    end
    pkg := value.ObjectGet(doc, "package")
    println value.AsString(value.ObjectGet(pkg, "name")), value.AsString(value.ObjectGet(pkg, "version"))
    println "authors:", value.ArrayLen(value.ObjectGet(pkg, "authors"))

    deps := value.ObjectGet(doc, "dependencies")
    names := value.ObjectKeys(deps)
    sort.QuickSort(names)
    each n in names:
        d := value.ObjectGet(deps, n)
        if value.IsString(d):
            println "dep", n, value.AsString(d)
        else:
            println "dep", n, value.AsString(value.ObjectGet(d, "version")), "(optional)"
        end
    end

    bins := value.ObjectGet(doc, "bin")
    repeat value.ArrayLen(bins) in i:
        b := value.ArrayGet(bins, i)
        println "binary", value.AsString(value.ObjectGet(b, "name")), "from", value.AsString(value.ObjectGet(b, "path"))
    end
end
```

Output:

```text
shop 1.4.0
authors: 2
dep http 2.1
dep json 1.0 (optional)
dep log 0.9
binary shop from src/main.salam
binary shop-admin from src/admin.salam
```

A dependency can be a plain version string or an inline table with more detail, so the program asks `IsString` before reading it. Objects do not keep the order of their keys; sorting `ObjectKeys` with `sort.QuickSort` gives a stable listing.

## Guide: TOML into a struct

For settings you use all over a program, load them into a struct once. Encode the decoded value as JSON with `json.EncodeDefault` and let `json.UnmarshalLenient` fill the struct: keys the file leaves out keep the struct's defaults, and a `[server]` table fills a nested struct.

encoding-toml-guide-struct.salam

```salam
import encoding.toml
import encoding.json
import encoding.encerr

struct Server:
    pub host: str = "127.0.0.1"
    pub port: int = 8000
end

struct Settings:
    pub title: str = ""
    pub debug: bool = false
    pub server: Server = Server {}
    pub allowed: Vector<str> = Vector {}
end

func main:
    text := `title = "Shop admin"
allowed = ["10.0.0.0/8", "192.168.1.0/24"]

[server]
port = 9090
`
    mut ok := false
    doc := toml.DecodeStrict(text, ok)
    mut s := Settings {}
    mut e := encerr.NoError()
    if not ok or not json.UnmarshalLenient(json.EncodeDefault(doc), s, e):
        println "bad settings"
        ret 1
    end
    println s.title, "debug:", s.debug
    println "listen on", s.server.host, s.server.port
    println "allowed networks:", s.allowed.len(), s.allowed.get(0)
end
```

Output:

```text
Shop admin debug: false
listen on 127.0.0.1 9090
allowed networks: 2 10.0.0.0/8
```

## Guide: write a TOML file

To write TOML, build a Value object and pass it to `Encode` or `EncodeStrict`. A nested object becomes a `[table]`. The top level must be an object, since a TOML document is always a table; `EncodeStrict` reports `false` for anything else.

encoding-toml-guide-write.salam

```salam
import encoding.toml
import encoding.value

func replica(host: str, weight: int): value.Value:
    mut r := value.NewValueObject()
    value.ObjectSet(r, "host", value.ValueString(host))
    value.ObjectSet(r, "weight", value.ValueInt(weight))
    ret r
end

func main:
    mut db := value.NewValueObject()
    value.ObjectSet(db, "url", value.ValueString("postgres://localhost/shop"))
    value.ObjectSet(db, "pool", value.ValueInt(8))
    value.ObjectSet(db, "timeout", value.ValueFloat(30.0))
    value.ObjectSet(db, "password", value.ValueNull())

    mut replicas := value.NewValueArray()
    value.ArrayPush(replicas, replica("10.0.0.2", 2))
    value.ArrayPush(replicas, replica("10.0.0.3", 1))
    value.ObjectSet(db, "replicas", replicas)

    mut root := value.NewValueObject()
    value.ObjectSet(root, "database", db)

    mut ok := false
    text := toml.EncodeStrict(root, ok)
    println "encoded:", ok
    print text

    back := value.ObjectGet(toml.Decode(text), "database")
    println "timeout is still a float:", value.IsFloat(value.ObjectGet(back, "timeout"))
    println "password written:", value.ObjectHas(back, "password")
    println "replicas read back:", value.ArrayLen(value.ObjectGet(back, "replicas"))
end
```

Output:

```text
encoded: true
[database]
replicas = [{host = "10.0.0.2", weight = 2}, {host = "10.0.0.3", weight = 1}]
timeout = 30.0
pool = 8
url = "postgres://localhost/shop"
timeout is still a float: true
password written: false
replicas read back: 2
```

Three things show in the output. The null `password` is left out, because TOML has no null. The array of replica objects is written inline on one line. The float `30.0` keeps its `.0`, so it reads back as a float and not as the integer `30`. Keys come out in no particular order, so never compare the text with a fixed string; compare the data, for example with `value.Equal` after decoding the text again.

## Guide: catching mistakes

Use `DecodeStrict` or `Valid` on any file a person edits. They catch broken syntax: a key without a value, an unclosed string, array or table header.

encoding-toml-guide-errors.salam

```salam
import encoding.toml

func check(label: str, text: str):
    mut ok := false
    _ := toml.DecodeStrict(text, ok)
    println label, ok
end

func main:
    check("good:            ", "a = 1\nb = 'two'\n")
    check("no value:        ", "a = \n")
    check("unclosed string: ", "a = \"open\n")
    check("unclosed array:  ", "a = [1, 2\n")
    check("unclosed table:  ", "[server\nport = 1\n")
    check("multi-line text: ", "a = \"\"\"x\"\"\"\n")
    check("duplicate key:   ", "a = 1\na = 2\n")
    check("unquoted string: ", "mode = fast\n")
    println "Valid agrees:", toml.Valid("a = 1"), toml.Valid("a = ")
end
```

Output:

```text
good:             true
no value:         false
unclosed string:  false
unclosed array:   false
unclosed table:   false
multi-line text:  false
duplicate key:    true
unquoted string:  true
Valid agrees: true false
```

The last two lines are the leniency described above: a duplicate key is accepted and the later value wins, and `mode = fast` passes as the string `"fast"`, although real TOML requires quotes. If either would hide a real mistake in your files, check the keys you care about after decoding, for example with `value.IsString` and a list of allowed values.

## Functions

### `DecodeStrict`

```salam
func DecodeStrict(text: str, ok &: bool): value.Value
```

Reads TOML, setting `ok` false when the text is not valid.

encoding-toml-Decode.salam

```salam
import encoding.toml
import encoding.value

func main:
    text := "title = \"salam\"\n\n[server]\nhost = \"localhost\"\nport = 8080\ntags = [\"a\", \"b\"]\n"
    println toml.Valid(text), toml.Valid("= no key")
    v := toml.Decode(text)
    server := value.ObjectGet(v, "server")
    println value.AsString(value.ObjectGet(v, "title")), value.AsInt(value.ObjectGet(server, "port"))
    println toml.Encode(v)
    mut read := false
    _ := toml.DecodeStrict("a = \n", read)
    println read
    mut wrote := false
    println toml.EncodeStrict(value.ValueInt(1), wrote), wrote
end
```

Output:

```text
true false
salam 8080
title = "salam"
[server]
host = "localhost"
tags = ["a", "b"]
port = 8080

false
 false
```

The example for this item is shown with the ones above: encoding-toml-Decode.salam

# encoding/url

https://salamlang.github.io/Salam/std/encoding-url/

Taking a web address apart, building and editing its parameters, and resolving relative addresses.

This package works with whole web addresses. `Parse` splits a URL such as `https://user@shop.example.co.uk:8443/path?page=2#top` into a `URL` struct with the fields `scheme`, `userinfo`, `host`, `port`, `path`, `raw_query` and `fragment`, and `String` puts it back together. Around that come helpers to edit query parameters, resolve relative links with `Join`, and find the registrable domain of a host.

Use it whenever you have a full address. For the `a=1&b=2` part on its own, such as a form body, use encoding/query; for percent-encoding a single string, `encoding.URLEncode` in encoding; to fetch the address, net/http.

### Raw and decoded parts

The fields hold the text exactly as it appeared, percent escapes included, so `String(Parse(x))` normally gives back `x`. Read the human form with `DecodedPath`, `DecodedUserinfo` or `Query`. When you set a field yourself, put encoded text in it: escape path segments with `EncodePathSegment` and build queries with `SetQuery`.

### What trips people up

- `Parse` never fails. It does no validation: a port that is not a number becomes `0`, and text without `://` (including `mailto:sara@example.com`) has no scheme or host and lands whole in `path`. Check `scheme` and `host` yourself before trusting an address from a user.

- Nothing is lowercased. `HTTPS://Shop.Example.COM` keeps its case in `scheme` and `host`, and `Domain` returns `Example.COM`. Lowercase with `str.Lower` before you compare hosts or domains.

- Editing one parameter rewrites the whole query. `RemoveParam`, `SetParam` and `KeepParams` decode the query and encode it again: `%20` becomes `+`, characters such as `*` get escaped, a bare `flag` becomes `flag=`, and repeated keys are grouped together. The meaning stays the same; the text may not.

- `Join` with only `?query` or `#fragment` loses the file name of the base, unlike a browser. See the links guide.

## Guide: strip tracking parameters

Links copied from email and social media carry `utm_` and click id parameters that only serve analytics. Before you store or compare links, parse them, drop those parameters with `RemoveParam`, clear the fragment and print the result with `String`. The parameters that stay keep their order.

encoding-url-guide-clean.salam

```salam
import encoding.url

func clean(raw: str): str:
    mut u := url.Parse(raw)
    names := url.ParamNames(u)
    each n in names:
        if n.starts_with("utm_") or n == "fbclid" or n == "gclid":
            _ := url.RemoveParam(u, n)
        end
    end
    u.fragment = ""
    ret url.String(u)
end

func main:
    println clean("https://shop.example/item/42?color=red&utm_source=news&utm_medium=email#reviews")
    println clean("https://blog.example/post?fbclid=IwAR0abc")
    println clean("https://example.com/search?q=salam%20lang&utm_campaign=fall&page=2&debug")
end
```

Output:

```text
https://shop.example/item/42?color=red
https://blog.example/post
https://example.com/search?q=salam+lang&page=2&debug=
```

`ParamNames` returns a copy of the names, so removing parameters inside the loop is safe. The fields of `URL` are plain strings you can set directly, as `u.fragment = ""` does. The last line shows the rewrite described above: `salam%20lang` comes out as `salam+lang` and the bare `debug` as `debug=`. Both mean the same to a server, but if you use the cleaned link as a cache or database key, clean every link the same way so equal links give equal text.

## Guide: resolve the links of a page

A crawler or a link checker finds relative links like `../api/json.html` in a page and needs the full address. `Join` resolves a reference against the page's own URL the way a browser does: `./` and `../` move through the folders, a leading `/` starts at the site root, `//host` keeps the scheme, and a full URL replaces everything.

encoding-url-guide-links.salam

```salam
import encoding.url

func main:
    page := url.Parse("https://docs.example.com/guide/start/index.html?lang=en")
    hrefs := ["install.html", "./setup/linux.html", "../api/json.html", "/blog/", "https://other.example/x", "//cdn.example.com/app.js"]
    each h in hrefs:
        println h, "->", url.String(url.Join(page, h))
    end
end
```

Output:

```text
install.html -> https://docs.example.com/guide/start/install.html
./setup/linux.html -> https://docs.example.com/guide/start/setup/linux.html
../api/json.html -> https://docs.example.com/guide/api/json.html
/blog/ -> https://docs.example.com/blog/
https://other.example/x -> https://other.example/x
//cdn.example.com/app.js -> https://cdn.example.com/app.js
```

A reference that is only a query (`?lang=fa`) or only a fragment (`#top`) does not keep the file name of the base yet, so resolve those yourself by setting `raw_query` or `fragment` on a copy of the base.

## Guide: is it the same site?

To allow redirects only within your own site, or to group links by owner, compare the registrable domain instead of the host name. `Domain` is the part a person registers, such as `example.co.uk`; `PublicSuffix` is the part under which anyone can register; `Subdomain` is what is left on the left. An address made of an IP has no domain, so compare the host name there. Host names are not case sensitive but the package keeps their case, so the program lowercases both addresses before parsing them.

encoding-url-guide-site.salam

```salam
import encoding.url
import str

func same_site(a: str, b: str): bool:
    ua := url.Parse(str.Lower(a))
    ub := url.Parse(str.Lower(b))
    if url.IsIP(ua) or url.IsIP(ub):
        ret url.Hostname(ua) == url.Hostname(ub)
    end
    ret url.Domain(ua) == url.Domain(ub)
end

func main:
    u := url.Parse("https://api.eu.shop.example.co.uk:8443/v1/orders")
    println "host:", url.Hostname(u), "port:", u.port
    println "domain:", url.Domain(u), "suffix:", url.PublicSuffix(u), "sub:", url.Subdomain(u)

    println same_site("https://www.example.com/a", "https://login.example.com/b")
    println same_site("https://WWW.Example.com/", "https://example.com/cart")
    println same_site("https://example.com/", "https://example.org/")
    println same_site("http://10.0.0.5:8080/", "http://10.0.0.5/")
end
```

Output:

```text
host: api.eu.shop.example.co.uk port: 8443
domain: example.co.uk suffix: co.uk sub: api.eu.shop
true
true
false
true
```

The package knows the common public suffixes such as `com`, `co.uk` and `com.au`, not the complete Public Suffix List, so hosting platforms that give every customer a subdomain may count as one site. Check those hosts by name when it matters.

## Guide: build a URL from user input

When parts of the address come from users, escape each path segment with `EncodePathSegment`, which also escapes `/` so a file name cannot add folders. Put the parameters in a QueryMap and attach it with `SetQuery`; `Add` allows the same key more than once.

encoding-url-guide-build.salam

```salam
import encoding.url
import encoding.query

func main:
    folder := "My Files"
    name := "report 2026/Q3.pdf"
    mut u := url.Parse("https://files.example.com")
    u.path = "/users/sara/" + url.EncodePathSegment(folder) + "/" + url.EncodePathSegment(name)

    mut q := query.NewQueryMap()
    query.Set(q, "download", "1")
    query.Add(q, "tag", "finance")
    query.Add(q, "tag", "سه‌ماهه")
    url.SetQuery(u, q)

    full := url.String(u)
    println full

    back := url.Parse(full)
    println "path:", url.DecodedPath(back)
    println "tags:", query.GetAll(back.raw_query, "tag")
end
```

Output:

```text
https://files.example.com/users/sara/My%20Files/report%202026%2FQ3.pdf?download=1&tag=finance&tag=%D8%B3%D9%87%E2%80%8C%D9%85%D8%A7%D9%87%D9%87
path: /users/sara/My Files/report 2026/Q3.pdf
tags: ["finance", "سه‌ماهه"]
```

`DecodedPath` gives the readable path but turns `%2F` back into `/`, so it cannot tell a slash inside a name from a folder boundary. Split `u.path` at `/` first and decode each segment when you need the names exactly.

## Types

### `URL`

```salam
struct URL
```

A parsed web address.

| Name | Type | Description |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `scheme` | `str = ""` | The scheme, such as `https`. |
| `userinfo` | `str = ""` | The user name and password before the `@`, still encoded. |
| `host` | `str = ""` | The host name or numeric address. |
| `port` | `int = 0` | The port, or zero when none was given. |
| `path` | `str = ""` | The path, still encoded. |
| `raw_query` | `str = ""` | The query after the `?`, still encoded. |
| `fragment` | `str = ""` | The part after the `#`. |

encoding-url-Parse.salam

```salam
import encoding.url
import encoding.query

func main:
    mut u := url.Parse("https://user%20a:pw@shop.example.co.uk:8443/books/%D8%B3%D9%84%D8%A7%D9%85?page=2&sort=new#top")
    println u.scheme, u.host, u.port, u.path, u.raw_query, u.fragment
    println url.Hostname(u), url.HostPort(u), url.IsIP(u)
    println url.Labels(u), url.PublicSuffix(u), url.Domain(u), url.Subdomain(u)
    println url.DecodedPath(u), url.DecodedUserinfo(u)
    println url.ParamNames(u), query.Size(url.Query(u))
    url.SetParam(u, "page", "3")
    println url.RemoveParam(u, "sort"), url.String(u)
    mut keep := Vector {} as Vector<str>
    keep.push("page")
    url.KeepParams(u, keep)
    mut q := query.NewQueryMap()
    query.Add(q, "q", "hello world")
    url.SetQuery(u, q)
    println url.String(u)
    url.ClearQuery(u)
    println url.String(u)
    println url.String(url.Join(u, "../img/a.png")), url.EncodePathSegment("a b/c")
    println url.IsIP(url.Parse("http://127.0.0.1/"))
end
```

Output:

```text
https shop.example.co.uk 8443 /books/%D8%B3%D9%84%D8%A7%D9%85 page=2&sort=new top
shop.example.co.uk shop.example.co.uk:8443 false
["shop", "example", "co", "uk"] co.uk example.co.uk shop
/books/سلام user a:pw
["page", "sort"] 2
true https://user%20a:pw@shop.example.co.uk:8443/books/%D8%B3%D9%84%D8%A7%D9%85?page=3#top
https://user%20a:pw@shop.example.co.uk:8443/books/%D8%B3%D9%84%D8%A7%D9%85?q=hello+world#top
https://user%20a:pw@shop.example.co.uk:8443/books/%D8%B3%D9%84%D8%A7%D9%85#top
https://user%20a:pw@shop.example.co.uk:8443/img/a.png a%20b%2Fc
true
```

## Functions

### `Parse`

```salam
func Parse(raw: str): URL
```

Takes an address apart into its pieces. It never fails and does no validation: only text with `://` (or a leading `//`) gets a scheme and host, and a port that is not a number becomes 0.

# encoding/query

https://salamlang.github.io/Salam/std/encoding-query/

Reading and building the query string of a web address, such as `q=hello&page=2`.

A query string is the `key=value&key=value` text after the `?` in a web address, and the same format is the body of an HTML form posted as `application/x-www-form-urlencoded`. This package reads and writes that text: it undoes the percent escapes and `+` for spaces, and builds correctly escaped strings from your values.

Use it when you hold the query text alone: a form body, the `raw_query` of a request, a signed API call. When you have a whole address and want to change its parameters, encoding/url has `SetParam`, `RemoveParam` and `KeepParams` on top of this package. Inside a net/http handler, `http.Query` and `http.Form` read single values for you; take `http.RawQuery` and this package when you need repeated keys or want to rewrite the query.

### Two ways to work

- On the text. `Get`, `GetAll` and `Has` take the query string itself. Each call decodes the whole string again, which is fine for reading a handful of values.

- On a `QueryMap`. `Decode` turns the text into a map you can change with `Set`, `Add`, `Remove` and `Retain`, then write back with `Encode`. One key may have several values (`tag=a&tag=b`), so each key holds a list, and the map remembers the order in which keys first appeared.

### What trips people up

- There is no getter on a `QueryMap`. Read the text with `Get`, or read the map directly: `m.data.has("tag")` and `m.data.get("tag").items`.

- Missing and empty look the same to `Get`. Both `page=` and no `page` at all return `""`; ask `Has` when it matters. A bare `flag` counts as present with an empty value, and `Encode` writes it back as `flag=`.

- Numbers are not checked. `"12abc".to_int()` is 12 and `"abc".to_int()` is 0, so bound every number you read before using it.

- Repeated keys are grouped. `a=1&b=2&a=3` encodes back as `a=1&a=3&b=2`. That is the same data, but if a signature or cache key covers the exact text, sign what you send, not what you received.

- Keys are case sensitive, and a leading `?` is skipped by `Decode`.

## Guide: read the parameters of a search page

A search page reads a few parameters, gives the missing ones a default, and converts the numbers. `Get` already decodes the value, so `green+tea` arrives as `green tea`. `GetAll` returns every value of a repeated key, which is how checkbox filters arrive.

encoding-query-guide-search.salam

```salam
import encoding.query

func main:
    qs := "q=green+tea&brand=nik&brand=pars&min=20&page=3&limit=500"

    words := query.Get(qs, "q")
    mut page := 1
    if query.Has(qs, "page"):
        page = query.Get(qs, "page").to_int()
    end
    mut limit := 20
    if query.Has(qs, "limit"):
        limit = query.Get(qs, "limit").to_int()
    end
    if page < 1: page = 1 end
    if limit < 1 or limit > 100: limit = 100 end
    brands := query.GetAll(qs, "brand")

    println "search for:", words
    println "brands:", brands.len(), brands
    println "min price:", query.Get(qs, "min").to_int()
    println "rows", (page - 1) * limit + 1, "to", page * limit
end
```

Output:

```text
search for: green tea
brands: 2 ["nik", "pars"]
min price: 20
rows 201 to 300
```

`Get` returns an empty string both for a missing key and for `key=`, so use `Has` when the difference matters, as the defaults for `page` and `limit` do here. Never trust the numbers: the visitor asked for 500 rows, and the handler caps `limit` at 100 and keeps `page` at 1 or more, so a bad value cannot make it read the whole table or a negative offset.

## Guide: next and previous page links

Pagination links must keep every filter the visitor chose and change only the page number. Decode the current query into a `QueryMap`, `Set` the page (it replaces all values of that key, or adds the key when it is new) and `Encode` it again.

encoding-query-guide-pages.salam

```salam
import encoding.query
import str

func page_link(current: str, page: int): str:
    mut m := query.Decode(current)
    query.Set(m, "page", str.FromInt(page))
    ret "/products?" + query.Encode(m)
end

func main:
    current := "category=books&sort=price&tag=new&tag=sale&page=2"
    println "prev:", page_link(current, 1)
    println "next:", page_link(current, 3)
    println "first visit:", page_link("category=books", 2)
end
```

Output:

```text
prev: /products?category=books&sort=price&tag=new&tag=sale&page=1
next: /products?category=books&sort=price&tag=new&tag=sale&page=3
first visit: /products?category=books&page=2
```

`Set` keeps an existing key in its place, so the links differ from the address the visitor came from only in the page number, and a cache sees one address per page instead of one per parameter order.

## Guide: HTML form bodies

A form sent with `method="post"` has the body type `application/x-www-form-urlencoded`, which is the same format as a query string. Decode it with the same functions. Spaces arrive as `+` and everything else outside plain ASCII as `%XX` bytes, Persian text included.

encoding-query-guide-form.salam

```salam
import encoding.query

func main:
    body := "name=Sara+Ahmadi&city=%D8%B4%DB%8C%D8%B1%D8%A7%D8%B2&note=50%25+off%3F&agree=on"
    form := query.Decode(body)
    println "fields:", query.Keys(form)
    println "name:", query.Get(body, "name")
    println "city:", query.Get(body, "city")
    println "note:", query.Get(body, "note")
    println "agreed:", query.Get(body, "agree") == "on"

    mut reply := query.NewQueryMap()
    query.Set(reply, "status", "saved ok")
    println "form style:", query.Encode(reply)
    println "URL style: ", query.EncodeWith(reply, query.QueryOptions { space_as_plus = false })
end
```

Output:

```text
fields: ["name", "city", "note", "agree"]
name: Sara Ahmadi
city: شیراز
note: 50% off?
agreed: true
form style: status=saved+ok
URL style:  status=saved%20ok
```

`Encode` writes spaces as `+`, as forms do. Some APIs want `%20` instead; `EncodeWith` with `space_as_plus = false` writes that.

## Guide: keep only the parameters you know

Parameters you do not use still change the address, which splits a cache into many copies of the same page and lets anyone pass odd flags along. `Retain` keeps only a list of allowed keys; `Remove` drops one and says whether it was there.

encoding-query-guide-allow.salam

```salam
import encoding.query

func main:
    incoming := "q=lamp&page=2&utm_source=ad&debug=1&sort=new&callback=x"

    mut m := query.Decode(incoming)
    mut allowed := Vector {} as Vector<str>
    allowed.push("q")
    allowed.push("page")
    allowed.push("sort")
    query.Retain(m, allowed)
    println "kept:", query.Encode(m)

    println "removed sort:", query.Remove(m, "sort")
    println "removed again:", query.Remove(m, "sort")
    println "cache key:", query.Encode(m), "with", query.Size(m), "keys"
end
```

Output:

```text
kept: q=lamp&page=2&sort=new
removed sort: true
removed again: false
cache key: q=lamp&page=2 with 2 keys
```

## Text functions or a QueryMap

| Job | Use |
| --- | --- |
| Read one or two values once | `Get`, `GetAll`, `Has` on the text |
| Change a query and write it back | `Decode`, then `Set`, `Add`, `Remove`, `Encode` |
| Filter untrusted parameters | `Retain` |
| Change the query of a full URL | `url.SetParam` and the other functions of encoding/url |

## Types

### `QueryOptions`

```salam
struct QueryOptions
```

The encoding options.

| Name | Type | Description |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `space_as_plus` | `bool = true` | Form style, true by default: a space is written as `+` and a `+` is read as a space. When false, `%20` is written and a `+` is read as a plus sign. |

encoding-query-Query.salam

```salam
import encoding.query

func main:
    text := "q=hello&page=2&tag=a&tag=b&empty="
    println query.Get(text, "q"), query.Get(text, "page"), query.Has(text, "empty"), query.Has(text, "x")
    println query.GetAll(text, "tag")
    mut m := query.Decode(text)
    println query.Size(m), query.Keys(m)
    query.Add(m, "tag", "c")
    query.Set(m, "page", "3")
    println query.Remove(m, "empty")
    println query.Encode(m)
    mut keep := Vector {} as Vector<str>
    keep.push("q")
    query.Retain(m, keep)
    println query.Encode(m)
    opts := query.QueryOptions {}
    println query.EncodeWith(query.DecodeWith("b=2&a=1", opts), opts)
    empty := query.NewQueryMap()
    println query.Size(empty)
end
```

Output:

```text
hello 2 true false
["a", "b"]
4 ["q", "page", "tag", "empty"]
true
q=hello&page=3&tag=a&tag=b&tag=c
q=hello
b=2&a=1
0
```

# encoding/envfile

https://salamlang.github.io/Salam/std/encoding-envfile/

Reading and writing `.env` files, with variable substitution.

A `.env` file holds a program's settings and secrets as one `KEY=value` per line, the format used by Docker Compose, most twelve-factor apps and tools such as dotenv. This package reads such a file into a `Doc`, an ordered list of keys and string values, substitutes `${NAME}` references, and writes a `Doc` back as text.

It works on text and never touches the process environment. If you only want a `.env` file's variables available to the program, `env.Load(path)` in env puts them into the environment in one call (and `env.Overload` lets the file win over variables already set). `config.LoadEnv` in config reads one into a `Config` with typed getters such as `GetInt` and `GetBool`. Use this package when you need the file itself: its order, its references, a strict check, or to write it back. For nested settings with numbers and lists, encoding/toml or encoding/yaml fit better.

### What a line may contain

- Blank lines and lines starting with `#` are skipped, and a UTF-8 byte order mark at the start is ignored. `export ` before a key is allowed, so a file a shell can `source` also parses.

- Keys are letters, digits, `_`, `.` and `-`. Spaces around the `=` are allowed.

- An unquoted value runs to the end of the line, minus trailing spaces. A `#` starts a comment only after a space, so `https://x/#top` keeps its `#`.

- A double-quoted value understands `\n`, `\t`, `\"` and `\\`, may span several lines, and takes `${NAME}` substitution. A single-quoted value is taken literally, with no escapes and no substitution.

- A key that appears twice keeps its first position and its last value.

### What trips people up

- Every value is a string. `PORT=8080` gives `"8080"`; convert it yourself, and remember that `"abc".to_int()` is 0, not an error.

- References only look upward. `${NAME}` is resolved from lines above it (then from the `base` document, if you pass one). A name defined further down, or not at all, silently becomes an empty string. Use `RefNames` on a `ParseRaw` result to see what a file expects.

- `Parse` skips bad lines without a word. A line like `SECRET KEY 8f2c` just disappears. Load files with `ParseStrict` at startup.

- `Format` drops comments and blank lines; it writes only keys and values.

## Guide: shared defaults and local overrides

Most projects commit a `.env` with safe defaults and let each developer keep a `.env.local` with their own ports and passwords. Parse both and `MergeInto` the local one: its keys replace the shared ones, and keys that only exist in the shared file stay. `GetOr` covers settings neither file has.

encoding-envfile-guide-layers.salam

```salam
import encoding.envfile

func main:
    shared := `# committed to the repository
APP_NAME=shop
PORT=8080
LOG_LEVEL=info
DB_URL=postgres://localhost/shop
`
    local := `# .env.local, kept out of git
PORT=9000
DB_URL=postgres://sara:secret@localhost/shop_dev
`
    mut cfg := envfile.Parse(shared)
    mut over := envfile.Parse(local)
    envfile.MergeInto(cfg, over)

    port := envfile.Get(cfg, "PORT").to_int()
    println envfile.Get(cfg, "APP_NAME"), "on port", port
    println "log level:", envfile.GetOr(cfg, "LOG_LEVEL", "warn")
    println "workers:", envfile.GetOr(cfg, "WORKERS", "2").to_int()
    println "keys in order:", envfile.Keys(cfg)

    envfile.Free(over)
    envfile.Free(cfg)
end
```

Output:

```text
shop on port 9000
log level: info
workers: 2
keys in order: ["APP_NAME", "PORT", "LOG_LEVEL", "DB_URL"]
```

Every value is a string; convert numbers with `to_int()`. A merged key keeps its original place, so `Keys` still lists them in the order of the shared file. In a real program the two texts come from `file.ReadAll` in fs/file.

## Guide: comments, quotes and multi-line values

Real `.env` files mix comments, URLs with `#` in them, PEM keys pasted over several lines and prices with a `$` in them. The program below reads one of each, so you can see where each rule from the list above applies.

encoding-envfile-guide-syntax.salam

```salam
import encoding.envfile

func main:
    text := `export APP_NAME=shop   # trailing comment
HOME_URL=https://shop.example/#top
MOTD="Welcome!\nOrders ship daily."
TLS_KEY="-----BEGIN KEY-----
MIIEvQIBADANBg
-----END KEY-----"
PRICE_NOTE='$5 off, literally'
EARLY=${LATER}
LATER=set below
PORT=8080
PORT=9090
`
    mut d := envfile.Parse(text)
    println "APP_NAME:", envfile.Get(d, "APP_NAME")
    println "HOME_URL:", envfile.Get(d, "HOME_URL")
    println "MOTD:", envfile.Get(d, "MOTD")
    key := envfile.Get(d, "TLS_KEY")
    println "TLS_KEY lines:", key.split("\n").len()
    println "PRICE_NOTE:", envfile.Get(d, "PRICE_NOTE")
    println "EARLY: [" + envfile.Get(d, "EARLY") + "]"
    println "PORT:", envfile.Get(d, "PORT"), "keys:", envfile.Len(d)
    envfile.Free(d)
end
```

Output:

```text
APP_NAME: shop
HOME_URL: https://shop.example/#top
MOTD: Welcome!
Orders ship daily.
TLS_KEY lines: 3
PRICE_NOTE: $5 off, literally
EARLY: []
PORT: 9090 keys: 8
```

The trailing comment after `shop` is dropped because a space comes before the `#`; the one in `HOME_URL` stays. The double-quoted `MOTD` turns `\n` into a real line break, and `TLS_KEY` keeps its three lines. `EARLY` is empty because `LATER` is defined after it, and `PORT` holds the second value but is counted once.

## Guide: references between variables

Values can refer to other keys with `${NAME}` or `$NAME`, and `${NAME:-default}` falls back when the key is not set. `Parse` resolves references within the file. To fill some of them from elsewhere, for example secrets that only the server knows, read the file with `ParseRaw` and resolve it with `ExpandDoc` and a second `Doc` of base values.

encoding-envfile-guide-expand.salam

```salam
import encoding.envfile

func main:
    text := `DB_HOST=localhost
DB_PORT=5432
DB_NAME=shop
DATABASE_URL=postgres://${DB_USER}@${DB_HOST}:${DB_PORT}/${DB_NAME}
CACHE_URL=redis://${REDIS_HOST:-127.0.0.1}:6379
GREETING='costs $5, not expanded'
`
    mut raw := envfile.ParseRaw(text)
    println "references:", envfile.RefNames(raw)

    mut base := envfile.New()
    envfile.Set(base, "DB_USER", "app")

    mut env := envfile.ExpandDoc(raw, base)
    println envfile.Get(env, "DATABASE_URL")
    println envfile.Get(env, "CACHE_URL")
    println envfile.Get(env, "GREETING")
    println "template:", envfile.Expand("${DB_NAME}_test", env, base)

    envfile.Free(env)
    envfile.Free(base)
    envfile.Free(raw)
end
```

Output:

```text
references: ["DB_USER", "DB_HOST", "DB_PORT", "DB_NAME", "REDIS_HOST"]
postgres://app@localhost:5432/shop
redis://127.0.0.1:6379
costs $5, not expanded
template: shop_test
```

Single quotes turn expansion off, as in a shell, so `$5` stays as written; in a double-quoted or bare value write `\$` for a literal dollar sign. `${NAME:-x}` uses `x` when the name is missing or empty, `${NAME-x}` only when it is missing. `RefNames` lists every name a file refers to, which is a quick way to tell an operator which variables a deployment needs. To use the process's own environment as the base, copy the variables you need into it with `env.Get` from env.

## Guide: fail early on a broken file

`Parse` is forgiving and skips lines it cannot read. At startup it is better to stop with a clear message: `ParseStrict` fills an `EncodingError` with the reason and the byte where the bad line starts. After that, check the keys the program cannot run without.

encoding-envfile-guide-validate.salam

```salam
import encoding.envfile
import encoding.encerr

func load(name: str, text: str):
    mut e := encerr.NoError()
    mut d := envfile.ParseStrict(text, e)
    if encerr.IsError(e):
        println name, "error at byte", e.position, "->", e.message
        envfile.Free(d)
        ret
    end
    required := ["DB_URL", "SECRET_KEY"]
    mut missing := 0
    each k in required:
        if not envfile.Has(d, k) or envfile.Get(d, k) == "":
            println name, "missing", k
            missing += 1
        end
    end
    if missing == 0:
        println name, "ok with", envfile.Len(d), "keys"
    end
    envfile.Free(d)
end

func main:
    load("prod:", "DB_URL=postgres://db/shop\nSECRET_KEY=8f2c\n")
    load("dev: ", "DB_URL=postgres://localhost/shop\nSECRET_KEY=\n")
    load("typo:", "DB_URL=postgres://db/shop\nSECRET KEY 8f2c\n")
    load("open:", "DB_URL=\"postgres://db/shop\n")
end
```

Output:

```text
prod: ok with 2 keys
dev:  missing SECRET_KEY
typo: error at byte 26 -> envfile: expected KEY=VALUE
open: error at byte 0 -> envfile: unterminated quoted value
```

Treat an empty value like a missing one for required keys, because `SECRET_KEY=` is a common leftover from a template.

## Guide: change a file and write it back

Tools that edit settings, such as an installer, change a `Doc` with `Set` and `Remove` and write it with `Format`. Values are quoted only when they need it, and quotes inside are escaped, so `Parse` reads the text back to the same values. `FormatExport` puts `export` before each line, for a file a shell can `source`.

encoding-envfile-guide-write.salam

```salam
import encoding.envfile

func main:
    mut d := envfile.Parse("APP_NAME=shop\nPORT=8080\n")
    envfile.Set(d, "PORT", "9090")
    envfile.Set(d, "WELCOME", "Hello, \"friend\"")
    envfile.Set(d, "SEARCH_URL", "http://127.0.0.1:7700")
    println "removed APP_NAME:", envfile.Remove(d, "APP_NAME")

    print envfile.Format(d)
    println "---"
    print envfile.FormatExport(d)
    println "---"
    println envfile.Quote("no-spaces"), envfile.Quote("two words")

    mut again := envfile.Parse(envfile.Format(d))
    println "round trip:", envfile.Get(again, "WELCOME")
    envfile.Free(again)
    envfile.Free(d)
end
```

Output:

```text
removed APP_NAME: true
PORT=9090
WELCOME="Hello, \"friend\""
SEARCH_URL=http://127.0.0.1:7700
---
export PORT=9090
export WELCOME="Hello, \"friend\""
export SEARCH_URL=http://127.0.0.1:7700
---
no-spaces "two words"
round trip: Hello, "friend"
```

`Format` writes keys in order and drops comments, so use it for files your program owns. For a file people maintain by hand, prefer telling them which line to change.

## Types

### `Doc`

```salam
struct Doc
```

The contents of an env file.

| Name | Type | Description |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `m` | `collections.OrderedMap` | The keys and values, in order. |
| `flags` | `Vector` | For each key, whether its value takes substitution; single quotes turn it off. |

encoding-envfile-Parse.salam

```salam
import encoding.envfile
import encoding.encerr

func main:
    text := "# settings\nHOST=localhost\nPORT=8080\nexport NAME=\"hello world\"\nURL=http://${HOST}:${PORT}/\n"
    mut doc := envfile.Parse(text)
    println envfile.Len(doc), envfile.Keys(doc)
    println envfile.Get(doc, "NAME"), envfile.Has(doc, "DEBUG"), envfile.GetOr(doc, "DEBUG", "false")
    println envfile.KeyAt(doc, 0), envfile.ValueAt(doc, 1)
    println envfile.Get(doc, "URL")
    raw := envfile.ParseRaw(text)
    println envfile.Get(raw, "URL"), envfile.RefNames(raw)
    mut base := envfile.New()
    expanded := envfile.ExpandDoc(raw, base)
    println envfile.Get(expanded, "URL")
    println envfile.Expand("${HOST}/api", doc, base), envfile.RefNamesIn("$A and ${B}")
    envfile.Set(doc, "DEBUG", "true")
    println envfile.Remove(doc, "URL")
    println envfile.Format(doc)
    println envfile.FormatExport(base) == "", envfile.Quote("a b")
    mut other := envfile.Parse("PORT=9090\nMODE=prod\n")
    envfile.MergeInto(doc, other)
    println envfile.Get(doc, "PORT"), envfile.Get(doc, "MODE")
    mut e := encerr.NoError()
    _ := envfile.ParseStrict("=no key\n", e)
    println encerr.IsError(e), envfile.Valid("A=1\n")
    println envfile.ParseScalar(`"a\tb"`), envfile.ParseScalarEx("x ; comment", true)
    envfile.Free(doc)
    envfile.Free(raw)
    envfile.Free(base)
    envfile.Free(expanded)
    envfile.Free(other)
end
```

Output:

```text
4 ["HOST", "PORT", "NAME", "URL"]
hello world false false
HOST 8080
http://localhost:8080/
http://${HOST}:${PORT}/ ["HOST", "PORT"]
http://localhost:8080/
localhost/api ["A", "B"]
true
HOST=localhost
PORT=8080
NAME="hello world"
DEBUG=true

true "a b"
9090 prod
true true
a	b x
```

### `ParseScalarEx`

```salam

```

Like `ParseScalar`; when `semi` is true, `;` starts a comment as well as `#`.

### `ExpandDoc`

```salam

```

Builds a new document with the references substituted. A name is looked up among the keys above it in the document, then in `base`; a name found in neither becomes an empty string. The result is fully expanded, so `RefNames` finds nothing in it.

The example for this item is shown with the ones above: encoding-envfile-Parse.salam

### `Expand`

```salam

```

Substitutes the references in a string from the document and `base`.

The example for this item is shown with the ones above: encoding-envfile-Parse.salam

```salam
func RefNames(d &: Doc): Vector<str>
```

The names of the variables the document's values refer to, in order of first use. Call it on a `ParseRaw` result; after `Parse` the references are already gone.

The example for this item is shown with the ones above: encoding-envfile-Parse.salam

### `RefNamesIn`

```salam
func RefNamesIn(raw: str): Vector<str>
```

The names of the variables referred to in a string, in both the `$A` and the `${A}` form.

The example for this item is shown with the ones above: encoding-envfile-Parse.salam
