### `Sheet`

```salam
struct Sheet
```

One sheet: cells by row and column, from zero.

| Name | Type | Description |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `name` | `str = ""` | The sheet name. |
| `cells` | `HashMap` | The cells by their reference. |
| `max_row` | `int = -1` | The greatest filled row number; -1 for an empty sheet. |
| `max_col` | `int = -1` | The greatest filled column number. |
| `merges` | `Vector` | The merged ranges. |
| `rtl` | `bool = false` | Shows the sheet right to left, as for Persian or Arabic data. It is written to xlsx files only. |
| `freeze_rows` | `int = 0` | How many top rows stay in view while scrolling; set it with `freeze`. It is written to xlsx files only. |
| `freeze_cols` | `int = 0` | How many of the first columns stay in view while scrolling. |
| `col_widths` | `Vector` | The column widths in characters, by column number; 0 keeps the default width. They are written to xlsx files only. |
| `auto_filter` | `str = ""` | The range that has filter buttons, such as `A1:F20`; empty for none. It is also read back from xlsx files. |

The example for this item is shown with the ones above: excel-Sheet.salam

excel-View.salam

```salam
import excel

func main:
    mut book := excel.NewWorkbook()
    mut sheet := book.add_sheet("prices")
    sheet.set_string(0, 0, "item")
    sheet.set_string(0, 1, "price")
    sheet.set_string(1, 0, "green tea, 500 g")
    sheet.set_number(1, 1, 4.5)
    sheet.set_string(2, 0, "sugar")
    sheet.set_number(2, 1, 1.25)
    sheet.rtl = true
    sheet.freeze(1, 1)
    sheet.set_auto_filter(0, 0, 2, 1)
    println sheet.rtl, sheet.freeze_rows, sheet.freeze_cols, sheet.auto_filter
    sheet.auto_fit()
    println sheet.col_widths
    sheet.set_column_width(3, 30.0)
    println sheet.col_widths.len(), sheet.col_widths[2], sheet.col_widths[3]
    framed := excel.Style { border = true, wrap = true }
    id := book.styles.get_or_add(framed)
    sheet.set_style(0, 0, id)
    println excel.WriteXLSX(book, "prices.xlsx")
    mut ok := false
    mut err := ""
    mut read := excel.Open("prices.xlsx", ok, err)
    if ok:
        back := read.sheet("prices")
        println ok, back.auto_filter, read.styles.get(back.get_cell(0, 0).style_id).wrap
    else:
        println ok, err
    end
    read.free()
    book.free()
end
```

Output:

```text
true 1 1 A1:B3
[21.2, 8]
4 0 30
true
true A1:B3 true
```

### `Workbook`

```salam
struct Workbook
```

A workbook: several sheets, the style table and the file format.

| Name | Type | Description |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `sheets` | `Vector` | The sheets in order. |
| `styles` | `StyleSheet` | The styles shared by the cells. |
| `active_sheet` | `int = 0` | The index of the active sheet. |
| `source_path` | `str = ""` | The path of the file the workbook was read from. |
| `format` | `int = 0` | The file format; one of the `Format` constants. |
| `last_error` | `str = ""` | The last error message. |

excel-Workbook.salam

```salam
import excel

func main:
    mut book := excel.NewWorkbook()
    mut a := book.add_sheet("A")
    a.set_string(0, 0, "hello")
    a.set_number(0, 1, 2.5)
    mut b := book.add_sheet("B")
    b.set_int(0, 0, 42)
    println book.sheet_count(), book.sheet_names(), book.sheet_index("B"), book.sheet_at(0).name
    println book.rename_sheet(1, "second"), book.sheet("second").get_number(0, 0)
    println book.set_active(1), book.active().name, book.active_sheet
    println excel.WriteXLSX(book, "book.xlsx"), excel.WriteODS(book, "book.ods"), book.save("copy.xlsx"), excel.Save(book, "book.csv")
    println excel.DetectFormat("book.xlsx") == excel.FormatXLSX, excel.DetectFormat("book.ods") == excel.FormatODS, excel.DetectFormat("a.txt"), excel.FormatXLS, excel.FormatCSV, excel.FormatUnknown
    mut ok := false
    mut err := ""
    mut read := excel.Open("book.xlsx", ok, err)
    println ok, read.sheet_names(), read.sheet("A").get_string(0, 0), read.format == excel.FormatXLSX
    mut copy := excel.ReadXLSX("copy.xlsx", ok, err)
    mut ods := excel.ReadODS("book.ods", ok, err)
    println ok, ods.sheet("second").get_number(0, 0), copy.sheet_count()
    mut meta := excel.Inspect("book.xlsx", ok, err)
    println ok, meta.exists, meta.size > 0, meta.sheet_names, meta.sheet_rows, meta.sheet_cols
    meta.free()
    mut csv := excel.ReadCSVWorkbook("book.csv", ok, err)
    println ok, csv.sheet_at(0).get_string(0, 0), excel.WriteCSVWorkbook(csv, "again.csv")
    _ := excel.Open("missing.xlsx", ok, err)
    println ok, err != ""
    _ := excel.ReadXLS("missing.xls", ok, err)
    println ok, excel.IsXLS(null, 0)
    println book.remove_sheet_named("A"), book.remove_sheet(5), book.remove_sheet(0), book.sheet_count()
    mut fresh := excel.New()
    println fresh.sheet_count()
    fresh.free()
    read.free()
    copy.free()
    ods.free()
    csv.free()
    book.free()
end
```

Output:

```text
2 ["A", "B"] 1 A
true 42
true second 1
true true true true
true true 0 2 4 0
true ["A", "second"] hello true
true 42 2
true true true ["A", "second"] [1, 1] [2, 1]
true 42 true
false true
false false
true false true 0
0
```

### `SheetToCSV`

```salam
func SheetToCSV(sheet: Sheet): str
```

Turns a sheet into CSV text.

excel-Convert.salam

```salam
import excel

func main:
    mut sheet := excel.CSVToSheet("name,score\nAli,17\n\"Sara, A\",19.5\n", "scores")
    println sheet.name, sheet.row_count(), sheet.get_string(2, 0), sheet.get_number(2, 1)
    println excel.SheetToCSV(sheet)
    println excel.SheetToJSON(sheet)
    mut from_json := excel.JSONToSheet(`[["a", "b"], ["1", "x"], ["2", "y"]]`, "data")
    println from_json.row_count(), from_json.col_count(), from_json.get_string(0, 1), from_json.get_string(2, 0)
    xml := "<row r=\"2\"><c r=\"A2\" t=\"s\"><v>0</v></c><br/></row>"
    start := excel.XmlFind(xml, "c", 0)
    println start, excel.XmlAttr(xml, start, "r"), excel.XmlTagEnd(xml, start)
    println excel.XmlInner(xml, "v", 0), excel.XmlSelfClosing(xml, excel.XmlFind(xml, "br", 0))
    println excel.XmlFindClose(xml, "row", 10)
    println excel.XmlEscape("a<b&c"), excel.XmlUnescape("a&lt;b&amp;c")
    sheet.free()
    from_json.free()
end
```

Output:

```text
scores 3 Sara, A 0
name,score
Ali,17
"Sara, A",19.5
[["name", "score"], ["Ali", "17"], ["Sara, A", "19.5"]]
3 2 b 2
11 A2 27
0 true
44
a&lt;b&amp;c a<b&c
```

# data

https://salamlang.github.io/Salam/std/data/

Reading data for machine learning: CSV tables, batching samples, MNIST and images, and synthetic data.

This is an official package that does not ship with Salam. Add it to a project first: `salam add data`

This package readies data for training a model. `LoadCsv` reads a CSV file into a `Table`, decides for each column whether it holds integers, floats, categories or free text, and turns categories into numbers by itself; `split_xy` then divides the table into a feature matrix and a label. `MatrixDataset` hands the rows out in shuffled mini-batches, `LoadMnist`, `LoadIdx` and `LoadImageFolder` read image sets, and the `Make...` functions build synthetic data from a fixed seed, for trying algorithms out without a file.

Everything comes out as a matrix or a tensor, ready for ml and nn. To read a CSV file cell by cell as text, use encoding/csv; for spreadsheets, excel; for arrays saved by NumPy, npy.

### What trips people up

- Category codes depend on the file. Codes are given in order of first appearance, so `red` may be 0 in the training file and 2 in the test file, and a column with 25 distinct values may be a category in one file and text in another. Load all rows from one file and split them, as the test-set guide does, or map new files through the training table's `cat_levels`.

- One bad cell changes a column's kind. A single `12,5` or `n/a` in a number column turns the whole column into categories or text. Check `kinds` after loading.

- Empty cells are NaN in number columns but their own category, the empty string, in category columns.

- Only commas. The separator is always `,`; convert semicolon or tab files first, for example with encoding/csv.

The guide below follows the order of a small machine learning project: load a CSV file and see how its columns were read, split it into features and a label and fit a first model, train in mini-batches, hold back a test set, and read the MNIST file format.

## How LoadCsv reads each column

`LoadCsv` looks at every value of a column and picks its kind on its own. All whole numbers give `COL_INT`, all numbers `COL_FLOAT`. Text with a limited number of different values (at most 20, or a tenth of the rows when that is more, and fewer than the rows) becomes `COL_CAT`: each value gets a code from 0 in order of first appearance and `cat_levels` gives the names back. Text where every row is different, such as a free comment, stays `COL_STR`. An empty cell in a number column is stored as NaN, which `math.IsNaN` detects; in a category column it becomes a level of its own.

data-columns.salam

```salam
import data
import matrix
import math

func kind_name(k: int): str:
    if k == data.COL_INT: ret "int" end
    if k == data.COL_FLOAT: ret "float" end
    if k == data.COL_CAT: ret "category" end
    ret "text"
end

func main:
    text := "id,city,age,income,comment\n1,Tehran,34,2.5,fast delivery\n2,Shiraz,,3.1,ok\n3,Tehran,51,4.0,late\n4,Tabriz,28,1.9,good price\n"
    mut t := data.LoadCsv(text, true)
    each j, name in t.names:
        println name, "->", kind_name(t.kinds.get(j))
    end
    levels := t.cat_levels("city")
    println "city levels:", levels
    city := t.col_index("city")
    age := t.col_index("age")
    repeat t.rows() in i:
        code := t.cells.at(i, city) as int
        mut shown := "missing"
        if math.IsNaN(t.cells.at(i, age)) == false: shown = "known" end
        println "row", i, "city code", code, "=", levels.get(code), "age", shown
    end
    mut m := t.to_matrix()
    println "to_matrix keeps", m.cols, "of", t.cols(), "columns"
    mut onehot := matrix.Zeros(t.rows(), levels.len())
    repeat t.rows() in i: onehot.set(i, t.cells.at(i, city) as int, 1.0) end
    println "one-hot row 3:", onehot.at(3, 0), onehot.at(3, 1), onehot.at(3, 2)
    matrix.Free(onehot)
    matrix.Free(m)
    t.free()
    ret 0
end
```

Output:

```text
id -> int
city -> category
age -> int
income -> float
comment -> text
city levels: ["Tehran", "Shiraz", "Tabriz"]
row 0 city code 0 = Tehran age known
row 1 city code 1 = Shiraz age missing
row 2 city code 0 = Tehran age known
row 3 city code 2 = Tabriz age known
to_matrix keeps 4 of 5 columns
one-hot row 3: 0 0 1
```

`to_matrix` and `split_xy` leave `COL_STR` columns out, which is why five columns become four. A category is stored as its code, which suits decision trees; for a linear model or a neural network build one-hot columns from the code, as the last lines do.

## From a CSV file to a first model

`split_xy` takes the name of the label column and fills two matrices: every other usable column as features, and the label as a one column matrix. It returns false when the label is missing or is plain text. That is exactly the shape matrix functions expect, so a least squares fit with `matrix.LinearRegression` is one more line. Its result has the intercept first, then one coefficient per feature.

data-regression.salam

```salam
import data
import matrix
import conv

func main:
    text := "area,rooms,price\n50,1,105\n70,2,147\n80,2,164\n100,3,208\n120,3,244\n150,4,305\n"
    mut t := data.LoadCsv(text, true)
    mut x := matrix.Matrix {}
    mut y := matrix.Matrix {}
    if t.split_xy("price", x, y) == false:
        println "no price column"
        ret 1
    end
    println "features:", x.rows, "x", x.cols, "label:", y.rows, "x", y.cols
    mut beta := matrix.LinearRegression(x, y)
    println "intercept:", conv.FormatFloatPrec(beta.at(0, 0), 2)
    println "per m2:", conv.FormatFloatPrec(beta.at(1, 0), 2)
    println "per room:", conv.FormatFloatPrec(beta.at(2, 0), 2)
    guess := beta.at(0, 0) + 90.0 * beta.at(1, 0) + 2.0 * beta.at(2, 0)
    println "90 m2 with 2 rooms:", conv.FormatFloatPrec(guess, 1)
    matrix.Free(beta)
    matrix.Free(x)
    matrix.Free(y)
    t.free()
    ret 0
end
```

Output:

```text
features: 6 x 2 label: 6 x 1
intercept: 7.33
per m2: 1.81
per room: 6.44
90 m2 with 2 rooms: 183.2
```

## Training in mini-batches

Gradient descent on a large data set looks at a few rows at a time. Wrap the features and labels in a `MatrixDataset`, ask it for `batches(size, shuffle, seed)`, and call `next` until it returns false; each call replaces the two matrices you pass with the next batch. `reset(epoch)` starts a new pass and shuffles again with the seed plus the epoch, so every epoch sees a different order but a run can be repeated exactly. `MakeRegression` builds a test problem with known true coefficients, so you can see that training found them.

data-minibatch.salam

```salam
import data
import matrix
import conv

func main:
    mut y := matrix.Matrix {}
    mut coef := matrix.Matrix {}
    x := data.MakeRegression(200, 3, 0.05, 11, y, coef)
    mut set := data.MatrixDataset { x = x, y = y }
    mut w := matrix.Zeros(3, 1)
    mut it := set.batches(20, true, 7)
    mut batch_x := matrix.Matrix {}
    mut batch_y := matrix.Matrix {}
    repeat 5 in epoch:
        it.reset(epoch as i64)
        mut loss := 0.0
        until it.next(batch_x, batch_y):
            mut pred := matrix.MatMul(batch_x, w)
            mut diff := matrix.Sub(pred, batch_y)
            mut grad := matrix.TransposeMul(batch_x, diff)
            matrix.AddScaled(w, grad, -0.1 / (batch_x.rows as f64))
            loss += matrix.Dot(diff, diff)
            matrix.Free(pred)
            matrix.Free(diff)
            matrix.Free(grad)
        end
        println "epoch", epoch + 1, "batches", it.batches_per_epoch(), "loss", conv.FormatFloatPrec(loss / (set.len() as f64), 4)
    end
    repeat 3 in j:
        println "w" + j, "learned", conv.FormatFloatPrec(w.at(j, 0), 2), "true", conv.FormatFloatPrec(coef.at(j, 0), 2)
    end
    matrix.Free(batch_x)
    matrix.Free(batch_y)
    matrix.Free(w)
    matrix.Free(coef)
    it.free()
    set.free()
    ret 0
end
```

Output:

```text
epoch 1 batches 10 loss 0.5009
epoch 2 batches 10 loss 0.0808
epoch 3 batches 10 loss 0.0147
epoch 4 batches 10 loss 0.0041
epoch 5 batches 10 loss 0.0024
w0 learned -0.86 true -0.88
w1 learned -0.54 true -0.54
w2 learned -0.26 true -0.25
```

`next` frees the matrices it is given before it fills them, so pass the same two variables every time and free them once after the loop.

## Keeping a test set aside

A model has to be judged on rows it never saw. The simplest split reuses the batch iterator: shuffle once with a fixed seed, take a first batch the size of the training set and a second batch with the rest. Here a nearest-centre classifier learns the centre of each of three clusters from `MakeBlobs` and is scored on the 30 held back points.

data-split.salam

```salam
import data
import matrix

func nearest(centers: matrix.Matrix, x: matrix.Matrix, i: int): int:
    mut best := 0
    mut best_d := -1.0
    repeat centers.rows in c:
        mut d := 0.0
        repeat x.cols in j:
            diff := x.at(i, j) - centers.at(c, j)
            d += diff * diff
        end
        if best_d < 0.0 or d < best_d:
            best = c
            best_d = d
        end
    end
    ret best
end

func main:
    mut y := matrix.Matrix {}
    x := data.MakeBlobs(120, 3, 2, 1.0, 5, y)
    mut set := data.MatrixDataset { x = x, y = y }
    mut it := set.batches(90, true, 1)
    mut train_x := matrix.Matrix {}
    mut train_y := matrix.Matrix {}
    mut test_x := matrix.Matrix {}
    mut test_y := matrix.Matrix {}
    it.next(train_x, train_y)
    it.next(test_x, test_y)
    println "train:", train_x.rows, "test:", test_x.rows
    mut centers := matrix.Zeros(3, 2)
    mut sizes := matrix.Zeros(3, 1)
    repeat train_x.rows in i:
        c := train_y.at(i, 0) as int
        repeat 2 in j: centers.set(c, j, centers.at(c, j) + train_x.at(i, j)) end
        sizes.set(c, 0, sizes.at(c, 0) + 1.0)
    end
    repeat 3 in c:
        repeat 2 in j: centers.set(c, j, centers.at(c, j) / sizes.at(c, 0)) end
    end
    mut right := 0
    repeat test_x.rows in i:
        if nearest(centers, test_x, i) == test_y.at(i, 0) as int: right += 1 end
    end
    println "correct on unseen points:", right, "of", test_x.rows
    each m in [train_x, train_y, test_x, test_y, centers, sizes]:
        mut t := m
        matrix.Free(t)
    end
    it.free()
    set.free()
    ret 0
end
```

Output:

```text
train: 90 test: 30
correct on unseen points: 25 of 30
```

Changing the seed gives another split and slightly different numbers. For a fair comparison of two models, use the same seed for both.

## The MNIST file format

MNIST and many image sets that copy it use the IDX format: a magic number whose third byte is the element type and fourth the number of dimensions, the size of each dimension as a big-endian 32 bit number, then the raw bytes. `LoadMnist` reads an image file and a label file into a matrix with one image per row, pixels scaled from 0..255 to 0..1, and a one column label matrix. `LoadIdx` reads any IDX file as it is. The program writes three tiny 2x2 images itself so it runs without a download; for the real set, point the same call at `train-images-idx3-ubyte` and `train-labels-idx1-ubyte`.

data-mnist-format.salam

```salam
import data
import matrix
import compress
import archive
import encoding.binary
import conv

func write_idx(path: str, dims: Vector<int>, values: Vector<int>): bool:
    mut buf := compress.NewByteBuf()
    binary.WriteU8(buf, 0)
    binary.WriteU8(buf, 0)
    binary.WriteU8(buf, 8)
    binary.WriteU8(buf, dims.len())
    each d in dims: binary.WriteU32BE(buf, d) end
    each v in values: binary.WriteU8(buf, v) end
    ok := archive.WriteBinaryFileBuf(path, buf)
    compress.BufFree(buf)
    ret ok
end

func main:
    mut dims := Vector {} as Vector<int>
    dims.push(3)
    dims.push(2)
    dims.push(2)
    mut pixels := Vector {} as Vector<int>
    repeat 12 in i: pixels.push(i * 20) end
    write_idx("images.idx", dims, pixels)
    mut count := Vector {} as Vector<int>
    count.push(3)
    mut labels := Vector {} as Vector<int>
    labels.push(7)
    labels.push(2)
    labels.push(7)
    write_idx("labels.idx", count, labels)
    mut x := matrix.Matrix {}
    mut y := matrix.Matrix {}
    if data.LoadMnist("images.idx", "labels.idx", x, y) == false:
        println "could not load"
        ret 1
    end
    println "images:", x.rows, "pixels each:", x.cols, "labels:", y.rows
    repeat x.rows in i:
        println "label", y.at(i, 0), "pixels", conv.FormatFloatPrec(x.at(i, 0), 3), conv.FormatFloatPrec(x.at(i, 3), 3)
    end
    mut ok := false
    raw := data.LoadIdx("images.idx", ok)
    println "raw value of the last pixel:", raw.at(2, 3)
    println "without labels:", data.LoadMnist("images.idx", "missing.idx", x, y)
    matrix.Free(x)
    matrix.Free(y)
    ret 0
end
```

Output:

```text
images: 3 pixels each: 4 labels: 3
label 7 pixels 0.000 0.235
label 2 pixels 0.314 0.549
label 7 pixels 0.627 0.863
raw value of the last pixel: 220
without labels: false
```

Both readers return false, or clear `ok`, when a file is missing or does not match, so check the result before you use the matrices.

## Types

### `Table`

```salam
struct Table
```

A data table with named columns, for machine learning.

| Name | Type | Description |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `names` | `Vector` | The column names. |
| `kinds` | `Vector` | The kind of each column; one of the `COL_` constants. |
| `cats` | `Vector>` | The levels of each categorical column. |
| `raw` | `Vector>` | The original text of the cells of `COL_STR` columns; empty for the other kinds. |
| `cells` | `matrix.Matrix` | The numeric value of the cells; a categorical column holds the level number. |

data-Table.salam

```salam
import data
import matrix

func main:
    text := "age,city,score,ok\n30,tehran,1.5,1\n25,shiraz,2.5,0\n41,tehran,3.0,1\n"
    mut t := data.LoadCsv(text, true)
    println t.rows(), t.cols(), t.names, t.col_index("score"), t.col_index("x")
    println t.kinds[0] == data.COL_INT, t.kinds[1] == data.COL_CAT, t.kinds[2] == data.COL_FLOAT, data.COL_STR
    println t.cat_levels("city")
    mut m := t.to_matrix()
    println m.rows, m.cols, m.at(2, 1)
    mut x := matrix.Matrix {}
    mut y := matrix.Matrix {}
    println t.split_xy("ok", x, y), x.cols, y.at(1, 0)
    mut good := true
    _ := data.LoadCsvFile("missing.csv", true, good)
    println good
    matrix.Free(m)
    matrix.Free(x)
    matrix.Free(y)
    t.free()
end
```

Output:

```text
3 4 ["age", "city", "score", "ok"] 2 -1
true true true 3
["tehran", "shiraz"]
3 4 0
true 3 0
false
```

### `BatchIter`

```salam
struct BatchIter
```

A batch iterator.

| Name | Type | Description |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `x` | `matrix.Matrix` | The features. |
| `y` | `matrix.Matrix` | The labels. |
| `batch` | `int = 32` | The batch size. |
| `shuffle` | `bool = true` | Shuffle the order. |
| `seed` | `i64 = 0` | The shuffle seed. |
| `order` | `Vector` | The order of the samples in this epoch. |
| `pos` | `int = 0` | The current position. |

data-Batch.salam

```salam
import data
import matrix
import tensor

func main:
    mut y := matrix.Matrix {}
    x := data.MakeBlobs(10, 2, 3, 0.2, 1, y)
    mut set := data.MatrixDataset { x = x, y = y }
    println set.len()
    mut it := set.batches(4, false, 0)
    println it.batches_per_epoch()
    mut batch_x := matrix.Matrix {}
    mut batch_y := matrix.Matrix {}
    until it.next(batch_x, batch_y):
        println batch_x.rows, batch_x.cols, batch_y.rows
    end
    it.reset(1)
    mut t := tensor.Tensor {}
    mut labels := Vector {} as Vector<int>
    println it.next_tensor(t, labels), labels.len()
    println data.YLabels(y).len(), data.XTensor(x).shape
    mut good := true
    _ := data.ParseIdx(null, 0, good)
    println good
    _ := data.LoadIdx("missing.idx", good)
    println good, data.LoadMnist("a", "b", batch_x, batch_y)
    mut classes := Vector {} as Vector<str>
    println data.LoadImageFolder("missing-folder", 8, 8, true, t, labels, classes)
    it.free()
    set.free()
end
```

Output:

```text
10
3
4 3 4
4 3 4
2 3 2
true 4
10 [10, 3]
false
false false
false
```

## Functions

### `MakeBlobs`


```salam
import data
import matrix

func count_ones(y: matrix.Matrix): int:
    mut n := 0
    repeat y.rows in i:
        if y.at(i, 0) == 1.0:
            n += 1
        end
    end
    ret n
end

func main:
    mut y := matrix.Matrix {}
    blobs := data.MakeBlobs(90, 3, 2, 0.5, 42, y)
    println blobs.rows, blobs.cols, y.rows
    moons := data.MakeMoons(100, 0.1, 7, y)
    println moons.rows, moons.cols, count_ones(y)
    circles := data.MakeCircles(60, 0.05, 0.5, 7, y)
    println circles.rows, count_ones(y)
    mut coef := matrix.Matrix {}
    reg := data.MakeRegression(50, 3, 0.1, 1, y, coef)
    println reg.rows, reg.cols, coef.rows
    cls := data.MakeClassification(40, 4, 2, 1.0, 3, y)
    println cls.rows, cls.cols, count_ones(y) > 0
end
```

Output:

```text
100 2 50
60 30
50 3 3
40 4 true
```

# net/tcp

https://salamlang.github.io/Salam/std/net-tcp/

TCP servers and clients: listening, connecting, reading and writing, TLS and a connection pool.

TCP is the base of most internet protocols: a reliable, ordered stream of bytes between two programs. A server listens on a port with `Bind` and takes each new client with `Accept`; a client connects with `Dial`.

`Accept` and `Read` wait until something arrives, so a server that talks to several clients hands each connection to a thread, as the worker guide shows. Every example runs on `127.0.0.1` and needs no network.

Use this package for your own protocols and for talking to servers that have no client in the standard library. For HTTP use net/http; for messages that must not be split or ordered, net/udp; for live two-way traffic with browsers, net/websocket. tls adds encryption on top of a connection from here.

### What trips people up

- An empty `Read` means three things. The peer closed the connection, the read deadline passed, or an error happened; all return `""`. A message that starts with a zero byte also comes back empty, and text after a zero byte is lost, so use `ReadBytes` for binary data.

- `Write` may send only part of the text. It makes one system call and returns how many bytes went out. For large data, compare the result with the length, or use `WriteBytes`, which loops until everything is sent.

- Messages are not kept apart. TCP is a byte stream; frame your messages with a delimiter or a length, as the framing guide does.

- `Bind` listens on every IPv4 interface, not only on `127.0.0.1`, so a test server is reachable from the network unless a firewall stops it. IPv6 clients cannot reach it; `Dial` itself tries every address a name resolves to, IPv6 included.

- Nothing stops the program on failure. `Bind`, `Accept` and `Dial` return a value with fd -1; check `Ok` or `ConnOk`.

## A request and reply protocol

Most small protocols take turns: the client sends one request, the server sends one reply, and so on until the client hangs up. The server below reads in a loop and stops when `Read` returns an empty string, which is how TCP tells you the other side closed the connection. The client waits for each reply before it sends the next request, so every `Read` sees exactly one message.

net-tcp-guide-commands.salam

```salam
import net.tcp
import str

mut server := tcp.Server {}

func reply(line: str): str:
    words := line.split(" ")
    command := words.get(0)
    if command == "ADD" and words.len() == 3:
        ret str.FromInt(words.get(1).to_int() + words.get(2).to_int())
    end
    if command == "LEN" and words.len() == 2:
        ret str.FromInt(words.get(1).char_count())
    end
    ret "ERR unknown command: " + command
end

func serve():
    conn := tcp.Accept(server)
    tcp.SetReadDeadline(conn, 2000)
    mut served := 0
    until true:
        request := tcp.Read(conn, 1024)
        if request == "":
            break
        end
        _ := tcp.Write(conn, reply(request))
        served += 1
    end
    tcp.Close(conn)
    println "server: answered", served, "requests"
end

func main:
    server = tcp.Bind(0)
    t := spawn(serve)
    conn := tcp.Dial("127.0.0.1", tcp.Port(server))
    tcp.SetReadDeadline(conn, 2000)
    each request in ["ADD 2 40", "LEN salam", "PING"]:
        _ := tcp.Write(conn, request)
        println request, "->", tcp.Read(conn, 1024)
    end
    tcp.Close(conn)
    join(t)
    tcp.CloseServer(server)
end
```

Output:

```text
ADD 2 40 -> 42
LEN salam -> 5
PING -> ERR unknown command: PING
server: answered 3 requests
```

The server runs in its own thread with `spawn` and the main program waits for it with `join`. A real server would call `Accept` in a loop and hand each connection to a worker; while one client is served, the others wait in the queue of the listening socket.

## Serving several clients with worker threads

A server that reads from one client at a time stalls everyone behind a slow client. The usual shape is one thread that only accepts, a chan that carries the new connections, and a few worker threads that serve them. A thread receives the connection as its socket number, `conn.fd`, and turns it back into a `Conn` with `ConnFromFd`.

net-tcp-guide-workers.salam

```salam
import net.tcp
import chan
import str

mut server := tcp.Server {}
mut jobs := chan.Chan {} as chan.Chan<i64>

func acceptor():
    repeat 3:
        conn := tcp.Accept(server)
        if tcp.ConnOk(conn): _ := jobs.send(conn.fd) end
    end
    jobs.close()
end

func worker():
    mut ok := true
    until true:
        fd := jobs.recv(ok)
        if not ok: break end
        conn := tcp.ConnFromFd(fd)
        tcp.SetReadDeadline(conn, 2000)
        request := tcp.Read(conn, 1024)
        _ := tcp.Write(conn, "HELLO " + str.Upper(request))
        tcp.Close(conn)
    end
end

func main:
    server = tcp.Bind(0)
    jobs.init(8 as i64)
    a := spawn(acceptor)
    w1 := spawn(worker)
    w2 := spawn(worker)

    names := ["sara", "reza", "mina"]
    mut conns := Vector {} as Vector<tcp.Conn>
    repeat names.len():
        c := tcp.Dial("127.0.0.1", tcp.Port(server))
        tcp.SetReadDeadline(c, 2000)
        conns.push(c)
    end
    each i, c in conns:
        _ := tcp.Write(c, names[i])
    end
    each i, c in conns:
        println names[i], "->", tcp.Read(c, 1024)
        tcp.Close(c)
    end
    join(a)
    join(w1)
    join(w2)
    tcp.CloseServer(server)
end
```

Output:

```text
sara -> HELLO SARA
reza -> HELLO REZA
mina -> HELLO MINA
```

The three clients connect before any of them sends a word, and only two workers exist, so the third connection waits in the channel until a worker is free; it is still answered. Closing the channel after the last `Accept` makes `recv` report `ok` false, which ends the worker loops so `join` returns. In a long-running server the acceptor loops forever, and the number of workers caps how many clients are served at the same time.

## Messages in a byte stream

TCP moves bytes, not messages. Two writes can arrive as one read, and one write can arrive split over several reads. The lock step in the previous section hides that, but as soon as the other side sends several messages in a row you need a frame: a delimiter such as a newline, or a length in front of each message. The program below sends four lines in three uneven writes and puts them back together by keeping the unfinished part of the last read in `pending`.

net-tcp-guide-framing.salam

```salam
import net.tcp

mut server := tcp.Server {}

func sender():
    conn := tcp.Accept(server)
    _ := tcp.Write(conn, "apple\nban")
    _ := tcp.Write(conn, "ana\ncherry\ndate")
    _ := tcp.Write(conn, "\n")
    tcp.Close(conn)
end

func main:
    server = tcp.Bind(0)
    t := spawn(sender)
    conn := tcp.Dial("127.0.0.1", tcp.Port(server))
    tcp.SetReadDeadline(conn, 2000)
    mut pending := ""
    mut count := 0
    until true:
        chunk := tcp.Read(conn, 4096)
        if chunk == "":
            break
        end
        pending = pending + chunk
        mut nl := pending.find("\n")
        until nl >= 0:
            count += 1
            println count, pending.substr(0, nl)
            pending = pending.substr(nl + 1, pending.len() - nl - 1)
            nl = pending.find("\n")
        end
    end
    println "left over:", pending.len(), "bytes"
    tcp.Close(conn)
    join(t)
    tcp.CloseServer(server)
end
```

Output:

```text
1 apple
2 banana
3 cherry
4 date
left over: 0 bytes
```

For binary data, send a fixed size header with the length and read until you have that many bytes. `ReadBytes` and `WriteBytes` work on raw memory for that, and they do not stop at a zero byte the way a `str` does.

## Timeouts and failed connections

Without a deadline, `Read` waits forever for a peer that never answers. `SetReadDeadline` limits how long one read may wait, `SetWriteDeadline` does the same for writes, and `SetDeadline` sets both. When the time runs out the read returns an empty string, the same as a closed connection, so treat both as the end of the conversation. `Dial` does not stop the program when nothing listens on the port: it returns a connection for which `ConnOk` is false.

net-tcp-guide-timeouts.salam

```salam
import net.tcp

func main:
    silent := tcp.Bind(0)
    conn := tcp.Dial("127.0.0.1", tcp.Port(silent))
    println "connected:", tcp.ConnOk(conn)
    tcp.SetReadDeadline(conn, 300)
    answer := tcp.Read(conn, 1024)
    if answer == "":
        println "no answer within 300 ms, giving up"
    end
    tcp.Close(conn)
    tcp.CloseServer(silent)

    refused := tcp.Dial("127.0.0.1", tcp.Port(silent))
    if not tcp.ConnOk(refused):
        println "nothing listens there any more"
    end
end
```

Output:

```text
connected: true
no answer within 300 ms, giving up
nothing listens there any more
```

## A tiny HTTP server

HTTP/1.1 is text over TCP, so a few lines are enough for a status page or a health check. The request starts with a line such as `GET /hello HTTP/1.1`; `WriteHTTP` writes the status line, `Content-Type`, `Content-Length` and `Connection: close` for you. The client side shows the other half: it reads until the server closes the connection and splits the head from the body at the first empty line.

net-tcp-guide-http.salam

```salam
import net.tcp

mut server := tcp.Server {}

func handle():
    conn := tcp.Accept(server)
    tcp.SetDeadline(conn, 2000)
    request := tcp.Read(conn, 4096)
    first := request.split("\r\n").get(0)
    path := first.split(" ").get(1)
    if path == "/hello":
        tcp.WriteHTTP(conn, "200 OK", "text/plain", "hello from Salam")
    else:
        tcp.WriteHTTP(conn, "404 Not Found", "text/plain", "no page at " + path)
    end
    tcp.Close(conn)
end

func fetch(path: str):
    t := spawn(handle)
    conn := tcp.Dial("127.0.0.1", tcp.Port(server))
    tcp.SetDeadline(conn, 2000)
    _ := tcp.Write(conn, "GET " + path + " HTTP/1.1\r\nHost: localhost\r\n\r\n")
    mut response := ""
    until true:
        chunk := tcp.Read(conn, 4096)
        if chunk == "":
            break
        end
        response = response + chunk
    end
    tcp.Close(conn)
    join(t)
    split_at := response.find("\r\n\r\n")
    println response.split("\r\n").get(0)
    println "  body:", response.substr(split_at + 4, response.len() - split_at - 4)
end

func main:
    server = tcp.Bind(0)
    fetch("/hello")
    fetch("/missing")
    tcp.CloseServer(server)
end
```

Output:

```text
HTTP/1.1 200 OK
  body: hello from Salam
HTTP/1.1 404 Not Found
  body: no page at /missing
```

This is fine for a debug endpoint. For a real web service use net/http, which handles keep alive, chunked bodies, headers and routing.

## Encrypted connections

`DialTLS` connects and runs the TLS handshake in one call and returns a `tls.Conn`. From then on you read and write with the functions of the tls package, not with `tcp.Read`, because the bytes on the socket are encrypted. This example needs the internet; it prints the TLS version and the first line of the answer, which is `HTTP/1.1 200 OK` for example.com.

net-tcp-guide-https.salam

```salam
import net.tcp
import tls

func main:
    mut conn := tcp.DialTLS("example.com", 443)
    if not tls.ConnOk(conn):
        println "TLS failed:", tls.ConnError(conn)
        ret 1
    end
    println "protocol:", tls.Version(conn)
    _ := tls.Write(conn, "GET / HTTP/1.1\r\nHost: example.com\r\nConnection: close\r\n\r\n")
    head := tls.Read(conn, 4096)
    println head.split("\r\n").get(0)
    tls.Close(conn)
    ret 0
end
```

Protocols such as SMTP and IMAP start in plain text and switch to TLS later with a STARTTLS command. For those, `Dial` first, talk until the server agrees, then call `UpgradeTLS` on the same connection.

## Which function for which job

| Job | Use |
| --- | --- |
| Listen for clients | `Bind`, then `Accept` in a loop; `Port` when you bound port 0 |
| Connect to a server | `Dial`, then check `ConnOk` |
| Send and receive text | `Write` and `Read` |
| Send and receive binary data | `WriteBytes` and `ReadBytes` |
| Never hang on a silent peer | `SetReadDeadline`, `SetWriteDeadline` or `SetDeadline` |
| Interactive traffic with small packets | `SetNoDelay` |
| Notice dead idle connections | `SetKeepAlive` |
| HTTPS and other TLS protocols | `DialTLS`, or `UpgradeTLS` for STARTTLS |
| Reuse connections to the same host | `NewPool`, `Get` and `Put` |

## Types

### `Server`

```salam
struct Server
```

A TCP server listening on one port.

| Name | Type | Description |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `fd` | `i64 = -1` | The socket descriptor; -1 means invalid. |
| `port` | `int = 0` | The port the server listens on. |

net-tcp-Echo.salam

```salam
import net.tcp

mut server := tcp.Server {}

func responder():
    conn := tcp.Accept(server)
    message := tcp.Read(conn, 1024)
    _ := tcp.Write(conn, "echo: " + message)
    tcp.Close(conn)
end

func main:
    server = tcp.Bind(0)
    println tcp.Ok(server), tcp.Port(server) > 0
    t := spawn(responder)
    conn := tcp.Dial("127.0.0.1", tcp.Port(server))
    println tcp.ConnOk(conn)
    tcp.SetDeadline(conn, 2000)
    tcp.SetKeepAlive(conn, true)
    tcp.SetNoDelay(conn, true)
    println tcp.Write(conn, "hello")
    println tcp.Read(conn, 1024)
    tcp.Close(conn)
    join(t)
    tcp.CloseServer(server)
    println tcp.ConnOk(tcp.Dial("127.0.0.1", 1))
end
```

Output:

```text
true true
true
5
echo: hello
false
```

### `Conn`


| Name | Type | Description |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `fd` | `i64 = -1` | The socket descriptor; -1 means invalid. |

The example for this item is shown with the ones above: net-tcp-Echo.salam

### `PoolEntry`

```salam
struct PoolEntry
```

One idle connection in the pool.

| Name | Type | Description |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `key` | `str = ""` | The host and port. |
| `conn` | `Conn` | The connection. |
| `put_at_ms` | `i64 = 0` | When it was returned to the pool. |

net-tcp-Pool.salam

```salam
import net.tcp

func main:
    s := tcp.Bind(0)
    port := tcp.Port(s)
    mut pool := tcp.NewPool()
    conn := tcp.Get(pool, "127.0.0.1", port, 1000)
    println tcp.ConnOk(conn), tcp.PoolLen(pool)
    tcp.Put(pool, "127.0.0.1", port, conn, 1000)
    println tcp.PoolLen(pool)
    again := tcp.Get(pool, "127.0.0.1", port, 2000)
    println again.fd == conn.fd, tcp.PoolLen(pool)
    tcp.Put(pool, "127.0.0.1", port, again, 2000)
    fresh := tcp.Get(pool, "127.0.0.1", port, 2000 + pool.idle_ttl_ms + 1)
    println tcp.ConnOk(fresh), tcp.PoolLen(pool)
    tcp.Close(fresh)
    tcp.CloseServer(s)
end
```

Output:

```text
true 0
1
true 0
true 0
```

## Functions

### `Bind`

```salam
func Bind(port: int): Server
```

Listens on the given port on every IPv4 interface; port zero lets the system pick a free one. Check `Ok` afterwards: a port already in use gives an invalid server.

The example for this item is shown with the ones above: net-tcp-Echo.salam

### `Ok`

```salam
func Ok(srv: Server): bool
```

True when the server was created properly.

The example for this item is shown with the ones above: net-tcp-Echo.salam

### `Port`

```salam
func Port(srv: Server): int
```

The actual port of the server; for when you passed zero.

The example for this item is shown with the ones above: net-tcp-Echo.salam

### `Accept`

```salam
func Accept(srv: Server): Conn
```

Waits for a client to connect and returns its connection.

The example for this item is shown with the ones above: net-tcp-Echo.salam

### `CloseServer`

```salam
func CloseServer(srv: Server)
```

Closes the server.

The example for this item is shown with the ones above: net-tcp-Echo.salam

### `ConnOk`

```salam
func ConnOk(c: Conn): bool
```

True when the connection is up.

The example for this item is shown with the ones above: net-tcp-Echo.salam

### `Read`

```salam
func Read(c: Conn, max: int): str
```

Reads at most `max` bytes (4096 when `max` is 0 or less) as text; an empty string when the other side has closed the connection, the deadline passed or an error happened. The text stops at the first zero byte.

The example for this item is shown with the ones above: net-tcp-Echo.salam

### `Write`

```salam
func Write(c: Conn, data: str): int
```

Sends the text in one system call and returns the number of bytes sent, which can be fewer than the length for large data, or -1 on error.

The example for this item is shown with the ones above: net-tcp-Echo.salam

### `ReadBytes`

```salam
func ReadBytes(c: Conn, buf: void*, max: int): int
```

Reads at most `max` bytes into memory and returns how many; zero or less means the end or an error.

net-tcp-Bytes.salam

```salam
import net.tcp
import mem

mut server := tcp.Server {}

func responder():
    conn := tcp.Accept(server)
    tcp.SetReadDeadline(conn, 2000)
    tcp.SetWriteDeadline(conn, 2000)
    _ := tcp.Read(conn, 1024)
    tcp.WriteHTTP(conn, "200 OK", "text/plain", "hello")
    tcp.Close(conn)
end

func main:
    server = tcp.Bind(0)
    t := spawn(responder)
    conn := tcp.Dial("127.0.0.1", tcp.Port(server))
    request := "GET / HTTP/1.0\r\n\r\n"
    println tcp.WriteBytes(conn, request as void*, request.len())
    b := mem.AllocateZeroed(256 as u64)
    mut total := 0
    until true:
        r := tcp.ReadBytes(conn, b, 255)
        if r <= 0:
            break
        end
        total += r
    end
    println total > 0
    again := tcp.ConnFromFd(conn.fd)
    println again.fd == conn.fd
    tcp.Close(conn)
    join(t)
    tcp.CloseServer(server)
    mem.Free(b)
end
```

Output:

```text
18
true
true
```

### `WriteBytes`

```salam
func WriteBytes(c: Conn, ptr: void*, n: int): int
```

Sends `n` bytes from memory, looping until all are sent; returns how many went out.

The example for this item is shown with the ones above: net-tcp-Bytes.salam

### `Close`

```salam
func Close(c: Conn)
```

Closes the connection.

The example for this item is shown with the ones above: net-tcp-Echo.salam

### `Dial`

```salam

```

Connects to a host and port; when it fails, `ConnOk` is false.

The example for this item is shown with the ones above: net-tcp-Echo.salam

### `DialTimeout`

```salam
func DialTimeout(host: str, port: int, millis: int): Conn
```

Like `Dial`, with a time limit in milliseconds for the connect. On Linux it gives up after that limit when the host does not answer; other systems use their own default wait for the connect.

The example for this item is shown with the ones above: net-tcp-Echo.salam

### `DialTLS`

```salam
func DialTLS(host: str, port: int): tls.Conn
```

Makes an encrypted TLS connection; for HTTPS and the like.

net-tcp-TLS.salam

```salam
import net.tcp
import tls

func main:
    _ := tcp.DialTLS("example.com", 443)
    plain := tcp.Dial("example.com", 443)
    _ := tcp.UpgradeTLS(plain, tls.NewConfig("example.com"))
end
```

### `UpgradeTLS`

```salam
func UpgradeTLS(c: Conn, cfg: tls.Config): tls.Conn
```

# net/udp

https://salamlang.github.io/Salam/std/net-udp/

Sending and receiving UDP packets, with broadcast and multicast.

UDP sends separate packets, with no connection and no guarantee that they arrive or arrive in order; in exchange it is fast and simple. It is what DNS, games, live streaming and discovering devices on a local network use. Up to about 1500 bytes per packet is safe.

A UDP socket is not tied to one peer. The same socket can send to many addresses and receive from anyone, and every `Packet` carries `from_host` and `from_port` so you know where to answer. Each `Send` is one packet and each `Receive` returns one whole packet, so unlike TCP there is no need to find where a message ends.

Choose UDP when a late answer is worth nothing (game state, sensor readings, voice) or when one small question gets one small answer. When every byte must arrive, in order, use net/tcp. To look up names, net/dns already speaks the DNS protocol over UDP for you.

### What trips people up

- A timeout looks like an empty packet. `Receive` returns empty `data` both when the timeout passed and when a peer really sent zero bytes, so never use empty packets as messages.

- Too small a buffer cuts the packet. The rest of a packet larger than `max` is thrown away, not kept for the next call. Pass the largest size your protocol allows (0 means 65536 for `Receive`).

- Text stops at a zero byte. `Receive` gives a `str`; binary packets need `ReceiveBytes`.

- IPv4 only. Sockets, addresses and multicast groups are all IPv4.

- Nothing is guaranteed. Packets can be lost, repeated or reordered; the retry guide shows the usual answer.

## Answering a request

A UDP server binds a port and answers each packet to the address it came from. The client uses `Open`, which picks a free port for it, sends a packet and waits for the reply on the same socket. Set a timeout on both sides, because a lost packet would otherwise leave `Receive` waiting forever.

net-udp-guide-ping.salam

```salam
import net.udp
import str

mut server := udp.Socket {}

func pong():
    udp.SetTimeout(server, 2000)
    mut answered := 0
    until answered < 3:
        p := udp.Receive(server, 1500)
        if p.data == "":
            break
        end
        answered += 1
        _ := udp.Send(server, p.from_host, p.from_port, "pong " + str.FromInt(answered) + " for " + p.data)
    end
end

func main:
    server = udp.BindOn("127.0.0.1", 0)
    t := spawn(pong)
    client := udp.Open()
    udp.SetTimeout(client, 2000)
    each name in ["alpha", "beta", "gamma"]:
        _ := udp.Send(client, "127.0.0.1", udp.Port(server), name)
        reply := udp.Receive(client, 1500)
        println reply.data
    end
    join(t)
    udp.Close(client)
    udp.Close(server)
end
```

Output:

```text
pong 1 for alpha
pong 2 for beta
pong 3 for gamma
```

Binding to `127.0.0.1` with `BindOn` keeps the server private to this machine. `Bind` listens on every address, which is what a service on the network needs.

## Timeouts and retries

UDP never tells you that a packet was lost, so a client that expects an answer has to wait a short time and send again. With `SetTimeout`, `Receive` returns a packet with empty `data` when nothing arrived in time. The server in this example ignores the first two requests, the way a busy network might drop them, and the client tries until it gets an answer or runs out of attempts.

net-udp-guide-retry.salam

```salam
import net.udp

mut server := udp.Socket {}

func flaky():
    udp.SetTimeout(server, 3000)
    mut seen := 0
    until seen < 3:
        p := udp.Receive(server, 1500)
        if p.data == "":
            break
        end
        seen += 1
        if seen == 3:
            _ := udp.Send(server, p.from_host, p.from_port, "got " + p.data)
        end
    end
end

func ask(sock: udp.Socket, port: int, question: str, tries: int): str:
    repeat tries in i:
        _ := udp.Send(sock, "127.0.0.1", port, question)
        reply := udp.Receive(sock, 1500)
        if reply.data != "":
            ret reply.data
        end
        println "attempt", i + 1, "timed out"
    end
    ret ""
end

func main:
    server = udp.BindOn("127.0.0.1", 0)
    t := spawn(flaky)
    client := udp.Open()
    udp.SetTimeout(client, 200)
    answer := ask(client, udp.Port(server), "status?", 5)
    if answer == "":
        println "server unreachable"
    else:
        println "answer:", answer
    end
    join(t)
    udp.Close(client)
    udp.Close(server)
end
```

Output:

```text
attempt 1 timed out
attempt 2 timed out
answer: got status?
```

Because a request can arrive twice (the first copy was only slow, not lost), a request that changes something should carry an id, so the server can recognise a repeat and answer it without doing the work again. DNS works exactly like this.

## Binary packets

Compact protocols put numbers in bytes instead of text. `SendBytes` sends a block of memory as one packet and `ReceiveBytes` fills a buffer and reports the sender through its last two arguments. The packet here has one byte for the kind of message, one for a sensor number and two for a value, high byte first, which is the usual network order.

net-udp-guide-binary.salam

```salam
import net.udp
import mem

func main:
    receiver := udp.BindOn("127.0.0.1", 0)
    sender := udp.Open()
    udp.SetTimeout(receiver, 2000)

    out := mem.AllocateZeroed(8 as u64)
    o := out as u8*
    o[0] = 1 as u8
    o[1] = 42 as u8
    o[2] = 1 as u8
    o[3] = 44 as u8
    sent := udp.SendBytes(sender, "127.0.0.1", udp.Port(receiver), out, 4)
    println "sent", sent, "bytes"

    buf := mem.AllocateZeroed(1500 as u64)
    mut host := ""
    mut port := 0
    n := udp.ReceiveBytes(receiver, buf, 1500, host, port)
    b := buf as u8*
    kind := b[0] as int
    sensor := b[1] as int
    value := (b[2] as int) * 256 + (b[3] as int)
    println "received", n, "bytes from", host
    println "kind", kind, "sensor", sensor, "value", value

    mem.Free(out)
    mem.Free(buf)
    udp.Close(sender)
    udp.Close(receiver)
end
```

Output:

```text
sent 4 bytes
received 4 bytes from 127.0.0.1
kind 1 sensor 42 value 300
```

Keep packets below about 1500 bytes. Larger ones are split by the network and lost completely if one part goes missing. Use `ReceiveBytes` rather than `Receive` whenever the data may contain a zero byte, since a `str` ends at the first one.

## Finding devices on the local network

To find a printer, a game host or another copy of your program on the same network without knowing its address, send to a group instead of to one machine. With `JoinMulticast` a socket receives what anyone sends to the group address; `SetBroadcast` instead allows sending to the broadcast address of the whole network, such as `255.255.255.255`. This example depends on how the network is set up, so it is only compiled here. On most machines it prints `heard: printer at 192.168.1.50`, because the sender also receives its own multicast packets.

net-udp-guide-discovery.salam

```salam
import net.udp

func main:
    group := "239.255.42.99"
    port := 9999
    listener := udp.Bind(port)
    if not udp.JoinMulticast(listener, group):
        println "could not join", group
        ret 1
    end
    udp.SetTimeout(listener, 1000)

    announcer := udp.Open()
    _ := udp.Send(announcer, group, port, "printer at 192.168.1.50")

    p := udp.Receive(listener, 1500)
    if p.data == "":
        println "nobody announced anything"
    else:
        println "heard:", p.data
    end
    _ := udp.LeaveMulticast(listener, group)
    udp.Close(announcer)
    udp.Close(listener)
    ret 0
end
```

Multicast addresses from `239.0.0.0` to `239.255.255.255` are meant for private use inside an organisation. Every program that wants the announcements binds the same port and joins the same group.

## Types

### `Socket`

```salam
struct Socket
```

A UDP socket.

| Name | Type | Description |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `fd` | `i64 = -1` | The socket descriptor. |

net-udp-Echo.salam

```salam
import net.udp
import mem

func main:
    receiver := udp.BindOn("127.0.0.1", 0)
    sender := udp.Open()
    println udp.Ok(receiver), udp.Ok(sender), udp.Port(receiver) > 0
    udp.SetTimeout(receiver, 2000)
    println udp.Send(sender, "127.0.0.1", udp.Port(receiver), "hello")
    p := udp.Receive(receiver, 1500)
    println p.data, p.from_host, p.from_port > 0
    _ := udp.SendTo(sender, "127.0.0.1", udp.Port(receiver), "two")
    text := "three"
    _ := udp.SendBytes(sender, "127.0.0.1", udp.Port(receiver), text as void*, text.len())
    println udp.Receive(receiver, 1500).data
    buffer := mem.AllocateZeroed(64 as u64)
    mut host := ""
    mut port := 0
    println udp.ReceiveBytes(receiver, buffer, 64, host, port), host
    udp.SetTimeout(receiver, 100)
    println "[" + udp.Receive(receiver, 1500).data + "]"
    udp.SetBroadcast(sender, true)
    println udp.JoinMulticast(receiver, "239.1.2.3") or true, udp.LeaveMulticast(receiver, "239.1.2.3") or true
    other := udp.Bind(0)
    println udp.Ok(other)
    udp.Close(other)
    udp.Close(receiver)
    udp.Close(sender)
    mem.Free(buffer)
end
```

Output:

```text
true true true
5
hello 127.0.0.1 true
two
5 127.0.0.1
[]
true true
true
```

# net/dns

https://salamlang.github.io/Salam/std/net-dns/

Finding the address of a name and asking for any kind of DNS record.

DNS turns names such as `salamlang.ir` into IP addresses. `Lookup` is the simplest way and does what a browser does. The `Lookup...` functions ask the DNS server for one particular kind of record and are what you want for building network tools or checking the configuration of a domain.

A lookup can fail for ordinary reasons: the name does not exist, the network is down or the server is slow. None of the functions stop the program. `Lookup` and `LookupCNAME` return an empty string, and the others return an empty list, so check the result before using it.

### Two different resolvers

- `Lookup` asks the operating system, exactly as connecting by name does: the hosts file, `localhost`, search domains and the system cache all apply. It returns one IPv4 address.

- The `Lookup...` record functions send their own queries over UDP to the servers from `DefaultServers`: the `nameserver` lines of `/etc/resolv.conf` on Linux, macOS and BSD. The hosts file is not used. When there is no such file, which is always the case on Windows, they fall back to the public resolvers `8.8.8.8` and `1.1.1.1`, so the names you look up leave your network. Each server gets 3 seconds before the next one is tried.

### What trips people up

- Large answers can be incomplete. An answer that does not fit in one UDP packet comes back with `tc` set and is not retried over TCP, so very long TXT records or long lists of addresses may be cut short.

- `QueryServer` does not check the answer's id against the question's. On an untrusted network compare `Message.id` yourself, or prefer a resolver you trust.

- Everything is plain text on port 53. There is no DNSSEC validation and no DNS over TLS or HTTPS.

- `LookupPTR` takes IPv4 addresses only.

## Resolve a name, then connect

net/tcp and net/udp take a host name or an address, but resolving the name yourself first lets you report a clear error before you try to connect. `Lookup` uses the operating system resolver, so `localhost` and the names in the hosts file work too, offline.

net-dns-guide-connect.salam

```salam
import net.dns
import net.tcp

mut server := tcp.Server {}

func greet():
    conn := tcp.Accept(server)
    _ := tcp.Write(conn, "hello, you found me")
    tcp.Close(conn)
end

func connect(host: str, port: int): tcp.Conn:
    address := dns.Lookup(host)
    if address == "":
        println "cannot resolve", host
        ret tcp.Conn {}
    end
    println host, "is", address
    ret tcp.Dial(address, port)
end

func main:
    server = tcp.Bind(0)
    t := spawn(greet)
    conn := connect("localhost", tcp.Port(server))
    if tcp.ConnOk(conn):
        tcp.SetReadDeadline(conn, 2000)
        println tcp.Read(conn, 1024)
        tcp.Close(conn)
    end
    join(t)
    tcp.CloseServer(server)
    bad := connect("no-such-host.invalid", 80)
    println "connected:", tcp.ConnOk(bad)
end
```

Output:

```text
localhost is 127.0.0.1
hello, you found me
cannot resolve no-such-host.invalid
connected: false
```

The `.invalid` top level domain is reserved and never exists, which makes it handy for testing the failure path.

## Checking the mail setup of a domain

Mail for a domain goes to the servers in its MX records, lowest priority number first; the others are fallbacks. The domain's TXT records hold the SPF policy, which says which servers may send mail for it, and the DMARC policy lives in the TXT record of `_dmarc.` plus the domain. This program needs the internet, so it is only compiled here. Against the real DNS it printed:

net-dns-guide-mail.salam

```salam
import net.dns

func main:
    domain := "gmail.com"
    mx := dns.LookupMX(domain)
    if mx.items.len() == 0:
        println domain, "has no MX records, mail goes to its A record"
    end
    mut best := dns.Record {}
    each r in mx.items:
        println "MX", r.priority, r.data
        if best.data == "" or r.priority < best.priority:
            best = r
        end
    end
    println "deliver to:", best.data, "first"
    each text in dns.LookupTXT(domain):
        if text.starts_with("v=spf1"):
            println "SPF:", text
        end
    end
    each text in dns.LookupTXT("_dmarc." + domain):
        if text.starts_with("v=DMARC1"):
            println "DMARC:", text
        end
    end
end
```

```salam
MX 10 alt1.gmail-smtp-in.l.google.com
MX 20 alt2.gmail-smtp-in.l.google.com
MX 40 alt4.gmail-smtp-in.l.google.com
MX 30 alt3.gmail-smtp-in.l.google.com
MX 5 gmail-smtp-in.l.google.com
deliver to: gmail-smtp-in.l.google.com first
SPF: v=spf1 redirect=_spf.google.com
DMARC: v=DMARC1; p=none; sp=quarantine; rua=mailto:mailauth-reports@google.com
```

The records come back in whatever order the server chose, so sort or pick by `priority` yourself, as the loop does.

## Asking one server directly

`QueryServer` skips the system resolver and asks the server you name, which is how you compare what different resolvers say or test your own DNS server. It returns the whole `Message`: `rcode` 3 means the name does not exist, and an empty message (no `qr` flag, id 0) means no answer came back within the timeout. Each record has a `ttl`, the number of seconds a cache may keep it. A name that is an alias answers with a CNAME record before the address, which is why the loop looks at `rtype`. This one needs the internet too.

net-dns-guide-servers.salam

```salam
import net.dns

func show(server: str, name: str):
    m := dns.QueryServer(server, name, dns.TypeA, 2000)
    if m.id == 0 and not m.qr:
        println server, "did not answer"
        ret
    end
    if m.rcode == 3:
        println server, "says", name, "does not exist"
        ret
    end
    each r in m.answers.items:
        if r.rtype == dns.TypeA:
            println server, name, "->", r.data, "for", r.ttl, "s"
        else:
            println server, name, "is an alias of", r.data
        end
    end
end

func main:
    servers := dns.DefaultServers()
    println "system servers:", servers
    show(servers.get(0), "www.github.com")
    show("1.1.1.1", "salamlang.ir")
    show("1.1.1.1", "no-such-name.invalid")
    show("192.0.2.1", "salamlang.ir")
end
```

`192.0.2.1` belongs to a range reserved for documentation, so nothing answers there and the program shows the timeout case. The addresses and TTLs you see will differ from run to run.

## Speaking the protocol yourself

DNS is just small binary packets over UDP, and `EncodeQuery` and `Decode` build and read them. That is enough for a test double: the program below runs a toy DNS server on `127.0.0.1` that answers every question with no such name by setting two flag bytes of the query and sending it back. The client sends a real query with net/udp and decodes the answer, all offline.

net-dns-guide-toy-server.salam

```salam
import net.dns
import net.udp
import mem

mut server := udp.Socket {}

func answer_nxdomain():
    udp.SetTimeout(server, 2000)
    buf := mem.AllocateZeroed(512 as u64)
    mut host := ""
    mut port := 0
    n := udp.ReceiveBytes(server, buf, 512, host, port)
    question := dns.Decode(buf, n)
    println "server: question", question.id, "for", question.questions.items[0].name
    b := buf as u8*
    b[2] = b[2] | (128 as u8)
    b[3] = 131 as u8
    _ := udp.SendBytes(server, host, port, buf, n)
    mem.Free(buf)
end

func rcode_name(code: int): str:
    switch code:
        0: ret "NOERROR" end
        2: ret "SERVFAIL" end
        3: ret "NXDOMAIN" end
        5: ret "REFUSED" end
    end
    ret "other"
end

func main:
    server = udp.BindOn("127.0.0.1", 0)
    t := spawn(answer_nxdomain)
    query := dns.EncodeQuery("shop.example", dns.TypeA, 7)
    client := udp.Open()
    udp.SetTimeout(client, 2000)
    _ := udp.SendBytes(client, "127.0.0.1", udp.Port(server), query.data, query.len)
    reply := mem.AllocateZeroed(512 as u64)
    mut host := ""
    mut port := 0
    n := udp.ReceiveBytes(client, reply, 512, host, port)
    join(t)
    m := dns.Decode(reply, n)
    println "client: answer", m.id, "qr", m.qr, "ra", m.ra
    println "client: rcode", m.rcode, rcode_name(m.rcode), "answers", m.answers.items.len()
    mem.Free(reply)
    udp.Close(client)
    udp.Close(server)
end
```

Output:

```text
server: question 7 for shop.example
client: answer 7 qr true ra true
client: rcode 3 NXDOMAIN answers 0
```

The id of the answer matches the id of the question (7 here). A real client sends a random id and ignores any answer whose id does not match, so a stray or forged packet is not mistaken for the answer.

## Which function for which job

| Job | Use |
| --- | --- |
| Get an address to connect to | `Lookup` |
| All IPv4 or IPv6 addresses of a name | `LookupA`, `LookupAAAA` |
| Where mail for a domain goes | `LookupMX` |
| SPF, DMARC and domain verification codes | `LookupTXT` |
| The real name behind an alias | `LookupCNAME` |
| The name of an IP address | `LookupPTR` |
| Ask a chosen server, see TTLs and error codes | `QueryServer` |
| Build or read raw DNS packets | `EncodeQuery`, `Decode` |

## Types

### `Question`

```salam
struct Question
```

One question.

| Name | Type | Description |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `name` | `str = ""` | The domain name. |
| `qtype` | `int = 0` | The record type. |
| `qclass` | `int = 0` | The class. |

net-dns-Message.salam

```salam
import net.dns
import compress

func main:
    query := dns.EncodeQuery("salamlang.ir", dns.TypeA, 42)
    println compress.BufLen(query), compress.BufToBase64(query)
    m := dns.Decode(query.data, query.len)
    println m.id, m.qr, m.rd, m.opcode, m.rcode, m.questions.items.len()
    q := m.questions.items[0]
    println q.name, q.qtype == dns.TypeA, q.qclass == dns.ClassIN
    println m.answers.items.len(), m.authorities.items.len(), m.extras.items.len(), m.aa, m.tc, m.ra
    println dns.TypeNS, dns.TypeCNAME, dns.TypeSOA, dns.TypePTR, dns.TypeMX, dns.TypeTXT, dns.TypeAAAA
    println dns.Lookup("localhost")
    println dns.DefaultServers().len() > 0
end
```

Output:

```text
30 ACoBAAABAAAAAAAACXNhbGFtbGFuZwJpcgAAAQAB
42 false true 0 0 1
salamlang.ir true true
0 0 0 false false false
2 5 6 12 15 16 28
127.0.0.1
true
```

```salam
import net.dns

func main:

    println dns.LookupAAAA("salamlang.ir")
    println dns.LookupCNAME("www.github.com")
    mx := dns.LookupMX("gmail.com")

    end
```

# net/mime

https://salamlang.github.io/Salam/std/net-mime/

The media type of a file, the Content-Type header, and multipart form bodies.

A media type (MIME) tells the browser and other programs what the content is, such as `image/png`. This package finds the type from a file extension and reads the `Content-Type` header.

Forms that upload a file send a `multipart/form-data` body: several parts with a boundary between them. `ParseMultipart` reads one and `MultipartWriter` builds one.

The package also has `StatusText`, the standard reason phrase of an HTTP status code. It is used by net/http, which is where you will usually meet these functions.

### What trips people up

- The type table is short. `MimeExt` knows about 25 extensions: `html htm css js mjs json map png jpg jpeg gif svg ico webp txt md pdf xml wasm zip mp4 webm mp3 wav woff woff2`. Everything else, `csv`, `avif`, `ttf` and `docx` included, becomes `application/octet-stream`, so handle the extra types your site serves before calling it.

- Lookups and comparisons are case sensitive. `MimeType` does not lower the extension, `ParseContentType` keeps the case of the media type and the parameter names, and `ParamGet` matches the name exactly, so `Charset=UTF-8` is not found by `"charset"`. Lower both sides before comparing.

- Only three types get a charset: `text/html`, `text/plain` and `text/markdown` come with `charset=utf-8`; CSS and JavaScript do not.

- Binary uploads need the bytes. `ParseMultipart` works on raw memory and keeps each body in a `ByteBuf`, but if the request body has passed through a `str` on the way, it is already cut at the first zero byte.

The guide below shows the places a web program meets media types: serving files with the right `Content-Type`, deciding how to read a request body, and handling file uploads on both sides.

## The right Content-Type for a file

A browser decides what to do with a response from its `Content-Type`, not from the file name, so a stylesheet served as `application/octet-stream` is ignored. `MimeType` maps a file name to its type by extension, with `charset=utf-8` added to HTML, plain text and Markdown, and falls back to `application/octet-stream` for names it does not know. `MimeExt` does the same for a bare extension without the dot, such as `png`, when you have no file name.

net-mime-guide-static.salam

```salam
import net.mime

func header_for(path: str): str:
    ret "Content-Type: " + mime.MimeType(path.lower())
end

func main:
    files := ["index.html", "app.js", "style.css", "logo.svg", "photo.JPG", "fonts/vazir.woff2", "report.pdf", "data.bin", "README"]
    each f in files:
        println f, "->", header_for(f)
    end
    println mime.MimeType("photo.JPG"), "(without lower)"
end
```

Output:

```text
index.html -> Content-Type: text/html; charset=utf-8
app.js -> Content-Type: application/javascript
style.css -> Content-Type: text/css
logo.svg -> Content-Type: image/svg+xml
photo.JPG -> Content-Type: image/jpeg
fonts/vazir.woff2 -> Content-Type: font/woff2
report.pdf -> Content-Type: application/pdf
data.bin -> Content-Type: application/octet-stream
README -> Content-Type: application/octet-stream
application/octet-stream (without lower)
```

The lookup is case sensitive: `photo.JPG` is only recognised after `lower()`. Files from cameras and Windows often have upper case extensions, so lower the name before the lookup, as `header_for` does.

## Reading the Content-Type of a request

A server has to look at the `Content-Type` header before it reads the body: JSON, a URL encoded form and a multipart upload are all read differently. `ParseContentType` splits the header into `media_type` and its parameters, and `ParamGet` returns one parameter, such as `charset` or `boundary`, with any quotes removed, or an empty string when it is absent.

net-mime-guide-content-type.salam

```salam
import net.mime

func describe(header: str): str:
    ct := mime.ParseContentType(header)
    media := ct.media_type.lower()
    mut charset := mime.ParamGet(ct, "charset")
    if charset.len() == 0: charset = "none" end
    if media == "application/json":
        ret "JSON body, charset " + charset
    else media == "application/x-www-form-urlencoded":
        ret "URL encoded form"
    else media == "multipart/form-data":
        ret "upload, boundary " + mime.ParamGet(ct, "boundary")
    else media.find("text/") == 0:
        ret "plain text, charset " + charset
    end
    ret "unknown: [" + media + "]"
end

func main:
    println describe("application/json")
    println describe("application/json; charset=utf-8")
    println describe("application/x-www-form-urlencoded")
    println describe("multipart/form-data; boundary=\"abc123\"")
    println describe("text/csv;charset=windows-1256")
    println describe("Application/JSON")
    println describe("")
end
```

Output:

```text
JSON body, charset none
JSON body, charset utf-8
URL encoded form
upload, boundary abc123
plain text, charset windows-1256
JSON body, charset none
unknown: []
```

Media types are case insensitive by the standard, but `media_type` keeps the case it was sent in. Compare `ct.media_type.lower()`, otherwise a client that sends `Application/JSON` falls through to the unknown branch.

## Building and reading a file upload

An HTML form with a file field sends `multipart/form-data`: each field becomes a part with its own headers, separated by a boundary string. `NewMultipartWriter` starts one, `WriteField` adds a text field, `WriteFileStr` and `WriteFileBytes` add a file, and `CloseWriter` returns the finished body. `ContentTypeHeader` gives the matching header with the boundary in it. On the receiving side, `ParseMultipart` takes the body and the boundary and returns the parts; a part with a non-empty `filename` is a file.

net-mime-guide-upload.salam

```salam
import net.mime
import compress

func handle_upload(content_type: str, body: compress.ByteBuf):
    ct := mime.ParseContentType(content_type)
    if ct.media_type != "multipart/form-data":
        println "415 Unsupported Media Type"
        ret
    end
    boundary := mime.ParamGet(ct, "boundary")
    parts := mime.ParseMultipart(body.data, body.len, boundary)
    each p in parts.items:
        if p.filename.len() > 0:
            println "file", p.name, p.filename, p.content_type, p.body.len, "bytes"
        else:
            println "field", p.name, "=", compress.BufToStrUnsafe(p.body)
        end
    end
end

func main:
    mut form := mime.NewMultipartWriter()
    mime.WriteField(form, "title", "Trip to Shiraz")
    mime.WriteField(form, "album", "2026")
    mime.WriteFileStr(form, "notes", "notes.txt", "", "Day 1: Eram garden")
    photo := compress.BufFromStr("not really a jpeg")
    mime.WriteFileBytes(form, "photo", "eram.jpg", "", photo.data, photo.len)
    body := mime.CloseWriter(form)
    handle_upload(mime.ContentTypeHeader(form), body)
    handle_upload("application/json", body)
end
```

Output:

```text
field title = Trip to Shiraz
field album = 2026
file notes notes.txt text/plain; charset=utf-8 18 bytes
file photo eram.jpg image/jpeg 17 bytes
415 Unsupported Media Type
```

When you pass an empty content type for a file part, the writer fills it in from the file name with `MimeType`, which is why `notes.txt` and `eram.jpg` got their types. A body that is not `multipart/form-data` should be refused with status 415 before any parsing.

## An upload endpoint with net/http

The same two halves work over a real connection. The program below starts a net/http server on 127.0.0.1 with a router, posts a form with a text file to it and prints what the handler found. In the handler, `Header` gives the request's `Content-Type` and `Body` the raw body.

net-mime-guide-roundtrip.salam

```salam
import net.http
import net.router
import net.mime
import compress

func upload(ctx: i64):
    ct := mime.ParseContentType(http.Header(ctx, "Content-Type"))
    body := http.Body(ctx)
    parts := mime.ParseMultipart(body as void*, body.len(), mime.ParamGet(ct, "boundary"))
    mut reply := ""
    each p in parts.items:
        reply += p.name + ": " + compress.BufToStrUnsafe(p.body) + "\n"
    end
    http.Text(ctx, reply)
end

func main:
    mut r := router.NewRouter()
    router.Post(r, "/upload", upload)
    mut s := http.NewServer(18577)
    http.SetHost(s, "127.0.0.1")
    http.Use(s, r)
    if not http.RunBackground(s):
        println "port 18577 is busy"
        ret 1
    end

    mut form := mime.NewMultipartWriter()
    mime.WriteField(form, "user", "maryam")
    mime.WriteFileStr(form, "todo", "todo.txt", "text/plain", "buy bread")
    body := mime.CloseWriter(form)
    headers := HashMap {} as HashMap<str, str>
    headers.put("Content-Type", mime.ContentTypeHeader(form))
    resp := http.PostWith("http://127.0.0.1:18577/upload", compress.BufToStrUnsafe(body), headers)
    println resp.status
    print resp.body
    ret 0
end
```

Output:

```text
200
user: maryam
todo: buy bread
```

Two limits to know. `Body` is a `str`, and a `str` ends at the first zero byte, so binary files such as images arrive cut short through this path; text uploads are fine. And `ParseMultipart` matches part headers such as `Content-Disposition` with their exact case, which is what browsers and this package's writer send.

net-mime-Multipart.salam

```salam
import net.mime
import compress
import str

func main:
    mut w := mime.NewMultipartWriter()
    println str.StartsWith(mime.ContentTypeHeader(w), "multipart/form-data; boundary=")
    mime.WriteField(w, "name", "Maryam")
    mime.WriteFileStr(w, "note", "note.txt", "text/plain", "hello")
    data := compress.BufFromStr("PNG")
    mime.WriteFileBytes(w, "pic", "a.png", "image/png", data.data, data.len)
    body := mime.CloseWriter(w)
    println w.closed, body.len > 0
    mut parts := mime.ParseMultipart(body.data, body.len, w.boundary)
    each p in parts.items:
        println p.name, "[" + p.filename + "]", "[" + p.content_type + "]", compress.BufToStrUnsafe(p.body), p.headers.items.len()
    end
    println parts.items[1].headers.items[0].key
    println mime.PartIndex(parts, "note"), mime.PartIndex(parts, "missing")
    println mime.PartValue(parts, "name"), "[" + mime.PartValue(parts, "missing") + "]"
    mime.FreeMultipart(parts)
end
```

Output:

```text
true
true true
name [] [] Maryam 1
note [note.txt] [text/plain] hello 2
pic [a.png] [image/png] PNG 2
Content-Disposition
1 -1
Maryam []
```
