# dom

https://salamlang.github.io/Salam/std/dom/

Working with a web page in the browser: elements, events, timers and JavaScript objects.

This package lets a Salam program drive a web page: find and create elements, change their text, classes and styles, react to clicks and keys, run timers and keep small values in `localStorage`. A program that uses it runs in the browser. Translate it to JavaScript with `salam js app.salam --output=app.js` and load it with a `<script src="app.js">` tag; `main` runs once the page is ready, and `println` writes to the browser console. That is why the examples on this page are only checked, not run. For drawing use web/canvas, for games that read the keyboard every frame web/keys, and for a desktop window around a page webview.

Elements and other JavaScript objects are held in an `i64` variable, and events and timers take an anonymous function such as `(): ... end`. Each function maps to one browser call (`SetText` is `textContent`, `SetStyle` is `style.setProperty` and so on), so the MDN documentation for that call applies.

Things that catch people out:

- A missing element is JavaScript `null`, not 0. `el == 0` is never true for it, and using it throws. Check with `Exists(id)` before `ById`, or with `CountOf(QueryAll(sel)) == 0` for a selector.

- `SetHtml` runs whatever HTML it gets. Put text from users in with `SetText`, never with `SetHtml`.

- `SetStyle` takes CSS names such as `background-color`, not the JavaScript form `backgroundColor`.

- `OnReady` does nothing when called from `main`, because `main` already runs after the page is ready and the browser does not repeat the ready event. Put start-up code straight in `main`.

- `OffEvent` needs the very function value you registered, so keep it in a variable; a second lambda with the same body is a different function.

## Running the examples

Each program below is a whole page's script. Save it as `app.salam`, translate it, and open an HTML file that loads the result:

```salam
salam js app.salam --output=app.js
echo '<!doctype html><meta charset="utf-8"><body><script src="app.js"></script>' > index.html
salam serve .
```

Then visit `http://127.0.0.1:8000`. Output from `println` appears in the browser console. With `--output=app.html` instead, `salam js` writes one self contained page.

## A to-do list

Most pages follow the same shape: build the elements once in `main`, keep the ones you need later in global variables, and react to events. A click handler that is created inside a function, like the one on each new list item, remembers the element it was made for. `StoreSetInt` and `StoreGetInt` keep a number in the browser's `localStorage`, so it survives a reload.

dom-todo.salam

```salam
import dom

mut list := 0 as i64
mut entry := 0 as i64
mut added := 0

func add_item(text: str):
    item := dom.Create("li")
    dom.SetText(item, text)
    dom.OnEvent(item, "click", ():
        dom.ToggleClass(item, "done")
    end)
    dom.Append(list, item)
    added += 1
    dom.StoreSetInt("todo-added", added as i64)
end

func main:
    dom.SetTitle("To do")
    entry = dom.Create("input")
    dom.SetAttr(entry, "placeholder", "What needs doing?")
    button := dom.Create("button")
    dom.SetText(button, "Add")
    list = dom.Create("ul")
    dom.Append(dom.Body(), entry)
    dom.Append(dom.Body(), button)
    dom.Append(dom.Body(), list)

    dom.OnEvent(button, "click", ():
        text := dom.GetValue(entry)
        if text.len() > 0:
            add_item(text)
            dom.SetValue(entry, "")
        end
    end)
    dom.OnEventE(entry, "keydown", (e: i64):
        if dom.EventKey(e) == "Enter":
            dom.PreventDefault(e)
            text := dom.GetValue(entry)
            if text.len() > 0:
                add_item(text)
                dom.SetValue(entry, "")
            end
        end
    end)
    println "items added on this device so far:", dom.StoreGetInt("todo-added")
end
```

`OnEvent` takes a handler without arguments; use `OnEventE` when you need the event itself, for example to read the key with `EventKey` or to stop the browser's default action with `PreventDefault`.

## Working with elements already on the page

When the HTML comes from a server or a template, the script finds the elements instead of creating them. This one filters a product table as the user types. It first checks with `Exists` that the page has what it needs, then takes every row with `QueryAll` and walks them with `CountOf` and `ItemAt`. Hiding a row is `SetStyle(row, "display", "none")`, and an empty value removes the style again.

dom-filter.salam

```salam
import dom
import str

func filter(rows: i64, word: str, counter: i64):
    mut shown := 0
    repeat dom.CountOf(rows) in i:
        row := dom.ItemAt(rows, i)
        name := str.Lower(dom.GetText(row))
        if word.len() == 0 or str.Contains(name, word):
            dom.SetStyle(row, "display", "")
            shown += 1
        else:
            dom.SetStyle(row, "display", "none")
        end
    end
    dom.SetText(counter, shown + " of " + dom.CountOf(rows) + " products")
end

func main:
    if not (dom.Exists("search") and dom.Exists("count")):
        println "this script needs #search and #count on the page"
        ret
    end
    search := dom.ById("search")
    counter := dom.ById("count")
    rows := dom.QueryAll("#products tr")
    if dom.CountOf(rows) == 0:
        dom.SetText(counter, "no products")
        ret
    end
    dom.SetStyle(dom.Query("#products"), "background-color", "#fafafa")
    dom.OnEvent(search, "input", ():
        filter(rows, str.Lower(str.Trim(dom.GetValue(search))), counter)
    end)
    filter(rows, "", counter)
end
```

It expects markup such as `<input id="search"> <p id="count"></p> <table id="products"><tr><td>Green tea</td></tr>...</table>`. `QueryAll` returns the rows that exist at that moment; rows added later are not in the list, so query again after you change the table.

## Checking a form as the user types

The `input` event fires on every change to a text box, which makes it the place for live checks. One function looks at all fields, writes the first problem into a message element and switches the button with `SetBool(el, "disabled", ...)`. Calling it once at the end of `main` puts the form in the right state before the user touches it.

dom-form-check.salam

```salam
import dom
import str

mut email := 0 as i64
mut password := 0 as i64
mut submit := 0 as i64
mut note := 0 as i64

func check():
    e := dom.GetValue(email)
    p := dom.GetValue(password)
    mut problem := ""
    if not str.Contains(e, "@"):
        problem = "Enter an email address."
    else p.len() < 8:
        problem = "The password needs at least 8 characters."
    end
    dom.SetText(note, problem)
    dom.SetBool(submit, "disabled", problem.len() > 0)
    if problem.len() > 0:
        dom.AddClass(note, "error")
    else:
        dom.RemoveClass(note, "error")
    end
end

func main:
    email = dom.Create("input")
    dom.SetAttr(email, "type", "email")
    password = dom.Create("input")
    dom.SetAttr(password, "type", "password")
    submit = dom.Create("button")
    dom.SetText(submit, "Sign up")
    note = dom.Create("p")
    each el in [email, password, submit, note]:
        dom.Append(dom.Body(), el)
    end
    dom.OnEvent(email, "input", ():
        check()
    end)
    dom.OnEvent(password, "input", ():
        check()
    end)
    dom.OnEvent(submit, "click", ():
        dom.Alert("Welcome, " + dom.GetValue(email))
    end)
    check()
end
```

An event wants a function value, so wrap a named function in a short lambda: `(): check() end`. Checks in the browser are for the user's comfort only; the server must check the same things again, for example with net/http/validate.

## A countdown with a timer

`SetInterval` calls a function every so many milliseconds and returns an id; keep it in a global so the function can stop itself with `ClearInterval`. For a single delayed call use `SetTimeout`, and for anything that moves on screen use `EveryFrame` instead, which follows the display's refresh rate.

dom-countdown.salam

```salam
import dom

mut left := 10
mut timer := 0 as i64
mut label := 0 as i64

func main:
    label = dom.Create("h1")
    dom.Append(dom.Body(), label)
    dom.SetText(label, "" + left)
    timer = dom.SetInterval(():
        left -= 1
        dom.SetText(label, "" + left)
        if left == 0:
            dom.ClearInterval(timer)
            dom.SetText(label, "Time is up")
            dom.SetStyle(label, "color", "crimson")
            dom.Tone(660, 300)
        end
    end, 1000)
end
```

`Tone` plays a short beep through the Web Audio API. Browsers only allow sound after the user has clicked or typed something on the page, so a beep from a timer that started on load may stay silent.

## Functions

### `Query`

```salam
func Query(sel: str): i64
```

The first element that matches the CSS selector; JavaScript `null` when there is none, which does not compare equal to 0.

dom-Elements.salam

```salam
import dom

func main:
    list := dom.Create("ul")
    dom.SetAttr(list, "id", "books")
    dom.Append(dom.Body(), list)
    repeat 3 in i:
        item := dom.Create("li")
        dom.SetText(item, "book " + (i + 1))
        dom.AddClass(item, "book")
        dom.Append(list, item)
    end
    println dom.Exists("books"), dom.Exists("nothing")

    all := dom.QueryAll("li.book")
    println dom.CountOf(all)
    second := dom.ItemAt(all, 1)
    println dom.GetText(second)
    dom.ToggleClass(second, "selected")
    println dom.GetAttr(second, "class")
    dom.RemoveClass(second, "book")
    println dom.GetAttr(second, "class")

    dom.SetStyle(second, "color", "red")
    println dom.GetStyle(second, "color")
    first := dom.Query("li")
    dom.Remove(first)
    println dom.CountOf(dom.QueryAll("li"))

    box := dom.ById("books")
    dom.SetHtml(box, "<li>new</li>")
end
```

```salam
import dom

func main:
    d := dom.Document()

    println dom.Call3(math, "max", 1, 2, 3), dom.Call4(math, "min", 4, 3, 2, 1)
    _ := dom.Call0(box, "focus")
    _ := dom.CallS1(box, "removeAttribute", "placeholder")
    _ := dom.CallS2(box, "setAttribute", "name", "q")

    println ctx != 0

    dom.StoreSetStr("name", "Maryam")

    r := dom.Random()
    println r >= 0.0 and r < 1.0, dom.RandomInt(6) < 6
    println dom.Now() >= 0.0

    button := dom.Create("button")
    greet := ():
        println "hello"
    end
    dom.OnEvent(button, "click", greet)
    dom.OffEvent(button, "click", greet)

    image := dom.LoadImage("logo.png")
    println dom.ImageReady(image)
    dom.Tone(440, 200)
    if dom.Confirm("shall we go on?"):
        name := dom.Prompt("what is your name?")
        dom.Alert("hello " + name)
    end
end
```

dom-Events.salam

```salam
import dom

mut count := 0

func main:
    button := dom.Create("button")
    dom.SetText(button, "click me")
    dom.SetAttr(button, "data-autofire", "click")
    dom.Append(dom.Body(), button)
    dom.OnEvent(button, "click", ():
        count += 1
        println "click", count
    end)

    box := dom.Create("input")
    dom.SetAttr(box, "data-autofire", "keydown")
    dom.Append(dom.Body(), box)
    dom.SetValue(box, "hello")
    println dom.GetValue(box)
    dom.OnEventE(box, "keydown", (e: i64):
        if dom.EventKey(e) == "Enter":
            dom.PreventDefault(e)
        end
        dom.StopPropagation(e)
        println "target:", dom.GetValue(dom.EventTarget(e))
    end)

    dom.OnWindowE("mousemove", (e: i64):
        println dom.EventX(e), dom.EventY(e)
    end)
    dom.OnWindowE("touchstart", (e: i64):
        println dom.TouchX(e), dom.TouchY(e)
    end)
    dom.OnWindow("scroll", ():
        println dom.ScrollX(), dom.ScrollY()
    end)
    dom.OnReady(():
        println "the page is ready"
    end)
    dom.OnResize(():
        println dom.WinWidth(), dom.WinHeight()
    end)
end
```

dom-Timers.salam

```salam
import dom

mut tick := 0
mut every := 0 as i64

func main:
    dom.SetTitle("timers")
    start := dom.Now()
    _ := dom.SetTimeout(():
        println "one second has passed"
    end, 1000)
    cancelled := dom.SetTimeout(():
        println "this never runs"
    end, 5000)
    dom.ClearTimeout(cancelled)
    every = dom.SetInterval(():
        tick += 1
        if tick == 3:
            dom.ClearInterval(every)
        end
    end, 200)
    dom.RequestFrame((now: f64):
        println "frame after", now - start
    end)
    dom.EveryFrame((now: f64):
        _ := now
    end)
end
```

# web/canvas

https://salamlang.github.io/Salam/std/web-canvas/

Drawing shapes, text and images on a browser canvas element.

This package gives plain functions for two dimensional drawing on a `<canvas>` element: charts, simple games, signatures, diagrams. As with dom, the program is translated for the browser with `salam js`, and the elements, events and timers around the drawing come from `dom`. For key presses in a game loop add web/keys; for pictures saved to a file on the server side, see image.

Get the drawing context with `Get` (by element id) or `Of` (for an element you hold) and pass it to every function. Each function is one call on the browser's `CanvasRenderingContext2D`. The coordinates are in canvas pixels, start at the top left corner, and the vertical axis points down, so angles turn clockwise.

Things that catch people out:

- Set the size with the `width` and `height` attributes, not CSS. CSS stretches the picture; the attributes set how many pixels there are.

- Shapes built from a path pile up until `BeginPath`; see the last section.

- An image draws nothing until it has loaded. Check `dom.ImageReady` before `DrawImage`.

- Mouse positions from `dom.EventX` are window coordinates. Subtract the canvas position from `getBoundingClientRect` to get canvas coordinates.

- Only the common calls are wrapped. Gradients, `measureText` and the rest are reached with `dom.Call...` and `dom.Set...` on the context.

## A bar chart from data

Drawing a chart is mostly arithmetic: turn each value into a height, each index into an x position, and draw from the bottom up because y grows downward. Set the canvas size with the `width` and `height` attributes rather than CSS; CSS only stretches the picture, while the attributes set how many pixels you draw on. `TextAlign(c, "center")` makes `FillText` centre each label on the x you give.

web-canvas-bar-chart.salam

```salam
import dom
import web.canvas

func main:
    el := dom.Create("canvas")
    dom.SetAttr(el, "id", "chart")
    dom.SetAttr(el, "width", "420")
    dom.SetAttr(el, "height", "240")
    dom.Append(dom.Body(), el)
    c := canvas.Get("chart")

    months := ["Jan", "Feb", "Mar", "Apr", "May", "Jun"]
    sales := [42.0, 55.0, 38.0, 71.0, 64.0, 80.0]
    top := 100.0
    base := 200.0
    bar := 40.0
    gap := 24.0

    canvas.StrokeStyle(c, "#999")
    canvas.LineWidth(c, 1)
    canvas.BeginPath(c)
    canvas.MoveTo(c, 30, base)
    canvas.LineTo(c, 410, base)
    canvas.Stroke(c)

    canvas.Font(c, "13px sans-serif")
    canvas.TextAlign(c, "center")
    each i, value in sales:
        x := 40.0 + (i as f64) * (bar + gap)
        h := value / top * 160.0
        canvas.FillStyle(c, "#3b82f6")
        canvas.BeginPath(c)
        canvas.RoundRect(c, x, base - h, bar, h, 4)
        canvas.Fill(c)
        canvas.FillStyle(c, "#222")
        canvas.FillText(c, months[i], x + bar / 2, base + 18)
        canvas.FillText(c, "" + (value as int), x + bar / 2, base - h - 6)
    end
end
```

These programs run in the browser, so they are only checked here; see how to run them.

## Animation: clear, move, draw

An animation redraws the whole picture on every frame. `EveryFrame` from dom calls your function before each repaint, usually 60 times a second. Each call moves the objects a little, paints the background over the last frame and draws everything again. Keep the state in globals so it lasts from one frame to the next.

web-canvas-bounce.salam

```salam
import dom
import web.canvas

mut x := 60.0
mut y := 60.0
mut dx := 3.0
mut dy := 2.0
mut c := 0 as i64

func main:
    el := dom.Create("canvas")
    dom.SetAttr(el, "id", "box")
    dom.SetAttr(el, "width", "360")
    dom.SetAttr(el, "height", "220")
    dom.Append(dom.Body(), el)
    c = canvas.Get("box")
    r := 14.0

    dom.EveryFrame((ms: f64):
        _ := ms
        w := canvas.Width(c)
        h := canvas.Height(c)
        x += dx
        y += dy
        if x < r or x > w - r:
            dx = 0.0 - dx
        end
        if y < r or y > h - r:
            dy = 0.0 - dy
        end
        canvas.FillStyle(c, "#10131a")
        canvas.FillRect(c, 0, 0, w, h)
        canvas.BeginPath(c)
        canvas.Arc(c, x, y, r, 0, 6.2832)
        canvas.FillStyle(c, "#f59e0b")
        canvas.Fill(c)
    end)
end
```

The speed here is per frame, so the ball moves faster on a 120 Hz screen. For the same speed everywhere, multiply by the argument of the frame function: it is the time since the last frame in milliseconds, at most 100 (so a hidden tab does not make things jump). The spinner below works that way.

## Clicks and images

A drawing that reacts to the mouse needs the click position in canvas coordinates. `dom.EventX` and `dom.EventY` are measured from the window, so the program asks the canvas for its box with `dom.Call0(board, "getBoundingClientRect")` and subtracts `left` and `top`. Each click stamps a picture there. `dom.LoadImage` starts the download at once and returns the image; until `dom.ImageReady` says it has arrived, the click does nothing. A right click clears the board, after `PreventDefault` stops the browser menu.

web-canvas-stamp.salam

```salam
import dom
import web.canvas

mut c := 0 as i64
mut board := 0 as i64
mut stamp := 0 as i64
mut placed := 0

func clear_board():
    canvas.FillStyle(c, "#f1f5f9")
    canvas.FillRect(c, 0, 0, canvas.Width(c), canvas.Height(c))
    canvas.FillStyle(c, "#334155")
    canvas.Font(c, "14px sans-serif")
    canvas.TextAlign(c, "left")
    canvas.FillText(c, "Click to place a stamp", 10, 20)
end

func main:
    board = dom.Create("canvas")
    dom.SetAttr(board, "width", "400")
    dom.SetAttr(board, "height", "260")
    dom.Append(dom.Body(), board)
    c = canvas.Of(board)
    stamp = dom.LoadImage("stamp.png")
    clear_board()

    dom.OnEventE(board, "click", (e: i64):
        if not dom.ImageReady(stamp): ret end
        box := dom.Call0(board, "getBoundingClientRect")
        x := dom.EventX(e) - dom.GetNum(box, "left")
        y := dom.EventY(e) - dom.GetNum(box, "top")
        canvas.DrawImage(c, stamp, x - 16, y - 16, 32, 32)
        placed += 1
        dom.SetTitle(placed + " stamps")
    end)
    dom.OnEventE(board, "contextmenu", (e: i64):
        dom.PreventDefault(e)
        clear_board()
        placed = 0
    end)
end
```

Put a `stamp.png` next to the page. When CSS makes the canvas larger or smaller than its `width` attribute, also scale the position by `canvas.Width(c) / box width`.

## Rotating with Save and Restore

`Translate`, `Rotate` and `Scale` move the coordinate system, not the shapes, and every later drawing call is affected. Wrap them in `Save` and `Restore` so the change ends where you want it to. The spinner below moves the origin to the centre, then draws the same small bar twelve times, turning a twelfth of a circle and raising `Alpha` each time.

web-canvas-spinner.salam

```salam
import dom
import web.canvas

mut c := 0 as i64
mut turn := 0.0

func main:
    el := dom.Create("canvas")
    dom.SetAttr(el, "id", "spin")
    dom.SetAttr(el, "width", "120")
    dom.SetAttr(el, "height", "120")
    dom.Append(dom.Body(), el)
    c = canvas.Get("spin")

    dom.EveryFrame((ms: f64):
        turn += ms / 400.0
        canvas.ClearRect(c, 0, 0, 120, 120)
        canvas.Save(c)
        canvas.Translate(c, 60, 60)
        canvas.Rotate(c, turn)
        repeat 12 in i:
            canvas.Alpha(c, (i as f64 + 1.0) / 12.0)
            canvas.FillStyle(c, "#0ea5e9")
            canvas.BeginPath(c)
            canvas.RoundRect(c, -4, -44, 8, 18, 4)
            canvas.Fill(c)
            canvas.Rotate(c, 6.2832 / 12.0)
        end
        canvas.Restore(c)
    end)
end
```

Angles are in radians: a full turn is about 6.2832. `Alpha` is part of the saved state too, so the `Restore` at the end also brings it back to 1.

One trap: `RoundRect`, `MoveTo`, `LineTo` and `Arc` add to the current path, and `Fill` fills all of it. Without `BeginPath` before each shape, the twelfth `Fill` here would paint all twelve bars again at full strength and the fading tail would disappear. `FillRect` and `StrokeRect` draw at once and do not touch the path.

```salam
import web.canvas

func main:
    el := dom.Create("canvas")
    dom.SetAttr(el, "id", "board")
    dom.SetAttr(el, "width", "320")
    dom.SetAttr(el, "height", "200")
    dom.Append(dom.Body(), el)
    c := canvas.Get("board")
    println canvas.Width(c), canvas.Height(c)

    canvas.FillStyle(c, "#f5f0e6")
    canvas.FillRect(c, 0, 0, canvas.Width(c), canvas.Height(c))
    canvas.FillStyle(c, "#2a7")
    canvas.RoundRect(c, 20, 20, 120, 60, 12)
    canvas.Fill(c)
    canvas.StrokeStyle(c, "#333")
    canvas.LineWidth(c, 2)
    canvas.StrokeRect(c, 160, 20, 120, 60)
    canvas.ClearRect(c, 170, 30, 20, 20)

    canvas.BeginPath(c)
    canvas.MoveTo(c, 20, 180)
    canvas.LineTo(c, 100, 100)
    canvas.LineTo(c, 180, 180)
    canvas.ClosePath(c)
    canvas.Stroke(c)
    canvas.BeginPath(c)
    canvas.Arc(c, 250, 140, 30, 0, 6.2832)
    canvas.Alpha(c, 0.5)
    canvas.Fill(c)
    canvas.Alpha(c, 1)

    canvas.Save(c)
    canvas.Translate(c, 160, 100)
    canvas.Rotate(c, 0.2)
    canvas.Scale(c, 1.5, 1.5)
    canvas.Font(c, "16px Inter")
    canvas.TextAlign(c, "center")
    canvas.FillStyle(c, "#000")
    canvas.FillText(c, "hello", 0, 0)
    canvas.Restore(c)

    image := dom.LoadImage("logo.png")
    if dom.ImageReady(image):
        canvas.DrawImage(c, image, 260, 10, 50, 50)
    end
    second := canvas.Of(dom.Create("canvas"))
    println second != 0
end
```

# web/keys

https://salamlang.github.io/Salam/std/web-keys/

Keyboard state for browser games.

In a game you usually ask once per frame which keys are down, rather than taking an event for every press. This package listens to the `keydown` and `keyup` events of the window for you and keeps the state of up to 32 keys. Call `Init` once, then ask `Down` or `Pressed` inside the `EveryFrame` function from dom, and draw with web/canvas. For a form or a text field, where you want each key as it comes, use `dom.OnEventE` with `dom.EventKey` instead.

Keys are named by the browser's `key` value: `ArrowLeft`, `Enter`, `" "` for the space bar, `a` for the A key. Things to know:

- Only tracked keys are seen. `Init` tracks the four arrows, Enter and the space bar; add others with `Track`. Asking about any other key returns false.

- Letters change with Shift and Caps Lock: `a` becomes `A`. Track and ask for both.

- Tracked keys stop doing their normal job on the page, so they cannot be typed into a text box while the game runs.

- A key can stay "down" after the window loses focus. When the player switches windows while holding a key, the browser sends no `keyup`, and `Down` stays true until that key is pressed and released again.

## Holding a key and pressing it once

The two questions are different. `Down` is true for as long as the key is held, which suits walking. `Pressed` is true once per press, the next time you ask after the key went down, which suits jumping, shooting or opening a menu: holding the space bar does not make the player jump again and again.

web-keys-jump.salam

```salam
import dom
import web.canvas
import web.keys

mut x := 40.0
mut y := 160.0
mut vy := 0.0
mut c := 0 as i64

func main:
    el := dom.Create("canvas")
    dom.SetAttr(el, "id", "level")
    dom.SetAttr(el, "width", "400")
    dom.SetAttr(el, "height", "200")
    dom.Append(dom.Body(), el)
    c = canvas.Get("level")
    keys.Init()
    floor := 160.0

    dom.EveryFrame((ms: f64):
        _ := ms
        if keys.Down("ArrowLeft"):
            x -= 3
        end
        if keys.Down("ArrowRight"):
            x += 3
        end
        jump := keys.Pressed(" ")
        if jump and y >= floor:
            vy = -9
        end
        vy += 0.5
        y += vy
        if y > floor:
            y = floor
            vy = 0
        end
        canvas.ClearRect(c, 0, 0, 400, 200)
        canvas.FillStyle(c, "#444")
        canvas.FillRect(c, 0, floor + 20, 400, 20)
        canvas.FillStyle(c, "#e11d48")
        canvas.FillRect(c, x, y, 20, 20)
    end)
end
```

Notice that the program asks `Pressed` on every frame and only then checks whether the player stands on the floor. If it wrote `y >= floor and keys.Pressed(" ")`, a press in mid air would not be asked about, would stay waiting, and the player would jump by itself on landing.

## Your own keys: pause with P

`Init` tracks the arrow keys, Enter and the space bar. Add any other key with `Track`, using the browser's `key` name: a letter, `Escape`, `Shift` and so on. The names are exact text, so with Shift or Caps Lock on, the P key arrives as `P`, not `p`; track both when it matters.

web-keys-pause.salam

```salam
import dom
import web.canvas
import web.keys

mut paused := false
mut angle := 0.0
mut c := 0 as i64

func main:
    el := dom.Create("canvas")
    dom.SetAttr(el, "id", "game")
    dom.SetAttr(el, "width", "200")
    dom.SetAttr(el, "height", "200")
    dom.Append(dom.Body(), el)
    c = canvas.Get("game")
    keys.Init()
    keys.Track("p")
    keys.Track("P")
    keys.Track("Escape")

    dom.EveryFrame((now: f64):
        _ := now
        if keys.Pressed("p") or keys.Pressed("P") or keys.Pressed("Escape"):
            paused = not paused
        end
        if not paused:
            angle += 0.05
        end
        canvas.ClearRect(c, 0, 0, 200, 200)
        canvas.Save(c)
        canvas.Translate(c, 100, 100)
        canvas.Rotate(c, angle)
        canvas.FillStyle(c, "#22c55e")
        canvas.FillRect(c, -30, -30, 60, 60)
        canvas.Restore(c)
        if paused:
            canvas.FillStyle(c, "#000")
            canvas.Font(c, "18px sans-serif")
            canvas.TextAlign(c, "center")
            canvas.FillText(c, "Paused, press P", 100, 190)
        end
    end)
end
```

A tracked key no longer does its usual job in the page, because the package calls `PreventDefault` for it. That is what stops the arrows and the space bar from scrolling during a game, but it also means a tracked letter cannot be typed into a text box on the same page.

Like the dom examples, these run in the browser and are only checked here.

## Smooth movement with arrows and WASD

Most games accept both the arrow keys and W, A, S and D. The helper `held` checks an arrow, a letter and its capital, so Caps Lock does not stop the player. Each axis becomes -1, 0 or 1; when both are set the program divides by the length, so moving diagonally is not faster than moving straight. The speed is in pixels per millisecond and is multiplied by `ms`, the time since the last frame that `EveryFrame` passes in, so the dot moves at the same speed on a 60 Hz and a 144 Hz screen.

web-keys-move.salam

```salam
import dom
import math
import str
import web.canvas
import web.keys

mut x := 200.0
mut y := 150.0
mut c := 0 as i64

func held(arrow: str, letter: str): bool:
    ret keys.Down(arrow) or keys.Down(letter) or keys.Down(str.Upper(letter))
end

func axis(minus_arrow: str, minus_letter: str, plus_arrow: str, plus_letter: str): f64:
    mut v := 0.0
    if held(minus_arrow, minus_letter): v -= 1.0 end
    if held(plus_arrow, plus_letter): v += 1.0 end
    ret v
end

func main:
    el := dom.Create("canvas")
    dom.SetAttr(el, "id", "field")
    dom.SetAttr(el, "width", "400")
    dom.SetAttr(el, "height", "300")
    dom.Append(dom.Body(), el)
    c = canvas.Get("field")
    keys.Init()
    each k in ["w", "a", "s", "d", "W", "A", "S", "D"]:
        keys.Track(k)
    end
    speed := 0.2

    dom.EveryFrame((ms: f64):
        mut dx := axis("ArrowLeft", "a", "ArrowRight", "d")
        mut dy := axis("ArrowUp", "w", "ArrowDown", "s")
        length := math.Sqrt(dx * dx + dy * dy)
        if length > 0.0:
            dx = dx / length
            dy = dy / length
        end
        x = math.ClampF(x + dx * speed * ms, 10.0, 390.0)
        y = math.ClampF(y + dy * speed * ms, 10.0, 290.0)
        canvas.FillStyle(c, "#0f172a")
        canvas.FillRect(c, 0, 0, 400, 300)
        canvas.FillStyle(c, "#22c55e")
        canvas.BeginPath(c)
        canvas.Arc(c, x, y, 10, 0, 6.2832)
        canvas.Fill(c)
    end)
end
```

## Functions

### `Track`

```salam
func Track(k: str)
```

Adds a key to the list of tracked keys; the key name is the browser `key` value, such as `a`. Up to 32 keys; more are ignored without a word. Works before or after `Init`.

web-keys-Game.salam

```salam
import dom
import web.canvas
import web.keys

mut x := 160.0
mut score := 0

func main:
    el := dom.Create("canvas")
    dom.SetAttr(el, "id", "game")
    dom.Append(dom.Body(), el)
    c := canvas.Get("game")
    keys.Init()
    keys.Track("a")
    keys.Track("d")
    dom.EveryFrame((now: f64):
        if keys.Down("ArrowLeft") or keys.Down("a"):
            x -= 4
        end
        if keys.Down("ArrowRight") or keys.Down("d"):
            x += 4
        end
        if keys.Pressed(" "):
            score += 1
        end
        canvas.ClearRect(c, 0, 0, canvas.Width(c), canvas.Height(c))
        canvas.FillRect(c, x - 10, 100, 20, 20)
        canvas.FillText(c, "score: " + score, 10, 20)
    end)
end
```

### `Init`

```salam

```

Starts listening on the window and tracks the arrow keys, Enter and the space bar. Tracked keys no longer scroll the page or type into fields. Call it once; a second call adds a second pair of listeners.

The example for this item is shown with the ones above: web-keys-Game.salam

### `Down`

```salam

```

The key is being held right now; for continuous movement.

The example for this item is shown with the ones above: web-keys-Game.salam

### `Pressed`

```salam

```

The key has been pressed since the last time you asked; every press returns true exactly once. For jumping or shooting.

The example for this item is shown with the ones above: web-keys-Game.salam

# webpush

https://salamlang.github.io/Salam/std/webpush/

Sending notifications to browsers from a server, with VAPID keys and the standard encryption.

This is an official package that does not ship with Salam. Add it to a project first: `salam add webpush`

A web push notification is a message a server sends to a user's browser even when the site is not open: a new chat message, a shipped order, a breaking news alert. This package is the server side. It makes the VAPID keys that identify your server, encrypts each message for one browser under RFC 8291 (`aes128gcm`) so the push service in between never sees its contents, signs the request, and posts it with net/http. The page side is plain JavaScript: a service worker and `pushManager.subscribe`.

The flow:

- Make a key pair once with `GenerateKeys` and keep it; load it later with `KeysFrom`.

- The page subscribes with the public key and sends you the subscription JSON; store it with the user as a `Subscription`.

- Send messages with `Send`, and delete a subscription when the result says `gone`.

Things that catch people out:

- New keys break every subscription. Each subscription is tied to the public key it was made with.

- A `ttl` of 0 is replaced by the 28 day default, so "deliver now or drop it" cannot be expressed; use a short value such as 60 instead.

- The payload size is not checked. More than 3993 bytes of text is still encrypted and sent, and the push service rejects it, usually with 413.

- `Send` waits as long as the push service takes; it has no time limit, so sending to thousands of users one after another can be slow. `KeysFrom` only checks that both keys are non-empty.

## Make the VAPID keys once

The VAPID key pair identifies your server to the push services, and every browser subscription is tied to its public key. If you make new keys at every start, all existing subscriptions stop working. So make them once, keep them somewhere safe, and load them with `KeysFrom` afterwards. The program keeps them in a file; a real server would more likely read them from its configuration or environment.

webpush-keys-file.salam

```salam
import webpush
import os
import str

func load_or_create(path: str): webpush.Keys:
    if os.Exists(path):
        lines := str.Split(os.ReadFile(path), "\n")
        if lines.len() >= 2:
            ret webpush.KeysFrom(lines.get(0), lines.get(1))
        end
    end
    fresh := webpush.GenerateKeys()
    os.WriteFile(path, fresh.public_key + "\n" + fresh.private_key + "\n")
    ret fresh
end

func main:
    path := "vapid-keys.txt"
    first := load_or_create(path)
    second := load_or_create(path)
    println "keys valid:", first.ok, second.ok
    println "same keys on the second start:", first.public_key == second.public_key
    println "public key length:", first.public_key.len()
    println "uncompressed point (starts with B):", str.StartsWith(first.public_key, "B")
    os.Remove(path)
end
```

Output:

```text
keys valid: true true
same keys on the second start: true
public key length: 87
uncompressed point (starts with B): true
```

The public key is the 87 character text that the page passes as `applicationServerKey` to `pushManager.subscribe`. The private key never leaves the server.

## Read the subscription the browser sends

After the user allows notifications, `pushManager.subscribe()` in the page returns a subscription. Its `toJSON()` form has an `endpoint` and two keys, `p256dh` and `auth`. Send that JSON to your server, read it into a `Subscription` with encoding/json and store it with the user. `Encrypt` reports through its `ok` argument whether the keys are usable, which is a cheap way to reject a broken subscription before you store it.

webpush-subscription.salam

```salam
import webpush
import encoding.json
import str

func from_browser(text: str): webpush.Subscription:
    ret webpush.Subscription {
        endpoint = json.Get(text, "endpoint"),
        p256dh = json.GetPath(text, "keys.p256dh"),
        auth = json.GetPath(text, "keys.auth")
    }
end

func main:
    posted := `{"endpoint":"https://fcm.googleapis.com/fcm/send/dQw4w9WgXcQ:APA91b","expirationTime":null,"keys":{"p256dh":"BCVxsr7N_eNgVRqvHtD0zTZsEc6-VV-JvLexhqUzORcxaOzi6-AYWXvTBHm4bjyPjs7Vd8pZGH6SRpkNtoIAiw4","auth":"BTBZMqHH6r4Tts7J_aSIgg"}}`
    sub := from_browser(posted)
    println "endpoint:", sub.endpoint
    println "push service:", str.StartsWith(sub.endpoint, "https://fcm.googleapis.com/")
    println "p256dh length:", sub.p256dh.len(), "auth length:", sub.auth.len()

    mut ok := false
    body := webpush.Encrypt(sub, "{\"title\":\"Welcome\"}", ok)
    println "keys usable:", ok, "encrypted body ready:", body.len() > 0

    broken := from_browser(`{"endpoint":"https://push.example.net/1","keys":{"p256dh":"abc","auth":"xyz"}}`)
    _ := webpush.Encrypt(broken, "hi", ok)
    println "broken keys usable:", ok
end
```

Output:

```text
endpoint: https://fcm.googleapis.com/fcm/send/dQw4w9WgXcQ:APA91b
push service: true
p256dh length: 87 auth length: 22
keys usable: true encrypted body ready: true
broken keys usable: false
```

## Keep the payload small

A push message carries at most 4096 bytes after encryption, which leaves 3993 bytes for your text. Most services also deliver small messages faster. Send a title, a short body and a link, and let the page fetch anything bigger when the user opens the notification. The program shows how the size grows: the encrypted body adds a fixed header and the padding, and base64url makes it a third longer again.

webpush-payload-size.salam

```salam
import webpush
import encoding.json

func payload(title: str, text: str, url: str): str:
    mut members := Vector {} as Vector<str>
    members.push(json.Member("title", title))
    members.push(json.Member("body", text))
    members.push(json.Member("url", url))
    ret json.Object(members)
end

func main:
    sub := webpush.Subscription {
        endpoint = "https://push.example.net/x",
        p256dh = "BCVxsr7N_eNgVRqvHtD0zTZsEc6-VV-JvLexhqUzORcxaOzi6-AYWXvTBHm4bjyPjs7Vd8pZGH6SRpkNtoIAiw4",
        auth = "BTBZMqHH6r4Tts7J_aSIgg"
    }
    small := payload("New reply", "Sara answered your question", "/q/1042")
    println small

    mut ok := false
    each n in [small.len(), 1000, 3000, 3993]:
        mut text := ""
        until text.len() < n:
            text = text + "x"
        end
        sealed := webpush.Encrypt(sub, text, ok)
        println "plain", n, "bytes, sealed and base64url encoded", sealed.len()
    end
end
```

Output:

```text
{"title": "New reply", "body": "Sara answered your question", "url": "/q/1042"}
plain 79 bytes, sealed and base64url encoded 243
plain 1000 bytes, sealed and base64url encoded 1471
plain 3000 bytes, sealed and base64url encoded 4138
plain 3993 bytes, sealed and base64url encoded 5462
```

## Send to many users and clean up

To notify everyone, loop over the stored subscriptions and call `Send` for each one. Look at the `Result`: `ok` means the push service accepted the message, `gone` (HTTP 404 or 410) means the user unsubscribed or the browser dropped the subscription, so delete it; anything else is worth trying again later. `ttl` says how long the service may hold the message for an offline device, `urgency` lets a phone save battery on low priority messages, and a message with the same `topic` replaces an older one that is still waiting.

webpush-broadcast.salam

```salam
import webpush

func main:
    keys := webpush.KeysFrom("BLmOwafYGSjiuCX_1RSCO_n0YmacxYMDqitMydKE4A1Wp2qmUuMXg2IM_hzcrmZLun4jEu_lKfVdtnAp0LMK4NE", "Nhh4m4Va4yhL-53i302044iqeAeMtnOEYlIT2KWRJmg")
    if not keys.ok:
        println "the VAPID keys are broken"
        ret 1
    end
    mut subs := Vector {} as Vector<webpush.Subscription>
    subs.push(webpush.Subscription { endpoint = "https://fcm.googleapis.com/fcm/send/abc", p256dh = "BCVxsr7N_eNgVRqvHtD0zTZsEc6-VV-JvLexhqUzORcxaOzi6-AYWXvTBHm4bjyPjs7Vd8pZGH6SRpkNtoIAiw4", auth = "BTBZMqHH6r4Tts7J_aSIgg" })
    subs.push(webpush.Subscription { endpoint = "https://updates.push.services.mozilla.com/wpush/v2/def", p256dh = "BCVxsr7N_eNgVRqvHtD0zTZsEc6-VV-JvLexhqUzORcxaOzi6-AYWXvTBHm4bjyPjs7Vd8pZGH6SRpkNtoIAiw4", auth = "BTBZMqHH6r4Tts7J_aSIgg" })

    mut o := webpush.NewOptions("mailto:ops@example.com")
    o.ttl = 3600
    o.urgency = "high"
    o.topic = "deploy"

    mut keep := Vector {} as Vector<webpush.Subscription>
    mut sent := 0
    each s in subs:
        r := webpush.Send(keys, s, `{"title":"Deploy finished","body":"Version 2.4 is live"}`, o)
        if r.ok:
            sent += 1
            keep.push(s)
        else r.gone:
            println "dropping", s.endpoint
        else:
            println "will retry", s.endpoint, r.status, r.error
            keep.push(s)
        end
    end
    println "sent", sent, "of", subs.len(), "and keeping", keep.len()
    ret 0
end
```

This program needs real subscriptions from a browser and network access, so it is only checked here. To try it, replace the sample endpoints with subscriptions taken from your own page.

## Types

### `Keys`

```salam
struct Keys
```

The VAPID keys of the server.

| Name | Type | Description |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `public_key` | `str = ""` | The public key as url safe base64; this is what you give to `applicationServerKey` in the page JavaScript. |
| `private_key` | `str = ""` | The private key; keep it secret. |
| `ok` | `bool = false` | The keys are valid. |

webpush-Keys.salam

```salam
import webpush
import str

func main:
    fresh := webpush.GenerateKeys()
    println fresh.ok, fresh.public_key.len(), fresh.private_key.len()

    k := webpush.KeysFrom("BLmOwafYGSjiuCX_1RSCO_n0YmacxYMDqitMydKE4A1Wp2qmUuMXg2IM_hzcrmZLun4jEu_lKfVdtnAp0LMK4NE", "Nhh4m4Va4yhL-53i302044iqeAeMtnOEYlIT2KWRJmg")
    println k.ok, webpush.KeysFrom("", "").ok
    at := webpush.VapidHeaderAt(k, "https://fcm.googleapis.com", "mailto:ali@example.com", 1700000000)
    println at
    now := webpush.VapidHeader(k, "https://fcm.googleapis.com", "mailto:ali@example.com")
    println str.StartsWith(now, "vapid t="), str.Contains(now, ", k=" + k.public_key)

    mut o := webpush.NewOptions("mailto:ali@example.com")
    println o.subject, o.ttl == webpush.DEFAULT_TTL, o.ttl / 86400
    o.urgency = "high"
    o.topic = "news"
    o.ttl = 3600
    println o.urgency, o.topic, o.ttl
end
```

Output:

```text
true false
```

### `Subscription`

```salam
struct Subscription
```

The subscription the browser makes with `pushManager.subscribe` and sends to your server.

| Name | Type | Description |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `endpoint` | `str = ""` | The address of the browser push service. |
| `p256dh` | `str = ""` | The public key of the browser, from the `keys` part of the subscription. |
| `auth` | `str = ""` | The authentication secret, from the same part. |

webpush-Encrypt.salam

```salam
import webpush

func main:
    sub := webpush.Subscription {
        endpoint = "https://push.example.net/x",
        p256dh = "BCVxsr7N_eNgVRqvHtD0zTZsEc6-VV-JvLexhqUzORcxaOzi6-AYWXvTBHm4bjyPjs7Vd8pZGH6SRpkNtoIAiw4",
        auth = "BTBZMqHH6r4Tts7J_aSIgg"
    }
    mut good := false
    body := webpush.EncryptWith(sub, "When I grow up, I want to be a watermelon", "yfWPiYE-n46HLnH0KqZOF1fJJU3MYrct3AELtAQ-oRw", "DGv6ra1nlYgDCS1FRnbzlw", good)
    println good
    println body

    one := webpush.Encrypt(sub, "hello", good)
    two := webpush.Encrypt(sub, "hello", good)
    println good, one != two, one.len() == two.len()
end
```

Output:

```text
true
DGv6ra1nlYgDCS1FRnbzlwAAEABBBP4z9KsN6nGRTbVYI_c7VJSPQTBtkgcy27mlmlMoZIIgDll6e3vCYLocInmYWAmS6TlzAC8wEqKK6PBru3jl7A_yl95bQpu6cVPTpK4Mqgkf1CXztLVBSt2Ks3oZwbuwXPXLWyouBWLVWGNWQexSgSxsj_Qulcy4a-fN
true true true
```

### `Options`

```salam
struct Options
```

The send options.

| Name | Type | Description |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `subject` | `str = ""` | Your contact address, as a `mailto:` or a web address; the services require it. |
| `ttl` | `int = 2419200` | How many seconds the service should hold the message for a browser that is off. 0 or less sends the 28 day default. |
| `urgency` | `str = ""` | The urgency: `very-low`, `low`, `normal` or `high`; empty sends no header, which services treat as normal. The value is not checked. |
| `topic` | `str = ""` | The topic; a new message with the same topic replaces an earlier undelivered one. |

The example for this item is shown with the ones above: webpush-Keys.salam

### `Result`

```salam
struct Result
```

The result of the send.

| Name | Type | Description |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `ok` | `bool = false` | The service accepted the message. |
| `status` | `int = 0` | The HTTP status code of the service. |
| `gone` | `bool = false` | The subscription is no longer valid (404 or 410); delete it from your database. |
| `error` | `str = ""` | Why the send failed: a network error, or the body of the service's answer when it is short. |

webpush-Send.salam

```salam
import webpush

func main:
    k := webpush.KeysFrom("BLmOwafYGSjiuCX_1RSCO_n0YmacxYMDqitMydKE4A1Wp2qmUuMXg2IM_hzcrmZLun4jEu_lKfVdtnAp0LMK4NE", "Nhh4m4Va4yhL-53i302044iqeAeMtnOEYlIT2KWRJmg")
    sub := webpush.Subscription {
        endpoint = "https://fcm.googleapis.com/fcm/send/abc",
        p256dh = "BCVxsr7N_eNgVRqvHtD0zTZsEc6-VV-JvLexhqUzORcxaOzi6-AYWXvTBHm4bjyPjs7Vd8pZGH6SRpkNtoIAiw4",
        auth = "BTBZMqHH6r4Tts7J_aSIgg"
    }
    o := webpush.NewOptions("mailto:ali@example.com")
    r := webpush.Send(k, sub, `{"title":"hello","body":"you have a new message"}`, o)
    if r.ok:
        println "sent", r.status
    else r.gone:
        println "the subscription has expired; delete it"
    else:
        println "error:", r.status, r.error
    end
end
```

## Functions

### `GenerateKeys`

Makes a fresh VAPID key pair; make it once and keep it, because the subscriptions are tied to the public key.

```salam

```

The `Authorization` header for the service at the given address, at the given time in Unix seconds. The signature is deterministic, so the same input gives the same output.

The example for this item is shown with the ones above: webpush-Keys.salam

### `VapidHeader`

```salam
func VapidHeader(keys: Keys, audience: str, subject: str): str
```

The same, at the current time.

The example for this item is shown with the ones above: webpush-Keys.salam

### `EncryptWith`

```salam
func EncryptWith(sub: Subscription, payload: str, as_private: str, salt: str, ok &: bool): str
```

Encrypts the message with the given key and salt under RFC 8291; for testing against the standard vectors. In real work use `Encrypt`.

The example for this item is shown with the ones above: webpush-Encrypt.salam

### `Encrypt`

```salam
func Encrypt(sub: Subscription, payload: str, ok &: bool): str
```

Encrypts the message for this subscription; with a fresh key and salt every time, so two outputs are never the same.

The example for this item is shown with the ones above: webpush-Encrypt.salam

### `Send`

```salam
func Send(keys: Keys, sub: Subscription, payload: str, opts: Options): Result
```

Encrypts the message and sends it to the browser push service with the VAPID header, which is valid for 12 hours. An empty message is a push with no body. There is no time limit and no check of the payload size.

The example for this item is shown with the ones above: webpush-Send.salam

### `NewOptions`

```salam

```

The default options with a contact address.

The example for this item is shown with the ones above: webpush-Keys.salam

### `KeysFrom`

```salam
func KeysFrom(public_key: str, private_key: str): Keys
```

Returns stored keys; `ok` is false when either one is empty. The keys themselves are not checked until the first `Send`.

The example for this item is shown with the ones above: webpush-Keys.salam


---

# crypto

https://salamlang.github.io/Salam/std/crypto/

SHA and MD5 digests, HMAC signatures, secure random numbers and password hashing.

This package has the basic cryptography tools, written in Salam: the SHA-1, SHA-2 and MD5 digests, HMAC, PBKDF2 password hashing, a constant time comparison and secure random bytes from the operating system. It covers hashing, signing and secrets; it does not encrypt. For encryption (AES-GCM, ChaCha20-Poly1305, key exchange) use tls, and for signed tokens that carry claims jwt.

Most functions come in three shapes: `...Hex` takes a `str` and returns hex text, the simplest; `...Bytes` and `...Raw` write the raw digest into memory you allocate; and `Sha256New`, `Sha256Update`, `Sha256Final` hash data that arrives in pieces.

Things to get right:

- `HashPassword` uses only 1000 PBKDF2 rounds. That is far below current advice (OWASP asks for 600,000 with SHA-256). For new systems build the same string with more rounds, as the second section shows; `VerifyPassword` reads the rounds from the stored string, so both kinds keep working.

- Compare secrets with `SecretEquals`, never with `==`.

- A `str` stops at the first zero byte. For binary data or a binary key, use the `...Bytes` and `...Raw` forms with a pointer and a length; `Sha256Hex` of a buffer that contains a zero hashes only the part before it.

- `HashStr`, `HashBytes` and `HashInt` are fast hash table hashes, not cryptographic ones; MD5 and SHA-1 are only for old systems that require them.

## Storing passwords

A login system keeps one string per user: the output of `HashPassword`. It has four fields separated by `$`: the algorithm, the number of PBKDF2 rounds, a random salt and the derived key. Because the salt is new every time, two users with the same password get different strings, and a leaked table cannot be attacked with one precomputed list. At login, `VerifyPassword` reads the rounds and the salt back out of the stored string, so the stored value is all you need to keep.

crypto-passwords.salam

```salam
import crypto
import str

struct User:
    pub name: str = ""
    pub hash: str = ""
end

func register(users &: Vector<User>, name: str, password: str):
    users.push(User { name = name, hash = crypto.HashPassword(password) })
end

func login(users: Vector<User>, name: str, password: str): bool:
    each u in users:
        if u.name == name:
            ret crypto.VerifyPassword(password, u.hash)
        end
    end
    ret false
end

func main:
    mut users := Vector {} as Vector<User>
    register(users, "sara", "correct horse battery")
    register(users, "omid", "correct horse battery")

    parts := str.Split(users.get(0).hash, "$")
    println "stored fields:", parts.len(), "algorithm:", parts.get(0), "rounds:", parts.get(1)
    println "same password, same hash?", users.get(0).hash == users.get(1).hash
    println "sara right password:", login(users, "sara", "correct horse battery")
    println "sara wrong password:", login(users, "sara", "correct horse")
    println "unknown user:", login(users, "nobody", "x")
end
```

Output:

```text
stored fields: 4 algorithm: pbkdf2-sha256 rounds: 1000
same password, same hash? false
sara right password: true
sara wrong password: false
unknown user: false
```

Answer "wrong user" and "wrong password" with the same message, so that a visitor cannot use the login form to find out which accounts exist.

## More rounds, and upgrading old hashes

The cost of a password hash is the number of rounds: every guess an attacker tries costs the same work as one login. `Pbkdf2HmacSha256Hex` takes the round count, so a stronger hash is the same four-field string as `HashPassword` writes, built by hand with 600,000 rounds. Existing users do not have to reset anything. At their next successful login the program sees that the stored hash has fewer rounds than the target and stores a new one, made from the password they just typed.

crypto-password-rounds.salam

```salam
import crypto
import str

const ROUNDS := 600000

func strong_hash(password: str): str:
    salt := crypto.RandomHex(16)
    ret "pbkdf2-sha256$" + ROUNDS + "$" + salt + "$" + crypto.Pbkdf2HmacSha256Hex(password, salt, ROUNDS, 32)
end

func rounds_of(stored: str): int:
    ret str.Split(stored, "$").get(1).to_int()
end

func login(stored &: str, password: str): bool:
    if not crypto.VerifyPassword(password, stored): ret false end
    if rounds_of(stored) < ROUNDS:
        stored = strong_hash(password)
        println "  upgraded the stored hash to", rounds_of(stored), "rounds"
    end
    ret true
end

func main:
    mut stored := crypto.HashPassword("tea at five")
    println "HashPassword uses", rounds_of(stored), "rounds"
    println "login:", login(stored, "tea at five")
    println "login again:", login(stored, "tea at five")
    println "wrong password:", login(stored, "coffee at six")
end
```

Output:

```text
HashPassword uses 1000 rounds
  upgraded the stored hash to 600000 rounds
login: true
login again: true
wrong password: false
```

600,000 rounds take a noticeable fraction of a second, which is the point, but it also means a login endpoint should be rate limited, or many parallel login attempts can keep the server busy.

## Checking a webhook signature

Payment providers, GitHub and most other services sign the requests they send you. They compute an HMAC of the raw body with a secret you both know and put it in a header. To check it, compute the same HMAC over the body exactly as it arrived and compare. Compare with `SecretEquals`, never with `==`: `==` stops at the first different character, and the time that takes tells an attacker how much of a forged signature was right.

crypto-webhook.salam

```salam
import crypto

func verify(secret: str, body: str, header: str): bool:
    expected := "sha256=" + crypto.HmacSha256Hex(secret, body)
    ret crypto.SecretEquals(expected, header)
end

func main:
    secret := "whsec_4f9a1c"
    body := "{\"event\":\"order.paid\",\"id\":1042}"
    header := "sha256=" + crypto.HmacSha256Hex(secret, body)
    println "signature: " + header

    println "genuine request:", verify(secret, body, header)
    println "changed body:", verify(secret, "{\"event\":\"order.paid\",\"id\":9999}", header)
    println "wrong secret:", verify("guess", body, header)
end
```

Output:

```text
signature: sha256=9d396fc7d426c8baf9dd3da910e4cd8bc378e42dfc08dc2bdf1681692f33554b
genuine request: true
changed body: false
wrong secret: false
```

Sign the bytes you received, not a version you decoded and encoded again: a JSON library may reorder keys or change spaces, and then the signature no longer matches.

## Checksums of large data

`Sha256Hex` needs the whole text at once. For a file or a download that arrives in pieces, keep a running state: `Sha256New` starts it, `Sha256Update` feeds each piece and `Sha256Final` writes the 32 byte digest. The result is the same as hashing everything in one go, as the program shows.

crypto-checksum.salam

```salam
import crypto
import encoding
import mem

func main:
    chunks := ["first block of the file, ", "second block, ", "and the last one."]
    mut whole := ""
    mut h := crypto.Sha256New()
    each c in chunks:
        crypto.Sha256Update(h, c as void*, c.len())
        whole = whole + c
    end
    out := mem.Allocate(32 as u64)
    crypto.Sha256Final(h, out)
    streamed := encoding.Base64EncodeBytes(out, 32)

    crypto.Sha256Bytes(whole as void*, whole.len(), out)
    oneshot := encoding.Base64EncodeBytes(out, 32)
    mem.Free(out)

    println "streamed: " + streamed
    println "one shot: " + oneshot
    println "match:", streamed == oneshot
    println "hex form: " + crypto.Sha256Hex(whole)
end
```

Output:

```text
streamed: E+f0zAqMN9MLnvZXyBef5ki729TQh4fngTGDH5hLL1M=
one shot: E+f0zAqMN9MLnvZXyBef5ki729TQh4fngTGDH5hLL1M=
match: true
hex form: 13e7f4cc0a8c37d30b9ef657c8179fe648bbdbd4d08787e78131831f984b2f53
```

The `...Bytes` and `...Final` functions write raw bytes into memory you allocated; turn them into text with `Base64EncodeBytes` from encoding. The SHA-512 and SHA-384 states work the same way with `Sha512New`, `Sha384New`, `Sha512Update` and `Sha512Final`.

## API keys and tokens

An API key, a password reset link or a session id must be impossible to guess, so make it with `RandomToken`, which reads the operating system's secure random source. `RandomToken(n)` returns `n` random bytes as `2n` hex characters. Store only the SHA-256 digest of the key: a stolen database then gives no working keys, and checking a key that comes in with a request is one digest and one `SecretEquals`. A plain digest is enough here because the key is long and random; a password is short and chosen by a person, which is why it needs `HashPassword` instead.

crypto-api-keys.salam

```salam
import crypto

func main:
    key := "sk_" + crypto.RandomToken(24)
    println "key length:", key.len()

    stored := crypto.Sha256Hex(key)
    println "stored digest length:", stored.len()

    println "valid key accepted:", crypto.SecretEquals(crypto.Sha256Hex(key), stored)
    println "forged key accepted:", crypto.SecretEquals(crypto.Sha256Hex("sk_" + crypto.RandomToken(24)), stored)
    println "two keys differ:", crypto.RandomToken(24) != crypto.RandomToken(24)
end
```

Output:

```text
key length: 51
stored digest length: 64
valid key accepted: true
forged key accepted: false
two keys differ: true
```

## Which function for which job

| Job | Use |
| --- | --- |
| Store and check a user password | `HashPassword`, `VerifyPassword` |
| Sign a message or check a signed request | `HmacSha256Hex` and `SecretEquals` |
| A file checksum or a content id | `Sha256Hex`, or `Sha256New`, `Sha256Update`, `Sha256Final` for data in pieces |
| A token, key or nonce | `RandomToken`, `RandomHex`, `RandomBytes` |
| A key derived from a passphrase | `Pbkdf2HmacSha256Hex` |
| A hash table key, not for security | `HashStr`, `HashBytes`, `HashInt` |
| Talking to an old system that wants MD5 or SHA-1 | `Md5Hex`, `Sha1Hex`; do not use them for anything new |

For signed tokens that carry claims, see jwt; for encryption, see tls.

## Types

### `Sha256`

```salam
struct Sha256
```

The SHA-256 state for data that arrives in pieces, such as a large file.

| Name | Type | Description |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `h` | `u32[]` | The internal state. |
| `blk` | `u8[]` | The partial block. |
| `blen` | `int = 0` | The length of the partial block. |
| `total` | `u64 = 0` | The total number of bytes. |

crypto-Hash.salam

```salam
import crypto
import encoding
import mem

func main:
    println crypto.Sha256Hex("abc")
    println crypto.Sha512Hex("abc").len()
    println crypto.Sha1Hex("abc")
    println crypto.Sha1Base64("abc")
    println crypto.Md5Hex("abc")

    text := "abc"
    out := mem.Allocate(64 as u64)
    crypto.Sha256Bytes(text as void*, 3, out)
    println encoding.Base64EncodeBytes(out, 32)
    crypto.Sha384Bytes(text as void*, 3, out)
    println encoding.Base64EncodeBytes(out, 48)
    crypto.Sha512Bytes(text as void*, 3, out)
    println encoding.Base64EncodeBytes(out, 16).len()
    crypto.Sha1Bytes(text as void*, 3, out)
    println encoding.Base64EncodeBytes(out, 20)
    crypto.Md5Bytes(text as void*, 3, out)
    println encoding.Base64EncodeBytes(out, 16)

    mut h := crypto.Sha256New()
    crypto.Sha256Update(h, "a" as void*, 1)
    crypto.Sha256Update(h, "bc" as void*, 2)
    crypto.Sha256Final(h, out)
    println encoding.Base64EncodeBytes(out, 32)
    mut b := crypto.Sha512New()
    crypto.Sha512Update(b, text as void*, 3)
    crypto.Sha512Final(b, out)
    println b.outlen
    mut s := crypto.Sha384New()
    crypto.Sha512Update(s, text as void*, 3)
    crypto.Sha512Final(s, out)
    println s.outlen, encoding.Base64EncodeBytes(out, 48)
    mem.Free(out)

    println crypto.HashStr("hello") == crypto.HashStr("hello"), crypto.HashStr("a") != crypto.HashStr("b")
    println crypto.HashBytes(text as void*, 3 as u64) == crypto.HashStr("abc")
    println crypto.HashInt(42 as u64) != crypto.HashInt(43 as u64)
end
```

### `Sha512`

```salam
struct Sha512
```

The SHA-512 or SHA-384 state for data in pieces.

| Name | Type | Description |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `h` | `u64[]` | The internal state. |
| `blk` | `u8[]` | The partial block. |
| `blen` | `int = 0` | The length of the partial block. |
| `total` | `u64 = 0` | The total number of bytes. |
| `outlen` | `int = 64` | The digest length: 64 for SHA-512 and 48 for SHA-384. |

The example for this item is shown with the ones above: crypto-Hash.salam

## Functions

### `BcryptHashWithSalt`

```salam
func BcryptHashWithSalt(password: str, cost: int, salt: void*): str
```

Like `BcryptHash`, with your own 16 byte salt from a pointer instead of a random one, so the same input always gives the same string; for tests and known answers, not for storing real passwords.

crypto-Bcrypt.salam

```salam
import crypto
import mem
import str

func main:
    stored := crypto.BcryptHash("s3cret-password", 10)
    println str.StartsWith(stored, "$2y$10$"), stored.len()
    println crypto.IsBcryptHash(stored), crypto.BcryptCost(stored)
    println crypto.BcryptVerify("s3cret-password", stored), crypto.BcryptVerify("wrong", stored)
    println stored != crypto.BcryptHash("s3cret-password", 10)

    salt := mem.Allocate(16 as u64)
    bytes := salt as u8*
    repeat 16 in i:
        bytes[i] = (i * 7) as u8
    end
    fixed := crypto.BcryptHashWithSalt("s3cret-password", 4, salt)
    println fixed
    println fixed == crypto.BcryptHashWithSalt("s3cret-password", 4, salt)
    mem.Free(salt)

    println crypto.BcryptVerify("U*U", "$2a$05$CCCCCCCCCCCCCCCCCCCCC.E5YPO9kmyuRGyh0XouQYb4YMJKvyOeW")
    println crypto.IsBcryptHash("pbkdf2-sha256$1000$aa$bb"), crypto.BcryptCost("not a hash")
end
```

Output:

```text
true 60
true 10
true false
true
$2y$04$..aMDPuhIhC2NyXLTDrgYOsyOe2m5.9j9drn3MfYolopNUBwAMWjy
true
true
false -1
```

### `BcryptHash`

```salam
func BcryptHash(password: str, cost: int): str
```

Hashes the password with bcrypt and a random 16 byte salt, and returns the 60 character `$2y$cost$salt+hash` string that PHP `password_hash` also writes. The cost is the base 2 log of the rounds: each step up doubles the work; 10 is a common choice, and values are kept between 4 and 31. Only the first 72 bytes of the password count.

The example for this item is shown with the ones above: crypto-Bcrypt.salam

### `IsBcryptHash`

```salam
func IsBcryptHash(encoded: str): bool
```

True when the string looks like a bcrypt hash: 60 characters starting with `$2a$`, `$2b$` or `$2y$`. Useful when a database holds both bcrypt and `HashPassword` strings.

The example for this item is shown with the ones above: crypto-Bcrypt.salam

### `BcryptCost`

```salam
func BcryptCost(encoded: str): int
```

The cost written in a bcrypt hash, such as 10 for `$2y$10$...`; -1 when the string is not a bcrypt hash. Compare it with your target cost to know when to hash a password again.

The example for this item is shown with the ones above: crypto-Bcrypt.salam

### `BcryptVerify`

```salam
func BcryptVerify(password: str, encoded: str): bool
```

Checks a password against a stored `$2a$`, `$2b$` or `$2y$` string, with the cost and salt it holds, in constant time; hashes from PHP and other bcrypt libraries work. False for any other format.

The example for this item is shown with the ones above: crypto-Bcrypt.salam

### `Sha256Hex`

```salam
func Sha256Hex(data: str): str
```

The SHA-256 digest as hex, 64 characters.

The example for this item is shown with the ones above: crypto-Hash.salam

### `Pbkdf2HmacSha256Hex`

```salam
func Pbkdf2HmacSha256Hex(password: str, salt: str, iterations: int, keylen: int): str
```

Derives a key with PBKDF2-HMAC-SHA256 from a password and a salt, at the given iteration count.

crypto-Password.salam

```salam
import crypto
import str
import mem

func main:
    stored := crypto.HashPassword("s3cret-password")
    println str.StartsWith(stored, "pbkdf2-sha256$")
    println crypto.VerifyPassword("s3cret-password", stored), crypto.VerifyPassword("wrong", stored)
    println stored != crypto.HashPassword("s3cret-password")

    println crypto.Pbkdf2HmacSha256Hex("password", "salt", 1, 32)
    println crypto.SecretEquals("abc", "abc"), crypto.SecretEquals("abc", "xyz")

    println crypto.RandomHex(16).len(), crypto.RandomToken(32).len() > 0
    b := mem.Allocate(8 as u64)
    crypto.RandomBytes(b, 8)
    mem.Free(b)
end
```

### `HashPassword`

```salam
func HashPassword(password: str): str
```

Hashes the password with PBKDF2-HMAC-SHA256, 1000 rounds and a random 16 byte salt, and returns `pbkdf2-sha256$1000$salt$hash` to keep in your database. The output is different every time. 1000 rounds is low by today's standards; see the guide for a stronger hash.

The example for this item is shown with the ones above: crypto-Password.salam

### `VerifyPassword`

```salam
func VerifyPassword(password: str, encoded: str): bool
```

Checks a password against a `pbkdf2-sha256$rounds$salt$hash` string, with the rounds and salt it holds, in constant time. False for any other format.

The example for this item is shown with the ones above: crypto-Password.salam

### `SecretEquals`

```salam
func SecretEquals(a: str, b: str): bool
```

Compares two secrets in constant time, so the answer time gives nothing away about their contents (only whether the lengths differ); for tokens and signatures.

The example for this item is shown with the ones above: crypto-Password.salam

### `HmacSha256Hex`

```salam
func HmacSha256Hex(key: str, msg: str): str
```

The HMAC-SHA256 signature of a message under a key, as hex; for checking that the message is untouched and comes from whoever holds the key. Key and message stop at a zero byte; use `HmacSha256Raw` for binary ones.

crypto-Hmac.salam

```salam
import crypto
import encoding
import mem

func main:
    key := "key"
    message := "The quick brown fox jumps over the lazy dog"
    println crypto.HmacSha256Hex(key, message)
    println crypto.HmacSha1Hex(key, message)
    println crypto.HmacSha1Base64(key, message)
    println crypto.HmacSha384Hex(key, message).len(), crypto.HmacSha512Hex(key, message).len()

    out := mem.Allocate(64 as u64)
    crypto.HmacSha256Bytes(key, message, out)
    a := encoding.Base64EncodeBytes(out, 32)
    crypto.HmacSha256Raw(key as void*, 3, message as void*, message.len(), out)
    println a == encoding.Base64EncodeBytes(out, 32)
    crypto.HmacSha1Bytes(key, message, out)
    b := encoding.Base64EncodeBytes(out, 20)
    crypto.HmacSha1Raw(key as void*, 3, message as void*, message.len(), out)
    println b == encoding.Base64EncodeBytes(out, 20), b == crypto.HmacSha1Base64(key, message)
    crypto.HmacSha384Bytes(key, message, out)
    c := encoding.Base64EncodeBytes(out, 48)
    crypto.HmacSha384Raw(key as void*, 3, message as void*, message.len(), out)
    println c == encoding.Base64EncodeBytes(out, 48)
    crypto.HmacSha512Bytes(key, message, out)
    d := encoding.Base64EncodeBytes(out, 64)
    crypto.HmacSha512Raw(key as void*, 3, message as void*, message.len(), out)
    println d == encoding.Base64EncodeBytes(out, 64)
    mem.Free(out)
end
```

Output:

```text

de7c9b85b8b78aa6bc8a7a36f70a90701c9db4d9
3nybhbi3iqa8ino29wqQcBydtNk=
96 128
true
true true
true
true
```

# jwt

https://salamlang.github.io/Salam/std/jwt/

Making and checking JWT tokens, and guarding API routes.

A JWT is a token the server signs after a user logs in and the client sends with every request; by checking the signature the server knows who the user is without going to the database. This package signs and checks tokens with the HMAC algorithms HS256, HS384 and HS512, never accepts the `none` algorithm, and has helpers for net/http handlers. Every service that checks a token needs the same secret, so it suits one backend or a few services you trust; there are no RS256 or ES256 public key signatures. When the client is a browser on your own site, a server side net/http/session is often simpler and can be revoked at once.

For an API, make a `Guard` with the secret and call `Require` or one of its siblings at the top of every handler; when the token is missing or wrong, the 401 or 403 answer is sent for you. The secret has to be long and random, for instance from `RandomToken` in crypto.

Things that catch people out:

- A token without `exp` is accepted forever unless you set `opts.require_exp`. Tokens from `Issue` always have one, but a token signed some other way may not.

- The secret is not checked for strength. Any non-empty string is used as it is; a short one can be guessed offline from a single token.

- The claims are signed, not encrypted. Anyone holding a token can read them with a base64 decoder, so put no secrets in them.

- A token cannot be taken back before it expires; keep access tokens short, as the refresh section shows.

## Protecting API routes with a Guard

The usual shape: `/login` checks the user (left out here) and answers with a token from `Issue`, which adds `exp`, `iat` and the guard's algorithm. Every protected handler starts with a `Require...` call and returns at once when it is false. `RequireScope` reads the space separated `scope` claim, so the same token opens `/orders` but gets a 403 at `/admin`. The last request uses a token signed with the right secret but without `exp`; because the guard sets `require_exp`, it is refused.

jwt-guard.salam

```salam
import encoding.json
import jwt
import net.http
import net.router

mut guard := jwt.NewGuard("k8R2pX7wQ4mZ9vL1cT6yB3nH5sD0fG2a")

func login(ctx: i64):
    mut c := jwt.NewClaims()
    c.sub = http.Form(ctx, "user")
    jwt.SetStr(c, "scope", "orders:read")
    mut err := 0
    token := jwt.Issue(guard, c, 900, err)
    http.Json(ctx, "{\"token\":\"" + token + "\"}")
end

func orders(ctx: i64):
    mut t := jwt.Token {}
    if not jwt.RequireScope(ctx, guard, "orders:read", t): ret end
    http.Json(ctx, "{\"orders_for\":\"" + t.claims.sub + "\"}")
end

func admin(ctx: i64):
    mut t := jwt.Token {}
    if not jwt.RequireScope(ctx, guard, "admin", t): ret end
    http.Text(ctx, "welcome, admin")
end

func call(path: str, token: str):
    mut headers := http.NewHeaders()
    if token.len() > 0: headers.insert("Authorization", "Bearer " + token) end
    r := http.GetWith("http://127.0.0.1:18661" + path, headers)
    println path, http.Status(r), http.Body(r)
end

func main:
    guard.opts.require_exp = true
    mut r := router.NewRouter()
    router.Post(r, "/login", login)
    router.Get(r, "/orders", orders)
    router.Get(r, "/admin", admin)
    mut s := http.NewServer(18661)
    http.SetHost(s, "127.0.0.1")
    http.Use(s, r)
    if not http.RunBackground(s):
        println "port 18661 is busy"
        ret 1
    end
    answer := http.Post("http://127.0.0.1:18661/login", "user=sara")
    token := json.Get(http.Body(answer), "token")
    call("/orders", "")
    call("/orders", token)
    call("/admin", token)

    mut forever := jwt.NewClaims()
    forever.sub = "sara"
    jwt.SetStr(forever, "scope", "orders:read")
    mut err := 0
    call("/orders", jwt.SignHS256(forever, guard.secret, err))
    ret 0
end
```

Output:

```text
/orders 401 {"error":"unauthorized","reason":"missing bearer token"}
/orders 200 {"orders_for":"sara"}
/admin 403 {"error":"forbidden","reason":"missing scope: admin"}
/orders 401 {"error":"unauthorized","reason":"required claim missing"}
```

`Require` takes the token from the `Authorization: Bearer` header, or from the cookie named in `guard.cookie` when there is no header. A 401 also carries a `WWW-Authenticate` header, as the HTTP rules ask.

## Why a token is rejected

`Verify` checks, in order, that the token has three parts, that its algorithm is the one you expect, that the signature matches, and then the times and the claims you asked for in `Options`. The first failure goes into `err`, and `ErrorText` turns it into a short reason. The program below fixes `now` so that it prints the same lines every time; in a server leave `now` at 0 and the current clock is used.

jwt-errors.salam

```salam
import jwt
import str

func report(label: str, token: str, secret: str, o: jwt.Options):
    mut err := 0
    _ := jwt.Verify(token, secret, o, err)
    if err == jwt.JWT_OK:
        println label + ": ok"
    else:
        println label + ": " + jwt.ErrorText(err)
    end
end

func main:
    secret := "a-long-random-secret-for-this-demo"
    mut c := jwt.NewClaims()
    c.sub = "7"
    c.iss = "auth.example.com"
    c.iat = 1790000000
    c.nbf = 1790000000
    c.exp = 1790000900
    mut err := 0
    token := jwt.SignHS256(c, secret, err)

    mut o := jwt.DefaultOptions()
    o.issuer = "auth.example.com"
    o.now = 1790000300
    report("fresh token", token, secret, o)
    report("wrong secret", token, "guess", o)

    parts := str.Split(token, ".")
    forged := parts.get(0) + "." + jwt.B64UrlEncode("{\"sub\":\"1\",\"iss\":\"auth.example.com\"}") + "." + parts.get(2)
    report("edited payload", forged, secret, o)

    o.now = 1790001000
    report("100 s after exp", token, secret, o)
    o.leeway = 120
    report("same, 120 s leeway", token, secret, o)

    o.leeway = 0
    o.now = 1789999000
    report("before nbf", token, secret, o)

    o.now = 1790000300
    o.issuer = "evil.example.com"
    report("other issuer", token, secret, o)

    strong := jwt.SignHS512(c, secret, err)
    mut only256 := jwt.OptionsFor(jwt.JWT_HS256)
    only256.now = 1790000300
    report("HS512 token, HS256 expected", strong, secret, only256)
end
```

Output:

```text
fresh token: ok
wrong secret: signature does not match
edited payload: signature does not match
100 s after exp: token expired
same, 120 s leeway: ok
before nbf: token not yet valid
other issuer: issuer mismatch
HS512 token, HS256 expected: algorithm mismatch
```

Three things to notice. Changing even one claim breaks the signature, so a client cannot raise its own rights. `leeway` forgives a small clock difference between the machine that signed and the one that checks; a minute or two is usual. And a token signed with HS512 is refused when the options say HS256: the algorithm comes from your options, never from the token, which is how this package avoids the classic `alg` attacks.

## Short access tokens and a refresh token

A token cannot be taken back once issued, so access tokens should live for minutes, not days. To spare the user a new login every fifteen minutes, issue a second, long lived refresh token at login and accept it at one route only, where it buys a new access token. Mark each token with what it is for, so that a refresh token is refused as an access token. `IssuePair` on a `Guard` issues both in one call; the program does it by hand to show the checks.

jwt-refresh.salam

```salam
import jwt

func issue(subject: str, use: str, iat: i64, ttl: i64, secret: str): str:
    mut c := jwt.NewClaims()
    c.sub = subject
    c.iat = iat
    c.exp = iat + ttl
    jwt.SetStr(c, "use", use)
    mut err := 0
    ret jwt.SignHS256(c, secret, err)
end

func accept(token: str, want: str, now: i64, secret: str): bool:
    mut o := jwt.DefaultOptions()
    o.now = now
    o.require_exp = true
    mut err := 0
    t := jwt.Verify(token, secret, o, err)
    if not t.valid:
        println "  rejected:", jwt.ErrorText(err)
        ret false
    end
    if jwt.Str(t, "use") != want:
        println "  rejected: wanted", want, "but got", jwt.Str(t, "use")
        ret false
    end
    ret true
end

func main:
    secret := "server-side-secret-of-at-least-32-bytes"
    login := 1790000000 as i64
    access := issue("42", "access", login, 900, secret)
    refresh := issue("42", "refresh", login, 30 * 86400, secret)

    println "request after 5 minutes:", accept(access, "access", login + 300, secret)
    println "request after 20 minutes:", accept(access, "access", login + 1200, secret)
    println "refresh after 20 minutes:", accept(refresh, "refresh", login + 1200, secret)
    new_access := issue("42", "access", login + 1200, 900, secret)
    println "request with the new token:", accept(new_access, "access", login + 1300, secret)
    println "refresh token used as access:", accept(refresh, "access", login + 1300, secret)
end
```

Output:

```text
request after 5 minutes: true
  rejected: token expired
request after 20 minutes: false
refresh after 20 minutes: true
request with the new token: true
  rejected: wanted access but got refresh
refresh token used as access: false
```

Keep the refresh token in an `HttpOnly` cookie (`SetSessionCookie`) rather than in JavaScript, and store its `jti` on the server if you need to revoke it before it expires.

## Rotating the secret

Sooner or later the secret has to change. If you switch at once, every user is logged out. Instead, give each secret a key id and put it in the token header with `SignWithKid`. To check a token, read its header with `Decode`, which does not verify anything, pick the secret for that `kid`, and only then call `Verify`. Sign new tokens with the new key and keep the old one until the last token signed with it has expired.

jwt-key-rotation.salam

```salam
import jwt

func secret_for(kid: str): str:
    keys := HashMap {} as HashMap<str, str>
    keys.put("2026-09", "old-secret-kept-for-one-more-week")
    keys.put("2026-10", "current-secret-used-for-new-tokens")
    if keys.has(kid):
        ret keys.get(kid)
    end
    ret ""
end

func check(token: str):
    mut err := 0
    header := jwt.Decode(token, err)
    secret := secret_for(header.kid)
    if secret.len() == 0:
        println "kid", header.kid, "rejected: unknown key"
        ret
    end
    mut o := jwt.DefaultOptions()
    o.now = 1790000100
    t := jwt.Verify(token, secret, o, err)
    println "kid", header.kid, "valid:", t.valid, "user:", t.claims.sub
end

func main:
    mut c := jwt.NewClaims()
    c.sub = "user-17"
    c.iat = 1790000000
    c.exp = 1790003600
    mut err := 0
    old := jwt.SignWithKid(c, jwt.JWT_HS256, "2026-09", "old-secret-kept-for-one-more-week", err)
    fresh := jwt.SignWithKid(c, jwt.JWT_HS256, "2026-10", "current-secret-used-for-new-tokens", err)
    stray := jwt.SignWithKid(c, jwt.JWT_HS256, "2025-01", "a-secret-nobody-has-anymore", err)
    check(old)
    check(fresh)
    check(stray)
end
```

Output:

```text
kid 2026-09 valid: true user: user-17
kid 2026-10 valid: true user: user-17
kid 2025-01 rejected: unknown key
```

Never trust anything else from `Decode`: the claims it returns are unverified, and only the key id is safe to use, because it only chooses which secret the real check runs with.

## Which function for which job

| Job | Use |
| --- | --- |
| Protect HTTP routes | `NewGuard`, then `Require`, `RequireScope`, `RequireClaim` or `RequireSubject` in each handler |
| Log a user in | `Issue` or `IssueFor`, and `SetSessionCookie` for browsers |
| Access and refresh tokens together | `IssuePair` |
| Sign a token outside HTTP | `NewClaims`, `SetStr` and friends, then `SignHS256` |
| Check a token and read its claims | `Verify`, then `Str`, `Int`, `Bool`, `HasScope` |
| Only a yes or no answer | `IsValid` |
| Read the key id before checking | `Decode` |

## Types

### `Token`

```salam
struct Token
```

A decoded token.

| Name | Type | Description |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `alg` | `str = ""` | The signing algorithm, such as `HS256`. |
| `typ` | `str = ""` | The type, usually `JWT`. |
| `kid` | `str = ""` | The key id, when the header carries one. |
| `claims` | `Claims` | The standard claims. |
| `header_json` | `str = ""` | The JSON text of the header. |
| `payload_json` | `str = ""` | The JSON text of the body. |
| `signing_input` | `str = ""` | The part that was signed: the header and the body with a dot between them. |
| `signature` | `str = ""` | The signature as url safe base64. |
| `valid` | `bool = false` | The signature and the times were checked and were right. |

jwt-Sign.salam

```salam
import jwt

func main:
    mut c := jwt.NewClaims()
    c.iss = "salamlang.ir"
    c.sub = "42"
    c.aud = "api"
    c.iat = 1700000000
    c.exp = 1700003600
    jwt.SetStr(c, "name", "Maryam")
    jwt.SetInt(c, "level", 3)
    jwt.SetBool(c, "admin", false)
    jwt.SetRaw(c, "scope", `"read write"`)
    jwt.SetRaw(c, "roles", `["editor","viewer"]`)
    println jwt.ClaimsJSON(c)

    mut err := 0
    token := jwt.SignHS256(c, "a-long-random-secret", err)
    println err == jwt.JWT_OK
    println token

    mut o := jwt.DefaultOptions()
    o.now = 1700001000
    o.issuer = "salamlang.ir"
    o.audience = "api"
    t := jwt.Verify(token, "a-long-random-secret", o, err)
    println t.valid, t.alg, t.typ, t.claims.sub
    println jwt.Str(t, "name"), jwt.Int(t, "level"), jwt.Bool(t, "admin"), jwt.Has(t, "email")
    println jwt.Raw(t, "level"), jwt.HasScope(t, "write"), jwt.HasAudience(t, "api"), jwt.ListHas(t, "roles", "editor")

    _ := jwt.Verify(token, "another-secret", o, err)
    println err == jwt.JWT_ERR_SIGNATURE, jwt.ErrorText(err)
    o.now = 1800000000
    _ := jwt.Verify(token, "a-long-random-secret", o, err)
    println err == jwt.JWT_ERR_EXPIRED, jwt.ErrorText(err)
    o.now = 1700001000
    o.issuer = "example.com"
    println jwt.IsValid(token, "a-long-random-secret", o)
    _ := jwt.Decode("abc", err)
    println err == jwt.JWT_ERR_MALFORMED
end
```

Output:

