aws-Objects.salam

```salam
import aws

func main:
    cfg := aws.FromEnvironment("photos")
    if not aws.Configured(cfg):
        println "set AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID and AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY"
        ret
    end

    put := aws.S3Put(cfg, "notes/hello.txt", "hello world", "text/plain; charset=utf-8")
    println put.ok, put.status, put.etag, put.request_id
    o := aws.PutOptions { content_type = "text/html", cache_control = "max-age=3600", storage_class = "STANDARD_IA", acl = "public-read" }
    aws.HeaderSet(o.meta, "owner", "ali")
    _ := aws.S3PutWith(cfg, "site/index.html", "<h1>hello</h1>", o)
    data := "salam"
    _ := aws.S3PutBytes(cfg, "raw.bin", data as void*, data.len(), "application/octet-stream")
    _ := aws.S3PutBytesWith(cfg, "raw2.bin", data as void*, data.len(), o)

    got := aws.S3Get(cfg, "notes/hello.txt")
    if got.ok:
        println got.body, got.length, aws.ResultHeader(got, "Content-Type")
    else:
        println got.status, got.code, got.error
    end
    _ := aws.S3GetWith(cfg, "notes/hello.txt", aws.GetOptions { if_none_match = got.etag })
    mut b := aws.S3GetBytes(cfg, "raw.bin")
    println b.ok, b.len, aws.BytesHeader(b, "ETag")
    aws.FreeBytes(b)
    mut b2 := aws.S3GetRange(cfg, "raw.bin", 0, 1)
    aws.FreeBytes(b2)
    mut b3 := aws.S3GetBytesWith(cfg, "raw.bin", aws.GetOptions { range_start = 2, range_end = 4 })
    aws.FreeBytes(b3)

    info := aws.S3Stat(cfg, "site/index.html")
    println info.ok, info.size, info.content_type, info.last_modified, info.storage_class
    _ := aws.S3StatVersion(cfg, "site/index.html", info.version_id)
    println aws.S3Head(cfg, "raw.bin").status, aws.S3Exists(cfg, "raw.bin"), aws.S3Size(cfg, "raw.bin")
    println aws.S3ObjectChecksum(cfg, "raw.bin")

    _ := aws.S3Copy(cfg, "notes/hello.txt", "notes/copy.txt")
    _ := aws.S3CopyWith(cfg, "notes/hello.txt", "archive/hello.txt", aws.CopyOptions { storage_class = "GLACIER" })
    _ := aws.S3Move(cfg, "notes/copy.txt", "notes/moved.txt")
    _ := aws.S3Touch(cfg, "notes/moved.txt", aws.CopyOptions {})
    _ := aws.S3Restore(cfg, "archive/hello.txt", 2, "Standard")

    _ := aws.S3SetObjectTags(cfg, "raw.bin", aws.NewTags())
    _ := aws.S3AddObjectTag(cfg, "raw.bin", "team", "web")
    mut t := aws.S3ObjectTags(cfg, "raw.bin")
    println aws.TagString(t)
    aws.HeaderFree(t)
    mut t2 := aws.S3ObjectTagsVersion(cfg, "raw.bin", "")
    aws.HeaderFree(t2)
    _ := aws.S3DeleteObjectTags(cfg, "raw.bin")
    _ := aws.S3MakePublic(cfg, "raw.bin")
    _ := aws.S3MakePrivate(cfg, "raw.bin")
    _ := aws.S3SetObjectAcl(cfg, "raw.bin", "private")
    println aws.S3ObjectAcl(cfg, "raw.bin").len() > 0
    _ := aws.S3SetLegalHold(cfg, "raw.bin", true)
    println aws.S3LegalHold(cfg, "raw.bin")
    _ := aws.S3SetRetention(cfg, "raw.bin", "GOVERNANCE", 1893456000 as i64)

    mut l := aws.S3List(cfg, aws.ListOptions { prefix = "notes/", max_keys = 100 })
    each e in l.items:
        println e.key, e.size
    end
    aws.ListFree(l)
    mut l2 := aws.S3ListPrefix(cfg, "site/")
    aws.ListFree(l2)
    mut l3 := aws.S3ListFolder(cfg, "")
    println aws.ListPrefixCount(l3)
    aws.ListFree(l3)
    mut l4 := aws.S3ListAll(cfg, "")
    println aws.ListCount(l4), aws.ListTotalSize(l4)
    aws.ListFree(l4)
    mut l5 := aws.S3ListAllWith(cfg, aws.ListOptions { prefix = "site/" })
    aws.ListFree(l5)
    mut l6 := aws.S3ListV1(cfg, aws.ListOptions {}, "")
    aws.ListFree(l6)
    mut l7 := aws.S3ListVersions(cfg, aws.ListOptions { prefix = "raw" }, "", "")
    aws.ListFree(l7)
    mut keys := aws.S3Keys(cfg, "notes/")
    _ := aws.S3DeleteMany(cfg, keys)
    aws.KeyFree(keys)
    _ := aws.S3DeletePrefix(cfg, "site/")
    _ := aws.S3DeleteVersion(cfg, "raw2.bin", "")
    println aws.S3Delete(cfg, "raw.bin").ok
end
```

aws-Services.salam

```salam
import aws

func main:
    chain := aws.DefaultChain()
    creds := aws.Resolve(chain)
    if not creds.ok:
        println "no credentials were found:", creds.error
        ret
    end
    println aws.DescribeCredentials(creds)
    cfg := aws.ResolveConfig("photos", "eu-central-1", chain)
    println aws.FromEnvironmentCredentials().ok, aws.FromProfileCredentials("default", chain).ok
    println aws.FromWebIdentityCredentials(chain).ok, aws.FromContainerCredentials(1000).ok
    println aws.FromInstanceCredentials(1000).ok, aws.InstanceRegion(1000)

    who := aws.GetCallerIdentity(cfg)
    println who.ok, who.account, who.arn, who.user_id
    role := aws.AssumeRole(cfg, "arn:aws:iam::123456789012:role/deploy", "salam", 900)
    if role.ok:
        cfg2 := aws.Apply(cfg, role)
        println aws.Describe(cfg2)
    end
    _ := aws.AssumeRoleWith(cfg, "arn:aws:iam::123456789012:role/partner", "salam", 3600, "ext-42", "")
    _ := aws.AssumeRoleWithWebIdentity(cfg, "arn:aws:iam::123456789012:role/ci", "ci", "token", 900)
    _ := aws.GetSessionToken(cfg, 3600, "arn:aws:iam::123456789012:mfa/ali", "123456")
    _ := aws.GetFederationToken(cfg, "guest", "", 900)

    created := aws.SqsCreateQueue(cfg, "jobs", aws.NewHeaders())
    queue := aws.SqsQueueUrl(cfg, "jobs")
    println created == queue, aws.SqsQueueArn(cfg, queue)
    mut queues := aws.SqsListQueues(cfg, "")
    repeat aws.QueueCount(queues) in i:
        println aws.QueueAt(queues, i)
    end
    aws.QueueListFree(queues)

    sent := aws.SqsSend(cfg, queue, "invoice 42")
    println sent.ok, sent.id, sent.md5, sent.sequence
    _ := aws.SqsSendWith(cfg, queue, aws.OutMessage { body = "later", delay = 60 })
    mut messages := aws.SqsReceive(cfg, queue, aws.ReceiveOptions { max_messages = 5, wait_seconds = 10 })
    each msg in messages.items:
        println msg.body
        _ := aws.SqsDelete(cfg, queue, msg.receipt)
    end
    aws.MessageListFree(messages)
    mut batch := aws.SqsReceiveBatch(cfg, queue, 10)
    _ := aws.SqsDeleteBatch(cfg, queue, batch)
    aws.MessageListFree(batch)
    mut waiting := aws.SqsPoll(cfg, queue)
    if aws.MessageCount(waiting) > 0:
        receipt := aws.MessageAt(waiting, 0).receipt
        _ := aws.SqsChangeVisibility(cfg, queue, receipt, 120)
        _ := aws.SqsRelease(cfg, queue, receipt)
    end
    aws.MessageListFree(waiting)
    println aws.SqsDepth(cfg, queue)
    mut attrs := aws.NewHeaders()
    aws.HeaderSet(attrs, "RedrivePolicy", aws.SqsRedrivePolicy("arn:aws:sqs:eu-central-1:123456789012:dead", 5))
    _ := aws.SqsSetAttributes(cfg, queue, attrs)
    aws.HeaderFree(attrs)
    mut current := aws.SqsAttributes(cfg, queue)
    println aws.HeaderGet(current, "VisibilityTimeout")
    aws.HeaderFree(current)
    _ := aws.SqsPurge(cfg, queue)
    _ := aws.SqsDeleteQueue(cfg, queue)

    mut call := aws.NewJsonCall("dynamodb", "DynamoDB_20120810.ListTables", "{}")
    result := aws.Invoke(cfg, call)
    println result.status, result.body
    aws.CallFree(call)

    req := aws.NewRequest("GET", "notes/hello.txt")
    println aws.Do(cfg, req).status
    mut raw := aws.DoBytes(cfg, req)
    aws.FreeBytes(raw)
end
```

aws-Sign.salam

```salam
import aws

func example(): aws.Config:
    ret aws.Config {
        endpoint = "https://s3.amazonaws.com", bucket = "examplebucket", access_key = "AKIAIOSFODNN7EXAMPLE", secret_key = "wJalrXUtnFEMI/K7MDENG/bPxRfiCYEXAMPLEKEY", path_style = false
    }
end

func main:
    at := 1369353600 as i64
    date := aws.AmzDate(at)
    println date, aws.DateStamp(date), aws.Scope(aws.DateStamp(date), "us-east-1", aws.SERVICE_S3)
    println aws.EncodeKey("photos/a b+c.png"), aws.UriEncode("a b/c", true), aws.UriEncode("a b/c", false)
    println aws.ALGORITHM, aws.UNSIGNED_PAYLOAD
    println aws.EMPTY_SHA256 == aws.Sha256Bytes(null, 0)

    headers := "host:examplebucket.s3.amazonaws.com\nrange:bytes=0-9\nx-amz-content-sha256:" + aws.EMPTY_SHA256 + "\nx-amz-date:" + date + "\n"
    signed := aws.SignRequest(example(), "GET", "/test.txt", "", headers, "host;range;x-amz-content-sha256;x-amz-date", aws.EMPTY_SHA256, at)
    println signed.ok, signed.amz_date
    println signed.authorization
    println aws.SignString(example(), aws.DateStamp(date), "text").len()
    println aws.SignQuery(example(), "GET", "/test.txt", "", "examplebucket.s3.amazonaws.com", at).len() > 0
    println aws.SignQueryHeaders(example(), "GET", "/test.txt", "", "host:examplebucket.s3.amazonaws.com\n", "host", at).len() > 0

    mut req := aws.NewRequest("GET", "test.txt")
    aws.SetHeader(req, "Range", "bytes=0-9")
    aws.SetQuery(req, "versionId", "v1")
    aws.SetQueryInt(req, "partNumber", 2)
    aws.SetFlag(req, "acl")
    print aws.CanonicalRequest(example(), req, at)
    println ""
    mut put := aws.NewRequest("PUT", "notes/a.txt")
    aws.SetText(put, "hello")
    head := aws.PreparedHead(example(), put, at)
    println head.find("PUT /notes/a.txt HTTP/1.1") == 0, head.find("Content-Length: 5") >= 0
    mut big := aws.NewRequest("PUT", "big.bin")
    aws.SetUnsignedPayload(big)
    println big.body_hash
    other := aws.NewBucketRequest("GET", "other", "")
    println other.bucket, aws.NewServiceRequest("GET").service_level

    text := "salam"
    aws.SetBody(big, text as void*, text.len())
    println big.body_len
    println aws.S3ContentHash(text as void*, text.len())
    println aws.S3ContentMd5(text as void*, text.len()), aws.S3ChecksumSha256(text as void*, text.len())
    println aws.S3ContentHashMd5(text as void*, text.len()), aws.S3MultipartEtag(text as void*, text.len(), 4)

    mut h := aws.NewHeaders()
    aws.HeaderSet(h, "Content-Type", "text/plain")
    aws.HeaderSet(h, "content-type", "text/html")
    aws.HeaderAdd(h, "x-amz-meta-tag", "a")
    aws.HeaderAdd(h, "x-amz-meta-tag", "b")
    println aws.HeaderCount(h), aws.HeaderGet(h, "CONTENT-TYPE"), aws.HeaderHas(h, "range")
    println aws.HeaderNameAt(h, 2), aws.HeaderValueAt(h, 2)
    aws.HeaderFree(h)

    mut tags := aws.NewTags()
    aws.TagSet(tags, "team", "web")
    aws.TagSet(tags, "env", "prod test")
    println aws.TagString(tags)

    println aws.Unquote("\"9b2cf5\"")
    err := "<Error><Code>NoSuchKey</Code><Message>The key does not exist</Message></Error>"
    println aws.ResultErrorCode(err), aws.ResultTag(err, "Message")
    println aws.ResultErrorMessage(err, 404)
    println aws.ResultErrorMessage("", 503)
end
```

### `PresignOptions`

```salam
struct PresignOptions
```

Options for a presigned URL.

| Name | Type | Description |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `expires` | `int = 0` | How long it is valid, in seconds; seven days at most. |
| `version_id` | `str = ""` | The version. |
| `content_type` | `str = ""` | The content type the uploader must send. |
| `acl` | `str = ""` | The ACL. |
| `storage_class` | `str = ""` | The class. |
| `response_content_type` | `str = ""` | The content type of the response. |
| `response_content_disposition` | `str = ""` | The Content-Disposition of the response; for the downloaded file name. |
| `response_cache_control` | `str = ""` | The Cache-Control of the response. |

aws-Presign.salam

```salam
import aws

func main:
    mut cfg := aws.ForAws("", "examplebucket")
    cfg = aws.WithCredentials(cfg, "AKIAIOSFODNN7EXAMPLE", "wJalrXUtnFEMI/K7MDENG/bPxRfiCYEXAMPLEKEY")
    at := 1369353600 as i64
    println aws.S3Url(cfg, "cdn/42.png")
    println aws.S3PresignAt(cfg, "GET", "test.txt", 86400, at)

    o := aws.PresignOptions { expires = 600, content_type = "image/png" }
    url := aws.S3PresignWith(cfg, "PUT", "up.png", o, at)
    println url.find("X-Amz-SignedHeaders=content-type%3Bhost") >= 0, url.find("X-Amz-Expires=600") >= 0

    println aws.S3Presign(cfg, "DELETE", "old.txt", 60).find("X-Amz-Expires=60&") >= 0
    println aws.S3PresignGet(cfg, "report.pdf", 3600).find("https://examplebucket.s3.amazonaws.com/report.pdf?") == 0
    println aws.S3PresignPut(cfg, "avatar.png", "image/png", 300).find("content-type") >= 0
    println aws.S3PresignDownload(cfg, "r/123.pdf", "report.pdf", 300).find("response-content-disposition") >= 0

    po := aws.PostOptions {
        expires = 3600, key_is_prefix = true, content_type = "image/", content_type_is_prefix = true, max_bytes = 1048576 as i64, acl = "private"
    }
    form := aws.S3PresignPostAt(cfg, "incoming/", po, at)
    println form.ok, form.url
    println form.policy
    println aws.HeaderGet(form.fields, "x-amz-signature")
    println aws.PostFormHtml(form, "file").find("<form") >= 0
    println aws.S3PresignPost(cfg, "a.png", aws.PostOptions {}).ok
end
```

### `Config`

```salam
struct Config
```

The connection configuration: address, region, bucket and credentials.

| Name | Type | Description |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `endpoint` | `str = ""` | The service address. |
| `region` | `str = "us-east-1"` | The region; `us-east-1` by default. |
| `bucket` | `str = ""` | The default bucket. |
| `access_key` | `str = ""` | The access key id. |
| `secret_key` | `str = ""` | The secret key. |
| `session_token` | `str = ""` | The session token. |
| `path_style` | `bool = true` | Path addressing, `host/bucket/key`, instead of `bucket.host/key`. |
| `service` | `str = "s3"` | The service name in the signature. |
| `expires` | `int = 900` | The default expiry of presigned URLs, in seconds. |
| `retry` | `int = 3` | The number of attempts in all, from 1 to 10; network errors, 429 and 5xx answers are tried again. |
| `retry_base_ms` | `int = 100` | The base delay between attempts. |
| `anonymous` | `bool = false` | Unsigned, for public buckets. |
| `request_payer` | `bool = false` | The requester pays for the request. |
| `timeout_ms` | `int = 0` | The timeout of each request, in milliseconds. |

aws-Config.salam

```salam
import aws

func main:
    println aws.AwsEndpoint("eu-central-1"), aws.StsEndpoint("eu-central-1"), aws.ServiceEndpoint("sqs", "eu-west-1")
    println aws.ForAws("eu-central-1", "photos").endpoint, aws.ForMinio("http://127.0.0.1:9000/", "photos").endpoint
    println aws.ForR2("acct", "photos").endpoint, aws.ForSpaces("ams3", "photos").endpoint
    println aws.ForWasabi("eu-central-1", "photos").endpoint, aws.ForBackblaze("us-west-004", "photos").endpoint
    println aws.ForEndpoint("https://s3.example.ir", "ir-tehran", "photos").region

    mut cfg := aws.NewConfig("http://127.0.0.1:9000", "photos")
    println aws.Configured(cfg)
    cfg = aws.WithCredentials(cfg, "AKIDEXAMPLE", "secret")
    cfg = aws.WithBucket(cfg, "backup")
    cfg = aws.WithSessionToken(cfg, "token")
    cfg = aws.WithRetry(cfg, 5, 200)
    println aws.Configured(cfg), cfg.bucket, cfg.retry, cfg.retry_base_ms, cfg.path_style, cfg.service
    println aws.Describe(cfg)

    text := "[default]\nregion = eu-west-1\n\n[profile work]\nregion = me-central-1\n"
    println aws.ParseIni(text, "default", "region"), aws.ParseIni(text, "profile work", "region")
    println aws.CredentialsPath().len() > 0, aws.ConfigPath().len() > 0
    println aws.FromEnvironment("photos").bucket

    creds := aws.StaticCredentials("AKIDEXAMPLE", "secret")
    println creds.ok, creds.source, aws.ExpiredNow(creds), aws.SOURCE_CONTAINER
    applied := aws.Apply(aws.ForAws("", "photos"), creds)
    println applied.access_key

    body := `<AssumeRoleResponse><AssumeRoleResult><Credentials><AccessKeyId>ASIAEXAMPLE</AccessKeyId><SecretAccessKey>s</SecretAccessKey><SessionToken>t</SessionToken><Expiration>2030-01-01T00:00:00Z</Expiration></Credentials></AssumeRoleResult></AssumeRoleResponse>`
    temp := aws.ParseCredentials(body, 200, "sts")
    println temp.ok, temp.access_key, temp.session_token, temp.expires, temp.source
    now := 1893455000 as i64
    println aws.Expired(temp, now, aws.STS_DEFAULT_SKEW), aws.SecondsRemaining(temp, now)
    println aws.DescribeCredentials(temp)
    println aws.SOURCE_ENV, aws.SOURCE_PROFILE, aws.SOURCE_WEB_IDENTITY, aws.SOURCE_INSTANCE
    println aws.STS_VERSION, aws.STS_MIN_DURATION, aws.STS_MAX_DURATION

    chain := aws.DefaultChain()
    println chain.use_env, chain.use_profile, chain.use_instance, aws.ContainerChain().use_instance

    failed := aws.Failure("no network")
    println failed.ok, failed.error
end
```

# llvm

https://salamlang.github.io/Salam/std/llvm/

Building, optimizing, running and linking code with LLVM.

LLVM is the compiler infrastructure behind Salam's own native backend. This package binds its C API so that a Salam program can be a compiler: build or read IR in a `Module`, check it with `Verify`, optimize it, then run it at once with the JIT or write an object file and link it into an executable. Use it when you are writing a language, a query compiler or a code generator. To run Salam code itself you do not need it; `salam build` already goes through LLVM.

### Core ideas

- Context, module, builder. A `Context` owns everything LLVM allocates. A `Module` is one translation unit of functions and globals inside it. A `Builder` is a cursor that appends instructions to the end of a block.

- Values are not numbers. `Add`, `Load` and the other instruction functions return a `Value`: the result the generated code will compute when it runs, not a result now.

- Two ways in. Write IR as text and read it with `ParseIR`, or build it call by call. Both end in the same `Module`.

- Two ways out. `RunJIT` compiles in memory and calls `main`. `Run` with an `Options` value, or `NewTargetMachine`, `RunOpt` and `EmitObject` step by step, write files for any target LLVM knows.

### Things that trip people up

- `ParseIR`, `RunJIT` and `Run` take the path of a `.ll` file, not the IR text. Write the text to a file first, as the examples do.

- `RunJIT` parses that file again by itself; it does not run a module you already have. Its `rc` is the `i32` that `main` returned.

- Invalid IR can crash LLVM later instead of producing an error. Call `Verify` on everything you build before you optimize or emit it.

- The linker inside the program (`LinkAuto`) still needs the target's C library files: a musl sysroot for Linux, MinGW for Windows, a WASI sysroot for WebAssembly. Without one the link fails with a message naming the directory it looked in; point `$SALAM_SYSROOTS` or `Options.sysroot` at one.

- Free in reverse order: builder, then module, then context.

Programs that use this package link against `libsalam_llvm`, so the site only compiles them. Build the library as the repository's LLVM backend instructions describe, then run them with `salam run`. The output shown is what they printed with LLVM 22 on x86-64 Linux.

## Running IR you wrote as text

The shortest way in is to write LLVM IR as text, the same `.ll` format `clang -S -emit-llvm` prints, and save it to a file. `ParseIR` reads that file into a module in a fresh context and reports syntax errors in `err`; `Verify` then checks the rules the parser does not, such as every block ending in a branch or a return. `RunJIT` compiles the same file in memory and calls its `main`.

llvm-guide-text.salam

```salam
import llvm
import io
import os

func main:
    path := os.TempDir() + "/salam_guide_sum.ll"
    _ := io.WriteFile(path, `define i32 @main() {
entry:
  br label %loop
loop:
  %i = phi i32 [ 1, %entry ], [ %next, %loop ]
  %acc = phi i32 [ 0, %entry ], [ %sum, %loop ]
  %sum = add i32 %acc, %i
  %next = add i32 %i, 1
  %more = icmp sle i32 %next, 10
  br i1 %more, label %loop, label %done
done:
  ret i32 %sum
}
`)
    parsed := llvm.ParseIR(path)
    if not parsed.ok:
        println "parse error:", parsed.err
        ret 1
    end
    checked := llvm.Verify(parsed.mod)
    println "valid:", checked.ok
    llvm.FreeModule(parsed.mod)
    llvm.FreeContext(parsed.ctx)
    r := llvm.RunJIT(path)
    println "sum of 1..10 =", r.rc
end
```

The loop adds 1 to 10, so the program prints `valid: true` and then `sum of 1..10 = 55`. The value of `main` comes back as `rc`, just like an exit code, which keeps the round trip simple while you are experimenting.

## A tiny compiler with the builder

A real compiler does not glue strings together; it walks its own syntax tree and calls the builder. This one reads arithmetic in reverse Polish notation: a number pushes a constant on a stack, and an operator pops two values and pushes the instruction that combines them. A `Value` stands for a result that will exist at run time, so the stack holds instructions, not numbers.

llvm-guide-rpn.salam

```salam
import llvm
import io
import os
import str

func main:
    program := "2 3 + 4 * 6 -"
    ctx := llvm.NewContext()
    mod := llvm.NewModule(ctx, "rpn")
    b := llvm.NewBuilder(ctx)
    i32 := llvm.Int32Type(ctx)
    none := Vector {} as Vector<llvm.Type>
    fn := llvm.AddFunction(mod, "main", llvm.FunctionType(i32, none, false))
    llvm.PositionAtEnd(b, llvm.AppendBlock(ctx, fn, "entry"))
    mut stack := Vector {} as Vector<llvm.Value>
    each word in str.Split(program, " "):
        if word == "+" or word == "-" or word == "*":
            r := stack.pop()
            l := stack.pop()
            if word == "+": stack.push(llvm.Add(b, l, r, "t")) end
            if word == "-": stack.push(llvm.Sub(b, l, r, "t")) end
            if word == "*": stack.push(llvm.Mul(b, l, r, "t")) end
        else:
            stack.push(llvm.ConstInt(i32, str.ToInt(word) as i64))
        end
    end
    _ := llvm.Ret(b, stack.pop())
    println llvm.Verify(mod).ok
    path := os.TempDir() + "/salam_guide_rpn.ll"
    _ := io.WriteFile(path, llvm.ModuleToString(mod))
    println program, "=", llvm.RunJIT(path).rc
    llvm.FreeBuilder(b)
    llvm.FreeModule(mod)
    llvm.FreeContext(ctx)
end
```

`(2 + 3) * 4 - 6` is 14, and that is what the JIT returns. With constants only, LLVM's builder folds the whole expression while you build it, so the IR is just `ret i32 14`; with parameters or loaded values you would see the `add`, `mul` and `sub` instructions.

## Let Verify catch your mistakes

Bugs in a code generator usually produce IR that is not valid, and LLVM may crash on it later instead of reporting it. Call `Verify` after building a module and before optimizing or running it. Here the block computes a value but never returns, so the module is rejected with a message that names the problem.

llvm-guide-verify.salam

```salam
import llvm

func main:
    ctx := llvm.NewContext()
    mod := llvm.NewModule(ctx, "broken")
    b := llvm.NewBuilder(ctx)
    i32 := llvm.Int32Type(ctx)
    none := Vector {} as Vector<llvm.Type>
    fn := llvm.AddFunction(mod, "answer", llvm.FunctionType(i32, none, false))
    llvm.PositionAtEnd(b, llvm.AppendBlock(ctx, fn, "entry"))
    _ := llvm.Add(b, llvm.ConstInt(i32, 40), llvm.ConstInt(i32, 2), "x")
    checked := llvm.Verify(mod)
    if not checked.ok:
        println "rejected:", checked.err
    end
    llvm.FreeBuilder(b)
    llvm.FreeModule(mod)
    llvm.FreeContext(ctx)
end
```

## An object file and a static program

`Run` takes the whole pipeline from one `Options` value: the optimization level, the target triple and what to produce. `OUT_OBJ` writes an object file for the chosen triple, even one that is not the machine you are on. For `x86_64-unknown-linux-musl`, LLD inside the program links it into a static executable with no system linker involved; `CanLinkTriple` says whether that is possible for a triple.

llvm-guide-static.salam

```salam
import llvm
import io
import os

func main:
    dir := os.TempDir()
    ll := dir + "/salam_guide_static.ll"
    _ := io.WriteFile(ll, `define i32 @main() {
entry:
  ret i32 7
}
`)
    mut opts := llvm.OptionsDefault()
    opts.opt_level = llvm.OPT_O2
    opts.target_triple = "x86_64-unknown-linux-musl"
    opts.output_mode = llvm.OUT_OBJ
    opts.output_file = dir + "/salam_guide_static.o"
    built := llvm.Run(ll, opts)
    if not built.ok:
        println "compile failed:", built.error
        ret 1
    end
    println "can link here:", llvm.CanLinkTriple(opts.target_triple)
    linked := llvm.LinkAuto(opts.output_file, dir + "/salam_guide_static", opts)
    if not linked.ok:
        println "link failed:", linked.err
        ret 1
    end
    println "built", dir + "/salam_guide_static"
end
```

On a machine without musl's files in `/usr/lib/x86_64-linux-musl` (the `musl-dev` package) or under `$SALAM_SYSROOTS`, the object is still written but the link step reports `no musl sysroot`. `CanLinkTriple` only tells you that LLD is built in and knows the triple; it does not look for the sysroot. The program it builds just exits with 7. For a Windows target use `x86_64-w64-windows-gnu` and an output ending in `.exe`; to work out sizes and file names from a triple without LLVM at all, see `llvm/triple`.

## Optimize, then read the result

Looking at the optimized IR and the machine code is how you check that your generator produces what you meant. `NewTargetMachine` describes the target CPU; give the module the same triple and its data layout with `SetTargetTriple` and `ApplyDataLayout`, then `RunOpt` runs LLVM's standard `O2` pipeline on it in place. `ModuleToString` prints the module as text and `EmitAsm` writes assembly to a file.

llvm-guide-opt.salam

```salam
import llvm
import io
import os
import str

func main:
    path := os.TempDir() + "/salam_guide_square.ll"
    _ := io.WriteFile(path, `define i32 @square_sum(i32 %n) {
entry:
  %a = alloca i32
  store i32 0, ptr %a
  %x = mul i32 %n, %n
  %old = load i32, ptr %a
  %new = add i32 %old, %x
  store i32 %new, ptr %a
  %r = load i32, ptr %a
  ret i32 %r
}
`)
    parsed := llvm.ParseIR(path)
    if not parsed.ok:
        println parsed.err
        ret 1
    end
    made := llvm.NewTargetMachine("x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu", llvm.OPT_O2, false)
    if not made.ok:
        println made.err
        ret 1
    end
    llvm.SetTargetTriple(parsed.mod, "x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu")
    llvm.ApplyDataLayout(parsed.mod, made.tm)
    opt := llvm.RunOpt(parsed.mod, made.tm, llvm.OPT_O2)
    if not opt.ok:
        println opt.err
        ret 1
    end
    text := llvm.ModuleToString(parsed.mod)
    each line in str.Split(text, "\n"):
        if str.StartsWith(line, "define") or str.StartsWith(line, "  "):
            println line
        end
    end
    asm := os.TempDir() + "/salam_guide_square.s"
    emitted := llvm.EmitAsm(parsed.mod, made.tm, asm)
    if not emitted.ok:
        println emitted.err
        ret 1
    end
    each line in str.Split(io.ReadFile(asm), "\n"):
        if str.StartsWith(line, "\t") and not str.StartsWith(line, "\t."):
            println str.Trim(str.Replace(line, "\t", " "))
        end
    end
    llvm.FreeTargetMachine(made.tm)
    llvm.FreeModule(parsed.mod)
    llvm.FreeContext(parsed.ctx)
end
```

```salam
define i32 @square_sum(i32 %n) local_unnamed_addr #0 {
  %x = mul i32 %n, %n
  ret i32 %x
movl %edi, %eax
imull %edi, %eax
retq
```

The input stores through a stack slot the way a naive code generator would. The optimizer turns the slot into registers, drops the add of zero and leaves one multiply, which becomes two x86 instructions. A front end can emit simple, slow-looking code like this and leave the cleanup to LLVM; that is the usual design. `OPT_OS` optimizes for size instead, and `EmitObject` writes a `.o` instead of assembly.

## Which function for which job

| Job | Functions |
| --- | --- |
| Read IR text | `ParseIR`, then `Verify` |
| Build IR from code | `NewContext`, `NewModule`, `NewBuilder`, then `AddFunction`, `AppendBlock` and the instruction functions |
| Run it now | `RunJIT`, `RunJITArgs` |
| The whole pipeline from a file | `Run` with `OptionsDefault` |
| Fine control over optimizing and emitting | `NewTargetMachine`, `RunOpt`, `EmitObject`, `EmitAsm` |
| Link an object | `LinkAuto`, or `LinkExternal` for the system linker |

## Types

### `OptResult`

```salam
struct OptResult
```

The result of optimizing.

| Name | Type | Description |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `ok` | `bool = false` | It worked. |
| `err` | `str = ""` | The error message. |

llvm-Target.salam

```salam
import llvm
import os

func build(ctx: llvm.Context): llvm.Module:
    mod := llvm.NewModule(ctx, "calc")
    b := llvm.NewBuilder(ctx)
    i32 := llvm.Int32Type(ctx)
    mut two := Vector {} as Vector<llvm.Type>
    two.push(i32)
    two.push(i32)
    fn := llvm.AddFunction(mod, "salam_add", llvm.FunctionType(i32, two, false))
    llvm.PositionAtEnd(b, llvm.AppendBlock(ctx, fn, "entry"))
    _ := llvm.Ret(b, llvm.Add(b, llvm.Param(fn, 0), llvm.Param(fn, 1), "s"))
    llvm.FreeBuilder(b)
    ret mod
end

func main:
    llvm.InitTargets()
    println llvm.DefaultTriple().len() > 0
    println llvm.CodeGenLevelOf(llvm.OPT_O2) == llvm.CODEGEN_LEVEL_DEFAULT, llvm.PassPipelineOf(llvm.OPT_O3)
    println llvm.OPT_O0, llvm.OPT_O1, llvm.OPT_OS, llvm.OPT_OZ
    println llvm.CODEGEN_LEVEL_NONE, llvm.CODEGEN_LEVEL_LESS, llvm.CODEGEN_LEVEL_AGGRESSIVE
    println llvm.CODEGEN_FILE_ASSEMBLY, llvm.CODEGEN_FILE_OBJECT, llvm.RELOC_DEFAULT, llvm.RELOC_PIC, llvm.CODE_MODEL_DEFAULT

    machine := llvm.NewTargetMachine("", llvm.OPT_O2, false)
    if not machine.ok:
        println "the target machine was not built:", machine.err
        ret
    end
    ctx := llvm.NewContext()
    mod := build(ctx)
    llvm.ApplyDataLayout(mod, machine.tm)
    optimized := llvm.RunOpt(mod, machine.tm, llvm.OPT_O2)
    println optimized.ok
    dir := os.TempDir()
    println llvm.EmitAsm(mod, machine.tm, dir + "/salam_add_en.s").ok
    println llvm.EmitObject(mod, machine.tm, dir + "/salam_add_en.o").ok
    println llvm.EmitBitcode(mod, dir + "/salam_add_en.bc").ok

    println llvm.ParallelJobs() > 0
    parts := llvm.ParallelPartitions(mod, 4)
    println parts >= 1
    mod2 := build(ctx)
    parallel := llvm.OptimizeEmitParallel(mod2, machine.tm, llvm.OPT_O2, 2, dir + "/salam_part_en")
    println parallel.ok, parallel.objects.len() >= 1
    llvm.FreeModule(mod)
    llvm.FreeModule(mod2)
    llvm.FreeTargetMachine(machine.tm)
    llvm.FreeContext(ctx)
end
```

### `RunResult`

```salam
struct RunResult
```

The result of running with the JIT.

| Name | Type | Description |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `ok` | `bool = false` | It worked. |
| `rc` | `int = 0` | What main returned. |
| `err` | `str = ""` | The error message. |

llvm-Build.salam

```salam
import llvm
import io
import os

func main:
    ctx := llvm.NewContext()
    mod := llvm.NewModule(ctx, "fib")
    b := llvm.NewBuilder(ctx)
    i32 := llvm.Int32Type(ctx)

    none := Vector {} as Vector<llvm.Type>
    main_type := llvm.FunctionType(i32, none, false)
    entry_fn := llvm.AddFunction(mod, "main", main_type)
    start := llvm.AppendBlock(ctx, entry_fn, "entry")
    body := llvm.AppendBlock(ctx, entry_fn, "loop")
    tail := llvm.AppendBlock(ctx, entry_fn, "done")

    llvm.PositionAtEnd(b, start)
    _ := llvm.Br(b, body)
    llvm.PositionAtEnd(b, body)
    counter := llvm.Phi(b, i32, "i")
    a := llvm.Phi(b, i32, "a")
    c := llvm.Phi(b, i32, "b")
    total := llvm.Add(b, a, c, "sum")
    next := llvm.Add(b, counter, llvm.ConstInt(i32, 1), "inext")
    more := llvm.ICmp(b, llvm.INT_SLT, next, llvm.ConstInt(i32, 10), "more")
    _ := llvm.CondBr(b, more, body, tail)

    mut sources := Vector {} as Vector<llvm.BasicBlock>
    sources.push(start)
    sources.push(body)
    mut counter_in := Vector {} as Vector<llvm.Value>
    counter_in.push(llvm.ConstInt(i32, 0))
    counter_in.push(next)
    llvm.AddIncoming(counter, counter_in, sources)
    mut a_in := Vector {} as Vector<llvm.Value>
    a_in.push(llvm.ConstInt(i32, 0))
    a_in.push(c)
    llvm.AddIncoming(a, a_in, sources)
    mut c_in := Vector {} as Vector<llvm.Value>
    c_in.push(llvm.ConstInt(i32, 1))
    c_in.push(total)
    llvm.AddIncoming(c, c_in, sources)
    llvm.PositionAtEnd(b, tail)
    _ := llvm.Ret(b, c)

    checked := llvm.Verify(mod)
    println checked.ok
    print llvm.ModuleToString(mod)
    path := os.TempDir() + "/salam_fib_en.ll"
    _ := io.WriteFile(path, llvm.ModuleToString(mod))
    r := llvm.RunJIT(path)
    println r.ok, r.rc
    llvm.FreeBuilder(b)
    llvm.FreeModule(mod)
    llvm.FreeContext(ctx)
end
```

| `ok` | `bool = false` | It worked. |
| `err` | `str = ""` | The error message. |

llvm-Run.salam

```salam
import llvm
import io
import os
import mem

func main:
    println llvm.Available()
    dir := os.TempDir()
    ll := dir + "/salam_args_en.ll"
    _ := io.WriteFile(ll, `define i32 @main(i32 %argc, ptr %argv) {
entry:
  %n = mul i32 %argc, 10
  ret i32 %n
}
`)

    parsed := llvm.ParseIR(ll)
    println parsed.ok
    checked := llvm.Verify(parsed.mod)
    println checked.ok, llvm.VERIFY_RETURN_STATUS
    llvm.SetTargetTriple(parsed.mod, llvm.DefaultTriple())
    println llvm.TargetTripleOf(parsed.mod) == llvm.DefaultTriple()
    llvm.FreeModule(parsed.mod)
    llvm.FreeContext(parsed.ctx)

    mut args := Vector {} as Vector<str>
    args.push("a")
    args.push("b")
    println llvm.RunJITArgs(ll, args).rc

    mut opts := llvm.OptionsDefault()
    println opts.opt_level, opts.output_mode
    opts.output_mode = llvm.OUT_JIT
    opts.run_args = args
    println llvm.Run(ll, opts).rc
    opts.output_mode = llvm.OUT_OBJ
    opts.output_file = dir + "/salam_args_en.o"
    println llvm.Run(ll, opts).ok
    opts.output_mode = llvm.OUT_ASM
    opts.output_file = dir + "/salam_args_en.s"
    println llvm.Run(ll, opts).ok
    println llvm.OUT_IR, llvm.OUT_BITCODE, llvm.OUT_EXEC

    println llvm.HostLinkTriple(), llvm.LldAvailable()
    println llvm.CanLinkTriple("x86_64-unknown-linux-musl"), llvm.CanLinkTriple("x86_64-w64-windows-gnu"), llvm.CanLinkTriple("aarch64-apple-darwin")
    println llvm.LLD_ELF, llvm.LLD_MINGW, llvm.LLD_COFF, llvm.LLD_MACHO, llvm.LLD_WASM
    linked := llvm.LinkExternal(dir + "/salam_args_en.o", dir + "/salam_args_en", llvm.OptionsDefault())
    println linked.ok, linked.err
    if linked.ok:
        println os.Run(dir + "/salam_args_en x y")
    end

    mut musl := llvm.OptionsDefault()
    musl.target_triple = "x86_64-unknown-linux-musl"
    println llvm.LinkAuto(dir + "/salam_args_en.o", dir + "/salam_args_en_musl", musl).ok
    _ := llvm.LinkElf(dir + "/a.o", dir + "/a", musl)
    _ := llvm.LinkMingw(dir + "/a.o", dir + "/a.exe", musl)
    _ := llvm.LinkWasi(dir + "/a.o", dir + "/a.wasm", musl)
    mut argv := mem.Allocate(64 as u64) as str*
    argv[0] = "ld.lld"
    argv[1] = "--version"
    println llvm.Link(llvm.LLD_ELF, argv as void*, 2)
    mem.Free(argv as void*)
end
```

### `Options`

```salam
struct Options
```

The options of the `Run` pipeline.

| Name | Type | Description |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `opt_level` | `int = 0` | The optimization level. |
| `debug_info` | `bool = false` | Keep the debug information. |
| `verify_module` | `bool = false` | Verify the module before generating. |
| `native_cpu` | `bool = false` | Optimize for this machine's own CPU. |
| `output_mode` | `int = 0` | The output kind, one of the `OUT_...` constants. |
| `output_file` | `str = ""` | The output path. |
| `target_triple` | `str = ""` | The target triple; empty means the module's triple. |
| `link_libs` | `Vector` | The libraries that are linked. |
| `link_kinds` | `Vector` | Each library's kind: static or dynamic. |
| `sysroot` | `str = ""` | The target system's root for cross linking. |
| `lib_paths` | `Vector` | The library search paths. |
| `extra_objects` | `Vector` | Other object files to link. |
| `run_args` | `Vector` | The arguments for running with the JIT. |

## Constants and variables

### `INT_EQ`

```salam
const INT_EQ: i32 = 32
```

Integer comparison predicate: equal.

llvm-Program.salam

```salam
import llvm
import io
import os

func main:
    ctx := llvm.NewContext()
    mod := llvm.NewModule(ctx, "hello")
    b := llvm.NewBuilder(ctx)
    i32 := llvm.Int32Type(ctx)
    i64 := llvm.Int64Type(ctx)
    f64 := llvm.DoubleType(ctx)
    ptr := llvm.PointerType(ctx)
    _ := llvm.Int1Type(ctx)
    _ := llvm.Int8Type(ctx)
    _ := llvm.Int16Type(ctx)
    _ := llvm.FloatType(ctx)
    _ := llvm.ArrayType(i32, 4)

    mut fmt_params := Vector {} as Vector<llvm.Type>
    fmt_params.push(ptr)
    fmt_type := llvm.FunctionType(i32, fmt_params, true)
    _ := llvm.AddFunction(mod, "printf", fmt_type)
    printer := llvm.NamedFunction(mod, "printf")

    mut two_numbers := Vector {} as Vector<llvm.Type>
    two_numbers.push(i64)
    two_numbers.push(i64)
    calc_type := llvm.FunctionType(i64, two_numbers, false)
    calc := llvm.AddFunction(mod, "calc", calc_type)
    llvm.SetLinkage(calc, llvm.LINKAGE_INTERNAL)
    llvm.PositionAtEnd(b, llvm.AppendBlock(ctx, calc, "entry"))
    l := llvm.Param(calc, 0)
    r := llvm.Param(calc, 1)
    t := llvm.Sub(b, llvm.Mul(b, l, r, "m"), llvm.SDiv(b, l, r, "d"), "t")
    _ := llvm.Ret(b, llvm.Add(b, t, llvm.SRem(b, l, r, "r"), "x"))

    count := llvm.AddGlobal(mod, i64, "count")
    llvm.SetInitializer(count, llvm.ConstInt(i64, 40))
    pi := llvm.AddGlobal(mod, f64, "pi")
    llvm.SetInitializer(pi, llvm.ConstReal(f64, 3.14))
    llvm.SetGlobalConstant(pi, true)

    none := Vector {} as Vector<llvm.Type>
    entry_fn := llvm.AddFunction(mod, "main", llvm.FunctionType(i32, none, false))
    llvm.PositionAtEnd(b, llvm.AppendBlock(ctx, entry_fn, "entry"))
    println llvm.InsertBlock(b).handle != null
    slot := llvm.Alloca(b, i64, "n")
    _ := llvm.Store(b, llvm.Load(b, i64, count, "c"), slot)
    mut args := Vector {} as Vector<llvm.Value>
    args.push(llvm.Load(b, i64, slot, "n1"))
    args.push(llvm.ConstInt(i64, 8))
    result := llvm.Call(b, calc_type, calc, args, "v")
    mut fmt_args := Vector {} as Vector<llvm.Value>
    fmt_args.push(llvm.GlobalString(b, "calc(40, 8) = %lld\n", "fmt"))
    fmt_args.push(result)
    _ := llvm.Call(b, fmt_type, printer, fmt_args, "")
    _ := llvm.Ret(b, llvm.ConstInt(i32, 0))

    empty := Vector {} as Vector<llvm.Type>
    noop := llvm.AddFunction(mod, "noop", llvm.FunctionType(llvm.VoidType(ctx), empty, false))
    llvm.SetLinkage(noop, llvm.LINKAGE_PRIVATE)
    llvm.PositionAtEnd(b, llvm.AppendBlock(ctx, noop, "entry"))
    _ := llvm.RetVoid(b)
    println llvm.LINKAGE_EXTERNAL, llvm.Verify(mod).ok
    println llvm.INT_EQ, llvm.INT_NE, llvm.INT_UGT, llvm.INT_UGE, llvm.INT_ULT, llvm.INT_ULE
    println llvm.INT_SGT, llvm.INT_SGE, llvm.INT_SLT, llvm.INT_SLE

    path := os.TempDir() + "/salam_hello_en.ll"
    _ := io.WriteFile(path, llvm.ModuleToString(mod))
    println llvm.RunJIT(path).rc
    llvm.FreeBuilder(b)
    llvm.FreeModule(mod)
    llvm.FreeContext(ctx)
end
```

### `ICmp`

# llvm/triple

https://salamlang.github.io/Salam/std/llvm-triple/

The data layout and target features worked out from a triple, with no LLVM needed.

A target triple, such as `x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu`, names the architecture, the vendor, the operating system and the environment. Without linking against LLVM, this package gives from it what a compiler needs before it generates code, such as the pointer size and the data layout.

The parts are separated by dashes and the later ones may be missing: `x86_64-linux-musl` has no vendor, and `aarch64-apple-darwin` no environment. The functions here only read the text, so they work the same on every machine and for targets you cannot run, which is what a cross compiler needs. Salam's own LLVM backend uses them to pick the data layout and the C library of the target. To create a real LLVM target machine for a triple, use `llvm`.

### Things to know

- The functions look for known words anywhere in the triple, such as `x86_64`, `windows` or `musl`. They do not validate it: a misspelled triple quietly gets the wrong answer.

- An empty triple means the host machine. So does an architecture `PointerBits` does not know: it falls back to the host's pointer size instead of reporting an error.

- `Datalayout` knows x86-64 (Linux, Windows and macOS), 32 bit x86 outside Windows and macOS, AArch64, RISC-V 64 and 32 bit ARM. For anything else, WebAssembly included, it returns an empty string. Windows on ARM gets the Linux AArch64 layout.

- `IsGlibc` means "Linux and not musl". An Android triple such as `aarch64-linux-android` contains `linux`, so it counts as glibc although Android uses Bionic.

## Laying out a struct for another target

The size of a pointer decides the size of every struct that holds one, and therefore every offset a code generator writes. `PointerBits` gives it for any triple. The program below lays out a list node with a name pointer, a 32 bit age and a next pointer, aligning each field to its own size as C does.

llvm-triple-guide-sizes.salam

```salam
import llvm.triple

func align_up(n: int, a: int): int:
    ret (n + a - 1) / a * a
end

func node_size(target: str): int:
    ptr := triple.PointerBits(target) / 8
    mut size := ptr
    size = align_up(size, 4) + 4
    size = align_up(size, ptr) + ptr
    ret align_up(size, ptr)
end

func main:
    each target in ["x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu", "i686-unknown-linux-gnu", "wasm32-unknown-wasi", "aarch64-apple-darwin"]:
        println target, triple.PointerBits(target), "bit pointers, node is", node_size(target), "bytes"
    end
end
```

Output:

```text
x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu 64 bit pointers, node is 24 bytes
i686-unknown-linux-gnu 32 bit pointers, node is 12 bytes
wasm32-unknown-wasi 32 bit pointers, node is 12 bytes
aarch64-apple-darwin 64 bit pointers, node is 24 bytes
```

The node is twice as big on 64 bit targets: two eight byte pointers plus a four byte integer padded to eight. On a 32 bit target, WebAssembly included, every field is four bytes and nothing is padded. For an exact answer for every type, give the string from `Datalayout` to LLVM, as the `llvm` package does.

## Choosing the file name and libc

A build tool makes a few decisions straight from the triple: Windows programs end in `.exe`, a glibc program needs a compatible glibc wherever it runs, and a musl program can be linked fully static and copied to any Linux machine. `IsWindows` and `IsGlibc` answer the first two; anything else can be read from the triple with `str`.

llvm-triple-guide-output.salam

```salam
import llvm.triple
import str

func output_name(name: str, target: str): str:
    if triple.IsWindows(target):
        ret name + ".exe"
    end
    ret name
end

func libc_note(target: str): str:
    if triple.IsWindows(target):
        ret "links against the Windows C runtime"
    else triple.IsGlibc(target):
        ret "needs glibc on the machine it runs on"
    else str.Contains(target, "musl"):
        ret "can be fully static"
    end
    ret "uses the system C library"
end

func main:
    each target in ["x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu", "x86_64-linux-musl", "x86_64-w64-windows-gnu", "aarch64-apple-darwin"]:
        println output_name("app", target), "for", target
        println "  " + libc_note(target)
    end
end
```

Output:

```text
app for x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu
  needs glibc on the machine it runs on
app for x86_64-linux-musl
  can be fully static
app.exe for x86_64-w64-windows-gnu
  links against the Windows C runtime
app for aarch64-apple-darwin
  uses the system C library
```

When `Datalayout` returns an empty string the target is one this package does not know. That is not an error: leave the data layout out of the module and LLVM fills in its own default for the triple.

## What the package knows about a target

This program asks every function about six targets. The first letter of a data layout string is the byte order: `e` for little endian, `E` for big endian. The rest lists the size and alignment of pointers and integer types, in LLVM's own format.

llvm-triple-guide-layout.salam

```salam
import llvm.triple
import str

func byte_order(data_layout: str): str:
    if data_layout.len() == 0:
        ret "unknown"
    end
    if str.StartsWith(data_layout, "E"):
        ret "big endian"
    end
    ret "little endian"
end

func main:
    targets := ["x86_64-pc-windows-msvc", "aarch64-apple-darwin", "riscv64-unknown-linux-gnu", "armeb-unknown-linux-gnueabi", "wasm32-unknown-wasi", "aarch64-linux-android"]
    each t in targets:
        data_layout := triple.Datalayout(t)
        println t
        println "  pointers:", triple.PointerBits(t), "bits,", byte_order(data_layout)
        println "  windows:", triple.IsWindows(t), "| glibc:", triple.IsGlibc(t)
        if data_layout.len() == 0:
            println "  no built-in layout, let LLVM choose"
        end
    end
end
```

Output:

```text
x86_64-pc-windows-msvc
  pointers: 64 bits, little endian
  windows: true | glibc: false
aarch64-apple-darwin
  pointers: 64 bits, little endian
  windows: false | glibc: false
riscv64-unknown-linux-gnu
  pointers: 64 bits, little endian
  windows: false | glibc: true
armeb-unknown-linux-gnueabi
  pointers: 32 bits, big endian
  windows: false | glibc: true
wasm32-unknown-wasi
  pointers: 32 bits, unknown
  windows: false | glibc: false
  no built-in layout, let LLVM choose
aarch64-linux-android
  pointers: 64 bits, little endian
  windows: false | glibc: true
```

Two answers deserve a second look. WebAssembly has no built-in layout, so its byte order is unknown here even though WebAssembly is little endian. Android reports `glibc: true`; a build tool that ships Android binaries should test for `android` itself before it trusts `IsGlibc`.

## Functions

### `HostDatalayout`


llvm-triple-Layout.salam

```salam
import llvm.triple

func main:
    each target in ["x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu", "aarch64-unknown-linux-musl", "aarch64-apple-darwin", "x86_64-pc-windows-msvc", "i686-w64-windows-gnu", "wasm32-unknown-wasi"]:
        println target, triple.PointerBits(target), triple.IsWindows(target), triple.IsGlibc(target)
        dl := triple.Datalayout(target)
        if dl.len() > 0:
            println "  ", dl
        else:
            println "  unknown; LLVM works it out itself"

end
```

Output:

```text
x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu 64 false true
   e-m:e-p270:32:32-p271:32:32-p272:64:64-i64:64-i128:128-f80:128-n8:16:32:64-S128
aarch64-unknown-linux-musl 64 false false
   e-m:e-i8:8:32-i16:16:32-i64:64-i128:128-n32:64-S128
aarch64-apple-darwin 64 false false
   e-m:o-i64:64-i128:128-n32:64-S128
x86_64-pc-windows-msvc 64 true false
   e-m:w-p270:32:32-p271:32:32-p272:64:64-i64:64-i128:128-f80:128-n8:16:32:64-S128
i686-w64-windows-gnu 32 true false
  unknown; LLVM works it out itself
wasm32-unknown-wasi 32 false false
  unknown; LLVM works it out itself
true
```

# optim

https://salamlang.github.io/Salam/std/optim/

Neural network optimisers: SGD, Adam, RMSProp and learning rate schedules.

This is an official package that does not ship with Salam. Add it to a project first: `salam add optim`

An optimiser turns gradients into better parameters. This package has the three that cover almost all neural network training (`SGD` with optional momentum, `Adam` and AdamW, `RMSProp`), gradient clipping, and learning rate schedules. It works on the parameters of an nn `ParamStore` whose gradients autograd has filled in. For classical models that train themselves, such as linear regression, trees or k-means, use ml instead.

Every training loop has the same five steps:

- `tape.reset()` and `store.zero_grad()`

- run the model and compute the loss

- `autograd.Backward(tape, loss)`

- optionally `ClipGradNorm`, and set `lr` from a schedule

- `opt.step(store)`

### Things that trip people up

- `step` does not clear the gradients. Gradients add up, so forgetting `zero_grad` makes every step use the sum of all earlier ones.

- Momentum and Adam keep one state tensor per parameter, matched by position in the store and created on the first `step`. Use one optimiser per store and add every parameter before training starts.

- `weight_decay` applies to every parameter in the store, biases and norm scales included.

- The defaults differ: `lr` is 0.01 for `SGD` and `RMSProp` but 0.001 for `Adam`. The updates are computed in `f32`, like the tensors.

- Optimisers with state hold memory; call `free` when training is done.

## Choosing an optimiser

The three optimisers here minimize the same bowl, `x&#178; + 50y&#178;`, from the same start for forty steps. The bowl is fifty times steeper in one direction than the other, which is what real losses look like. Plain `SGD` must keep its learning rate below the limit the steep direction allows (here anything at or above 0.02 never settles), so it crawls along the flat one. Momentum keeps a running velocity, carrying the step along the flat direction while the bouncing in the steep one cancels out.

optim-guide-compare.salam

```salam
import optim
import nn
import autograd
import tensor
import conv

func run(kind: int): f64:
    mut store := nn.ParamStore {}
    start := tensor.Full(tensor.Shape1(2), 1.0)
    handle := store.add("xy", start)
    mut scale_data := Vector {} as Vector<f32>
    scale_data.push(1.0 as f32)
    scale_data.push(50.0 as f32)
    scale_shape := tensor.Shape1(2)
    scale := tensor.FromArray(scale_shape, scale_data)
    mut plain := optim.SGD { lr = 0.019 }
    mut heavy := optim.SGD { lr = 0.01, momentum = 0.9 }
    mut adam := optim.Adam { lr = 0.1 }
    mut tape := autograd.NewTape(1)
    mut last := 0.0
    repeat 40:
        tape.reset()
        store.zero_grad()
        p := nn.Bind(tape, store, handle)
        loss := autograd.Sum(tape, autograd.Mul(tape, autograd.Constant(tape, scale), autograd.Square(tape, p)))
        autograd.Backward(tape, loss)
        last = autograd.Value(tape, loss).at(0)
        if kind == 0: plain.step(store) end
        if kind == 1: heavy.step(store) end
        if kind == 2: adam.step(store) end
    end
    tape.free()
    plain.free()
    heavy.free()
    adam.free()
    store.free()
    ret last
end

func main:
    names := ["SGD", "SGD with momentum", "Adam"]
    repeat 3 in kind:
        println names[kind], conv.FormatFloatPrec(run(kind), 4)
    end
end
```

Output:

```text
SGD 0.0622
SGD with momentum 0.0063
Adam 0.5352
```

`Adam` scales each weight's step by its own gradient history, so it needs the least tuning and is the usual first choice for a network. On this tiny problem its steps of about `lr` make it hover near the minimum instead of settling, which is a good reminder to lower the rate as training goes on. `NewAdamW` is Adam with decoupled weight decay, the common choice for transformers.

## Learning rate schedules

A schedule is just a function from the step number to a learning rate; you assign the result to the optimiser's `lr` field before each `step`. `WarmupCosine` climbs linearly for the warmup steps, then follows half a cosine down to the minimum. `StepLR` multiplies the rate by `gamma` every so many steps.

optim-guide-schedule.salam

```salam
import optim
import conv

func main:
    base := 0.01
    total := 100 as i64
    warmup := 10 as i64
    println "step  warmup+cosine  step decay"
    each step in [0, 4, 9, 10, 30, 55, 80, 99]:
        at := step as i64
        smooth := optim.WarmupCosine(base, at, warmup, total, 0.0001)
        stairs := optim.StepLR(base, at, 30, 0.5)
        println step, conv.FormatFloatPrec(smooth, 5), conv.FormatFloatPrec(stairs, 5)
    end
end
```

Output:

```text
step  warmup+cosine  step decay
0 0.00100 0.01000
4 0.00500 0.01000
9 0.01000 0.01000
10 0.01000 0.01000
30 0.00884 0.00500
55 0.00505 0.00500
80 0.00126 0.00250
99 0.00010 0.00125
```

Warmup matters most for Adam and for large models: the first gradients are noisy and the moment estimates are still empty, so full sized steps at the start can throw the weights far off.

## Clipping gradients

One bad batch can produce a huge gradient and undo many steps of training. `ClipGradNorm` measures the length of all gradients together and, when it is above the limit, scales them down to that length while keeping their direction. It returns the length before clipping, which is worth logging: a norm that keeps growing is an early sign the learning rate is too high. Call it after `Backward` and before `step`.

optim-guide-clip.salam

```salam
import optim
import nn
import autograd
import tensor
import conv

func main:
    mut store := nn.ParamStore {}
    handle := store.add("w", tensor.Full(tensor.Shape1(2), 1.0))
    mut tape := autograd.NewTape(1)
    mut sgd := optim.SGD { lr = 0.1 }
    repeat 3 in step:
        tape.reset()
        store.zero_grad()
        sgd.lr = optim.StepLR(0.1, step as i64, 1, 0.5)
        w := nn.Bind(tape, store, handle)
        loss := autograd.Sum(tape, autograd.Scale(tape, autograd.Square(tape, w), 500.0))
        autograd.Backward(tape, loss)
        before := optim.ClipGradNorm(store, 1.0)
        mut p := store.at(handle)
        println "step", step, "lr", sgd.lr, "norm", conv.FormatFloatPrec(before, 1), "clipped grad", conv.FormatFloatPrec(p.grad.at(0), 3), conv.FormatFloatPrec(p.grad.at(1), 3)
        sgd.step(store)
        println "  w is now", conv.FormatFloatPrec(p.value.at(0), 3), conv.FormatFloatPrec(p.value.at(1), 3)
    end
    tape.free()
    sgd.free()
    store.free()
end
```

Output:

```text
step 0 lr 0.1 norm 1414.2 clipped grad 0.707 0.707
  w is now 0.929 0.929
step 1 lr 0.05 norm 1314.2 clipped grad 0.707 0.707
  w is now 0.894 0.894
step 2 lr 0.025 norm 1264.2 clipped grad 0.707 0.707
  w is now 0.876 0.876
```

The loss is `500w&#178;` for each weight, so the raw gradient is about 1400 long, and clipping cuts it to exactly 1. The program also halves the learning rate every step with `StepLR`. `ClipGradValue` is the blunter tool: it caps every single gradient value, which changes the direction too.

## The whole recipe on a real model

Here everything comes together on a small delivery-time model: a `Linear` layer from nn learns how many minutes each kilometre and each item adds. AdamW trains it, `WarmupCosine` sets the rate before every step, and `ClipGradNorm` guards against a bad start. The inputs and targets are divided by 10 first; optimisers work best when the numbers are near 1.

optim-guide-recipe.salam

```salam
import optim
import nn
import autograd
import tensor
import conv

func main:
    km := [1.0, 2.5, 4.0, 5.5, 7.0, 8.5, 3.0, 6.0]
    items := [1.0, 3.0, 2.0, 5.0, 1.0, 4.0, 6.0, 2.0]
    minutes := [14.0, 22.5, 26.0, 37.5, 37.0, 48.5, 33.0, 36.0]
    mut x := tensor.Zeros2(8, 2)
    mut y := tensor.Zeros2(8, 1)
    repeat 8 in i:
        x.set_at2(i, 0, km[i] / 10.0)
        x.set_at2(i, 1, items[i] / 10.0)
        y.set_at2(i, 0, minutes[i] / 10.0)
    end
    mut rng := tensor.NewRng(1)
    mut store := nn.ParamStore {}
    model := nn.NewLinear(store, "eta", 2, 1, rng)
    mut opt := optim.NewAdamW(0.1, 0.01)
    mut tape := autograd.NewTape(1)
    total := 400 as i64
    repeat 400 in step:
        tape.reset()
        store.zero_grad()
        guess := model.forward(tape, store, autograd.Input(tape, x))
        loss := autograd.MSELoss(tape, guess, autograd.Constant(tape, y))
        autograd.Backward(tape, loss)
        norm := optim.ClipGradNorm(store, 5.0)
        opt.lr = optim.WarmupCosine(0.1, step as i64, 20, total, 0.001)
        opt.step(store)
        if step % 100 == 0 or step == 399:
            println "step", step, "lr", conv.FormatFloatPrec(opt.lr, 4), "loss", conv.FormatFloatPrec(autograd.Value(tape, loss).at(0), 4), "grad norm", conv.FormatFloatPrec(norm, 3)
        end
    end
    w := store.at(model.w).value
    b := store.at(model.b).value
    println "minutes =", conv.FormatFloatPrec(b.at(0) * 10.0, 1), "+", conv.FormatFloatPrec(w.at(0), 2), "per km +", conv.FormatFloatPrec(w.at(1), 2), "per item"
    tape.free()
    opt.free()
    store.free()
    x.free()
    y.free()
end
```

Output:

```text
step 0 lr 0.0050 loss 15.9842 grad norm 8.950
step 100 lr 0.0896 loss 0.2397 grad norm 0.208
step 200 lr 0.0546 loss 0.0787 grad norm 0.109
step 300 lr 0.0170 loss 0.0456 grad norm 0.078
step 399 lr 0.0010 loss 0.0411 grad norm 0.073
minutes = 11.8 + 3.12 per km + 1.83 per item
```

The first gradient norm is almost 9, so the clip at 5 trims it, and after that the norm never comes near the limit. The rate climbs for 20 steps, peaks and falls to 0.001 by the last step, where the loss has flattened out. Because the inputs were scaled by the same factor as the target, the weights read directly as minutes per kilometre and per item; only the bias has to be multiplied back by 10.

## Types

### `Adam`

```salam
struct Adam
```

The Adam optimiser; a good default for most networks.

| Name | Type | Description |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `lr` | `f64 = 0.001` | The learning rate; 0.001 by default. |
| `beta1` | `f64 = 0.9` | The coefficient of the gradient average. |
| `beta2` | `f64 = 0.999` | The coefficient of the squared gradient average. |
| `eps` | `f64 = 1e-08` | A small number that keeps a division by zero from happening. |
| `weight_decay` | `f64 = 0` | Weight decay. |
| `decoupled` | `bool = false` | Apply the weight decay apart from the gradient, meaning AdamW. |

optim-Train.salam

```salam
import optim
import nn
import autograd
import tensor

func train(method: int, steps: int, target &: tensor.Tensor): f64:
    mut store := nn.ParamStore {}
    handle := store.add("w", tensor.Zeros1(4))
    mut adam := optim.Adam { lr = 0.1 }
    mut adamw := optim.NewAdamW(0.1, 0.01)
    mut rms := optim.RMSProp { lr = 0.05 }
    mut sgd := optim.SGD { lr = 0.05, momentum = 0.9 }
    mut tape := autograd.NewTape(1)
    repeat steps:
        tape.reset()
        store.zero_grad()
        w := nn.Bind(tape, store, handle)
        t := autograd.Input(tape, target)
        loss := autograd.Sum(tape, autograd.Square(tape, autograd.Sub(tape, w, t)))
        autograd.Backward(tape, loss)
        _ := optim.ClipGradNorm(store, 10.0)
        optim.ClipGradValue(store, 5.0)
        if method == 0:
            adam.step(store)
        else method == 1:
            adamw.step(store)
        else method == 2:
            rms.step(store)
        else:
            sgd.step(store)
        end
    end
    mut p := store.at(handle)
    result := p.value.at(3)
    tape.free()
    adam.free()
    adamw.free()
    rms.free()
    sgd.free()
    store.free()
    ret result
end

func main:
    mut target := tensor.Arange(4)
    each method in [0, 1, 2, 3]:
        rounded := (train(method, 400, target) * 100.0 + 0.5) as int
        println method, rounded
    end
    tensor.Free(target)
    println optim.StepLR(1.0, 25, 10, 0.5), optim.CosineLR(1.0, 50, 100, 0.0), optim.WarmupCosine(1.0, 0, 10, 110, 0.0)
end
```

Output:

```text
0 300
1 299
2 300
3 300
0.25 0.5 0.1
```

## Functions

### `NewAdamW`

```salam
func NewAdamW(lr: f64, weight_decay: f64): Adam
```

Adam with decoupled weight decay, meaning AdamW.

The example for this item is shown with the ones above: optim-Train.salam

### `ClipGradNorm`

```salam
func ClipGradNorm(ps &: nn.ParamStore, max_norm: f64): f64
```

Shrinks the gradients so their total norm does not pass the limit, and returns the norm before clipping; it keeps gradients from exploding.

The example for this item is shown with the ones above: optim-Train.salam

### `ClipGradValue`

```salam
func ClipGradValue(ps &: nn.ParamStore, limit: f64)
```

Holds every gradient within minus the limit to the limit.

The example for this item is shown with the ones above: optim-Train.salam

### `StepLR`

```salam
func StepLR(base: f64, step: i64, every: i64, gamma: f64): f64
```

A step learning rate: `base` times `gamma` once for every full `every` steps.

The example for this item is shown with the ones above: optim-Train.salam

### `CosineLR`

```salam
func CosineLR(base: f64, step: i64, total: i64, min_lr: f64): f64
```

A cosine learning rate: it falls from the base rate at step 0 to the minimum at step `total` along half a cosine wave, and stays there.

The example for this item is shown with the ones above: optim-Train.salam

### `WarmupCosine`

```salam
func WarmupCosine(base: f64, step: i64, warmup: i64, total: i64, min_lr: f64): f64
```

A linear warmup over the first `warmup` steps (step 0 already gets `base/warmup`), then a cosine decay that reaches `min_lr` at step `total`; the usual choice for training transformers.

The example for this item is shown with the ones above: optim-Train.salam

# onnx

https://salamlang.github.io/Salam/std/onnx/

Reading and running ONNX models with no outside dependency.

This is an official package that does not ship with Salam. Add it to a project first: `salam add onnx`

ONNX is the common exchange format for trained machine learning models. Train in PyTorch, TensorFlow or scikit-learn, export to `.onnx` once, and this package runs the model inside a Salam program with no Python and no ONNX Runtime library. `LoadOnnx` reads the file, `Run` computes the outputs from your input tensors, and the results are ordinary tensor values.

Use it for inference: scoring, classifying, embedding. To train or fine tune a network in Salam itself, build it with nn and optim. For large language models in the GGUF format, see gguf and llm.

### Core ideas

- A `Model` is the graph from the file: `nodes` in the order they run, the weights (`inits`), and the names of the graph's inputs and outputs.

- `feed_names` lists the inputs you supply, in order; `Run` takes one tensor for each and returns one tensor per graph output.

- Nothing stops the program. Every failure sets the `ok` argument to false and puts the reason in `model.error`.

### Limits to know before you export

- Every tensor is `f32` inside. Integer and double weights are converted when the file is read, so an `int64` above 16777216 loses precision.

- About 65 operators are implemented, enough for feed forward, convolutional and normalization layers (the list is below). Anything else, such as `LSTM`, `Resize` or the quantized operators, fails with `unsupported op: NAME`.

- `Conv` has no groups (so no depthwise convolutions), no dilations and only symmetric padding. `MaxPool` and `AveragePool` have no padding.

- Weights must be inside the `.onnx` file. Models exported with external data (a separate `.data` file, used above 2 GB) do not load.

- Input shapes are not checked against the file and the opset version is ignored. A wrong shape shows up as an error from the first operator that cannot use it.

## Checking every step

Both `ParseOnnx` (or `LoadOnnx`) and `Run` report success through their last argument, a `bool` they set, and leave the reason in the model's `error` field. Check it after each call: a file that is not ONNX, a graph with an operator this package does not implement, or the wrong number of inputs all come back this way instead of stopping the program. The model in this example is built in memory with encoding/protobuf, a single `Relu`, so the program runs without any file.

onnx-guide-errors.salam

```salam
import onnx
import tensor
import compress
import encoding.protobuf

func text(b &: compress.ByteBuf, field: int, value: str):
    protobuf.WriteTag(b, field, protobuf.WT_LEN)
    protobuf.WriteLenPrefixedStr(b, value)
end

func sub(b &: compress.ByteBuf, field: int, message: compress.ByteBuf):
    protobuf.WriteTag(b, field, protobuf.WT_LEN)
    protobuf.WriteLenPrefixedBytes(b, message.data, compress.BufLen(message))
end

func relu_model(): compress.ByteBuf:
    mut node := compress.NewByteBuf()
    text(node, 1, "x")
    text(node, 2, "y")
    text(node, 4, "Relu")
    mut input_x := compress.NewByteBuf()
    text(input_x, 1, "x")
    mut output_y := compress.NewByteBuf()
    text(output_y, 1, "y")
    mut graph := compress.NewByteBuf()
    sub(graph, 1, node)
    sub(graph, 11, input_x)
    sub(graph, 12, output_y)
    mut m := compress.NewByteBuf()
    protobuf.WriteTag(m, 1, protobuf.WT_VARINT)
    protobuf.WriteVarint(m, 8 as u64)
    sub(m, 7, graph)
    ret m
end

func main:
    mut ok := false
    junk := "this is not a model"
    _ := onnx.ParseOnnx(junk as void*, junk.len(), ok)
    println "junk parsed:", ok

    mut bytes := relu_model()
    mut model := onnx.ParseOnnx(bytes.data, compress.BufLen(bytes), ok)
    println "model parsed:", ok, "inputs:", model.feed_names().len()

    mut nothing := Vector {} as Vector<tensor.Tensor>
    _ := onnx.Run(model, nothing, ok)
    println "run without inputs:", ok, "|", model.error

    mut feeds := Vector {} as Vector<tensor.Tensor>
    feeds.push(tensor.Arange(4) - tensor.Full(tensor.Shape1(4), 2.0))
    results := onnx.Run(model, feeds, ok)
    println "run with x:", ok, tensor.ToString(results.get(0))
    model.free()
    compress.BufFree(bytes)
end
```

Output:

```text
junk parsed: false
model parsed: true inputs: 1
run without inputs: false | expected 1 inputs, got 0
run with x: true tensor(4)[0 0 0 1]
```

`feed_names` lists the inputs you must supply, in order. It leaves out the graph inputs that are really weights stored in the file, which older exporters list as inputs too.

## Looking inside a model file

Before wiring a model into a program, look at what it expects. This tool prints the inputs and outputs, how many nodes of each operator the graph has, and how many numbers the weights hold. Run it on any `.onnx` file:

```salam
salam build onnx-guide-inspect.salam
./onnx-guide-inspect model.onnx
```

onnx-guide-inspect.salam

```salam
import onnx
import os

func main:
    args := os.Args()
    if args.len() < 2:
        println "usage: onnx-guide-inspect model.onnx"
        ret 1
    end
    mut ok := false
    mut model := onnx.LoadOnnx(args.get(1), ok)
    if not ok:
        println "could not read the model:", model.error
        ret 1
    end
    println "IR version", model.ir_version
    println "feeds", model.feed_names(), "outputs", model.outputs
    mut counts := HashMap {} as HashMap<str, int>
    mut order := Vector {} as Vector<str>
    each node in model.nodes:
        if counts.has(node.op):
            counts.put(node.op, counts.get(node.op) + 1)
        else:
            counts.put(node.op, 1)
            order.push(node.op)
        end
    end
    each name in order:
        println "  " + name, counts.get(name)
    end
    mut weights := 0
    each t in model.inits:
        weights += t.numel()
    end
    println model.inits.len(), "weight tensors,", weights, "numbers"
    model.free()
end
```

Run on the small model that the reference example at the bottom of this page writes, it prints:

```salam
IR version 8
feeds ["x"] outputs ["y"]
  Mul 1
  LeakyRelu 1
1 weight tensors, 3 numbers
```

Check the operator counts against the supported list before you build anything on a model:

| Kind | Operators |
| --- | --- |
| Linear algebra | `MatMul`, `Gemm`, `Conv` |
| Element-wise math | `Add`, `Sub`, `Mul`, `Div`, `Pow`, `Sqrt`, `Exp`, `Log`, `Abs`, `Neg`, `Reciprocal`, `Floor`, `Ceil`, `Round`, `Sign`, `Erf`, `Min`, `Max`, `Sum`, `Mean`, `Clip` |
| Activations | `Relu`, `LeakyRelu`, `PRelu`, `Elu`, `Selu`, `Gelu`, `Sigmoid`, `HardSigmoid`, `Tanh`, `Softplus`, `Softmax`, `LogSoftmax` |
| Normalization and pooling | `BatchNormalization`, `InstanceNormalization`, `LayerNormalization`, `MaxPool`, `AveragePool`, `GlobalAveragePool`, `Dropout` (does nothing at inference) |
| Reductions and logic | `ReduceSum`, `ReduceMean`, `ReduceMax`, `ReduceMin`, `Equal`, `Greater`, `Less`, `Where` |
| Shapes | `Reshape`, `Flatten`, `Transpose`, `Concat`, `Split`, `Slice`, `Gather`, `Squeeze`, `Unsqueeze`, `Expand`, `Shape`, `Cast`, `Constant`, `Identity` |

## Running a trained classifier

Train the model where it is convenient, export it once, and run it from Salam with no Python at run time. With PyTorch, a classifier of the iris flowers with four inputs and three outputs is exported like this:

```salam
torch.onnx.export(model, torch.zeros(1, 4), "iris.onnx",
    input_names=["x"], output_names=["logits"],
    dynamic_axes={"x": {0: "batch"}})
```

The program feeds two flowers at once as a `2x4` tensor, turns the logits into probabilities with `tensor.Softmax` and takes the most likely class of each row.

onnx-guide-classify.salam

```salam
import onnx
import tensor

func main:
    mut ok := false
    mut model := onnx.LoadOnnx("iris.onnx", ok)
    if not ok:
        println "could not read iris.onnx:", model.error
        ret 1
    end
    species := ["setosa", "versicolor", "virginica"]
    mut features := Vector {} as Vector<f32>
    each v in [5.1, 3.5, 1.4, 0.2, 6.7, 3.0, 5.2, 2.3]:
        features.push(v as f32)
    end
    shape := tensor.Shape2(2, 4)
    mut feeds := Vector {} as Vector<tensor.Tensor>
    feeds.push(tensor.FromArray(shape, features))
    outputs := onnx.Run(model, feeds, ok)
    if not ok:
        println "the model did not run:", model.error
        ret 1
    end
    probs := tensor.Softmax(outputs.get(0))
    best := tensor.ArgMaxAxis(probs, 1, false)
    repeat 2 in i:
        println "flower", i, "is", species[best.at(i) as int]
    end
    model.free()
end
```

The `dynamic_axes` setting is what lets the batch size change: without it PyTorch may write the batch size of 1 into `Reshape` and `Expand` nodes as a constant, and a batch of two then fails inside the graph. The model must be given the same preprocessing it was trained with, here the raw measurements in centimetres.

## Types

### `Attr`

```salam
struct Attr
```

One node attribute, such as alpha.

| Name | Type | Description |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `name` | `str = ""` | The name. |
| `kind` | `int = 0` | The value kind in the ONNX format: 1 float, 2 integer, 3 string, 4 tensor, 6 and 7 lists. |
| `f` | `f64 = 0` | The float value. |
| `i` | `i64 = 0` | The integer value. |
| `s` | `str = ""` | The string value. |
| `t` | `tensor.Tensor` | The tensor value. |
| `floats` | `Vector` | The float list. |
| `ints` | `Vector` | The integer list. |

onnx-Run.salam

```salam
import onnx
import tensor
import compress
import encoding.protobuf
import archive
import os

func submessage(b &: compress.ByteBuf, field: int, message: compress.ByteBuf):
    protobuf.WriteTag(b, field, protobuf.WT_LEN)
    protobuf.WriteLenPrefixedBytes(b, message.data, compress.BufLen(message))
end

func text(b &: compress.ByteBuf, field: int, value: str):
    protobuf.WriteTag(b, field, protobuf.WT_LEN)
    protobuf.WriteLenPrefixedStr(b, value)
end

func number(b &: compress.ByteBuf, field: int, value: i64):
    protobuf.WriteTag(b, field, protobuf.WT_VARINT)
    protobuf.WriteVarint(b, value as u64)
end

func node(b &: compress.ByteBuf, op: str, input1: str, input2: str, output: str):
    text(b, 1, input1)
    if input2 != "":
        text(b, 1, input2)
    end
    text(b, 2, output)
    text(b, 4, op)
end

func model(m &: compress.ByteBuf):
    mut graph := compress.NewByteBuf()
    mut mul := compress.NewByteBuf()
    node(mul, "Mul", "x", "w", "h")
    submessage(graph, 1, mul)
    mut relu := compress.NewByteBuf()
    node(relu, "LeakyRelu", "h", "", "y")
    mut alpha := compress.NewByteBuf()
    text(alpha, 1, "alpha")
    number(alpha, 20, 1)
    protobuf.WriteTag(alpha, 2, protobuf.WT_FIXED32)
    protobuf.WriteFloat(alpha, 0.1)
    submessage(relu, 5, alpha)
    submessage(graph, 1, relu)
    mut weight := compress.NewByteBuf()
    number(weight, 1, 3)
    number(weight, 2, 1)
    mut payload := compress.NewByteBuf()
    each factor in [2.0, 2.0, 2.0]:
        protobuf.WriteFloat(payload, factor)
    end
    submessage(weight, 4, payload)
    text(weight, 8, "w")
    submessage(graph, 5, weight)
    mut input_x := compress.NewByteBuf()
    text(input_x, 1, "x")
    submessage(graph, 11, input_x)
    mut output_y := compress.NewByteBuf()
    text(output_y, 1, "y")
    submessage(graph, 12, output_y)
    number(m, 1, 8)
    submessage(m, 7, graph)
end

func main:
    mut buffer := compress.NewByteBuf()
    model(buffer)
    mut good := false
    mut m := onnx.ParseOnnx(buffer.data, compress.BufLen(buffer), good)
    println good, m.ok, m.ir_version, m.nodes.len(), m.inits.len(), m.init_names.get(0)
    mut relu := m.nodes.get(1)
    println relu.op, relu.inputs.get(0), relu.outputs.get(0), relu.attr_index("alpha")
    println (relu.attr_float("alpha", 0.0) * 100.0 + 0.5) as int, relu.attr_int("axis", -1)
    attr := relu.attrs.get(0)
    println attr.name, attr.kind
    println m.feed_names().len(), m.inputs.get(0), m.outputs.get(0)

    mut shape := tensor.Shape2(1, 3)
    mut x := tensor.Full(shape, -1.5)
    x.set_at(2, 4.0)
    mut inputs := Vector {} as Vector<tensor.Tensor>
    inputs.push(x)
    mut outputs := onnx.Run(m, inputs, good)
    mut y := outputs.get(0)
    println good, (y.at(0) * 100.0 - 0.5) as int, y.at(2)

    path := os.TempDir() + "/salam_tiny_en.onnx"
    _ := archive.WriteBinaryFileBuf(path, buffer)
    mut m2 := onnx.LoadOnnx(path, good)
    println good, m2.nodes.len()
    m2.free()
    m.free()
    compress.BufFree(buffer)
end
```

Output:

```text
true true 8 2 1 w
LeakyRelu h y 0
10 -1
alpha 1
1 x y
true -30 8
true 2
```
